[SEP] (see attached) [SEP] At the request of the USCG, the regional NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator investigated the potential oil spill trajectory for two grounded barges near Texas City Light #14 The barges CTCO 336 and 358 are each loaded with a reported 20K gallons of a light crude oil and were being pushed by the tug HENRI CENAC. It would appear from the information provided that the barges have grounded S of the Texas City Dike. High tide was at 5:56 AM (local time), and low tide is predicted for 9:09 PM this evening. Winds are predicted to be S at 15 to 20 kts. The winds at Station GPST2, Galveston Pleasure Pier, have been around 15 kts S-SSW over the last hour. In the absence of a tidal influence, any spilled oil transport would be wind dominated pushing the oil into the Texas City Dike. Any breaks in the dike would allow oil movement into Lower Galveston Bay. Should a spill occur during the ebb tide cycle late afternoon and early evening, oil could migrate toward the pass between Galveston Island and Bolivar Peninsula due to the effect of tidal currents. The extent of movement and the treat to sensitive areas on the western portion of Bolivar Peninsula would be driven in part by the timing of any release. Should there be an indication of actual oil in the water, this initial trajectory forecast would need to be updated immediately to provide an accurate prediction. Tide predictions and a brief weather summary follow. I will work up the RAR shortly. If you have any questions or if there is an observation of a spill, please contact me immediately. [SEP] (image credit, google) [SEP] On Wednesday, 10 July 2009, at 1530 hrs, the NRC received a report of a ???€?mystery sheen???€? in Green Canyon Block 645 (report number 912389). USCG Marine Safety Unit Morgan City followed up on the report and asked NOAA to provide a trajectory analysis. The mystery slick is reported to be 3.5 by 2 miles in size. Note, the information available is based on observations from personnel at the BP platform who state that the slick is at their location, but not associated with their operation. The person making the report also stated to the USCG that there is a natural seep in the area, but it is unknown if this slick and the seep are connected. The reported location at 1530 hrs was 27?? 19???€? 16???€? N Lat. 90?? 32???€? 8???€? W Long. This position is more than 100 miles off the Louisiana coast in the Gulf of Mexico. Preliminary Trajectory Analysis Given the light winds and sea state, the reported slick is not expected to move very fast. It may slowly drift to the NE over the next 12-36 hrs. The slick is reported to be composed of rainbow sheen. The volume is unknown, but if 100% cover???€? the slick may be in the 1500 gallon range (or much less if the color is light rainbow and patchy). Given that the type of oil is an unknown, the actual volume unknown, and the winds and sea state are light it is very difficult to provide an estimate as to how long the slick might persist before dissipating with any accuracy. That stated, the slick is not expected to persist more than a couple of days. The slick would not be a threat to the shoreline or nearshore resources at this distance offshore. Offshore birds feeding in the area of the slick could be at risk until the slick dissipates. Weather and Current Information The on-scene observations at the time of the report were W winds at 4 knots. The current marine forecast for this area suggest that winds are light and variable, maybe 5 to 10 knots and seas 1 to 2 feet. The Shell Brutus platform is currently reports winds of 4 to 6 knots. Currents at Green Canyon 858 are very light at less than 0.01 knots to the E. In short, there are no strong drivers at present to move the quickly or in a predictable direction. The current winds are thought to have a net SW component this evening. The NOAA Marine Forecast prediction for this general area for Thursday through the weekend are SE to S winds at 5 to 10 knots maybe increasing 10 to 15 knots this weekend. Seas may strengthen to 2 to 3 feet this weekend. Note, the weather could change and change quickly, but there just isn???€?t much happening at present that far offshore.

[SEP] To Charlie Henry August 18. 2009 How far up the coast do we expect tarballs this summer the originate from Mexico or Southern Texas? Tarballs may impact as far north as Galveston Island with an outside chance of reaching Bolivar Peninsula into September. Data: TABS buoy: The daily overview from today indicates a strong south to north current off Brownsville, a persistent East to West Current off Lake Sabine. Buoy B just south of Freeport is weak and variable with a slight downcoast (NE to SW bias). The record over the past few days from the buoys reflect this pattern. This would make it difficult for tarballs to move north of the Freeport area. SST (Sea Surface Temp) Analysis: This shows a strong upwelling signal to about 28 degrees north. This indicates at south to north current along the coast from about 20 degrees north in Mexico to about Matagorda Island. SSH (Sea Surface Height) Analysis of surface currents: This shows a south to north coastal current extending to about Matagorda Island to the north. Stat wind table from buoy 42035 off Galveston: The wind stats indicate persistent winds from 110 to 220 degrees in August. This is from the SE, S, and SW directions. In Sept the winds begin to shift and become 020 to 190. This is from the NE, E, SE, and S. We expect the northward migration of tarballs to stop in September if the statistical winds hold true to form. IXTOC oil spill: During the summer of 1979 oil extended as far north as Galveston Island from the IXTOC oil well blowout. Discussion: Historically tarballs from Mexico have gone as far as Galveston Island. Data from various sources listed above indicate that this will probably be the case again this summer. The most likely northern most extent from looking at currents appear to be in the Matagorda Island. However winds could carry some tarballs as far north as Galveston Island and under just the right conditions, some oil could be carried as far as Bolivar Peninsula. Note that any oil spilled between in the coastal zone south of Matagorda Island could end up on the beach along the South Texas coast. The oil does not have to originate in Mexico.
On 7/21/09 USCG Sector North Carolina notified the NOAA SSC about a vessel sinking offshore of Diamond Shoals, Cape Hatteras, North Carolina. The F/V TINA RAY, a 76 foot long wooden vessel carrying approximately 1600 gallons of #2 diesel fuel collided with the R/V LOCURA, a  33 foot sailboat.  Fuel on-board sailboat is unknown.  Location was approximately 10nmi offshore.  USCG reported a sheen about one mile long by 1/2 mile wide. USCG requested verbal trajectory.  Based on NE currents (1-2 knots) and SW winds (5-7 knots) the sheen was moving in a NE direction away from shore.  Based on 80 degree water temps and 90 degrees air temps, SSC expected sheen to dissipate within 12-24 hours depending upon rate of discharge of diesel fuel from fuel tanks. Sailboat involved in incident was secured and towed to shore.  A vessel is enroute to salvage the F/V TINA RAY which sank.

On June 16, 2009, NOAA ERD was notified of a stranded sailing yacht on Rose Atoll in American Samoa.   The 35-foot aluminum vessel is believed to have approximately 40 gallons of diesel onboard, but reports are very sketchy at this time.  The yacht is reported to be intact and not leaking.  A private yacht is enroute to provide assistance.  Rose Atoll is located approximately 130 nautical miles east-southeast of Pago Pago Harbor, American Samoa, and is the easternmost Samoan island. It is the southernmost unit of the National Wildlife Refuge System. On January 6, 2009, Rose Atoll Marine National Monument was established, which includes Rose Atoll National Wildlife Refuge within its boundaries. [SEP] Additional information is at: http://sanctuaries.noaa.gov/news/features/0209_rose.html http://www.fws.gov/roseatollmarinemonument/ On January 6, 2009, President George W. Bush established Rose Atoll Marine National Monument under the authority of the Antiquities Act of 1906. The monument incorporates approximately 13,451 square miles within its boundaries, which extend 50 nautical miles from the mean low water line of Rose Atoll Presidential Proclamation 8337, which established the monument, gave the Secretary of the Interior management responsibility for the monument, including Rose Atoll National Wildlife Refuge, in consultation with the Secretary of Commerce. It prohibits commercial fishing within the monument, but gives the Secretary of Commerce, through the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, primary responsibility for managing fishery-related activities. The proclamation further provides that the Secretary of Commerce initiate the process to add the marine areas of the monument to the Fagatele Bay National Marine Sanctuary. On January 16, 2009, the Secretary of the Interior delegated his management responsibilities for the monument to the Fish and Wildlife Service through Secretary???€?s Order 3284. FWS is working with NOAA and the Government of American Samoa to carry out the requirements of the Presidential Proclamation and Secretary???€?s Order. The Alaska SSC was notified early Wednesday morning that the 262 foot Barge SCT282 came into hard contact with the 113 foot Tug Pacific challenger, owned and operated by K-Sea Transportation.  This collision cracked the #1 cargo tank causing an approximate 4-6 inch X 3/16 inch crack two to three feet above the water line and releasing unleaded gasoline into Cook Inlet, approximately 1 mile SSE of the KPL dock at Nikiski.  The barge had a total of around 70,000 BBL of unleaded gas that it was delivering to several south-central ports.   The crack is very close to the top of the tank and was seeping gasoline into the water.  There no injuries to report.  The vessels were expected to arrive in Homer on Wednesday night, May 27th, where actual measurements will determine the size of the spill. [SEP] John was called at about 0600 PDT by CG and he consulted with Bushy by phone. About 30K gallons of gasoline was lost into the water. The concern wasn't the pollution threat but whether folks were gonna get sick from the fumes. School kids were gonna be out later in the morning catching buses near the site. John and Bushy (me) concluded that in a few hours the entire slick would be gone. Remember it was about 0500 ADT when John called. We also noted that with the 4 - 5 knot max currents (spill happened at min before flood) the gasoline was going to move out of the area quickly and exposure times to the fumes would be short. John called CG back and verbally gave them the message. [SEP] Crash spills gas: Boats collide in Cook Inlet By Joseph Robertia | Peninsula Clarion An early morning marine collision in Cook Inlet that resulted in an unknown amount of unleaded gasoline leaking into the water sent personal from the Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation and the U.S. Coast Guard scrambling. "I got a call from the duty officer at 3 a.m.," said Gary Folley of ADEC, in regard to the incident, which took place at roughly 1 a.m. Wednesday, approximately 1 mile from the Tesoro KPL dock in Nikiski. The 113-foot Pacific Challenger tug and the 262-foot, 48,000 barrel barge SCT 282 -- both owned by New Jersey-based K-Sea Transportation -- crashed into each other as a result of choppy seas. "It occurred while the barge was leaving the KPL dock," Folley said. The crew began inspecting the vessels, which was when a crack in the tank -- carrying roughly 70,000 gallons of gasoline -- was noticed. "The crack was about 4- to 6-inches long, and just above the water line," Folley said. Within 20 minutes, the crew transferred the gasoline into undamaged tanks on the barge, and a temporary epoxy patch was applied over the pierced area. A Coast Guard flight over the spill area late Wednesday morning did not detect any signs of a sheen or gasoline in the water. "They couldn't see any signs of the spill. Gasoline evaporates pretty fast, but also there probably wasn't much spilled," Folley said. The tug and the barge headed to Homer, where they were scheduled to undergo a detailed accident investigation by the Coast Guard and the state. Measurements also will be taken to determine the amount of gas that did spill. Joseph Robertia can be reached at joseph.robertia@peninsulaclarion.com.

[SEP] On 12 May 2009, the regional NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator (SSC) was notified of a crude oil spill in Venice, Louisiana (NRC Report 905256). The USCG reported that 20 bbls of oil was lost into an adjacent marsh from a pipe failure during a pressure test. The oil is contained in a small pond and fringe marsh area immediately adjacent to the facility. The USCG requested that we assess the potential use of in-situ burning to mitigate the spill. Based on the follow up discussion, it was the consensus of the Federal On-Scene Coordinator???€?s Representative (FOSCR) and the SSC that a conventional response would probably be the best course of action. The incident was adjacent to the small town of Venice and immediately adjacent to infrastructure at the facility. The volume of oil was small and recoverable to expected cleanup standards using drum skimmers and some flushing. In-situ burning is a viable for many marsh spills, but the benefit gained must be weighted with the potential losses. In this situation, the close proximity of members of the general public (smoke plume concern) as well as potential for collateral burn in excess of the area threatened by the spill tipped the scale against the use of in-situ burning and toward a conventional response.

At 1130local, April 1, 2009, as a result of a collision while docking, roughly 2300gal (estimate as of noon, 2Apr09)) of waste oil (slops) was discharged from a barge owned by Diversified Environmental Services, Inc., into McKay Bay, a secondary bay of Tampa Bay, FL.  Location of the spill was at the "Shrimp Docks" on the southwest side of the 22nd St. Causeway.  The majority of the spill was apparently contained in the immediate vicinity of the dockside facility by the responsible party, since they are also an oil spill cleanup contractor whose HQ is at the dock where the oil was discharged.  The collision opened a 2 foot long gash in the port forward quarter of the barge, puncturing one of the barges tanks.  It is a single skin barge.  NOAA ERD was apparently not notified, and the SSC learned of it through ARD personnel at 1850 local, 1Apr09, although the earliest reports indicated the spill was less than 1000 gallons and contained.  A site visit on 2Apr09 by the SSCr in St. Petersburg collected further information. [SEP] DES barge with 2 foot long gash on port side. Photo by NOAA (Jeansonne)2Apr09. On Saturday, 28 March 2009, the Regional NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator was contacted by USCG Sector New Orleans relative to a 200 yard long mystery slick reported as black oil.  The observation was in the Mississippi River at MM 112.  The USCG requested trajectory support. [SEP] (image credit, google) [SEP] On Saturday, 28 March 2009, the Regional NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator (SSC) was contacted by USCG Sector New Orleans relative to a 200-yard long mystery slick reported as black oil. The observation was in the Mississippi River at MM 112 at 1:10 PM. The USCG requested trajectory support. The SSC looked at the trajectory implications based on location, river flow, and wind conditions and provided a verbal report to the USCG. In short, the river was relatively high and flowing maybe 4 knots (educated guess only) and the winds were predicted to continue out of the W at 10 to 15 mph. At the time of the request for support, the New Orleans Airport was showing 17 mph W winds. The reported location was favoring the Left Descending Bank (LDB). It was most likely that the oil would strand along the LDB entrained in batture or staged barges fleeting areas. If any oil made it past the first bend of the river, it would likely strand on the RDB near Ama. It would be highly unlikely for the oil to travel as far as Harahan (and if it made it that far, it would have already reached that location when the SSC was notified). This volume of oil was not thought to be very large, and biggest concern might be oiling of barges in fleeting areas. The battures are of environmental concern, but, again, the volume is small. The USCG reported that initial reports from some of the fleeting area reported no oil. No additional support was requested.
The USS New Orleans, a US Navy amphibious ship, collided with the USS Hartford, a US Navy submarine in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday morning at about 0100 local time.  The collision resulted in an estimated release of 25,000 gallons of marine diesel oil.US Navy Supervisor of Salvage contacted the NOAA SSC as per a joint contingency plan and modeling estimates are being prepared. [SEP] MANAMA, Bahrain (AP) ???€? Two U.S. Navy vessels ???€? a nuclear-powered submarine and an amphibious ship ???€? collided during the early morning hours Friday in the Strait of Hormuz between Iran and the Arabian peninsula, the U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet reported. There was no damage to the sub's nuclear propulsion system, said Lt. Nate Christensen, a 5th Fleet spokesman. The military said in a statement that the incident occurred around 1:00 a.m. local time on Friday (5 p.m. ET, Thursday), when the USS Hartford, a submarine, and the USS New Orleans, an amphibious ship, collided. According to the Bahrain-based 5th Fleet, 15 sailors aboard the Hartford were slightly injured but able to return to duty. No injuries were reported aboard the New Orleans. Both ships were heading to port and were going in the same direction when the incident occurred in the narrow strait, said 5th Fleet spokesman, Lt. Nate Christensen. He said the incident occurred at night and the submarine was submerged at the time but that he could give no further details as the collision is still under investigation. FIND MORE STORIES IN: California | Connecticut | San Diego | Iran | Navy | Fleet | Strait of Hormuz | Arabian | Groton | Bahrain-based | USS New Orleans Both vessels are now heading to port for repairs and evaluation, but Christensen said that following standard security procedures he could not say where the vessels were headed. The New Orleans suffered a ruptured fuel tank, resulting in an oil spill of approximately 25,000 gallons of diesel fuel. Both ships are currently operating under their own power. The Navy said both ships were on regularly scheduled deployments to the region and conducting security operations. Oil prices rose after news of the collision which happened in a busy shipping route. As much as 17 million barrels of oil a day went through the narrow strait in the first half of 2008, or about 40% of all seaborne traded oil or 20% of all oil traded globally. The Hartford is based in Groton, Conn., and the New Orleans is based in San Diego, Calif., the Navy said. As are all U.S. submarines, the Hartford is nuclear powered. The New Orleans is an amphibious transport dock ship. ---Source: USA Today online [SEP] Date: FRIDAY, 20 MARCH, 2009 To: NOAA SSC STEVE LEHMANN FROM: NOAA/ORR, Seattle, WA 98115 SUBJECT: Diesel spill in the Straits of Hormuz FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION, PLEASE CONTACT Bill Lehr ORR, NOAA, SEATTLE, WA 98115. Mitchel oceanographic survey, Hormuz is an area of current shear with inflow into the Persian Gulf on the Iranian side and outflow on the Arabian side. The USCG notified the NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator of both the damaged rail car leaking molten sulfur and several reported empty hazmat rail cars that contained only residuals of anhydrous ammonia and styrene monomer. The USCG notified the NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator of both the damaged rail car leaking molten sulfur and several reported empty hazmat rail cars that contained only residuals of anhydrous ammonia and styrene monomer. The hot molten sulfur created an air threat forcing an evacuation. The incident occurred where the bridge crosses Plaquemine Bayou in the city of Plaquemine, LA (30?? 17.59???€? N Lat. 091?? 14.32???€? W Long.).  The threat was mostly from the rotten egg smell of hydrogen sulfide that has a very low odor threshold. Nobody was hurt. The five cars that derailed were near the rear of a 67-car train that was going 16 mph at the time of the accident. NOAA provided only verbal consultation to the USCG responding to the incident in conjunction with state authorities. The sulfur itself once cooled is not considered a major environmental concern. The NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator will follow up with the USCG on this incident to assess if there are any residual issues that would be of concern. If there are no follow up issues that involve the USCG and NOAA, this report will serve as the Initial and Final Hotline report. This could have been much worse.
The Alaskan SSC was notified at 0600 March 5 by Sector Anchorage that the 112 foot FV Mar-Gun grounded on the north side of St. George Island, the more southern of the two Pribilof Islands in the SE Bering Sea, Alaska. Five POB and the vessel had 15,000 gallons of diesel and grounded in 18 to 25 ft. of water. At the moment the Coast Guard is treating the incident strictly as a SAR case, although NOAA SSC and Sector Anchorage personnel are gearing up to treat this as a pollution case, and have called for a UC meeting morning of March 5. NOAA is providing weather, tides, ADIOS runs, and possible trajectories and impacts. Dan Magone from Dutch Harbor was hired as the vessel salvor to extricate it from its rocky grounding on the shoreline on the N. side of St. George Island. After several fits and starts, bad weather, labor difficulties, broken equipment,etc, etc. the vessel was finally refloated around the first of May and was taken to Dutch Harbor for final repairs. No significant amounts of oil were released during the incident. (206) 526-4911. _______________________________________________________ The reported scenario: A 36 foot yacht ran aground at around 1600-1700 EDT near buoy 22 off Wassaw Sound. It was hard aground and carrying about 170 gal. gasoline. As of 1750 EDT vessel was under tow by SeaTow. The location was given as 31??55.895'N--087??57.776'W, and is 3/4 of a Mile or more from shoreline in all directions. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP as it would affect any trajectory implications. _______________________________________________________ 1) Winds Forecast Tornado watch in effect untill 3am EST Sunday. Small craft advisory in effect from midnight tonight through monday afternoon. Tonight: Winds for the SW 15 to 20 knots increasing to 20 to 25 knots with gust up to 30 knots late. Sunday: Winds from the SW at 20 to 25 knots with gusts up to to 30 knots 2) Trajectory Analysis Gasoline is a very light fuel and will evaporate and disperse rapidly. In the strong winds, and waves, we expect any spilled fule to disperse very quickly, probably not leaving even a visible sheen for any length of time. That ship locatio is almost a mile from shore, so we do not ecpect any shoreline contact at all. 3) Resources at risk With the strong winds, much of the spilled fuel is likely to be dispersed into the water column. This can create a toxic hazard, but it will be highly localized. Some local biota could be killed in a small area. It is unlikely that any effects will be noticable in the longer term. 4) Oil Fate Gasoline is a light refined product with a specific gravity that can range from 0.76 to 0.70 at 15??C (54 to 70 API). The product typically has a very high evaporation rate and does not tend to create persistent slicks. For a release this small, in open water conditions and with wind speeds greater than 10 knots, 90% of the gasoline is expected to evaporate within the first 1 hour or sooner of the initial release. When spilled, the gasoline spreads quickly into thin films by forming patches of rainbow and silver sheens. If the sheens reach the shoreline in a few hours, a slight staining, or greasy film is common. Normally, this type of release does not become an involved cleanup problem. There is a high flammability hazard associated with gasoline spills. Specifically, if a spill is kept from spreading freely by natural or man-made structures the gasoline slick might be thick enough to support ignition. In addition, vapor concentrations near the source of spill or vapors collected in sheltered areas can present an explosion hazard. Please note that gasoline does have a relatively high concentration of light aromatic compounds and tends to be more soluble and more toxic then heavier oils. In high energy environments, the gasoline is likely to disperse as small droplets in the water column. Gasoline spills can result in an initial toxic shock to biota and persist as a biological threat, particularly in low energy marine environments such as shallow bays and inlets.
Early morning of Wed., Feb. 25, Sector Anchorage received word that the 58' FV Icy Mist was taking on water north of Akutan Island with 4 POB along with 2700 gallons of diesel, 150 gallons of hydraulic oil,  200 gallons of lube oil, and 60,000 lbs of Pacific Cod.  Conditions were horrific with  sustained winds of 60 to 70 kts and  gusts approaching 100 kts.   Vessel was intentionally beached on a rocky shoreline shadowed by a high vertical cliff face.  The 4 POB were rescued by Coast Guard helo, and the status of the fuel onboard is unknown at this time.Initially, from an overflight, no pollution was reported, and the vessel appeared to be in good condition.  However on up close examination, the bottom of the vessel was found to be badly damaged causing a release of all the diesel and all the hydralic oil.   The 200 gallons of lube oil was removed.    NOAA SSC  provided weather forecast support throughout as well as information on the fate of the oil if a release occurred.   The state of Alaska will managed both the disposal of the Pacific cod and the vessel. [SEP] The USCG reported that the grounded tank ship Yasa Golden Dardanelles was successfully refloated at 1208 a.m. this morning (24 Feb.). The ship, an 800-foot tanker with 26 crewmembers, was carrying 621,000 barrels of home heating oil when it ran aground off the coast of Galveston on Friday, February 21. The tank ship did not discharge oil nor did salvage operations impede other vessel traffic. A Unified Command consisting of the Coast Guard, the ship's owner, Texas General Land Office, United States Mineral Management Service, National Oceanic and Atmospheric Association, Titan Salvage, O'Brien's Response Management and the Marine Spill Response Corporation has worked around-the-clock over the past four days to free the vessel expeditiously while minimizing environmental impact. The ship was freed by lightering over 80,000 barrels of oil to another tank ship. The transfer was conducted safely ensuring no harm to the personnel working, no pollution release into the environment, and no damage to the vessel. Coast Guard personnel on-scene oversaw the operation. This morning, commercial divers will perform an underwater hull inspection, and naval engineers and inspectors from the ship's classification society will examine the ship before it enters port. Unless the situation changes, this entry will serve as the final report for the grounding. [SEP] http://www.dallasnews.com/sharedcontent/APStories/stories/D96G5R0O6.html Coast Guard working to free grounded tanker 02/21/2009 Associated Press An oil tanker remained grounded Saturday off the Texas coast in the Gulf of Mexico, but no fuel had spilled from it, officials said. [SEP] On 18 February 2009, NOAA was notified by the Texas General Land Office (TGLO) of an offshore gas and gas condensate release near Matagorda Island, Texas. The initial NRC report (#897816) stated that a 1 mile x 1 mile sheen was observed associated with a 24???€? natural gas line failure at a platform. Clearly, the potential for fire and explosion near source was the most immediate issue. Secondly, would be the threat of the release to the marine and costal environment. The reported position was 27?? 57' 36" N Long. 096?? 33' 54" W Long. This location is approximately 20 miles offshore due E of Rockport, Texas. TGLO???€?s Scientific Support Coordinator evaluated the potential fate and trajectory of the observed slick. In short, the analysis suggested that the slick would move parallel to shore and dissipate. NOAA is monitoring the situation. Preliminary Trajectory Analysis Preliminary trajectory indicated a spill originating at 27?? 57' 36" N Long. 096?? 33' 54" W Long. traveling parallel to the coast about 15 miles to the southwest from its original position from 8am this morning to 8am tomorrow morning (see GNOME Model Predictions). The oil was reported at one point as a 32 API condensate crude. The value was later updated to an API gravity of 50.2???€? a value more in-line with a condensate. Such light oils generally dissipate by evaporation and natural dispersion into the water column. At the end of the day, there was no update as to the status of the release.

Currents have had a southerly component since the evening of the 15th, and at times been over 1 knot. ++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++ So how far from the south could the oil have come from? Let's suppose upcoast currents that average 1/3 knots since midnight between the 15th and 16th. That would be about 42 hours before the oil showed up at Santa Cruz. So that means 14 nm just from the currents. The winds average about 15 knots over this period along the outer coast so that would be about 21 nm from the windage. That means a total of about 35 nm of transport since midnight Sunday Santa Barbara Channel is about 180 nm from Monterey Bay. For the oil to have come from Pt Conception would take about a week. Did the oil come from the Monterey Formation? It could. Could the oil have come from the offshore shipping lanes? It could.

[SEP] NOAA SSCr (Jeansonne) participated in an environmental survey of the areas around the collision site between 0930 and 1100 hours local. Aditionally, a U.S. Coast Guard helicopter surveyed the entire middle and lower Tampa Bay area for signs of the diesel spilled. No sign of diesel was observed or smelled at the Port Manatee Island near the entrance to Port Manatee. No sheens were observed during the survey and at the time visibility was unrestricted. Current estimate of the amount spilled is 800-1000 gallons diesel. During the night and through about 0700 local, heavy fog resulted in very limited visibility. However, responders did report transiting through diesel sheens and the strong smell of diesel as they moved around the area and to/from shore. During the night, the leak was stopped. The shrimper was anchored and stablized with a deliberate port list to raise the leak site above the level of fuel and all but 100 gallons of fuel was transfered to other tanks. the Tug/barge combination did not appear to have been significantly damaged. A FWC research fish hatchery at Port Manatee was notified by the SSCr at 0730 and they have secured their water intakes as needed. At noon they were advised that no diesel was currently being observed or expected in the vicinity of their facility. The Captain of the Port (COTP), on advice from his staff and the on-scene responders, released the two vessels involved to return to their docks and was in the process of re-opening the port to vessel traffic. At that time the COTP decided to begin shutting down the active pollution response. SSCr departed the scene at 1115 local and proceeded to the office in St. Petersburg. U.S Coast Guard Sector Honolulu notified the NOAA SSC that the USS Port Royal, a Pearl Harbor-based navy guided missile cruiser, is hard aground at the entrance to Pearl Harbor at coordinates 21 degrees 17.48 north, 157 degrees 55.23 west. The location is approximately a half a mile south of Honolulu Airport's Reef Runway and a mile and a half from the entrance of Pearl Harbor.No oil has been released at this time. The vessel is taking on water, however, the water is contained in the space adjacent to the sonar array. It is believed that only the sonar array is aground. Operations to free the vessel, reportedly grounded on sand and crushed coral rock, are in progress. The vessel is reported to be carrying 250,000 gallons of navy marine diesel and 1000 gallons of JP5 aboard. [SEP] The USS Port Royal was successfully freed between 0200 and 0300 this morning and then towed into Naval Station Pearl Harbor for further inspection, assessment, and development of repair plans. An overflight at first light indicated a small sheen, which dissipated within a few hours. NOAA ERD provided a trajectory forecast for the small oil sheen observed and a weather spot-forecast update. The U.S. Navy and US Coast Guard Sector Honolulu thanked NOAA ERD for the technical support and assistance during the incident response over the weekend. The Navy says it has freed the $1 billion warship that ran aground close to the coast of Honolulu. The Navy issued a statement saying the USS Port Royal was removed from a rock and sand shoal early Monday. Crews had to remove about 500 tons of water and 100 tons of anchors and other equipment to lighten the vessel. After that work was completed it took a salvage ship and seven tugs about 40 minutes to work the ship loose. The guided missile cruiser ran aground Thursday just off Honolulu International Airport. It was visible to everyone flying in and out of Oahu and also was in clear view from a nearby public beach park. The Port Royal, based at Pearl Harbor, is one of the Navy's most advanced ships. Brierley Ostrander Phone: 907-463-2980 Alaska State Ferry breaks free from mooring, aground JUNEAU, Alaska - The Alaska State Ferry Lituya, a 180-foot motor vessel home ported in Metlakatla, Alaska, broke loose from its moorings at the ferry pier in Metlakatla and is reported aground one mile north on Scrub Island, Alaska, in Port Chester at 1 a.m. Friday. Coast Guard Cutter Anthony Petit, a 175-foot buoy tender home ported in Ketchikan, Alaska, is making preparations to get underway and is scheduled to arrive on scene at sunrise. Coast Guard Air Station Sitka and Coast Guard Station Ketchikan will launch assets as soon as weather conditions permit. No one was on board the Lituya at the time of the incident. Current weather conditions in the vicinity are winds from the southeast at 26 mph with gusts up to 80 mph, visibility is 3 miles, overcast with heavy rain and seas of six to eight-feet. The Alaska Marine Highway System, Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation and Coast Guard Sector Juneau are working together to respond. ### The United States Coast Guard -- Proud History. [SEP] January 22, 2009 Public Affairs (212) 668-7114 Press Release Heating oil barge runs aground near Execution Rocks NEW YORK-A barge carrying more than 5 million gallons of home heating oil reportedly struck an unknown object and began taking on water near City Island, N.Y., at approximately 2:30 p.m., today. No pollution is reported at this time. The commercial tug Meredith C. Reinauer was pushing a barge to Boston, Mass., when they reportedly struck the object near Execution Rocks, N.Y. The master of the tug contacted the Coast Guard and reported the barge was taking on water in a ballasting void. The tug brought the barge to anchor off of Hart Island, N.Y. A Coast Guard 41-foot response boat crew from Coast Guard Station Kings Point was quickly on scene to confirm that the vessel was not discharging any oil. Commercial divers from Randive, Inc. were quickly on-scene and conducted an underwater survey of the barge hull. Miller Environmental Group, a commercial oil spill removal company, has placed a boom around the barge as a precautionary measure and is lightering fuel from it. The Coast Guard and Nassau County Police are currently enforcing a 200-yard safety zone around the tug and barge while lightering operations take place. "Coast Guard personnel on-scene will be monitoring this case throughout its entirety," said LT Brandon Link, Command Duty Officer at Coast Guard Sector New York. "So far no pollution has been reported, precautionary measures have been taken and we will ensure all the proper steps are taken to safely secure the cargo." The investigation into this incident is ongoing. ### For more information about the Coast Guard and Public Affairs Detachment New York you may use the following links. [SEP] Resources at Risk (RAR) Texas Petroleum Pipeline Spill, Near Kaplan, LA I. Spill Source Information This report was prepared on 20 January 2009 at 1000. Information in the report is based on the report of a spill in a marsh southwest of Kaplan, Louisiana. A reported 200 bbls of a mixture of crude oil and production water (high brine content formation water) was released. II. Geographic Region Covered This report covers the wetlands surrounding the production area where the release occurred. Consult other ResponseLink reports for trajectory information. III. Habitats at Risk Habitats around the release site are primarily freshwater marshes and forested wetlands with some upland/developed areas. IV. Biological Resources at Risk Birds Waterfowl commonly found in area wetlands include: American coot (high concentrations), American wigeon (high concentrations), blue-winged teal, canvasback, gadwall (high concentrations), green-winged teal, hooded merganser, lesser scaup, mallard, mottled duck, northern pintail, and northern shoveler. A rare wading bird winters within 2 miles of the release site. Colonial waterbirds nest within 5 miles of the release site. Fish Fish species present in the Intracoastal Waterway and other inland waters include: Atlantic croaker (very abundant), bay anchovy (very abundant), black drum, crevalle jack, Florida pompano, gizzard shad, gray snapper, gulf menhaden, gulf sturgeon, red drum, sand seatrout, sheepshead, silver perch, southern flounder, Spanish mackerel, spot, spotted seatrout, striped mullet, and tarpon. Spawning adults, eggs, larvae, and juveniles may be present. Invertebrates Invertebrates present in the Intracoastal Waterway and other inland waters include: bay squid (spawning), blue crab, brown shrimp (spawning), Florida stone crab, gulf stone crab, pink shrimp (spawning), and white shrimp (spawning). Reptiles and Terrestrial Mammals American alligators, raccoons, mink, muskrats, river otters, and nutria are present in wetlands. V. Human-Use Resources at Risk The spill site is within the White Lake Wetlands Conservation Area managed by Louisiana Wildlife and Fisheries and the Amoco Gueydan Mini-Refuge. The Flying J/Broussard Mini-Refuge occurs south of the release site. Based on imagery available, the observed pipeline spill location appears to be within a marsh adjacent to an oil production area, N of the ICW and just over10 miles SW of Kaplan, Louisiana. The spill site is within the White Lake Wetlands Conservation Area managed by Louisiana Wildlife and Fisheries and within an area identified as the AMOCO GUEYDAN MINI-REFUGE. This area is highly sensitive by designation as a refuge and the wildlife it supports. In general, all wetlands and marshes are considered sensitive habitat. This area has the added protection of state refuge status. The USCG team on-scene reports that the OSRO is deploying boom to contain a portion of the release, delineating the spill area, and working to contain the spill in as small an area as possible. The SSC has been in communication with the field team several times this afternoon, and will follow up again tomorrow. New maps have been added to Hotline. [SEP] Based on imagery available, the pipeline spill location appears to be within an agricultural rice field, just S of the ICW and just over 10 miles SW of Kaplan, Louisiana. Just to the W of this location is a freshwater marsh area that would be a holding site for waterfowl. The spill location appears to be just inside of the White Lake Wetlands Conservation Area managed by Louisiana Wildlife and Fisheries. It is not clear if the agriculture land is owned by the state, but it does appear within the management area given the resolution of LDWF on-line site map. Attached are several maps that provide some highlights of the natural features in the area. From a natural resources at risk prospective, the threat to migratory waterfowl would probably be the greatest immediate threat issue. Ideally, the spilled oil and production water is trapped within water control structures and can be contained. Bird hazing would probably be required to reduce the threat to migratory waterfowl, but some level on on-scene assessment is needed. On Sunday, January 18, the 800-foot bulk carrier CSL Argosy ran aground in the Chesapeake Bay in the lower Craig Hill Channel just north of Annapolis, MD.  The ship, with pilot aboard, was inbound to Baltimore with a cargo of iron ore when it ran aground. On the evening of 16 Jan. 2009, the USCG notified the regional NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator of an allision of the OSV C-ROVER with a MODU in the general area of the Flower Garden Banks National Marine Sanctuary (FGBNMS). While completing transfer operations of synthetic-based drilling mud, the C-ROVER hit Column No. 4 on the Semi-Submersible MODU. The reported position was 27° 22.9’ N Lat. 094° 38.99’ W Long. (S of the FGBNMS). [SEP] The reported location is some 100 miles offshore and S of the Flower Garden Banks National Marine Sanctuary. Synthetic-Based drilling mud is very heavy (much denser than seawater) and will immediately sink when spilled. Such products generally do not create a significant surface sheen. Given that the NOAA chart shown that this area is very deep, maybe 275 fathoms or 1650 feet, a release of 1000 gallons of drilling mud would have settled over the bottom as a light sprinkling. The worse case discharge, if discharged very rapidly, may generate a small seafloor lump smothering anything under it. We have no information as to what the present oceanographic currents are with depth at this location???€? subsurface current flow would disperse any released drilling mud more widely, but neither a 1000 gallon of 45,000 gallon release is thought to represent a significant environmental issue at this location based on this initial assessment. Most environmental tox data indicates that synthetic-based drilling mud formulations are much less toxic than traditional oil based products. [SEP] (Updated and Final Trajectory Analysis) Situation: An allission and hose separation during a transfer operation may have resulted in the loss of some diesel fuel. The max. worse case is estimated at 1,700 gallons of diesel fuel (the residual in the tank). The location of the release is more than 100 miles offshore and S of the Flower Garden Banks National Marine Sanctuary (FGBNMS). The TABS buoy at the Flower Gardens is indicating NE winds at 10 to 15 kts, which is in sync with the general offshore marine forecast. Any small release of diesel would be expected to dissipate rather quickly given the on-scene conditions. If the damaged OSV is releasing fuel in route to Freeport TX, small amounts of diesel released would not persist, but rather evaporate and naturally disperse. We would not want such a condition as the vessel enters nearshore waters and the port if it can be avoided safely (the vessel was not reported to be sheening). The winds were onshore on Sat. at Freeport, TX. It appears that the damage was only to a mostly empty (the #4 STBD) below the water line. As a result, the residual would be trapped in the tank. From what has been reported, there are no reported releases or observed sheens. Any release at the time of the separation would move to the SW and not persist given the sea state conditions on-scene. The offshore facility is also reporting no release. At present, there is little current, but 10 to 15 kt winds that would have transport any pollution to the SW, but the sheen would not have persisted very long. The fate of the unknown, but probably small, volume of diesel would have been evaporation and natural dispersion. The OSV reports only synthetic mud residue was in the damaged tank at the time of the allision and no sheen was observed on the water (note, any released synthetic drilling mud may not have generated a surface sheen). At this point (Friday night), the vessel???€?s master reports conducting internal water transfers for stability and the breached No. 4 tank is now filled with seawater. This would mean there was a potential for approximately 1,000 gallons to have released. Sector Anchorage notified the NOAA SSC at 0615, Thursday morning, that the Ocean Marine Services, Inc. workboat, the M/V Monarch, had become pinned against the leg of the Granite Pt. platform, as the combined result of a strong flood tidal current and extreme ice. The vessel has about 38,000 gallons of diesel onboard, is currently listing at around 30 degrees, and has been successfully abandoned. In addition, the Granite Pt. platform has been shut-in and abandoned, as the result of concern for possible damage to the platform. It appears that SSC may be headed on-scene. The CG and the SSC headed on-scene via a CG C-130 which overflew the Granite Pt. platform and the overturned Monarch hull just barely showing above the surface of the water. A couple of hours later it was reported that the Monarch had sunk to the seafloor in rougly 80 to 90 feet of water. Due to the ice and strong currents, it was decided to attempt a salvage operation in the spring. However, in March it was announced that the Monarch would be left on the bottom of Cook Inlet adjacent to the Granite Pt. platform. [SEP] Thursday Evening report: Sector Anchorage notified the NOAA SSC at 0615, Thursday morning, that the oil field workboat, the M/V Monarch (roughly 150 feet long), had become pinned against the leg of the Granite Pt. platform, as the combined result of a strong flood tidal current and extreme ice conditions. The vessel has about 38,000 gallons of diesel onboard After listing at around 30 degrees up against the platform for several hours, the vessel completely sank shortly after noon. In the process the vessel was completely abandoned, and the platform was shut-in and abandoned as a precaution against possible damage and oil release to the environment. Shortly after noon on Thursday, the vessel completely sank in the turbid waters of Cook Inlet in roughly 60 feet of water. At this point the response transitioned from one of pollution to one of salvage. At this point nodoby knows exactly where the vessel is. If it was neutrally buoy, it could be carried for a considerable distance by the strong Cook Inlet tidal currents, before coming to rest on the seafloor. Placing a marker buoy on the vessel was futile as the extensive ice would only destroy such a device. The platform was re-occupied Thursday afternoon and is in the process of being evaluated for damage and is being re-started. The responsible party has committed to attempting a salvage effort to raise and remove the fuel from the Monarch, and is in the process of developing a plan and finding the resources necessary to carry out such a plan. A side scan sonar survey will be necessary, divers have been contacted, and heavy equipment is being arranged. All this will take several days to orchestrate and carry out. Over twenty years of experience dealing with accidents and vessels and platforms in this portion of Cook Inlet tells me that this is going to be an extremely difficult operation, very time and labor intensive, and that ultimately may not succeed. As a result, the CG released me from an on-scene presence, to a stand-by status back home in Anchorage, in order to take care of a medical emergency with my wife. In addition, I have also learned, over the years, that the fate of much greater amounts of diesel than what are on board the Monarch, is extremely transient (on the order of hours) in this high energy, turbulent portion of Cook Inlet, particular in the presence of a large amounts of ice. Status reports will continue on a regular basis. On January 6, 2009, Sector Anchorage notified the NOAA SSC  of a potential incident in which a fiberglass 38' F/V American Way had engine problems enroute on a supply cruise between the villages of Kodiak  and Chignik, on the Alaskan Peninsula. and was intentionally grounded on Aghiyuk Island, SW of Kodiak Island.   The vessel had 650 gallons of diesel fuel in tanks and 4 drums of diesel on board.  After grounding, the 2-man crew abandoned the vessel and was rescued by the CG and taken to Chignik.   Aghiyuk Island is part of the Alaska Maritime NWR.   The CG requested weather and possible oil fate should any release occur.    Due to bad weather an initial CG overflight was unable to obtain any clear view or photos of the vessels.    In order to assess the condition and situation of the vessel, the CG hired Magone Marine out of Dutch Harbor.   Due to distance, however, their ETA was some time on Jan. 8.    Over the next several weeks, bad weather hampered Magone's efforts to get on-scene, and he was successful only a couple of times, until finally it was confirmed that the vessel had sunk. [SEP] Tidal heights - Jan. 8 through Jan. 14 [SEP] Thursday morning, Jan. 8, meeting with FOSC Capt Mark Hamilton and his staff: Capt. Hamilton had just returned to Anchorage from 5-6 days in the lower-48, and initially was fully briefed on the details of the incident. Good tidal height information (see next posting) was provided by NOAA in order to correlate the disposition of the vessel in the Jan. 7 photos (around 1100 to 1300 on Jan. 7) with the tidal conditions that occurred during the vessel???€?s initial grounding on Sun., Jan. 4 at around 1600 to 1800. It was concluded that in the Jan. 7 photos the vessel is most likely in its same position as when it initially grounded, and even though the photos show it partially submerged, it is also probably still partially grounded. Sector Anchorage personnel will attempt to get further information from the Master regarding status of the fuel drums on the vessel, fishing gear aboard the vessel, the Masters assessment of whether he thinks the vessel has moved, and attempt to further flush out how confident he is that no rats were onboard the vessel when it grounded. The latter issue is of extreme importance to USFWS and the Alaska Maritime NWR folks as this island is extremely rich in bird diversity and numbers during spring and summer. [SEP] Shortly after noon (local time) on Friday, 12 Dec. 2008, NOAA was notified of a slick from an unknown source off the Louisiana Coast. A passing aircraft reported a 0.25 x 2 mile dark slick some 4 to 5 miles offshore in the vicinity of Vermillion Block 29. The USCG requested a trajectory analysis. The current transport conditions are offshore, but no source information or if this is a continuous release is known at present. None of the facilities in the area are reporting a problem. The source remains a mystery. [SEP] (source, NOAA [SEP] On the evening of 11 December 2008, NOAA was requested to provide scientific support to USCG Marine Safety Unit Galveston for a grounded tug at the mouth of Dickerson Bayou, Texas. The Tug SABINE PASS had grounded earlier in the day, and was reported hard aground in soft mud and possibly an oyster reef. The tug is reported to have 4000 gallons of diesel onboard. No specific Lat. Long. position was known at the time of notification. [SEP] Situation: On the evening of 11 December 2008, USCG Marine Safety Unit Galveston requested NOAA Scientific Support for a grounded tug at the mouth of Dickinson Bayou, Texas. The Tug SABINE PASS had grounded earlier in the day, and was reported hard aground in soft mud and near an oyster reef. The tug is reported to have 4000 gallons of diesel onboard. Tide Analysis: At the time of grounding, the water level would have been approaching low tide. And the water level would have been significantly lower than that predicted due to the passing cold front. At the time of this analysis (roughly 12 hours later), the water level would be at near high tide, but still significantly less than predicted. The water level station at Eagle Point was recording a level nearly two feet below predicted for the evening high tide at 10:34 PM (local time). See attached water level chart for details. The next low tide and high tide for Eagle Point are 11:47 AM at -0.8 feet predicted and 11:28 PM (Friday Night) at +1.3, respectively. These tides will probably run below normal also as the wind remain out of the N. If the vessel doesn???€?t refloat tonight, this analysis will be updated after reviewing the water level trend during the evening and an updated weather forecast. Water levels during this time of year are often wind dominated: strong winds with a N component push water out and winds with a S component stack water in the small bay and bayou systems. Dickerson Bayou would also be affected by rainfall events, but the amount of precipitation was relatively minor. By Saturday, strong S wind are expected to reverse the current trend, i.e., higher than predicted tides might be expected. Weather Forecast: Overnight (tonight, 11 Dec.) the forecast is for clear skies, with a low around 39, and a N wind between 5 and 10 mph. On Friday (12 Dec.), sunny skies, a high near 60, and N wind around 5 mph becoming E is predicted increasing to between 5 and 15 mph Friday night. By Saturday, S wind between 15 and 20 mph, with gusts as high as 25 mph are predicted. Trajectory Analysis: Flood Tide Movement. Any diesel released on a rising tide would move up Dickerson Bayou. The extent of movement would be determined by the stage of the flood tide at release, but could easily extend a couple of miles (or more). Slack Tide Movement. It is unlikely that oil would be lost during slack tide conditions tonight unless the tug strikes an object such as a hard part of the reef after initially releasing from the soft mud. Any diesel released during this period would move to the S shore on the Dickerson Bayou and the immediate area of Dickerson Bay. Ebb Tide Movement. Any oil released before or during an ebb tide (falling tide) would migrate into Dickerson Bay and impact the shoreline near Skyline Drive. The rate of release (as well as total volume released) would dictate the extent of oiling and the extent of the observed slick. Since the winds are forecasted to be relatively light and out of the N switching to E, a worse case spill (4000 gallons) might extend into Galveston Bay, but would mostly strand (at least initially) along the S shore of Dickerson Bay. Initial Resources at Risk Analysis: This initial analysis covers Dickinson Bayou and Dickinson Bay. Diesel fuels are relatively nonpersistent, but can be toxic by exposure to be both surface oil and naturally dispersed oil. The shoreline of Dickinson Bay and Bayou is a mix of marshes, sheltered scarps, exposed scarps in clay, gravel beaches, exposed riprap, and seawalls. The only endangered species in the immediate area is the Atwater???€?s prairie chicken, which may be found about a mile south of Dickinson Bayou. Numerous species of fish are present in the area. Dickinson Bay is a nursery area for fish; gulf killifish, hardhead catfish, sheepshead minnow, spotted seatrout, red drum, and bay anchovy may be spawning in the bay at this time. Other larval and juvenile fish present include Atlantic croaker, southern flounder, sand seatrout, and striped mullet. Larval and juvenile life stages are the most sensitive to oil impacts. There are oyster beds at the mouth of Dickinson Bay and throughout the area of Galveston Bay in the vicinity of Dickinson Bay. Also present in the area are blue crab (larvae and juveniles), brown shrimp, and white shrimp (spawning, larvae, and juveniles). Also present in the area are numerous species of waterfowl, wading birds, terns, and rails. The American alligator may also be present, but mostly likely is a state of near hibernation due to the extreme cold weather. There is a marina and boat ramp at April Fool Point, and a marina where Highway 146 crosses Dickinson Bayou. There is a water intake for Houston L&P Robinson Plant at the mouth of Salt Bayou. Dickinson Bay is also used for recreational fishing.

[SEP] TIME: 1800 CST Monday, Nov. 24, 2008 TO: NOAA SSC Charlie Henry FROM: NOAA Office of Response and Restoration Emergency Response Division Seattle, WA 98115 SUBJECT: F/V Miss Marhanna For additional information, please contact Chris Barker, NOAA Emergency Response Division, Seattle, WA. Phone: (206) 526-4911. _______________________________________________________ Per your request, we have looked at trajectory implications of a release from the grounded fishing vessel Miss Marhanna. The F/V Miss Marhanna was reported grounded at 2300 on Nov. 21st. Soon after the grounding, a small sheen was reported. It is suspected that that was probably bilge water, and the the main fuel tanks have not yet been breached. However, there is concern that the vessel could be broken up in the strong winds expected this evening and for the next couple days. The vessel has a capacity of 40,000 gal of diesel fuel, but is thought to be carrying about 15,000 gal at this time. The location is at the end of the south .jetty of Brazon Santiago Pass, at approx: 26??3.5'N--097??9.0'W. If there is an actual release, we can provide a more precise trajectory given the conditions at the time of the release. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP, as it would affect any trajectory implications. _______________________________________________________ 1) WINDS: Tonight: Winds from the SE at 5-10 knots, increasing to 15-20 knots from the N later this evening. Tuesday: Winds from the NE at 15-20 knots. Wednesday: Winds from the SE at 15-10 knots. 2) TRAJECTORY: At the mouth of the Brazon Santiago Pass entrance, the oil movement will be dominated by the winds and the tidal currents through the entrance. Unfortunately, we have found no data about the strength of tidal currents though the entrance. However, the Aransas pass to the north has currents of about 2-2.5 knots. We expect that the currents in this entrance may by up to that large. If there is a release during a ebb current, the sheen will be carried into the Gulf, away from shore by the currents, while being moved by the winds to the southwest or northeast, depending on the direction of the winds at the time of the release. A a result, the sheen will travel twards shore, and be largely broken up by the surf. there may be some stainiing of the beach within a couple miles of the entrance. The visual sheen should last less than 10 hours or so in the strong winds and waves. If there is a release during a flood current, the sheen could be carried into the pass, into the south end of Laguna Madre. Once in the lagoon, it will be moved primarily by the wind, toward the southwest or northwest, depending on the wind direction at the time of the release. There would likely be shoreline impacts on the shores of Long Island and Port Isabel. Some sheen could get drawn into the Brownsville Ship Channel and into south Bay, perhaps effecting the mudflats along the west shore. The sheen will dissipate more slowly in the lagoon than it would in the open coast, but it will still dissipate fairly rapidly in the strong winds, with the visual sheen inside the lagoon lasting up to 24 hours or so. 3) OIL FATE: Light refined products, such as diesel (or Fuel Oil No 2), typically have very high evaporation rates and do not tend to create persistent slicks. However, the terminology for refined products is not standardized, and, sometimes, heavier intermediate fuel oils are referred to as ???€?marine diesel???€?. These heavier products are much less volatile than normal Fuel Oil no 2 and can form a more persistent slick. When spilled, the diesel spreads quickly into thin films often forming patches of rainbow and silver sheens. If the sheens reach the shoreline in a few hours, a slight staining, or greasy film-like bathtub ring is common. These oils usually do not form a stable emulsion and, as a result, do not form a heavy or sticky residual to clean up. Note that lighter refined products do have a relatively high concentration of light aromatic compounds and tend to be more soluble and more toxic than heavier oils. These oils do not generally present an involved cleanup problem. However, they can result in an initial toxic shock to biota and can persist as a biological threat in low energy marine environments. LCO is a complex mixture of hydrocarbons. Its exact composition depends on the source of the crude oil from which it was produced and the refining methods used. Most of these products are characterized as combustible liquids with respect to flammability. No specific information for this product was provided. [SEP] Butylene is an easily liquefied colorless gas boiling from 20.7 to 38??F. Insoluble in water. Contact with the unconfined liquid can cause frostbite by evaporative cooling. Any leak can be either liquid or vapor. Can asphyxiate by the displacement of air. Under prolonged exposure to intense heat containers may rupture violently and rocket. Highly flammable - Vapor is heavier than air and may travel long distance to a source of ignition and flash back. May act as an asphyxiant or slight anesthetic at high vapor concentrations especially in enclosed (or confined) spaces. Shoreline Resources at Risk Shoreline types around Chocolate Bayou are primarily sheltered scarps and salt and brackish water marshes. Bulrush, common reed, and other rushes are typical vegetation along the bayou shoreline. IV. Biological Resources at Risk Birds Birds commonly found in the area at this time of year include: clapper rail, Forster???€?s tern, gulls, and wading birds. Fish Fish species present in Chocolate Bayou include: red drum (spawning), bay anchovy (spawning), gulf menhaden (spawning), spotted seatrout (spawning), gizzard shad, and southern flounder. Invertebrates Species present in Chocolate Bayou include: oysters, blue crab, brown shrimp (spawning), and white shrimp (spawning). [SEP] (image credit, google) [SEP] 1993 CUMENE SPILL (CASE STUDY AS INFORMATION ONLY) At 0003 March 31, 1993, the USCG MSO Philadelphia was notified by Tioga Marine Terminal of an acetone-like odor in the area. At the time of the incident there were partly cloudy skies, winds east 5 to 10 knots, and a temperature of 60??F. MSO personnel estimated that between 32,000 to 600,000 gallons of cumene had been released from the M/V Ellen Knutsen into the Delaware River. The 442-foot Ellen Knutsen was docked at the GATX terminal in Port Richmond, Pennsylvania just south of the Betsy Ross Bridge on the Delaware River. The source of the release was a two-inch crack between the #5 starboard segregated ballast tank and the #10 starboard cargo tank. This crack permitted cargo to leak into the adjacent ballast tank. The ballast cumene mixture discharged into the river during deballasting. The spill spread downstream as far as Camden, New Jersey and upstream to near the Tacony-Palmyra Bridge. GATX personnel stopped transfer operations as soon as the spill was discovered. The total estimated release was 16,000 gallons. The Philadelphia Fire Department Hazardous Materials (HAZMAT) Team, New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection and Energy, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) for regions II and III, Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Resources, and USCG AST were onscene. Air monitoring revealed levels below two ppm at the dock and zero on the water. Behavior of Spilled Material: The product was a colorless, alkylated benzene liquid that produced a sheen in areas of heavy concentrations. The cumene moved with the flow of the river and tide and the odor of the material was detected several miles from the source. Although cumene is not very soluble in water and only a localized fish kill might be expected, it is highly toxic to birds. The spill???€?s proximity to downtown Philadelphia also caused concerns about public health. The Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry (ATSDR) indicated that this material was used as a motor fuel additive; was not immediately dangerous to life; was not very volatile; was combustible, but not flammable; was an irritant to eyes and the upper respiratory tract; and, depending on the concentration and duration of exposure, symptoms could include irritation, dermatitis, narcosis, and coma. The agency could not comment on specific public health concerns without knowing the exact concentrations in the air surrounding the source of the spill. The air monitoring devices HNU Systems Inc. Photoionization Detector or Organic Vapor Analyzer would be able to measure those concentrations in air. Due to the behavior of the product (similar to diesel fuel) and the possible health hazards involved from exposure to the chemical, the material was allowed to evaporate naturally and was washed out from under dock areas by fire hoses. None of the cumene spilled was recovered. Countermeasures and Mitigation: The Philadelphia Fire Department HAZMAT Team took control of the response at the incident site. Offloading and lightering operations were discontinued and the vessel remained at the GATX terminal until April 1 when it was moved to anchorage in the Delaware River to facilitate removing the product trapped under the piers. Commercial and public lands were closed until air monitoring revealed safe levels, and shipping lane and vehicle traffic route closures were in effect for the first few hours of the response. Diversionary and protective booms were placed at creek mouths and water intakes as precautionary protection for these sensitive areas. Open-water recovery or shoreline cleanup were not undertaken. Other Special Interest Issues: Because of the hazardous nature of the product, Tri-State Bird Rescue Research Center decided not to jeopardize the health of their volunteers by undertaking wildlife rehabilitation. No reports of injured animals were received. [SEP] GNOME generated movie (trajectory) for a release a max. flood tide. The pass was opened in 1955 to enhance bay water salinity and promote submerged vegetation development. The name, Rollover, was taken from the practice of smugglers during Spanish rule that would roll barrels of whiskey and rum from the Gulf of Mexico over the narrow peninsula to be recovered by a vessel on the bayside bypassing the customs office at Galveston. [SEP] Reported Situation: A small oil slick estimated at 3 bbls was observed at 29?? 21.28???€? N Lat. 089?? 14.14???€? W Long at 1000 hrs (local time). This position places the observed slick approximately 3 miles NW of Main Pass and roughly 6 to 8 miles SSW of Breton Island. Initial Trajectory Analysis The good news is that Breton Island is not at risk. The bad news is that the Delta National Wildlife Refuge is at risk. The risk is only limited by the reported spill volume observed (3 bbl). It is likely that light oiling could impact the marshes and tidal passes of Denesse Pass, Kimble Pass, and possibly even the marshes on the E side of Baptiste Collette Bayou this evening or tonight. These areas are all part of the refuge and migratory birds, shore birds, and pelicans utilize these areas. At present, the wind is reported to be E at between 5 and 10 mph and is expected to increase slightly during the evening hours. The tide is at the end of an ebb cycle and will flood through the evening with a high tide expected after midnight. Often, there is a long shore current that moves S along the delta near the 20-30 foot depth contour due to flow from the upper portions of Breton Sound. Whether the slick is in this flow or not, is not that important, because at some point (probably already), the slick would be expected to move past the influence of any down-coast current and into the shallow waters of the Mississippi Delta. At that point, the transport would be wind and tidal current dominated and both transport factors combined would result in an onshore condition. Because of the uncertainty in precisely predicting spill trajectories in such a dynamic area such as the Mississippi Delta, the risk to a wildlife refuge, and the unknown nature of the source, follow up observations are recommended. The Delta Wildlife Refuge should also be notified of the potential threat. Weather Forecast Saturday Afternoon: Mostly sunny, with a high near 85. East wind around 10 mph. Sector Anchorage receive a notification on Oct. 1 that the M/V Nunaniq had discharged 50 gallons of diesel fuel into Mekoryuk Bay during the night of Sept. 27.  The vessel had struck a rock while delivering cargo to the native village of Mekoryuk and a fuel tank suffered a pin hole size puncture.   The fuel in the damaged tank was transferred to another tank and the vessel's crew conducted a cleanup with sorbent pads.  USFWS personnel from the Yukon Delta NWR flew to the scene on Sept. 28, and made numerous observations and photos which are contained in a report posted on this hotline.   Sector Anchorage notified the NOAA Alaska SSC on Oct. 2 and asked for an evaluation of the situation.   Also on Oct. 2, a CG team was dispatched to Bethel and Nunivak Island to do an on-scene evaluation. [SEP] Nunivak I [SEP] ushy I know it may seem trivial, but I would like to put these communications into responselink so that we or others can find and make use of this information in the future. I especially value saving the report by the wildlife biologists. It is a small event with good observations. Especially what resource injuries were looked for and NOT found with the macrofauna. No fish kills, the seagrass looks OK, no bird injuries (including the photographed shorebirds on the Fucus rock), I am not totally convinced that the jellyfish were killed by the oil. In our numerous trips to Prince William Sound, in coves with active streams (ie, Snug harbor) during flood tide we frequently see congregations of jellyfish drifting 1/2 to several meters below the surface toward the stream source, while the surface water itself, above a fresher-water shear of a few inches, is moving out of the coves. This concentrates jellies near the stream mouth. Afew get stranded on the stream mouth flats. If was present in such a situation, stranded jellies could end up in pools of oil during the ebb. Those that did so would probably die. Those that stranded but not in oil would also probably die, naturally. Thus a look at a reference stream mouth would be and important comparison. I do not doubt that diesel has soaked into the soft sediment and is injuring the infauna. Observes should watch for amphipods, polychaetes, clams emerging on the sediment surface, possibly to be scavenged by shorebirds. That's a route of exposure. Wil diesel in the sediment there could be delayed or longer-term injuries to infauna and possibly their prey. Fortunately this may not be like the No. 2 fuel spill at WoodsHole Mass marshes 30 years ago where researchers are still finding fresh diesel a half foot below the sediment surface. This diesel is on and in the mudflat sediment where, with numerous tidal exchamges, it should leach out fairly quickly. No doubt the local populace will be watching this area, which is probably very well known to them. I would value seeing any future reports. It might be good to know the temperature and alinity history at a few points sorrounding the site. Also, the primary piece of information missing is the actual volume spilled. I hope that gets confirmed. So, can we please put this in ResponseLink? Alan

[SEP] On the evening of 17 September 2008, the regional NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator (SSC) was notified of a well blowout in Grand Bayou Blue at 29?? 28.011???€? N Lat. 090?? 22.901???€? W Long. This position places the release approximately 10 miles NNW of Galliano Louisiana. The USCG reported that the incident was observed at 1700 hrs (local time). The owner/operator reported that the christmas tree and small platform were missing. The cause is unknown, but may have been an allision. The initial report was a 8-10 foot gusher of oil, but by 2200 hrs, the gush had decreased to on 2-3 feet in height (possible bridging in). The amount of oil released is unknown. An Oil Spill Response Organization (OSRO) has been dispatched with 4000 feet of boom. The USCG is coordinating either a RP or USCG overflight in the morning to assess oil pollution and the status of the well. NOTE: The light winds predicted this evening may enhance the risk of fire and explosion near the well blowout. There will not be much wind. If there is significant natural gas escaping, the heavier components such as propane will not quickly dissipate and could accumulate and spread out from the wellhead. Proper safety precautions should be used to include establishment of a safety zone and air monitoring for personnel safety. The lack of wind will only increase any risk. The safe response is not to be near the source. If any of the above information is wrong, please contact the NOAA SSC as it may have a direct effect on the predicted fate and transport. Initial Trajectory. The area identified is essentially an open water lake surrounded by highly broken coastal marsh. The current water levels are back to near normal tides after the storm surge from Hurricane Ike created an estimated 4-foot surge above normal tides in this area. The winds this evening have had been primarily from the N between at 3 to 8 mph. The forecasted winds overnight are expected to be light with a slight N component. By Thursday afternoon, the winds will have shifted to the NE then E and there is a 20% chance of evening showers. The observed winds would initially transport the oil to the broken marsh and canals on the S side of Grand Bayou Blue. Any oil still releasing and uncontained by Thursday afternoon may move to the SW in the direction of Lake Bully Camp Ponds. Given that natural containment is limited by the broken marsh and he network of man-made canals and bayous, the oil may continue to spread due to the influence of both winds and tides. We don't know when the accident started but it is likely that by tomorrow morning the spill would have undergone at least one complete tide cycle. Within the canals, tidal currents could move the oil about 1 -2 miles in either direction. With moderate winds from the N oil would move into the canal system to the S and enter Grand Bayou (which is about 3 miles south of the spill location) within 2 tidal cycles. The next high tide is predicted for the early morning, which could move oil into and through the broken marsh to the N. Tides are difficult to predict in this area especially with the freshwater flow and any lingering effects of Hurricane Ike flooding. The point is, oil could move both N, S, and W over the next 24-hour period, but the dominate movement should be S and SW. Initial Recommendation to Consider. Insure safety (see above). The response actions should focus on source control, containment near source at a safe distance due to potential fire and explosive issues from any natural gas released, and booming the affected spill area???€? essentially, put a box around the problem to limit the impact by booming off the cuts and canals that would allow oil to escape Grand Bayou Blue. [SEP] The closest tide station is in Terrebone Bay and is about 20 miles away fro the spill location. It has a predicted range a range of a little over a foot. To estimate tides for Grand Bayou Blue, We took the average wave speed and water depth and came up with the following ???€?best guess???€? to support the initial trajectory. The times could be off by as much as plus or minus 2 hours without taking into account and freshwater flow which was also investigated. Probably max flow at less than 1/5 knot. In the canals into and out of Grand Bayou Blue, tidal currents will max out at about 1/3 knot with tidal excursion of about 2 miles. As previously stated, these are rough estimations only. Winds of 10 knots or more with windage of .3 knots will dominate over the tide. In the canals, the wind will push the oil to one shore and pile it up and smear it along the shoreline. [SEP] The source has been partially (mostly) controlled by divers securing an underwater valve, but some gas was reported to still be releasing. The current plan is to sting the well on Saturday to fully shut it in. The estimated release is 300 to 400 bbl of crude oil. The OSRO is continuing to secure the pockets of oil and recovery contamination. There is at least one open water skimmer still working in the area. NOAA will continue to provide remote assistance, but may go on scene to assist in any difficult cleanup issues. Such a reduced response posture is simply the balance of the potential impacts of this incident relative to the magnitude of activity post-Hurricanes Gustav and Ike. HOPE On the over flight of 30 SEPT, recoverable quantities of light crude were observed in the marsh pond SW of the tank farm at the Houston Oil Production Enterprises (HOPE) site. On 1 OCT, NOAA accompanied USCG FOSCR, TGLO and USFWS to HOPE facility and consulted with RP and OSRO on clean up tactics. The agreed upon response strategy involves staking a line of absorbent boom to contain oil along the SW shoreline of the pond and placing absorbent pads inside of boom to facilitate passive recovery of oil. Boom will be deployed by jon boat with minimal to no impact on the marsh. OSRO will check pads and replace them as necessary to continue passive recovery. Vac truck operations will continue to recovery oil in and around tank farm. Response progress will be monitored again on OCT 2 or 3. 2. Rainbow bridge: On OCT 1, NOAA examined tank in ICW at Rainbow bridge in Port Arthur and met with USCG and contractor to discuss removal operations. The contractor will approach that tank at high tide on OCT 2 and determine if the tank contains petroleum products and will maintain boom around tank during operations. Contractor will ensure that all valves on the tank are closed and will tow the tank to a public boat launch W of the bridge. No dredging will be required to remove tank. Contractor will submit a full recovery plan to USCG in the morning of OCT 2. Tomorrow NOAA will asseist with assessments at PAPCO. USFWS will depart Port Arthur tomorrow morning but will provide further input and contact/coordination details prior to leaving. NOAA will work to develop a final documentation strategy for the responses and cases under the USCG MA at Port Arthur. EPA and USCG leads are still discussing final documentation needs and formats needed. This will be addressed tomorrow at a meeting in Pasadena. During this meeting, there will also be discussion of the marsh recovery plan and required permitting to access wetlands and remove orphaned containers such as drums and tanks. Port Arthur SSC and EPA lead will participate in this meeting. Port Arthur was visited today by the Port Arthur MSU COTP, and EPA regional directors for Superfund and Emergency Response.
