If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP as it would affect any trajectory implications. _______________________________________________________ 1) Weather Forecast Overnight: East winds 9 to 14 knots. Seas 2 To 3 feet. Saturday: East northeast winds 12 to 17 knots. seas 1 to 3 feet. Saturday Night: East northeast winds 8 to 13 knots. Seas 2 feet. Sunday: East winds 8 to 13 knots. Seas 2 feet or less. 2) Trajectory Analysis Diesel fuel is a fairly light oil that tends to evaporate and disperse fairly quickly. We expect that the currents in the region are small, so any sheen that does persist will tend to move downwind, possibly causing staining of any impacted shorelines, but little persistent impacts. With the forecast winds from the east and east northeast, we expect the sheen to move to the west and west southwest, effecting the shoreline on the western shore of the Army terminal turning basin. We expect most of the sheen to remain near the Army terminal pier. If there is significant turbulence from the cooling water intake/outfall in the vicinity of the sheen, this could serve to disperse some of the oil into the water column a bit faster, perhaps resulting in the intake water being effected. 3) Oil Fate NOAA's Adios2 model predicts that 90% of the oil will be evaporated or dispersed within about 12 hours. If the diesel is contained in boom, or under piers, etc, it could persist longer. TIME: 1400 CDT Friday, September 12, 2008 TO: NOAA SSC Charlie Henry FROM: NOAA Office of Response and Restoration Emergency Response Division Seattle, WA 98115 SUBJECT: M/V Antalina For additional information, please contact Chris Barker, NOAA Emergency Response Division, Seattle, WA. At 0840-PDT NOAA was informed by NOAA ICC that the M/V Antalina was disabled approximately 114nm SE of Galveston, TX. M/V Antalina is a 585ft bulk cargo carrier fully loaded with 11,280 metric tons of green petroleum coke. No information on the amount of fuel in its bunkers is known. The ship was reported to be at position 28 03.1'N, 093 11.7'W and drifting SW. The ship has lost propulsion but not ship's power. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP, as it would affect any trajectory implications. _______________________________________________________ 1) WEATHER: That location was within the Hurricane-strength radius of Hurricane Ike at the time of the report, and the ship will likely remain within the Hurricane for some time. It will encounter very strong winds and large seas for about 18 hours before the hurricane moves ashore. 2) TRAJECTORY AND OIL FATE: The cargo is a Petroleum Coke, which a not particularly hazardous solid. The physical characteristics of petroleum coke are similar to coal dust and spilled coke would be expected to behave the same as spilled coal dust. The material that was released would likely form floating mats on the water surface, although some of the material would form dust clouds in the upper water layer. With the storm conditions, we expect the mats would be broken up rapidly, sinking in the vicinity of the release. The ship is carrying an unknown quantity of fuel oil, though it could be a substantial amount, given the size of the vessel. If the fuel were released in the hurricane, it would be broken up and widely dispersed by the severe winds and waves. After the storm, it is unlikely that the resulting widely scattered tarballs would be observable or have significant environmental effects. [SEP] As per USCG briefing on 09/14/2008: Both vessel and crew survived Hurricane Ike intact and without incident. M/V ANTALINA is operating under its own power and will make way for Port Arthur at first light on 14 SEP under escort by TUG SMITH ROTTERDAM. This will serve as a final report for this incident. [SEP] Petroleum coke (often abbreviated petcoke) is a carbonaceous solid derived from oil refinery coker units or other cracking processes. Other coke has traditionally been derived from coal. More data can be found about the substance from the MSDS here: http://www.marathonpetroleum.com/content/documents/mpc/msds/0109MAR019.pdf Petcoke is a fuel produced using the byproducts of the petroleum refining process. Crude oil must be refined to produce gasoline and other products. A residue is left over from this process that can be further refined by ???€?coking???€? it at high temperatures and under great pressure. The resulting product is petcoke, a hard substance that is similar to coal. Petcoke, like coal, is used by other electric utilities such as JEA and Lakeland. Petcoke has a much higher heating value than coal, at around 14,000 Btu per pound, compared with 12,500 Btu per pound for coal. The physical characteristics of petroleum coke are similar to coal dust and spilled coke would be expected to behave the same as spilled coal dust. We would not anticipate that all of the material would leak out, even with a significant hull breach. The material that was released would likely form floating mats on the water surface, although some of the material would form dust clouds in the upper water layer. The mats would be broken up over time by wave action. Given the approaching hurricane, this could be a quite rapid process. Petroleum coke does not weather rapidly. Only minute amounts would evaporate or dissolve into the water column. Biodegradation would also be very slow. Petroleum coke is also, relative to other petroleum products, not very toxic, although it does contain small amounts of heavy metals and PAH's. Compiled by Mark Dix, Deputy Chief, ERD

[SEP] Unified Command Established for Post-Hurricane Ike Pollution Response PASADENA, Texas - Four federal and state agencies established a unified command here Monday to efficiently coordinate efforts to contain and clean up oil and hazardous materials in the wake of Hurricane Ike. Members of the Environmental Protection Agency, Coast Guard, Texas General Land Office and Texas Commission on Environmental Quality comprise the Unified Command. Field workers from these agencies are working with local agencies to assess, contain and clean up spills and hazardous materials. The Unified Command are responding according to federal guidelines in Emergency Support Function (ESF) #10. This provides an outline for federal support and management of various spill sites to minimize their impact on the public and the environment. In addition to detailing the roles of federal agencies, it promotes close coordination with state, local and industry representatives to establish priorities and goals for response. Field personnel have identified 181 sites with reports of pollution in the Houston-Galveston area. Teams are assessing pollution sites in the Port Arthur area and will have a count of the pollution sites there later Monday. Date: Sept. 22, 2008 Contact: Public Information Office (252) 267-3662 Members of the public can report oil spills or displaced hazardous materials by contacting the National Response Center at (800) 424-8802. The public should report oiled or injured wildlife by calling Texas Parks & Wildlife at (281) 842-8100. Editor's note: More specific descriptions of the oil and hazardous material sites are forthcoming. For more information, contact the Public Information Office at (252) 267-3662 or (252) 267-4811. The EPA is planning to meet with Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality on Wednesday, and this is one of the topics. If a ESF-10 Mission is tasked, there would probably a request for NOAA support. Additional Information: Despite the impact of Hurricane Gustav to the infrastructure of Baton Rouge and SE Louisiana (more than 80% of Baton Rouge remains without power and recovery is expected to be very slow). Communication are fairly good and the SSC is able to maintain web access by charging the portable computer battery using an inverter and car battery. Without the use of the cellular internet access card, communication would have been significantly limited. Having a cellular phone from outside the affected area also seems to be a plus. The point being, even though plans to return to home bases may suggest that things are not that bad, it is far to early to make any real assessments. During the early morning hours of Thursday, 28 August 2008, the NOAA ERD HAZMAT Duty Officer was notified of an allision in Bolivar Roads.  The regional Scientific Support Coordinator (SSC) was notified and provided the support requested by USCG MSU Galveston.  The report was that a tow containing two red flagged barges had an illision with a stationary barge.  The actual details were unknown, but there was damage reported, but no release. [SEP] Position reported by USCG (image credit, Google). [SEP] Reported Situation Allision involving a tow with two red flag barges. One barge is reported to be carrying Crude Oil and the second Naphtha. There is reported damage to at least one of the barges, but the is no report of a release at present. The USCG has requested an initial trajectory and brief RAR. Initial Trajectory Analysis and Concerns The reported position shows the barges located in he ICW approximately 3 miles from the Port Bolivar entrance. Given the current winds, any release would initially slowly moved to the NE impacting the N side of the waterway toward Johnson Road. Once tide begins to drop in the afternoon, any pollution would be expected to move back toward the SW toward the Port Bolivar and toward the main Galveston Channel. A small spill should be largely contained with the ICW. Report any observed release to the NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator to initiate a review and update of this trajectory based on known observations. Both products, Crude Oil and Naphtha, are flammable liquids that would float on the surface of the water. If there is a significant release, or release into an exposed void, use caution to not create a potential ignition. Air monitoring would be initially required to insure safe exposure levels for both LEL and benzene should there be damage to the Crude Oil cargo or a significant release. Naphtha is a distillate cut of crude oil in the light to medium range and generally doesn???€?t persist long in the environment due to evaporative loss. While natural resources do utilize the ICW as a feeding area, the greater abundance of natural resources outside the waterway would be of greater risk. Any release should be contained with the ICW, if it can be done safely. Tides Forecast The area is currently in a flood tide condition and will ebb (drop) in the afternoon evening. The tides are currently a mixed semidiurnal so the will be some slight changes throughout the morning. The next true low tide is forecast for after 9:00 PM local time. Current Wx Observations The NOAA Weather Buoy Station 42035 is currently showing SSW winds at less than 10 mph. The PORT system is consistent with this observation. Initial Weather Forecast Thursday Day: Light winds, 5 to 10 out of the W becoming S winds at 5-10 mph are forecasted. Today: A 20 percent chance of showers and thunderstorms after 1pm. Partly cloudy, with a high near 91. Heat index values as high as 101. Thursday Night: A slight chance of showers and thunderstorms before 10pm, then isolated showers and thunderstorms after 1am. Partly cloudy, with a low around 79. Southeast wind around 10 mph. Chance of precipitation is 20%. Friday: A 30 percent chance of showers and thunderstorms, mainly after 1pm. Partly cloudy, with a high near 91. Heat index values as high as 102. North wind around 5 mph becoming east. [SEP] USCG inspectors and investigators visited the barge. No pollution or threat of pollution was reported.

On Friday, 8 August 2008, USCG MSU Galveston notified the NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator (SSC) of a pipeline leak near Dickerson Bay in Texas. [SEP] Resources at Risk for Dickinson Bayou I. Spill Source Information This report was prepared on August 8, 2008. Information in the report is based on a release of an unknown quantity of crude oil from a pipeline near Dickinson Bayou. II. Geographic Region Covered This report covers Dickinson Bayou and Dickinson Bay. This area does not necessarily correspond to actual or potential oil locations. Consult other Hotline reports for oil location information. III. Expected Behavior of the Spilled Material Assuming the oil is a crude oil, the product is expected coat the vegetation and intertidal organisms. There may also be a water-soluble component that could have an impact on subtidal organisms. If the release is in the marsh, as indicated by the initial report, there may be coating of the marsh sediments. IV. Shoreline Resources at Risk The shoreline of Dickinson Bay and Bayou is a mix of marshes, sheltered scarps, exposed scarps in clay, gravel beaches, exposed riprap, and seawalls. In the marshes the oil will coat the vegetation and possibly the sediments. The extent of sediment oiling will depend on water levels in the marsh and water level changes over time. Coating the vegetation will result in short-term impacts to the marsh with possible die-off of the vegetation this year. Oiled sediments can result in chronic, long-term, impacts including loss of marsh vegetation. On the clay scarps oil will typically not adhere to the wet sediment surfaces, but could penetrate root cavities if present and dry. On the exposed scarps the oil will typically not persist for any length of time. The riprap may be coated by the oil with accumulations in the cavities between the rocks. This accumulated oil can result in chronic sheening. The gravel beaches, composed mostly of shell, are very porous. Oil may coat the porous shells and penetrate into the sediments. If oiled, cleanup may require removal of all oiled shell material. In the sheltered areas formation of asphalt pavements are likely where accumulation is heavy. Seawalls may be coated by the oil. Areas of light oiling may leave a band at the high water line while areas of heavier oiling may coat most of the intertidal zone. V. Biological Resources at Risk The only endangered species in the area is the Atwater???€?s prairie chicken which may be found about a mile south of Dickinson Bayou. Fish - Numerous species of fish are present in the area. Dickinson Bay is a nursery area for fish; Gulf killifish, hardhead catfish, sheepshead minnow, spotted seatrout, red drum, and bay anchovy may be spawning in the bay at this time. Other larval and juvenile fish present include Atlantic croaker, southern flounder, sand seatrout, and striped mullet. Larval and juvenile life stages are the most sensitive to oil impacts. In addition they may be in shallow water and are more likely to be exposed to lethal and sublethal concentrations of oil in the water column. Shellfish - There are oyster beds at the mouth of Dickinson Bay and throughout the area of Galveston Bay in the vicinity of Dickinson Bay. Also present in the area are blue crab (larvae and juveniles), brown shrimp, and white shrimp (spawning, larvae, and juveniles). The crab and shrimp are mostly benthic species, so it is not likely that the adults will be impacted. However the juveniles and larvae can be found in shallow waters and may be impacted the water soluble component of the oil. Birds - Black skimmers and olivaceous cormorants are nesting in the area at this time of year. Also present in the area are numerous species of waterfowl, wading birds, terns, and rails. Diving birds, such as cormorants, are usually at high risk during oil spills because they spend nearly all their time on the water surface. Wading birds, marsh birds, and some shorebirds may be directly oiled on the upper body and feathers by coming in contact with oiled vegetation or wrack. Direct oiling of birds reduces the buoyancy, water repellency, and insulation provided by feathers, and may result in death by drowning or hypothermia. Preening of oiled feathers may also result in ingestion of oil resulting in irritation, sickness, or death. Bird oiling, particularly of wading birds, may continue even after the floating oil slicks have been removed, depending on the extent of oiled vegetation. Oil brought back to the nests by adult birds may kill or injure eggs and young birds. Reptiles - The American alligator (nesting and hatching), Texas diamondback terrapin, and diamondback terrapin are present in the area. Oiling of these animals can result in irritation of the eyes, nose, and mouth. Heavy oiling can lead to death. Oiling of alligator eggs may result in mortality of the eggs. VI. Human-Use Resources at Risk There is a marina and boat ramp at April Fool Point, and a marina where Highway 146 crosses Dickinson Bayou. There is a water intake for Houston L&P Robinson Plant at the mouth of Salt Bayou. Dickinson Bay is also used for recreational fishing. [SEP] On Friday, 8 August 2008, USCG MSU Galveston notified the NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator (SSC) of a pipeline leak near Dickerson Bay in Texas. The initial report was only that sheen was observed and that a pipeline spill was reported. The USCG requested a RAR for the immediate area around the reported release. Later it was discovered that the spill was mostly contained behind the weir o a canal that prevented the bulk of the release from entering the main waterway. The pipeline was shut in. An OSRO was in route, and the spill volume was estimated at 16 bbl. No additional support was requested. [SEP] Reported location provided by USCG (image credit, google).
The NOAA SSC was notified by MSU Valdez on the morning of August 8 of the intentional grounding of the 92' F/V Northern Mariner two hours before the high tide on the previous afternoon of August 7 after striking a rock. The vessel contains 25,000 gallons of diesel in 6 wing tanks, 3 on each side of the vessel and was loaded with fish, but no release has occurred. The captain reports that damage occurred about 6 ft. from the nearest fuel tank - a one foot long hole in the forward engine room. Four persons were successfully abandoned on the evening of August 7, and MSU Valdez has requested a trajectory for a possible release. The vessel's proximity to the San Juan fish hatchery is of paramount concern to the Coast Guard. Current efforts are being focused on litering both the fuel and the fish to lighten the vessel as well as to partially deploy the pre-staged boom around the hatchery. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP as it would affect any trajectory implications. _______________________________________________________ 1) Weather Forecast Calm winds becoming variable at less than 10 knots with seas less than 2 feet today through Sunday. Sunday night into Monday: Winds picking up to be from the north or northeast at 15 to 20 knots. 2) Trajectory Analysis Summary: The most probable scenario should a spill occur is for the oil to enter Prince of Wales Passage and impact shoreline along the Passage. However if most of the 25,000 gallons of diesel were to spill on a flood tide under calm wind conditions, a sheen could move to the SE along Knight Island Passage and potentially enter Latouche Passage during an ebb tide or NE wind conditions. Under this scenario a persistent sheen could impact Sawmill Bay. Discussion: Tide currents. Knight Island Passage: Weak and variable tide currents. We expect a net current from the NW to the SE in Knight Island Passage due to runoff into Prince William Sound, this time of the year. Latouche Passage: Tide predictions indicate an average net tidal excursion of about 2 - 3 miles with the flood to the NE and the ebb to the SW. We expect a net flow to the SW. Prince of Wales Passage: Tide predictions indicate an average net tidal excursion of about 3 - 4 miles with the flood direction to the NE and the ebb direction to the SW. We expect a net flow to the SW. For oil to impact Sawmill Bay would require oil to move down Knight Island Passage on an ebb, and enter Latouche Passage. From there it would take a full ebb cycle or persistent NE winds to get to Sawmill Bay. Overall travel time of the oil from the grounded vessel would be 12 hours or more depending upon the release scenario and winds. The most likely scenario would be to have oil enter Prince of Wales Passage and impact shoreline along Prince of Wales Passage, Flemming I, and the north side of Evans Island. 3) Oil Fate estimates from ADIOS II model for a 25,000 gallon diesel spill: Under 15 knots winds a visible sheen would persist for about 15 - 20 hours Under 10 knot winds a visible sheen would persist for 20 - 24 hours Under 5 knot winds a visible sheen would persist for 36 - 48 hours [SEP] Friday, Aug. 15, morning weather forecast-PWS & Resurrection Bay, Seward PKZ121-160200- RESURRECTION BAY 400 AM AKDT FRI AUG 15 2008 .TODAY...VARIABLE WIND 10 KT. The Crowley Barge 180-1 is grounded on a beach near the Togiak Fisheries Inc. Cannery in Togiak, Alaska.  According to loading reports the barge has approximately 175,000 gallons of diesel, 24,000 gallons of gasoline, and 23,000 gallons of jet A fuel onboard.  The double-hulled barge was intentionally grounded (on a soft, sandy bottom) for the delivery of the fuel; however, it grounded too high on the beach to re-float.  There has been no spillage of any product and the likelihood of a release is considered small, but a hotline has been opened as a precaution. The owner is preparing a "salvage" plan, which will likely include off-loading a portion of the fuel onto another barge on Saturday.  The USCG has requested information on potential resources at risk in the event that there is spillage of all or part of the fuel.  The incident location is 59 degrees, 3 minutes north latitude and 160 degrees 20 minutes west longitude. [SEP] As compiled by the Regional Environmental Officer - Alaska U.S. Department of the Interior As requested, here is preliminary information regarding potential resources at risk for the grounding of Barge 180-1 near the Village of Togiak based on contacts made with representatives of the following State and Federal natural resource trustee agencies: DOI-Fish and Wildlife Service: The Togiak National Wildlife Refuge Manager has been notified. Based on the location information provided to date, the incident is outside of the Togiak NWR boundaries; however, a significant release could affect refuge lands. Primary concern: Red Salmon fishery which is winding down and the Coho fishery that will be gearing up soon. Until you get out towards the cape there are only a few seabird colonies: Glaucous winged gulls, cormorants and pigeon guillemots. There is low potential for sea otters in the area. U.S. Department of the Interior - Bureau of Indian Affairs: There is one Native allotment located approximately 4 kilometers southwest of the Village of Togiak on the coast and a second Native allotment located approximately 3.5 kilometers southeast of the Village of Togiak on the coast. National Marine Fisheries Service: There are likely to be seals in the area and sea lions offshore and associated with salmon stream mouths. Next to the cannery there would be less concern. Alaska Department of Fish and Game: There are 4 anadromous fish streams near Togiak that support a variety of salmonid species: Kurtluk River (chum), an unnamed stream right near Togiak (king, sockeye), Togiak River (chum, coho, king, pink, sockeye, dolly varden and whitefish) and another unnamed stream across the bay from Togiak (chum, coho, king, pink, sockeye and arctic char). The Togiak River is currently open for commercial fishing, and will be closing on July 25. ESI maps indicate potential presence of harlequin ducks, black scoter, common eider, long-tailed duck, scaup and Steller???€?s eider. Bald eagle may also be present. The Togiak salmon fishery is at its peak this week with lots of effort and escapement. Subsistence fishing for salmon is likely to be occurring in the Togiak River with some effort on Togiak Bay area beaches especially near the communities of Togiak and Twin Hills at this time. There are significant sport fisheries occurring in the Togiak River (all the way down to it's outlet into Togiak Bay) for 5 species of Pacific salmon, Dolly Varden, rainbow trout, Arctic grayling, and other resident species from June through September. Alaska Office of History and Archaeology: There are a number of known village sites in the vicinity of Togiak and up the Togiak River. A significant release into the bay or river could potentially affect cultural sites. The following are some additional comments about the situation. WIND EFFECTS: ------------------------------- The winds at the time of a release would have two different effects in the oil. The winds will tend to move the oil, determining what shorelines are impacted. In addition, winds will greatly effect the evaporation of the an released oil. A low winds speed is indeed likely to be the worst case, as it will allow the oil to persist longer, as well as pushing the oil toward shore slowly, allowing it to move farther downstream with the currents. Based in historical data, we expect the winds to be greater than 10 knots about 10% of the time, and greater than 5 knots about 40% of the time. OIL FATE: ------------------------------- Diesel fuel tends to evaporate and disperse fairly quickly. moderate winds would length the persistence of a spill. NOAA's Adios model, run with the heaviest Diesel Fuel in its library, and using a wind speed of 5 knots, and a water temperature of 68F (the current temp at the Longview Weather Observation Station), indicates that a significant sheen could last for over 5 days. However, it is unlikely that the winds would remain that low for that long. With a 10 knot wind, it would persist for less that 3 days, and with a 15 knot wind, about a day. In addition, the sheen would likely be pushed ashore by the wind, so as not to travel more than a few miles downstream, depending on the direction and velocity of the wind. Lube oils will not evaporate, but they will disperse into the water column in high energy environment, and the quantities are likely to be much smaller. We don't expect them to be a long term or long range issue in this case. TRAJECTORY: ------------------------------- While the river is influenced by tides in the region, and will move faster and slower with the tides, the flow is continuously downstream. The estimate of about a knot average flow in the main channel is reasonable. The vessel is located in a slough off the main channel south of Lord Island. The flow in the slough will be substantially slower than the main channel, but will still be downstream. Any sheen that is moved down the slough will enter the main channel approximately four miles downstream. Depending on the wind speed and direction, much of the released oil is likely to have beached in the slough before entering the main channel, so the most likely effected area would be the slough southwest of Lord and Walker islands. GENERAL CONSIDERATIONS: ------------------------------- BEHAVIOR OF SPILLED DIESEL FUEL: Light refined products, such as diesel (or Fuel Oil No 2), typically have very high evaporation rates and do not tend to create persistent slicks. However, the terminology for refined products is not standardized, and, sometimes, heavier intermediate fuel oils are referred to as ???€?marine diesel???€?. These heavier products are much less volatile than normal Fuel Oil no 2 and can form a more persistent slick. When spilled, the diesel spreads quickly into thin films often forming patches of rainbow and silver sheens. If the sheens reach the shoreline in a few hours, a slight staining, or greasy film-like bathtub ring is common. These oils usually do not form a stable emulsion and, as a result, do not form a heavy or sticky residual to clean up. Note that lighter refined products do have a relatively high concentration of light aromatic compounds and tend to be more soluble and more toxic than heavier oils. These oils do not generally present an involved cleanup problem. However, they can result in an initial toxic shock to biota and can persist as a biological threat in low energy marine environments. BEHAVIOR OF LUBE OILS: Lubricating oils are ubiquitous. They are used in all types of engines operating on land, at sea, or in the air. All lubricating oils are composed mainly of high-boiling point (>400 ??C) hydrocarbons containing 25 to 40 carbon atoms per molecule. Compound classes that impart undesirable qualities to a lubricant (waxes, polar compounds, and others) are removed in the refining processes. To meet the requirements of many different engine types and operating conditions, a multitude of oil products have been developed. These can be divided into two groups: 1) oils used in continuous service, such as turbine oils and 2) oils used in intermittent service, such as motor oils. Oils used in continuous service operate at a fairly constant temperature for prolonged periods without frequent shutdown or renewal. Stability is of prime importance. Oils used in intermittent service must show little viscosity change with temperature (high viscosity indices). These oils must also be changed at frequent intervals to remove particulates collected during service. Stability of these oils is, therefore, a secondary consideration. Additives: Additives are used to improve or impart various properties to the highly refined lubricating base oil. Automotive engine oils can contain a wide variety of additives including metallic detergents or ashless dispersants for controlling deposits, oxidation inhibitors, corrosion inhibitors, anti-wear additives, low temperature flow improvers, viscosity and friction modifiers. Railway locomotive diesel engine oils and marine diesel engine oils typically contain ashless dispersants and metallic detergents. Zinc-free detergents and silver lubricity agents are used where silver bearings are present. Environmental Behavior: Lubricating oils, for all their differences in formulation, have many similarities. When spilled into a lake, river, or ocean they will spread rapidly to a thin slick. They will not evaporate, and they will disperse fairly readily in high energy conditions without the addition of chemical dispersants. In general, lubricating oils are of low to moderate aquatic toxicity. While the base oils used in the production of lubricating oils are generally of extremely low

[SEP] Resources at Risk Assessment The following represents an initial assessment of resources at risk for a potential release of Fuel Oil #6 in the Bolivar Roads area of Galveston Texas from the Barge GULFSTREAM. This area has a high concentration of natural resources that would be threaten by an oil spill including several species that are protected as federal and state threaten/endangered species. The east end of Galveston Island (the Big Reef Area), Bolivar Flats Shorebird Sanctuary, and Pelican Island are just examples of highly sensitive areas with a high density of birds at risk from a fuel oil spill. Please review the following information and contact the NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator if you have any questions. Emergency cellular contact number: (206) 849-9928. Note, this assessment was prepared during the emergency response and is intended only for response planning. It may be incomplete given the short time frame available for preparation, but it does provide adequate information for response planning. The report contains essentially the same information as that provided during the Barge Energy grounding in May 2008. Should there be an actual release, please contact the NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator immediately to refine the analysis based on actual spill information. Resources at Risk Assessment for Barge GULFSTREAM Grounding I. Spill Source Information The Barge reported aground at approximately 29?? 20.81N / 094?? 46.01W in the Bolivar Anchorage in Galveston, Texas. The estimated cargo onboard was reported as 63,100 bbls. II. Geographic Region Covered The area covered by this report includes the lower Houston Ship Channel and the west end of Bolivar Peninsula, Pelican Island, and eastern Galveston Island. This area does not necessarily correspond to actual or potential oil locations, and was prepared to provide an initial assessment of immediate Resources at Risk from a potential spill. III. Expected Behavior of the Spilled Material Heavy fuel oils have a relatively low water solubility and are highly persistant. Exposure to skin, mucous membranes, lungs, or the gastrointestinal tract may lead to toxic effects for birds, reptiles and marine mammals. IV. Shoreline Resources at Risk The following provides an assessment of shoreline types that may be impact from a fuel oil release: Bolivar Peninsula. Western tip of the Bolivar Peninsula shorelines are composed of coarse-grained sand beaches, fine-grained sand beaches, exposed man-mad structures, exposed riprap, and salt and brackish marshes. Shorelines along the northern and southern shores of the Bolivar Peninsula are primarily fine-grained sand beaches with portions of salt/brackish marshes. Bolivar Flats Shorebird Sanctuary is located just east of the ferry terminal and is a very special place with a high density of birds. Texas City Dike. The North and South Jetties and the Texas City Dike are composed of exposed riprap structures. Pelican Island. Northeastern Pelican Island is composed primarily of coarse-grained sand beaches. Southeastern Pelican Island is composed of coarse-grained and fine-grained sand beaches with some exposed riprap, exposed solid structures, and sheltered, solid man-made structures. The western shoreline of Pelican Island and the small spoil/marsh island to the west is primarily salt/brackish marsh and scarps/steep slopes in clay with some fine-grained sand beach. Galveston. The shoreline along Galveston Channel is primarily exposed, solid man-made structures with some exposed riprap and sheltered, solid, man-made structures. The Lagoon is a salt and brackish marsh. The shoreline adjacent to Bolivar Roads and the Gulf of Mexico on Galveston Island are primarily fine-grained sand beach. V. Biological Resources at Risk Threatened/Endangered Birds/Reptiles in Immediate Threat Area: Birds. Reddish egret (state threatened) may be present at the western edge of Bolivar Peninsula. Brown pelican (federally endangered) and white-faced ibis (state threatened) may also be present. Piping plover (state/federally threatened) may be present, but most would have migrated by this time of year to northern breeding areas. The peregrine falcon (federally endangered) should have also migrated from these region as well as the long-billed curlew (state species of special concern) and the Common loon (state species of special concern). Critical Habitat. Designated Critical Habitat for wintering piping plover occurs near Big Reef (Galveston Island) and Bolivar Flats (these areas are protected as habitat even without the species being present). Reptiles. Loggerhead (state endangered/federally threatened) and Kemp???€?s ridley (state/federally endangered) sea turtles may be present in low concentrations in Gulf waters. Other Biological Resources Present in Immediate Threat Area: Birds. Bird species potentially present on Bolivar Flats may include a high concentrations of shorebirds, wading birds, gulls, terns, diving birds (such as cormorant, American white pelican, black skimmer. Marsh birds (such as the clapper rail) would also be present. Birds present in Gulf waters include gulls, terns, and magnificent frigatebird. Fish and Invertebrates. Fish and invertebrates potentially present in the immediate shallow waters of Galveston Bay include: southern flounder, pinfish, striped mullet, red drum, bay anchovy, seatrout, Atlantic croaker (very high concentrations), crevalle jack, sand and seatrout, shrimp (white shrimp spawning), blue crab, and oysters. Other species present in the Gulf include gafftopsail catfish, pompano, sharks, menhaden, gray snapper, hardhead catfish, croaker, red drum, mullet, Spanish mackerel, southern kingfish, blue crab, brown shrimp, and white shrimp. Essential Fish Habitat . This area would be considered EFH for many marine/estuarine resources including brown shrimp, white shrimp, red drum, lane snapper, Spanish mackerel, cobia, dolphin, and bluefish. Reptiles. Diamondback terrapin may be present in Hanna Reef area and along western Bolivar Peninsula/Horseshoe Lake. Marine Mammals. Bottlenose dolphin may be present in Bay and Gulf waters. Marine mammals receive special protection under the Marine Mammal Protection Act. VI. Other Resources at Risk Human-Use Resources. Beach access points, boat ramps, heliports, and marinas are numerous in the area. Commercial ship traffic moves through Houston Ship Channel. [SEP] On the evening of 24 June 2008, the Regional NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator (SSC) was notified by Sector Mobile of two grounded barges carrying a combined total of 46,000 bbls of Vacuum Gas Oil near Dauphin Island. The M/V Mark L was piloting the two-barge tow and apparently just run outside of the channel. The barges are reported to be soft aground and no report of damage or release of product. A second tug is expected on-scene tonight to remove the vessels. High tide is predicted for 0900 hrs. The SSC will follow up with Sector Mobile in the morning. The potential risk of a failure and oil spill were report as low. [SEP] Vacuum Gas Oil, or VGO, is an intermediate petroleum process oil produced from a crude oil feedstock in a refinery vacuum distillation tower. Also known as cat feed, or catalytic cracker feedstock, VGO is further refined to make gasoline, No.2 oil, other products and byproducts. VGO is generally a waxy liquid, dark green to amber in color, with a boiling point range of between 315-560 ??C. VGO will float in fresh and saltwater (specific gravity generally near 0.90). [SEP] At 5:26 PM (local time) on 10 June 2008, the USCG notified the NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator (SSC) of a grounded sperm whale near Port Aransas, Texas. At that time, the whale was reported alive and the USCG was seeking guidance. The SSC contacted Jim Jeansonne, a member of the ERD SSC team, to coordinate the consultation with the Marine Mammal Stranding network and the USCG Sector Corpus Christi. Follow up communications with the USCG by the SSC confirmed that the NMFS was engaged. It was also reported that the whale, a 27-foot female, was euthanized, and a necropsy would be performed the following day. Unless the situation changes, this report will constitute the initial and final hotline entry. Additional Information About Sperm Whales Once quite common in the Gulf of Mexico, sperm whales are now only occasionally observed. They are listed as endangered species under ESA and protected under the Marine Mammal Protection Act. Sperm whales can swim down to depths greater than 3,000 meters; apparently, limited in depth only by the time it takes to swim down and back to the surface. They are the largest of all toothed whales, making them the Earth's largest living carnivore. Sperm whales feed mainly on squid (including colossal squid and the giant squid), octopus and deepwater fishes, but it also reported to feed on sharks and skates. The correct scientific name for the sperm whale is currently unclear or under debate. The species is generally known as Physeter catodon, but Physeter macrocephalus is the name most commonly listed by NOAA. A total of 17 sperm whale strandings were documented in the northern Gulf of Mexico between 1997 and 2002. The best estimate of the abundance of sperm whales in the northern Gulf of Mexico was approximately 1,300 whales in 2003 (NOAA report). Probably the most remembered sperm whale grounding was in 1970, when a dead, 45-foot whale of this species beached in Oregon. This was the whale that was filled with a half-ton of dynamite and exploded???€? you have probably seen the video. For more information on these unique marine animals, view the following web site: http://www.nmfs.noaa.gov/pr/species/mammals/cetaceans/spermwhale.htm

[SEP] Evening report, 14MAY2008: US Coast Guard's Sector San Francisco notified the NOAA SSC at 0140hrs on 14MAY2008 that the Tug Independence had allided with Tesoro's Avon Wharf in Martinez, CA and may have damaged three 6-8 inch pipelines containing gasoline and perhaps diesel fuel. Initial reports indicated an unknown quantity of gasoline had been released into the Carquinez Straits, though "major amounts" of product had been described in the water. A trajectory estimate was requested. The Avon Wharf is located east of the Benicia-Martinez Bridge on the south shoreline of the waterway. Information from the Incident Command Center indicated that the affected pipelines were static lines and that an estimated 1,500 gallons of gasoline were released. After daybreak, an overflight of the area revealed no discernable amounts of product on the water. Later on-scene information indicated that, though a 12-inch gas pipeline had been creased in the allision, only a small sampling line had actually been breached; releasing an estimated 5 gallons of gasoline. The USCG issued numerous press releases throughout the day and continues with the requisite accident investigation, though substantive pollution response efforts have concluded. Lee, Chronicle Staff Writer (05-14) 07:33 PDT MARTINEZ -- A tugboat struck and ruptured a pipeline near the Tesoro refinery in Martinez early today, spilling as much as 1,500 gallons of gasoline into the water, the Coast Guard said. The incident happened at 12:20 a.m. when the tugboat Independence struck three pipelines at the Avon wharf at Tesoro's Golden Eagle refinery on the southern shore of the Carquinez Strait, said Petty Officer Kevin Neff. One of the pipes, which is a foot in diameter, was damaged and began leaking fuel into the strait, which leads to San Francisco Bay. There were no vessels at the wharf and no activities there at the time of the collision, authorities said. No injuries have been reported. The pipe is considered a static line in that it was not actively transferring fuel at the time, Neff said. The fuel that spilled was any residual amount that was in the line, he said. The Avon wharf is used to load vessels for transport of motor fuels throughout the West Coast. The cause of the collision is under investigation. The four members of the crew on board the tugboat will be administered drug and alcohol tests as part of routine procedure, Neff said. Two Coast Guard boats from the Vallejo station responded to the scene, and a helicopter was sent to the area for a visual inspection. Coast Guard specialists in pollution response have also been dispatched from Novato. Vessel traffic in the area, about 1 1/2 miles east of the Benicia-Martinez Bridge, has been suspended temporarily until authorities determine the impact of the spill on the environment, authorities said. The spill is the latest release of pollutants into Bay Area waters. On May 5, about 3,300 gallons of toluene spilled from the Reaction Products plant in Richmond apparently killed between 200 and 300 fish in an irrigation canal leading to San Pablo Bay. Thieves had apparently climbed a chain link fence to get at the tanks and stole brass valve fittings, causing a leak. In November, the Cosco Busan container ship struck a tower of the Bay Bridge, spilling more than 50,000 gallons of fuel oil. In the past 16 years, bridges in the bay have been hit 50 times by ships. Eighteen of those were commercial vessels, according to the Coast Guard. On Jan. 10, a barge carrying 2 million gallons of oil crashed into the Richmond-San Rafael Bridge. No oil had spilled, but had that occurred, it would have dwarfed the Cosco Busan spill, authorities said. E-mail Henry K. Lee at hlee@sfchronicle.com. [SEP] Tide heights in Carquinez Straits

[SEP] More pic. and vessel specifications at http://www.boatnerd.com/pictures/fleet/dorothyann.htm [SEP] See http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azipod for more details and pictures For those non-mariners, an azipod is the registered brand name of the ABB Group for their azimuth thruster. These are marine propulsion units consisting of electrically driven propellers mounted on a steerable pod. The pod's propeller usually faces forward, as in this puller (or tractor) configuration, the propeller is more efficient. In addition, because it can rotate around its mount axis, the pod can apply its thrust force in any direction. Azimuth thrusters allow ships to be more maneuverable and enable them to travel backward nearly as easily as they can travel forward. Update provided by: MST1 Nathan Thompson, USCG Sector New Orleans, Incident Management Division [SEP] On Monday, 14 April 2008, the Regional NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator (SSC) was notified by USCG Sector New Orleans of a small spill near Bayou Couba in South Louisiana. The Louisiana Oil Spill Coordinator's office (LOSCO) also provided prompt notification and updates. At the time it was reported as a small spill, maybe 4 to 5 bbls, and contained. There were no issues identified that required direct NOAA support. Since then, there has been on-scene investigation by the USCG, and the USCG has asked for assistance relative to the response and cleanup. One concern identified was marsh and vegetation impacts during the cleanup (OSRO cut trees down/paths made in vegetation). USCG plans an overflight of the impacted area. The NOAA SSC will meet with the USCG in the morning. The location of the spill is within the Salvador State Wildlife Management Area. The following background Information was derived from a report provided by the USCG. On the evening of 13 April 2008, Sector New Orleans received a report of a 20 ft by 15 ft sheen on Bayou Couba in the Salvador State Wildlife Management Area. A USCG Pollution Investigation team was dispatched the next morning (Sunday, 13 April 2008). According to Dune Energy (the RP), the spill came from a dead 2 inch flow line from the North side of the Bayou Couba Facility. The facility noticed the spill because of dead hyacinth and vegetation in the area. Upon further investigation they noticed that the 2'' flow line was leaking. Dune Energy did not know how long the flow line had been leaking. Upon notice, the facility immediately shut in the North side of the facility and deployed 150 ft of hard boom in the affected area. The flow line was cut off and capped with a gauge to secure and determine if any pressure was still built up in the line. Dune Energy has accepted full responsibility for the spill and has hired an OSRO (E.S. & H) to clean up the spill. The OSRO arrived at approximately 0800 Sunday and deployed a drum skimmer to recover oil. Pads and absorbent boom was also deployed. The first reported amount of crude oil was 1 bbl, which was estimated in the dark. From further investigation by the USCG suggest that the spill is more likely 4-5 barrels. USCG Sector Tampa/St Petersburg notified the SSC that the tug Yankee with Barge DBL 151 grounded at 1700 EST today (2Apr08) south of marker 14 in Egmont Channel, just outside of Tampa Bay, FL at position 27-36.39 N: 082-48.92W. Vessel was successfully refloated after lightering a portion of the cargo without reported pollution before dark on Friday, April 4, 2008. [SEP] Resources at Risk for T/B DBL-151, Tampa Bay, FL I. Spill Source Information This report was prepared at 1200 on 3 April 2008 based on the grounding of the tug Yankee and the tank barge DBL-151 south of marker 14 in Egmont Channel, Tampa Bay, FL. The barge is fully loaded with 118,000 Bbls of #6 heavy fuel oil. Check ResponseLink for maps of the grounding site. II. Geographic Region Covered The area covered by this report extends from the entrance to Tampa Bay north to Indian Rocks Beach. Consult other ResponseLink reports for oil trajectory information. III. Expected Behavior of No. 6 Heavy Fuel Oils There can be large differences among heavy fuel oils in terms of how they are expected to behave when spilled in the environment. Depending on the density, they will float or not float; depending on the viscosity, pour point, and ambient temperatures, they will spread into slicks or congeal into tarballs and tarmats; depending on what they were blended with, they can change properties over time. A summary of their expected behavior when spilled on water is: - Floating heavy fuel oil will usually spread into thick slicks which can contain large amounts of oil. Oil recovery by skimmers and vacuum pumps can be very effective, particularly early in the spill. - Very little of these viscous oils is likely to mix into the water column. It can form thick streamers or, under strong wind conditions, break into patches and tarballs. - They will be very persistent oils and the spilled oil can be carried long distances by winds and currents. - The specific gravity of a particular No. 6 heavy fuel oil can vary widely, from 0.95 to greater than 1.03. - Floating oil could potentially sink once it strands on the shoreline, picks up sediment, and then is eroded by wave action. - Heavy fuel oil can be very viscous and sticky, meaning that stranded oil tends to remain on the surface rather than penetrate sediments. Light accumulations usually form a "bath-tub ring" at the high-water line; heavy accumulations can pool on the surface. - Shoreline cleanup can be very effective, particularly soon after the spill before the oil weathers, becoming stickier and even more viscous. Removal is needed because degradation rates for heavy oils are very slow, taking months to years. IV. Shoreline Resources at Risk The shoreline habitats along the outer shore are dominated by sand beaches. The tidal inlets are bordered by seawalls and riprap structures. Inside the bays, there are extensive seawalls in developed areas and mangroves along natural shorelines. Heavy fuel oils tend to heavily coat the intertidal zone, be it seawalls or mangrove prop roots. Tidal heights are increasing for the next few days, so spilled oil could contaminate increasingly larger areas. V. Biological Resources at Risk Birds This area has a rich avifauna. Listed species of particular concern include: Federally and State threatened piping plovers that occur on outer beaches and sand flats; State threatened snowy plovers nesting on the north tip of Mullet Key; State threatened least terns nesting on Egmont and Passage Key and other small keys north of Mullet Key; and Florida scrub jay nesting on Passage Key. There are many shore birds and wading birds in the area, many of which are nesting (e.g., black skimmers, oystercatcher, royal tern). Double-crested cormorants are very common. A spill of heavy fuel oil poses a significant risk to all the birds in the region. Many of these birds feed and rest on intertidal beaches and flats in large numbers. This oil can heavily coat the feathers, leading to death by hyperthermia and ingestion during attempts to preen. Oiled birds can contaminate eggs and chicks in the nest. Fish and Shellfish There are numerous species of fish throughout the bay and coastal waters. Key species include: snook (spawning), drum (spawning), crevelle jack (juveniles and adults), seatrout(spawning), spot and pompano (juveniles), pinfish (spawning), and Gulf flounder and Spanish mackerel (adults). Therefore, there will be juveniles of many important commercial and recreational species present. Heavy fuel oils do not tend to cause significant acute mortality, but the persistent oil can cause very significant sublethal and chronic effects. Shellfish are also abundant and include oysters, blue crabs, hard clams, spiny lobster, and pink shrimp. Shrimp are spawning at this time. Oysters in the intertidal zone may be heavily coated. If the oil accumulates on the seafloor, many of these shellfish species are at risk from fouling and long-term exposure. Sea Turtles Three species of sea turtles are nesting at this time: Loggerhead sea turtles on many of the outer beaches, Kemp's ridley sea turtle on Treasure Island north to Indian Rocks Beach, and green sea turtles on Mullet Key. Adults will be concentrating in nearshore waters. Nesting females may crawl across oiled beaches to reach nest sites. Adults and juveniles can mistake tarballs for food items, leading to fouling of mouth and flippers. Marine Mammals The West Indian manatee (Federal and State endangered) is common inside the bays. Heavy fuel oil could irritate eyes, nose, and mouth parts. VI. Human-Use Resources The entire area has heavy recreational and commercial use and value. Managed areas along the outer coast include Egmont Key and Passage Key National Wildlife Refuges, Egmont Key State Park, Fort Desoto State Park on Mullet Key, Pinellas County Aquatic Preserve which covers 30,000 acres of submerged lands from Mullet Key to the Anclote River. Analysis of Available Information During the time of the grounding, sometime before 1100 hrs today, the winds were SW and the coastal current was from the E. On 14 March, there were S winds so the movement and grounding would seem to fit the information provided. The bigger question is if it remains aground? The high tide at the Mermentau River inlet, which is to the W of the grounding location, was at 1253 hrs on 15 March. That was only a few hours after the vessel was observed onshore and the winds were expected to shift with a northerly, offshore, component at about the same time. There is a chance that vessel refloated and drifted offshore. If it didn't drift off in the early afternoon, it is expected to still be in roughly the same location on the morning of 16 March. The next high tide is expected around 1300 hrs on Sunday, 16 March. At that time, the winds are forecasted to be out of the E at 10 to 20 mph. It is possible that the vessel could refloat under such a scenario and drift to the west. One determining factor would be just how hard aground the vessel rests. If the vessel did drift off the beach during the last high tide (sometime after lunch on 15 March), it would have been blown offshore by an N wind. The coastal current is to the west, so the combined movement would be to the SW then more westerly as the winds continued to clock around. Given the uncertainties and a lack of any real time observations, attempting to generate an accurate trajectory for the vessel would be difficult. Had there been an observation of the vessel afloat (if it did refloat) with a time and location this evening, NOAA could have provided a more detailed analysis. The NOAA SSC discussed the above analysis with one of the NOAA Emergency Response Division oceanographers (and that was fortunate because the initial tide information that the SSC had viewed on-line was wrong). In short, we both agreed that given the uncertainty and lack of any real-time observations since the morning report, we could not provide a more detailed trajectory analysis (or one with a high degree of accuracy) if the vessel had refloated. Pollution Threat Diesel fuel is not generally considered a persistent oil. Any released diesel fuel would be expected to spread rapidly and dissipate due to evaporation and natural dispersion. The reported volume was 1000 gallons of diesel fuel and probably less than 100 gallons of lube oil. This would suggest that the threat is relatively low based on volume, but diesel fuel is toxic and the vessel is already in the nearshore environment. Any diesel fuel spilled at the grounding site would be expected to be from a fracture and leak over a period of hours. With the falling tide and N winds forecasted for yesterday afternoon and into the night, this would generally suggest an offshore transport and the diesel would dissipate as described above. Diesel sheen extending several miles would be possible and threaten birds that may be feeding in the area as well as nearshore aquatic marine life. As the winds shift to the E by morning, the threat would extend several miles down the coast to the W. The USCG is expected to conduct a morning overflight to assess the position of the vessel and any pollution release. The NOAA SSC requested to be notified if there was any observation of sheen or if the vessel had moved. If the vessel was adrift, the SSC requested to be provided the time and location of the observation to coordinate a better estimate as to where it might drift and the potential to reground. [SEP] On Sunday afternoon, 2 March 2008, the regional NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator (SSC) was notified by the Texas General Land Office (TGLO) of a grounded tanker near Corpus Christi, TX. There is no oil reported spilled, but the State of Texas SSC, Dr. Buzz Martin, did generate a potential threat analysis and trajectory should the situation change. The M/V EOS, a double hulled tanker carrying 300,000 metric tons of crude (non-specified, but probably Venezuelan), lost propulsion and ran aground on the edge of the Corpus Christi Ship Channel. The reported grounding was at 27?? 49' 48.18" N Lat., 097?? 08' 17.34" W Long. Based on Dr. Buzz Martin's analysis, the strength of the forecasted winds make the winds the primary driver for any spilled oil movement over the next several days. In the event of an oil release, SE winds would drive the oil towards the islands and seagrass beds of Redfish Bay in the vicinity of Dagger Island and Dagger Point. As the winds shifts to the SW (Tuesday morning) the threat would move easterly towards Ransom Point. As the winds continue changing in a clockwise manner to the NW (Monday evening), the threat migrates to resources south of the grounding site such as Mustang and Pelican Island. See attached trajectory for additional information. Again, this is only a notification at present. There has not been a report of any oil released, and the USCG has not requested any additional support from NOAA. The location of the grounding is mostly muddy substrate, which would reduce the risk of a release. The NOAA SSC will follow up with both the USCG and TGLO to up date this report. USCG Sector Honolulu called the NOAA SSC Saturday evening (23Feb08) at 1730 to report a mystery sheen off Barbers Point, Hawaii. Reports of oil odor had first been received at approximately 0130. A USCG overflight reported observing a sheen approximately 100 feet wide stretching from Barbers point to the Kahe Power Plant. USCG observers on-scene reported the oil appeared to be thick diesel.  NOAA trajectory support was requested. [SEP] Conclusion: Oil spilled in Barbers Point Harbor early Friday evening could have exited the harbor and spread into coastal waters causing a slick that was was 2 - 3 miles long and parallel to shore on Saturday. We would expect oil that exited the harbor on Friday night and early Saturday morning to remain within about 1 nm from shore and move primarily alongshore under light variable wind conditions. We cannot determine exactly when and where the oil was spilled within the harbor. The harbor is small, the variability in the wind direction was large and the gravity spread of any spilled oil is difficult to quantify. The flood tide between 2300 Friday and 0530 Saturday would also bring oil back into the harbor and mix whatever oil remained in the harbor. Predicted tide heights from entrance to Pearl Harbor: We expect these to be similar to what Barber's Point Harbor would experience in both timing and height. Friday 1740 high tide 1.3 feet Friday 2310 low tide 0.01 feet Saturday 0531 high tide 1.6 feet Saturday 1151 low tide -01. feet Winds: Winds recorded from Kalaeloa Airport (Barbers Point) indicate that winds were 3 mph or less between 1853 HST(Friday) and 0253 HST (Saturday). Under these type of conditions, wind direction becomes highly variable. Windage on floating oil under these conditions would be negligible. Between 0353 and 0453 winds were actually from the NE at 3 mph. Wind observations from Waianae Harbor were from the NE (080 to 040) from 2049 on Friday night to 0949 on Saturday morning. The winds were 5 knots or less for this period. Analysis: The ebb tide excursion out of the harbor for the Friday night ebb is estimated to be about 300 to 500 yards. This means that oil that was spilled in the harbor near the start of the ebb could have been carried by the ebb tide several hundred yards off shore by midnight. Once the oil gets outside of the immediate vicinity of the entrance, it would be subject to coastal currents which would move the oil alongshore. Tidal currents alone could move the oil about 2 miles in about 6 hours. Winds were light and variable. This means that the oil spilled in the harbor would cover a significant portion of the small harbor due to gravity spreading and the variable winds. By about 0530 Saturday, the subsequent flood tide would probably have brought some oil back into the harbor and also into Ko Olina marina. Note the winds obs at 0353 and 0453 Saturday morning were FROM the NE at 3 mph. This would help to keep some oil offshore and moving along the coast. We would expect more oil to exit the harbor on the ebb that occurred on Saturday morning between 0531 and 1151 with winds being variable in direction until about noon. ??? ??? [SEP] Selected portions of siituation updates provided by Scott Kathey (MBNMS) on 22FEB2008: The 38-ft S/V SADIE (CF8587KY) went adrift on February 21 after its sails were damaged in heavy weather and the engine malfunctioned. Coast Guard Sector San Francisco mounted a vigorous rescue response by air and sea units and lifted the two POB from the vessel, leaving the vessel adrift without a crew. A Coast Guard helicopter fixed the position of the vessel approximately 1/2 mile offshore of Grimes Point at first light on February 22, and Vessel Assist, a contract towing service, deployed to take the vessel in tow. The California Fish & Game P/B SWORDFISH arrived on scene and monitored the status of the SADIE, which was held in place by a parted anchor chain that had snagged on the seafloor. Before Vessel Assist could arrive, the sea forced the anchor chain loose, and the SADIE drifted into the shoreline, grounding upright, high on rocks, at the base of a steep 600-ft coastal bluff. The vessel went aground 1/3 mile south of Grimes Point on the Big Sur Coast (36deg 12.15'N, 121deg 43.83'W) at approximately 1130 hours (PST), Friday, February 22, 2008. Seas on scene were reported at 8 - 10 feet with overcast skies and intermittent rain squalls. A salvage technician swam ashore and inspected the vessel, reporting that the hull had sustained several punctures and was unfit for re- floating. Vessel Assist left the scene. The wreck site is accessible by foot, but not by vehicle. A strong storm front is expected to move through the area over the next 24 hours and will likely destroy the vessel, releasing the 20-30 gallons of diesel from the vessel's fuel tank. Coast Guard Sector San Francisco has been notified of the grounding and potential spill. Grounding reports have been filed with the NRC (863126 and 863015) and the California Office of Emergency Services Warning Center (report #08-1485). The vessel owner does not have insurance on the boat or available funds to remove the fuel or vessel from the wreck site. The Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary has queried the Coast Guard regarding possible action by the Federal On Scene Coordinator Representative to remove fuel from the vessel. At 1650 hours today (22FEB2008) that an Incident Management Team is deploying to Monterey this evening. They will meet up with the vessel owner tomorrow (Feb 23) and inspect the wreck site to determine if fuel can be removed from the SADIE in a safe manner. Weather conditions are expected to worsen tonight, and rains could make access down the foot trails of the steep 600-ft slope untenable. The FOSCR will determine next steps following a survey of the area. On Feb. 17, 2008, the F/Vl Westward, an 82 ft wooden hulled fish tender built in 1943, grounded in the vicinity of Point Ildefonso on the SW side of Prince of Wales Island, 7 miles west of Klawock and 10 miles NW of Craig, discharging an unknown amount of diesel. At 6:30 a.m. a containment boom was set around the vessel by the Craig Harbormaster response boat (Josie J) to mitigate further discharge of oil.  A CG  helo conducted an overflight of the stricken vessel at approximately 8:50 a.m.and reported a 2.5 nautical mile long sheen coming off the vessel.   The helo crew also reported the containment boom transported to the scene had been deployed.   Meanwhile, the CG contracted with SEAPRO for site assessment and the SEAPRO oil spill response vessel M/V Rudyard Bay departed Ketchikan at 7:30 a.m.  but did not arrive on-scene until night fall of that day.   By early afternoon on Feb. 17, the owner of the vessel reported all the vents on the vessel's oil tanks were successfully plugged during the afternoon low tide.  A second CG overflight conducted during the morning of Feb. 18 reported only sheen on the water.   Being a Sunday followed by a holiday, the CG was unable to roust any potential salvors and/or divers who could sound the fuel tanks, although the CG is currently working to develop salvage and lightering plans.   The capacity of the vessel is 4000 gallons of diesel in four tanks, 150 gallons of lube oil and 150 gallons of hydraulic oil; however, at this time the amount of fuel remaining in the tanks is unknown.    No sensitive resources were identified by the CG within 45 miles of the grounding site.  Salvor and marine surveyor finally hired to deal with the situation.   In the interim the M/V Rudyard Bay had pumped out over 4000 gals of diesel, and the marine surveyor reported no visible signs of oil in the engine room and some residual bilge slop oil in the forward compartment.   Attention is now directed at removing and disposing the 130 tons of bait herring that was on board the vessel. At 0730 hrs on 16 February 2008, the NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator (SSC) was notified by USCG Marine Safety Unit Galveston of an allision between a vessel and oil and gas production rig in the GOM near the Flower Garden Banks National Marine Sanctuary (FGBNMS).  The vessel, the GRADY FAGAN, was damaged.  A 2-inch gash was reported in the STDB day tank and there was loss of an unknown quantity of marine diesel fuel. [SEP] The Flower Garden Banks National Marine Sanctuary (FGBNMS) is one of 14 federally designated underwater areas protected by NOAA's National Marine Sanctuary Program. Located 70 to 115 miles off the coasts of Texas and Louisiana, these underwater communities rise from the depths of the Gulf of Mexico atop underwater mountains called salt domes. The sanctuary actually protects three separate areas: East Flower Garden Bank, West Flower Garden Bank and Stetson Bank. These banks are separated from each other by miles of open ocean. The FGBMNS encompasses a variety of habitat types, including the northernmost coral reefs in the continental United States. The marine community built around the FGBMNS is very rich with about 23 species of corals, over 250 reef invertebrate species, 175 plus fish species, and 80 plus species of marine algae. For additional information on the FGBNMS, please visit the following web site: http://flowergarden.noaa.gov/ [SEP] Photograph from a 2003 Dive on the Flower Garden Banks National Marine Sanctuary (photo credit, Sarah Bernhardt, NOAA National Marine Sanctuaries Program). These few photographs are provided to provide the viewer a sense of the beauty and species richness of the FGBMNS. [SEP] At 0730 hrs on 16 February 2008, the NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator (SSC) was notified by USCG Marine Safety Unit Galveston of an allision between a vessel and oil and gas production rig in the GOM near the Flower Garden Banks National Marine Sanctuary (FGBNMS). The vessel, the GRADY FAGAN, was damaged. A 2-inch gash was reported in the STDB day tank and there was loss of an unknown quantity of marine diesel fuel. The GRADY FAGAN is a 193-foot Offshore Supply Vessel (OSV) reported to be carrying 9000 gallons of diesel in the STBD tank. The rig was reported as the Ocean Star The SSC participated in a conference call with the USCG and the ship's master. NOAA was asked to provide a trajectory analysis (see previous hotline reports). The trajectory analysis suggests that the risk to the FGBNMS was low: even is a relatively large percentage of the diesel was lost, it would not persist given the current sea conditions. Dilution of any naturally dispersed oil was expected to be rapid. To the credit of the USCG, they were very aware of the sensitivity of the FGBNMS and wanted to insure that all precautions were taken. The MSRC Texas Responder was placed on standby and a USCG Falcon jet was launched to assess the situation. The SSC notified the NMS Office so that they were aware of the situation. A map was created to relate the approximate position of the allision and track of the GRADY FAGAN. The overflight the same morning reported that there was very little sheen, or to quote the report, "not much of anything" observed. There appears to be no risk to the FGBNMS. This entry will serve as the final report for any offshore issues related to the GRADY FAGAN. The USCG remains concerned as to the safety of the vessel and any additional pollution discharge as it head into port for inspection and repair. The crew had initiated transfer of the residual fuel in the damaged STBD tank to another tank on board to mitigate release. Should the situation change, additional updates will be provided. [SEP] To support these predictions, the NOAA ADIOS2 Oil Weather model was run at a wind speed less than observed and forecasted to be conservative. A relatively high rate of diesel release was also factored into the analysis (again, to be conservative, or on the safe side, with respect to risk). The results are provided on the next page. In reality, a higher percentage would probably be dispersed with higher wind speeds. This screen save of the oil budget is provided characterize the probable fate of the spilled diesel fuel. It is only a model prediction, not a true mass balance. The volume of diesel released remains unknown. [SEP] Trajectory Analysis: OSV GRADY FAGAN Incident Prepared by: Charlie Henry NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator Situation The Offshore Supply Vessel, or OSV, GRADY FAGAN collided with the Ocean Star Rig sometime after 0400 hrs on 16 Feb. 2008. The Rig has reported no damage. The GRADY FAGAN has reported a 2-inch gash in a day tank. An unknown volume of diesel fuel has been released. The crew has started to transfer fuel oil to another tank. The reported position of the initial incident was 27?? 18' 35.8" N Lat. 093?? 34' 08.7" W Long. This position placed the accident more than 20 miles SSE of the West Flower Garden Bank. The OSV moved to the NW, and at 0640 hrs was located at approximately 27?? 35' N Lat. 093?? 42' W. Long. This position is closer to the Flower Garden Banks. The OSV then proceeded to the W at a heading of 290 degrees and a speed of 5 kts. It is unknown how much diesel was lost and if the vessel is still leaking fuel oil. USCG MSU Galveston has requested a trajectory analysis based on what information is known. Trajectory and Diesel Fate Analysis Weather. The on-scene weather current information from TABS Buoy N last reported at 0130 hrs that the winds were 14 kts from the SSE. After 0130 hrs, there have been no updates. Adjacent to the Flower Gardens is a Met Station at the Mariner Energy Platform. This station has been reporting winds at 14 to 19 kts from the SE and SSE throughout the morning hours. The NOAA Marine Forecast suggests that winds as high as 20 to 25 kts are possible through the day and rough seas. Expected Trajectory. Any spilled diesel from the vessel would be carried in a northerly direction by relatively strong winds and a relatively weak ocean current. Given the observed and reported sea conditions, any spilled diesel fuel is not expected to persist as a surface slick for more than a few hours. Evaporation and natural dispersion would rapidly transport most of the spilled diesel into the air and into the water column. Dilution rates of the naturally dispersed diesel fuel are expected to be very high given the conditions on-scene. While the vessel positions place the diesel threat near the West and East Flower Garden Banks, is doubtful that the any cohesive sheen will make it to the banks themselves. If a large amount of diesel was lost, some sheen may cross into Flower Garden National Marine Sanctuary boundary, but would not persist.

[SEP] Georges Bank, east of Cape Cod, is an extensive bank with depths of less than 50 fathoms that extend over 150 miles northeastward from the offshore end of Nantucket Shoals. (117) In heavy weather the danger area is the oval-shaped top of the bank, which is about 80 miles long in a northeast-southwest direction and 50 miles in maximum width. The bottom in this area is extremely broken and irregular, with a great number of ridges and shoal spots having depths of less than 10 fathoms. Between these shoals are channels of varying widths in which depths of about 20 fathoms may be found. All of this area lies within the 30-fathom curve, and so much of it has depths of less than 20 fathoms that it may practically all be considered to lie within a generalized 20-fathom curve. (119) The bottom is mostly sand, sometimes with shell, and in places pebbles. Bottom samples obtained during surveys are described in a great many places on the charts. (120) The two principal dangers on Georges Bank are Georges Shoal and Cultivator Shoal, which are near the center of the danger area. Around these shoals the sea breaks in depths of 10 fathoms during heavy weather, and the locality should be avoided by deep-draft vessels. (123) Cultivator Shoal, near the western end of Georges Bank, is a ridge nearly 15 miles long, on which depths of 3 to 10 fathoms are found. The 3-fathom spot is near the north end of the shoal. In December 1980, a submerged obstruction was reported about 8.7 miles northwest of the 3-fathom spot in about 41??43'N., 68??23'W.; vessels engaged in bottom operations are advised to exercise caution in the area. (124) The entire area within the 20-fathom curve has an extremely broken bottom. There are numerous ridges and shoal spots on which depths dangerous to navigation, particularly in heavy weather, may be found. These shoal spots generally have steep sides, and soundings give very little or no indication of their existence. Tide rips and swirls, as well as overfalls, are common in the vicinity of these spots, but are not always visible. They show best with a smooth sea and with the current flowing in certain directions. [SEP] Coast Guard Repair And Recovery Operations Continue After Two Vessel Collision In Newark Bay, N.J. By newsdesk - Posted on January 29th, 2008 New York - A unified command with representatives from the Great Lakes Dredge and Dock LLC (the owner of the Dredge New York), Coast Guard Sector New York, New York Department of Environmental Conservation (NY DEC), New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJ DEP) and the vessel Orange Sun continue to monitor the repair and recovery of a damaged dredge vessel after a collision with a freight ship in Newark Bay Thursday. The Orange Sun, a 669-foot Liberian flagged vessel and the dredging vessel New York were involved in a collision resulting in the New York taking on water and leaking a small amount of hydraulic fluid. The Dredge New York was carrying approximately 3,000 gallons of hydraulic oil, 50,000 gallons of main diesel fuel and 1,000 gallons of lube oil at the time of the incident. Crews from the Great Lakes Dredge and Dock LLC deployed booming equipment around the vessel as a precaution immediately after the incident. As an additional precautionary measure, Great Lakes Dredge and Dock LLC contracted Ken's Marine to deploy boom around Shooter's Island, Newark Channel, the Elizabeth Channel and Singer Flat due to sensitive environments and wildlife in those areas. A Coast Guard Sector New York Shoreline Cleanup Assessment Team, (SCAT) conducted a survey in the vicinity of the Bayonne Bridge and Staten Island at 8 a.m. Friday and reported minimal sheen in the water. There have been no reports of impact to the waterfowl, fish or aquatic vegetation in the vicinity of the collision as a result of the incident. Coast Guard Air Station Cape Cod and Atlantic City helicopter crews conducted over flights of the collision site at 2:30 p.m. Thursday and at 10 a.m. Friday. Both over flights reported a light sheen coming from the barge as well as in the vicinity of Shooters Island, Port Newark and Port Elizabeth. A second layer of booming equipment was deployed by Kens Marine around the dredge vessel as a result of the over flights. The Randive Company, also contracted by the Great Lakes Dredge and Dock LLC, began a dive survey of the Dredge New York at 6:45 p.m. Thursday. The survey revealed four holes in the bow of the ship and a rupture in the hull that spans vertically from its keel to deck. The rupture is about 12-feet to 15-feet long and ranges from two to 12 inches in width on the port side of the ship. The dive survey also revealed that the two forward compartments, which hold the dredge vessel's spud controls, are flooded. Dive surveys will continue until the vessel has been determined safe to move. Two commercial scow barges initially helped to stabilize the vessel and keep it in place, and a heavy lift crane is now on scene to provide additional lifting support if needed. The Coast Guard Cutter Sturgeon Bay, a 140-foot vessel home ported in Bayonne, N.J., will remain in the vicinity of the damaged vessel to monitor the status of the repair and to enforce a no wake zone until the salvage operations are completed. Newark Bay was initially closed to vessel traffic but reopened Thursday at 7 p.m. "The quick initial response from all the agencies involved helped to mitigate what could have been a much more serious situation" said Lt. j.g. Kristin Conville, a Coast Guard Sector New York Incident Management Division officer. "The continued cooperation from all involved parties has allowed crews to stabilize the damaged dredge, prevent impact to the environment and move forward with recovery efforts." The Liberian flagged vessel Orange Sun, owned by Arctic Reefer Corporation in Monrovia, Liberia, and operated by Atlanship Switzerland, was outbound at the time of the incident. After the collision, the vessel was escorted to the Southern Bay Ridge Anchorage in New York Harbor. A Captain of the Port Order has been issued for the vessel requiring a specified classification society to verify that the vessel is fit for route and service as well as to provide a dive survey assessing any damage that might have been done to the vessel. "We will continue the repair efforts on a round the clock basis with our own personnel and with the help of salvage and diving contractors," said Chris Gunsten, a representative for the Great Lakes Dredge and Dock LLC. "The safety of the environment, our crews and the users of the waterway is of the utmost importance as we continue with this difficult task."
