[SEP] Accident Closes Major Shipping Channel for Hours By KEN BELSON Published: January 25, 2008 A 669-foot tank ship carrying orange juice collided with a smaller dredging ship in Newark Bay on Thursday, forcing the Coast Guard to close a waterway that leads to some of the largest shipping terminals on the East Coast for about five hours. No one was injured in the collision, but the smaller ship, the 117-foot Dredge New York, took on water and started to sink before it was stabilized. The Coast Guard found a sheen of light hydraulic fluid in the surrounding water, but investigators had not determined its source. Several Coast Guard helicopters and boats with investigators were at the site, according to Petty Officer Angelia Rorison, a spokeswoman for the Coast Guard in New York. She added that the hydraulic fluid spill did not appear serious and that no other major pollutants were found. The collision, Officer Rorison said, occurred about 1:50 p.m. near Port Newark, on the west side of a channel between Bayonne, N.J., and Newark. The freighter, Orange Sun, which was flying a Liberian flag, collided with the dredging vessel, and several hours later, the ship was escorted by tugboats to Berth 24 at Port Newark. The dredging vessel was linked to a barge and tugboat after water was removed from the ship. The dredging vessel was working on a $2.5 billion project to deepen New York Harbor and the surrounding channels to 50 feet, from 45 feet, to allow bigger container ships to dock in New York and New Jersey. [SEP] VESSEL FREED FROM BEACH AT COPALIS SEATTLE - A third day of salvage attempts proved fruitful late afternoon Saturday, when the Anna Marie was finally pulled free from the beach during high tide at Copalis. The boat ran aground on Wednesday morning, and previous attempts to get the vessel off the sand on Thursday and Friday were unsuccessful. It took at least two hours of pulling during high tide, but the Anna Marie is now safely offshore while the salvage crew readies the boat for a tow into port for repairs. Responders from the Washington Department of Ecology (Ecology) and Coast Guard have been on scene since Wednesday to coordinate and monitor attempts to get the vessel into deep water again. The boat had been in a precarious position, also putting at risk 1,000 gallons of diesel and another 200 gallons of other petroleum products. Ecology and Coast Guard had plans in place and equipment staged to remove fuel from the Anna Marie had today's salvage attempt not gone well. The vessels owners are now working on a tow plan, which details how and where the Anna Marie will be taken for repairs. The Coast Guard must first approve the tow plan. The salvage effort was conducted by Fred Devine Diving and Salvage. [SEP] USCG Sector Portland notified the SSC that the F/V Anna Marie is grounded on Copalis Beach, north of Ocean Shores, WA. Tens of thousands of wintering waterfowl take advantage of the rich food resources found in the delta, and large numbers of other bird species can be found on the refuge. Bird populations generally peak during the spring and fall migrations. Large numbers of wading birds nest on the refuge, and thousands of shorebirds can be found on tidal mudflats and deltaic splays. Numerous furbearers and game mammals are year-round residents, and the marshes and waterways provide year-round and seasonal habitat for a diversity of fish and shellfish species. Raptors are not uncommon on Delta NWR. Ospreys are common winter visitors to the refuge. The following threatened and endangered species may be present within the refuge: American alligator, brown pelican, Arctic peregrine falcon, piping plover. Given the heavy seas and high winds, it is thought that most of the birds species would have moved to the interior of the delta marshes rather than the coastal margins and nearshore coastal habitats. When the wind and sea state subsides, they will return to these areas. [SEP] These were produced on Saturday, Jan 19th with no info on oil type, or oil amount. Apparently, the well was hit by something and is releasing a water/gas/oily mixture. The USCG had released a broadcast for vessels to stay clear that morning. It was reported that the plume extended about 20-30 feet in the air, and the volume of oil released was unknown. A 5 bbl/day estimate of the flow rate was provided by the RP. At the time of the notification, the winds had shifted with the passing of a cold front pushing the residual oil offshore. The Louisiana Oil Spill Coordinator's Office provided additional incident and response information, and much of that information was used to generate this report. While awaiting the results of an overflight (and before the NOAA SSC could provide a full trajectory analysis), the well had been reported shut in and only sheen remained on the water surface. Other than a verbal trajectory, no additional support was provided by NOAA on this incident in part because the SSC was initially engaged in meetings with FEMA and the USCG related to Marine Debris and unavailable. Once the results of the overflight were known, the incident was essentially closed and no additional trajectory support was required. During the overflight, the OSRO observed a silver and rainbow sheen adjacent to the well but no recoverable oil. The estimate flow rates provided by the RP for normal well production were 510 bbls of produced water (formation water) and 5 bbls of crude oil per day. Impact to the shoreline at Grand Isle were unknown, but there was thought to be minor impact initially before the wind direction changed. No additional details are known.

[SEP] CG Investigates Mystery Oil Sheen U.S. Coast Guard | December 31, 2007 NEW YORK - The Coast Guard is investigating a mystery oil sheen in Newark Bay, N.J., that was discovered at 11 a.m. today. Coast Guard Sector New York was initially notified by a Sandy Hook pilot aboard the motor vessel HS Bizet. The master of the tug boat James Turecamo subsequently reported a dense sheen of unknown substance near Port Elizabeth and Port Newark at 12 p.m. Other vessel operators also reported sighting the sheen throughout the afternoon. A Coast Guard Auxiliary overflight confirmed a sheen in the Kill Van Kull extending through Newark Bay and into the Hackensack River. Coast Guard pollution investigators collected samples of a deisel-like product. Investigators also conducted a port sweep to visibly inspect all merchant vessels moored at Port Elizabeth and Port Newark, but were unable to determine a spill source. Reports indicate the sheen is dissipating. The Coast Guard is asking merchant vessels in the port area to voluntarily provide oil and bilge samples for comparison. "Coast Guard investigators will examine the samples taken from the site and compare them to samples taken from vessels in the surrounding area," said Lt. j.g. Elisabeth Murtha, a watch officer at Coast Guard Sector New York. "If we can find a correlation between the sample collected from the water and a sample provided by a merchant vessel, we may take further action." Coast Guard Sector New York employs a Vessel Traffic Service that tracks vessel movements similarly to an air traffic control system. Coordinating with the Vessel Traffic Service, pollution investigators will be able to learn which vessels were in the Newark Bay area during the time leading up to the initial sightings of the sheen. "It's never a good thing when oil makes its way into our waterways, but we're fortunate that this is a lighter sheen that dissipates rather quickly and causes minimal environment impact," said Murtha. http://www.military.com/features/0,15240,159173,00.html

PHONE (206) 526-4911. _______________________________________________________ Per your request, we have looked at the air hazard implications of the release from the Phoenix Well blowout, Belle Pass, Iberia Parish, LA. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP, as it would affect hazard implications. _______________________________________________________ 1) WEATHER: Today: SE winds at 10 knots. Slight chance of showers. Tonight: SE winds at 5 knots. Slight chance of showers. Wednesday: SE winds at 10 knots increasing to 15 knots. chance of showers and thunderstorms. 2) AIR HAZARD: Fire Hazard: Methane is the dominant gaseous component of natural gas, though some higher molecular weight hydrocarbons can also be present in significant amounts. Flash fire is the main hazard associated with natural gas releases. As the natural gas travels downwind from the release point it mixes with air and forms a cloud consisting of a fuel-air mixture which can ignite; historically, significant numbers fatalities have been associated with flash fires from accidental releases. Lightning from possible thunderstorms could provide an ignition source, but it is unlikely. Under the wind conditions anticipated through Wednesday, the hazard zone from the gas, as defined by the possible flammable cloud, will extend as far as 300 yards downwind, Rain and higher winds will diminish the threat zone somewhat. A small fraction of the higher molecular weight material can be carried downwind and deposited on the water. This material is also flammable and if the wind corrals this material into a pocket along the shore, it could also generate sufficient vapors to form a localized fire hazard, though this is an unlikely scenario. Inhalation hazard: The major chemical components associated with natural gas wells exhibit low acute toxicity to inhalation. If the concentration of natural gas is high enough, it may cause asphyxiation by displacing oxygen. The toxic inhalation threat zone is expected to be smaller than the flammable threat zone. Higher molecular weight compounds can travel downwind as an aerosol cloud and rain out. These particulates can be toxic by inhalation. We cannot model this but recommend that responders use visual cues to assess this hazard. Some less dominant components from a natural gas well can be very toxic. Sulfur compounds, like hydrogen sulfide, are highly toxic by inhalation and can be hard to detect. We do not have any information suggesting that there are significant sulfur compounds from this spill; however, we think it is important for the responders to be aware of this possibility. [SEP] Evening Report The Regional NOAA SSC arrived on-scene at the Houma Command Post at approximately 1600 hrs. The situation had not significantly changed from the earlier update. NOAA met with the USCG on-scene representative and the incident management team representing the RP. The primary objective was to insure the protection of the public and responders by keeping duck hunters and fishermen out of the area and conduct monitoring to insure safe responder activities. NOAA had provided an assessment of the plume threat from a Lower Explosive Limit (LEL) prospective using a 10% of the LEL for Methane and modeling the plume as a heavy gas to account in part for the affect of the condensate and water vapor. The general safety guidelines established by the response was a 1-mile exclusion zone: this value was greater than the modeling distance provided by NOAA for fire and explosion risk. The wild well team had conducted a preliminary assessment and was considering a tactic of engaging the blowout prevention manually (not sure how that will be done, but more information may be available at the morning planning meeting). The SSC connected the USCG with the NWS to provide a warning broadcast on the National Weather Service Broadcast similar to the notice broadcast to mariners. Some boom has been deployed, but the slick from the condensate that has rained out in Belle Lake was reported as light. There was consideration of the placement of sorbent boom materials in key location if it could be done safely. PHONE (206) 526 4911. _______________________________________________________ Per your request, we have looked at trajectory implications of a release of oil from the M/V Algo North. These notes are based on the following information: At 2100 EST approximately 2500 gal of Diesel Fuel, and 1/2 ton of Heavy Fuel oil was released from the M/V Algo North in the Maumee River, Toledo, OH. The location is: 24d41.49'N - 83d28.01'W. There is ice in the river of less than two inches. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP, as it would affect any trajectory implications. _______________________________________________________ 1) WEATHER: Winds: Tonight and tomorrow, East winds between 10-15 knots are expected, shifting to the North at 15-20 knots Sunday River Flow: The Maumee river is currently above flood stage about 30 miles upstream of Toledo. Flow levels are now dropping, expected to drop below flood levels by Sunday morning. Estimated flow rate at the peak was 14,700 cfs. ten miles upstream from the mouth of the river, and is currently dropping. Ice: Ice cover is reported to be less than two inches thick on the lake. In the river, ice cover is expected to be minimal, with perhaps some ice around the shoreline. 2) TRAJECTORY: The spill location is very near the mouth of the river. The oil will likely be moved into the lake by the river flow, then the movement will be dominated by the winds. The predicted East wind will tend to move any oil in the lake to the West, toward the shore. Areas of shoreline impact are likely to be Grassy Island, the shore to the West, and perhaps as far as North Cape. In addition, if the dredge spoils liking the channel are exposed, they may see some impacts as well. Shoreline impacts from the diesel would be a bathtub ring stain. It is unclear the exact ice coverage. If there is significant shore ice, the oil will hang up on the ice, rather than the impacting the shoreline directly. 3) OIL FATE: Light refined products, such as diesel (or Fuel Oil No 2), typically have very high evaporation rates and do not tend to create persistent slicks. However, the terminology for refined products is not standardized, and sometimes, heavier intermediate fuel oils are referred to as 'marine diesel'. These heavier products are much less volatile than normal Fuel Oil no 2 and can form a more persistent slick. When spilled, the diesel spreads quickly into thin films often forming patches of rainbow and silver sheens. Note that lighter refined products do have a relatively high concentration of light aromatic compounds and tend to be more soluble and more toxic than heavier oils. In this case, the low temperatures will slow the evaporation of the diesel, so it will persist longer than usual. Shoreline impacts from the diesel would be a bathtub ring stain. Heavy fuel oil has a much greater persistence. At the low temperatures, it may be near its pour point. It may be observed tomorrow as scattered tarballs, or, if cold enough, as waxy clumps. It's possible that the oil may stick to sediments, making it heavier. If floating low in the water, these clumps will travel farther into the lake than the diesel sheen. The reported quantity of Fuel Oil is only about 130 gallons, so there may not be any visible tomorrow unless it was beached soon after being released. There is a chance that the heavy oil could sink, especially if there is a high sediment load in the river, but if that's the case then it won't be observed. [SEP] On 11 December 2007, the NOAA Regional Scientific Support Coordinator (SSC) was notified of a marine casualty and active SAR case. There was no pollution reported, but there was a potential for a release due to the vessel fuel tanks. The SSC coordinated with the NOAA Emergency Response Division Home Team to provide a trajectory analysis for the USCG. Additional Background Information: A crew boat struck a small wellhead platform last night in Main Pass 44, Breton Sound, Louisiana. There was no pollution in the water, but NOAA was requested to provide a trajectory on the potential threats should there be a spill. The vessel was estimated to be carrying approximately 7,000 gallons of fuel onboard and another 100 gallons of lube oil at the time of the incident. The reported position was 29?? 39' 69" N Lat. 089?? 10' 71" W Long. This position places the vessel in Breton Sound and just over nine miles N of Breton Island. The vessel is thought to be securely attached to the platform. Also, the collision bulkhead appears to be completely intact, so the vessel is expected to float once detached from the platform. The vessel owner has a surveyor en route to develop a salvage plan. The Platform is Chevron's MP 44 KC, Lease OCS-G 03338 in Federal waters based on a Supreme Court Decree Line (circa 1975). Chevron has shut-in the platform. [SEP] Map [SEP] The vessel remains attached to the platform. There are four wellheads contained within the structure. In the update from the USCG, one of the lines was reported to be "bent" by the vessel, and the vessel may actually be resting on or directly against it. Because of the potential for a release to this pipeline as well as the diesel aboard the vessel, the USCG has requested an updated trajectory to include both potential threats. The production rate for the well in question was reported to be 160 bbls/day of a 53 API oil, but a realistic worse case discharge would probably be less given that the system is reported shut in.A salvage plan was received for review. Additional information about the incident: M/V Lady Marie was reported to be in route to the MP 73 field when it struck what was reported as a caisson at approximately 0500 hours. There were injuries, but the number and extent are not known at present. A crane barge owned by Samsung collided with the M/V HEBEI SPIRIT on December 8, 2007, 10 km (6.2 miles) off the coast of South Korea, west of Taean county.  The M/V HEBEI SPIRIT sustained 3 large punctures and subsequently released an estimated 2.8 million gallons of crude oil.  The vessel is currently anchored and has temporary patches on all of the punctures.  Over 160 km (100 miles) of coastline have been impacted, with the heaviest concentrations of oil being Teaen county and points 30 miles to the north.Reports from the joint USCG/NOAA team assisting the Korean Coast Guard. [SEP] Buried oil on Mallipo beach. Photo credit: NOAA [SEP] Evening Report 16 December 2007 Hebei Spirit Korea Sunday we went to KCGHQ and meet with their Research and Development Lab manager. We had a tour of their facility and discussed the results of testing on the spilled oil. It turns out there were different cargos in each of the three tanks that were holed. The general description of the oils was Light Arabian Crude. The R&D manager promised to get us the testing results translated into English. We are still awaiting that report. I did get photos of the chromatography graphs and asked our chemists to send me an interpretation. Still awaiting this also. After the lab we spent time in the KCG International Affairs Office beginning to draft our recommendations report. Following that we had a meeting with the Deputy Director and Assistant Director of the Korean Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries (MOMAF). They were interested in our recommendations also. They have requested a C-130 with ADDS pack from EARL to Korea on standby while the tanker is moved to a dock for repairs. It was explained to us that the KCG is in charge of the on-water response (up to the high tide line) and MOMAF is coordinating the other response activities and issues with regional and local authorities. MOMAF will be attending the Tuesday meeting. Monday we are scheduled to drive to Seoul to brief the US Embassy staff and Ambassador on our activities. Tuesday the KCG is coordinating a meeting with all the international advisors (UNDP, UNEP, Japan, EU, ITOPF, and the US Team) now in country. The current plan is to use our draft report as an outline for the agenda. The group would have discussions on the issues we observed and make one report with recommendation, rather than six reports. Hopefully we will be able to reach a consensus. I anticipate that the report with have a range of options for the KCG to draw from. [SEP] Photo taken one week after internet news photo. Besides the natural gas, there is also crude in the line as the company did pump crude into it after Hurricane Katrina. Chevron has established an Incident Command Post in New Orleans at their corporate office downtown. An Oil Spill Response Organization (OSRO) was responded with hard boom/sorbent boom, drum skimmers, vacuum truck, a marco skimmer, and the Fast Response Unit (FRU) GRAND BAY. Boom has been placed around the source and is being deployed along the shoreline. 3,000 feet of boom has been deployed at this time. Additionally, USCG personnel are on scene overseeing the operations and have been coordinating with LADEQ, LOSCO, LAWLF, and NOAA SSC representatives. There have been no reports of wildlife impact or press related interest at this time. The current strategy is secure the source and maintain containment to minimize the area impacted. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP as it would affect any trajectory implications. _______________________________________________________ 1) Weather Forecast Tonight winds are expected to be NW becoming N tomorrow at 5 - 10 knots. 2) Trajectory Analysis A large oil spill between 1500 and 1700 today will result in oil moving upriver with the tidal current as far as Port Wentworth and Argyle Island by slack before ebb at 2300 tonight. On the subsequent ebb, the bulk of the oil would return downstream and extend downriver to Long Island. Depending on how the vessel leaks the oil over time, some oil could exit out into Tybee Roads by 0630 Wednesday morning. With the winds from the NW to N expected tonight the shoreline impacts will be along the south shore of the Savannah River. On the flood tide, the North end of Elba Island and downtown Savannah would get the heaviest impacts. Expect some impacts on the north side of Hutchinson I. On the ebb tide oil will enter South Channel and impact the north side of McQueen Island. Expect impacts to the Wilmingotn River and St Augustine Creek, south of McQueen Island. 3) Oil Fate From ADIOS II model. Heavy refined products, such as Fuel Oil No. 6 and HFO, have been refined to remove the lighter components and as a result are somewhat pre-weathered. As a result they are usually persistent floating pollutant problems. These oils can occasionally form a mousse, but usually only slowly, and after a period of days. Fuel Oil No. 6 and HFO may not spread into thin films and but rather break up into smaller patches and then tarballs. The resulting scattered tarballs are very difficult to observe using visual, or remote sensing techniques. This combined with the persistence of the tarballs makes of spills quite likely to result in long range, and occasionally unexpected, beach impacts. Around 2030 on November 23, Sector Juneau reported that a 120 ft. houseboat, owned by Evergreen Timber was aground in Coon Cove in George Inlet.   The vessel was taking on water via a small hole in its hull.  6000 gallons of diesel were onboard but none had yet leaked into the environment.   Sector Juneau requested support from NOAA for a trajectory, weather and tidal information.  SPOT weather forecasts were provided by the Juneau NWS office, and NOAA Hazmat provided the remaining information.  The Coast Guard initially provided one dewatering pump and planned to provide additional pumps.   By the morning of November 24, five additional pumps had fully dewatered the vessel, causing it to float high enough to expose and patch the hole in the hull.  No fuel was released into the water and the Coast Guard declared the incident closed. [SEP] The Juneau weather service office report that the dominant winds in the area were southerly around 25 knots with gusts to 35 kts. This pattern would continue through Saturday with southerly winds becoming 10-20 knots. [SEP] After consultation with Glen Watabayashi at Seattle Hazmat, Sector Juneau was given the following trajectory for a possible leak of the diesel. If the leak was slow (most likely case) then the southerly winds would tend to pin the oil at the head of Coon Cove. Tidal currents are relatively weak (max of 1 knot) in the adjacent deep channel of George Inlet and would be even less in Coon Cove. An Ebb tide may move a very small portion of the diesel out into this deeper channel. Sector St Petersburg contacted the HDO to request plume modeling for an anhydrous ammonia release.  SSC contacted the command center to request location, release volume and time and on scene weather.  Location of leak was later determined to be on the south end of the US Hwy 301 bridge over the Alafia R., east side.  NOAA assisted USCG to assess the hazards.  A teanager had drilled a 1/4-3/8" hole in a 6" diameter liquid ammonia pipeline.  Local authorities evacuated public from 1/4-1/2 radius toward the westsouthwest for about 40 hours. [SEP] Photo of repaired NH3 pipe at south end of bridge on east side looking north across river. Pipe is approx. 6 inches in diameter. A hole 1/4-3/8" diameter was drilled into the side of the pipe about 2' above the ground. Photo 18Dec07 by Jim Jeansonne, NOAA Hazmat. [SEP] Photo of Hwy 301 bridge and sidewalk directly over the NH3 pipe. View from south end of bridge on east side looking north across river. Photo 18Dec07 by Jim Jeansonne, NOAA Hazmat. [SEP] Some post incident information obtained during a Tampa Bay Port Spill Committee Mtg. The teenager took 2 days to drill through the approximately 1/4" thick steel wall of the pipeline using a cordless drill. He had to re-charge the battery overnight. When he broke through the pipe wall, the escaping liquid ammonia, which immediately turned to a cryogenic vapor cloud, burned him from neck to groin. The youth fell or jumped into the river, thereby probably saving his life by flushing away the ammonia and rewarming his skin (the water was relatively warm). He survived the incident, but his eventual fate is not known at this time. When the youth let go of the drill, the drill bit broke off in the hole, thus partially plugging it. This restricted the size of the opening and retarded the release of ammonia. Responders decided to allow the ammonia to continue to bleed off, rather than risk worker injuries. Responders apparently did not have specially designed insulated Level A suits to deal with the extremely cold ammonia gas cloud. Regular suits would become too brittle, crack, and leak. The total volume released is not known at this time. At the time of the incident, the pipeline was under repair, so the pressure was much lower than normal, 180-200psi, rather than the typical 400+psi. [SEP] Google Earth image showing leak location at Hwy 301 bridge over the lower Alafia R. [SEP] USCG Sector St Petersburg reported that the leaking pipeline had been successfully patched and have concluded the response. County representatives will continue to assess impacts to soil and water. The ship is carrying 720 bbl diesel but there have been no breaches in tanks or hull.  However, a 1000' sheen is reported on the water.  Ship is taking on water.  The spill is suspected to have resulted from a hydraulic system casualty as the vessel lost steering and was intentionally grounded to prevent sinking. [SEP] During the morning hours of Saturday, November 10, after the USCG Sector Hampton Roads aproved of the vessel's salvage plan, the C/S Spirit of Nantucket was successfully refloated and towed to a local shipyard for repairs. It appears that the C/S Spirit of Nantucket while transitting the Inter Coastal Waterway (ICW) hit the remnants of a derelict submerged vessel which resulted in damage to the ruddder and the rupturing of the bilge tank which then allowed a mix of oily water to be discharged from the vessel and water to inundate the hull. Initially it was beleived that hydraulic fluid was spilled. USCG provided several pumps to remove water from the hull so that vessel could be refloated. DISCUSSION: -------------------------------- The conditions look good for the operation today, with moderate winds expected to be from the North, swinging around to the East in the afternoon. However, the winds are expected to shift to be from the Southeast Saturday, when it's most likely that a leakage may occur. The winds will still be moderate, but the Southeasterly direction will tend to move any released oil toward shore, where it may impact the shoreline before evaporating and dispersing. Long term outlook: The long term forecast indicates possible windows next week, with light Northerly winds forecast for Wednesday and Friday. Little shoreline contact is expected unless there is a stronger Easterly or Southerly component of the wind than expected. If there is a release on Sunday, the expected Easterly winds could push the oil more towards shore, perhaps resulting in some small impacts to the shoreline between the spill location and Galveston Bay entrance. 3) OIL FATE: The oil is a light condensate crude, API 55. Observations from the previous releases from this same pipeline indicate that it rapidly spreads out into a very thin film (light sheen) that is difficult to recover. Even if a large quantity is released (several 100 bbls), we expect that a surface slick would last less than 24 hours in the forecast conditions. Sheens may persist longer. [SEP] At 0130 hrs on 24 October 2007, the NOAA HAZMAT Duty Officer (HDO) on call relayed a request from USCG Port Arthur to provide trajectory support for an overflight to investigate a reported pipeline leak. The report included an estimate that maybe 100 bbls of oil was lost. The reported position placed the suspected source of the spill just off-shore the beach and east of Sabine Pass. The NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator (SSC) investigated the trajectory implications and provided the USCG a verbal assessment of the area that morning overflight should concentrate. At the time, the winds were blowing offshore from the NW. The overflight on 24 October showed a slick some 2 miles long originating from the reported source location. It was estimated that slick was approximately 300 gallons of sheen. NOAA provided a follow up trajectory analysis (see earlier reports). No overflight was available to follow the slick the following day, but it was expected to remain offshore and dissipate naturally. A USCG pollution response team conducted a follow up beach survey on 24 October and did identify some light shoreline oiling immediately near the source location. A pollution cleanup contractor had already isolated the leak source. On 25 October, the source was secured using a clamp. From a response prospective, this entry will constitute the ResponseLink Final Report. [SEP] A photograph from a series of photographs taken by the USCG Pollution Investigation Team on 24 Oct. 2007. On the morning of October 5 Tank Barge OB6, operated by Delta Western, grounded in the lower Ugashik River three miles southeast from Smokey Pt. OB6 currently has 5,868 gallons of unleaded gasoline and 5,882 gallons of #2 diesel in its tanks. Attempts to refloat will commence on next high tide. If successful, OB6 intends to anchor in Ugashik River. Current wx conditions: West winds 35kts, overcast, 10kt vis. [SEP] The grounded barge OB6 was successfully refloated during last night's high tide. No pollution occurred and no holes in the barge were detected. Barge is securely anchored now in Ugashik Bay waiting for a better towing line and better weather to procede on its mission of delivering fuel to more villages in SW Alaska. Case Closed. [SEP] Sector Anchorage Command Center reported that the barge refloating effort late last night (Oct. 5) was unsuccessful. Apparently the seas were too choppy to be able to successfully conduct the operation. It was noted, however, that there seemed to be adequate water at high tide, and another effort will be made on the higher high tide late this evening to refloat the barge. The barge is steel construction and no reports of any petroleum leakage have occurred. [SEP] Today at 0600 the barge OB6, operated by Delta Western, broke free from its tow and grounded on a sandy/muddy beach near Pilot Point in Ugashik Bay. The barge is port side to the beach with 5,868 gallons of unleaded and 5,882 gallons of diesel #2 in the starboard tanks. All other tanks are empty. The tug Noatak and crew are safe and anchored about 1 mile from the barge in Dago Creek. There has been no report of a discharge as of now. Further details on the integrity of the hull will be reported after a visual inspection is conducted later today. Current weather is high winds 40 - 50 knots expected to diminish throughout the day. Periodic weather updates will be communicated to us throughout the day. The plan is to retrieve the barge from the beach between 2000 and 2100, weather permitting. The Delta Western VP of operations for Western Alaska has informed me that he will be making an NRC report for a potential discharge, which is justified since the barge now sits in a State critical habitat area. Our reports indicate that high tide could be between 2100 and 2234, and between 13.1 and 19.5 ft. At the time of the grounding the tides were between 8 and 10 ft. All this will be communicated to the on-scene incident commander. [SEP] SHIO was run and provided to the Coast Guard. It showed that the next high tide would be at 2000 on Oct. 5. The sailboat, Sweet Dreams, ran aground in Masonboro Inlet, adjacent to Wrightsville Beach, NC at approximately 2300 hours on 9/3/07.  USCG Wilmington, NC notified NOAA SSC at approximately 0930 hours on 9/4/07. It was reported to the SSC that the vessel sank and broke apart.  Approximately 375 gallons of #2 fuel oil was on board the vessel when she ran aground. Due to warm ocean temperatures in the mid-80's F. and warm air temps in the 90's F, most if not 100% of the fuel oil would be expected to evaporate and dissipate within 24 hours or less from the time of the incident.  Vessel owner hired salvage company to inspect vessel. Salvagers confirmed that fuel tank breached and empty. No reports of product observed in water or on shoreline. Surfwashing on Majagua Beach was started to remove buried oil. This operation was effective and the sorbent booms did a good job recovering the released oil. To the east along Pta Verraca workers continued to remove oiled wrack from the fringing mangroves. The majority of this will be completed tomorrow with only small rocky pockets along the northern end of Pta Verraca to be addressed the following day. USCG found heavily oiled mangroves in La Pargara today. The oil was extremely viscous and was estimated to be 1 to 3 inches thick in and area of about 100 sq yards. Tomorrow a team consisting of NOAA, USFWS, EQB and contractors will revisit this area by boat to more fully assess the impact and assess possible cleanup methodologies. Two other teams led by USCG will survey shoreline to the east and west to see if other areas of oiled mangroves exist. These areas were not visible from overflights due to the heavy foliage associated with the mangroves. USCG plans to move the command post to La Pargara tomorrow. [SEP] LT Ku, To follow-up on our telephone conversation earlier this evening, I provide the following answers to several questions that I posed to one of my oceanographers. If any of the initial sheen information is incorrect, please let me know ASAP as it would affect any trajectory implications. The two sheens in question: August 20 at 1400 PDT, 3nm x 3 nm, center at 32 deg 37' 18"N, 118 deg 38' 48" W. August 21 at 1400 PDT, 2nm x 6.6 nm, center at 32 deg 46'N, 117 deg 49' W. Both sheens are quite far offshore. Q1. Might these sheens be related? A1. There is a possibility that these sheens are related, but proving so would be difficult. We do not expect these to be the same sheen visualized twice. With wind conditions showing winds greater than 10 knots sheens on the water are unlikely to stay together for very long. Q2. What is the potential for shoreline impacts? A2. From such a long distance offshore, we would not expect these sheens to remain coherent long enough to reach the shoreline. Q3. How much are these sheens a threat to Mexican Waters. A3. With winds from the WNW-W, and the summer currents to the south, there is a very small possibility these sheens could reach Mexican territorial waters. We do not expect these sheens to contact any shorelines. Despite the small possiblity of reaching Mexican waters, we will attempt to provide you with an estimate tomorrow of how long it might take for oil to transit that distance given the conditions on-scene. (Official Coast Guard photo) ATLANTIC CITY -- The Coast Guard, along with state and local agencies, continue to respond Aug. 2 to a fishing boat, which ran aground Tuesday in Little Egg Inlet. The Rough Seas, a 59-foot fishing boat, ran aground with one person aboard at about 3:45 p.m. July 31. New Jersey State Police transferred the operator of the boat to awaiting EMTs on shore. A boatcrew from Coast Guard Station Barnegat Light, secured the fishing boat and deployed a boom around it and in the entrance to the inlet in an attempt to contain any pollution that may leak out. The Coast Guard has established a field command post at the Jacques Cousteau National Estuarine Research Reserve and is working closely with the New Jersey State Police, New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection and Sea Tow International on cleanup operations. A salvage plan has been approved by the Coast Guard, and salvage crews are staging equipment and personnel to begin salvage and cleanup operations. No sheen was visible today during a helicopter overflight assessment of the boat and shoreline. The Coast Guard is transmitting a broadcast notice to mariners alerting them of the situation. On Sunday morning, the NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator was notified by USCG Sector New Orleans of an oil spill in the GOM. At approximately 0200 hrs that same morning, an unidentified vessel was reported to have struck a wellhead platform in Breton Sound resulting in an oil spill. The reported position of the well and leak was 29° 33' 51" N Lat. 089° 20' 09" W Long. The well was secured at 1240 hrs the same day. The amount of oil released was reported as 80 bbls. [SEP] The following information was reported in a FWS website, http://www.fws.gov/breton/. The information is provided as part of an initial Resources at Risk (RAR) assessment only. Please see the website for complete details of the site. GENERAL INFORMATION: Breton National Wildlife Refuge is the second oldest refuge in the country and was 100 years old on October 4th, 2004. President Theodore Roosevelt heard about the destruction of birds and their eggs on Chandeleur and Breton Islands in 1904 and soon afterward created Breton NWR. He visited the Island in June of 1915, this is the only refuge Roosevelt ever visited. The island had been the site of a Lighthouse Station (destroyed by Hurricane Katrina). ENDANGERED & THREATENED SPECIES ON THE REFUGE: Brown Pelican, Least Tern, and Piping Plover OTHER WILDLIFE SPECIES: Breton NWR provides habitat for colonies of nesting wading birds and seabirds, as well as wintering shorebirds and waterfowl. Twenty-three species of seabirds and shorebirds frequently use the refuge, and 13 species nest on the various islands. The most abundant nesters are brown pelicans, laughing gulls, and royal, Caspian, and sandwich terns. Waterfowl winter near the refuge islands and use the adjacent shallows, marshes, and sounds for feeding and for protection during inclement weather. Redheads and lesser scaup account for the majority of waterfowl use. Other wildlife species found on the refuge include nutria, rabbits, raccoons, and loggerhead sea turtles. HABITAT DESCRIPTION: The dominant vegetation on Breton NWR are black mangrove, groundsel bush, and wax myrtle. Shallow bay waters around the islands support beds of manatee grass, shoal grass, turtle grass, and widgeon grass. [SEP] Photograph of oil spill source. The 127 foot F/V Nordic Viking ran around in eastern PWS at 10:35 pm on July 21, 2007, 55 miles SE of Valdez.  One tank containing 3500 gallons of diesel was breached and release into the water.  11,500 gallons remained in eight other tanks which were not damaged.  The PRP hired Hudson Marine as the IMT and Alaska CHADUX to handle the response and the litering of the remaining fuel on board the vessel.   Weather was overcast with little to no wind and calm seas. [SEP] Saturday, July 28, 2007 - Nordic Viking Final Report Alaskan SSC arrived in Valdez on Thursday morning and immediately became engaged in the SCAT portion of the Nordic Viking response. The weather on-scene continued to be very calm conditions. A SCAT team, comprised of Coast Guard, state, RP and land owner representatives had already been formed and was busy in the field assessing shoreline accumulations and impacts of the diesel. The SSC joined the team as an advisor. One major area of activity was concentrated in and around Hells Hole, a sensitive, sheltered lagoon-like area on the north side of Port Gravina, roughly 6-7 nautical miles west of the spill site at the mouth of Olsen Bay. The impacts were restricted to roghly a 300 meter section of the beach just inside the entrance to Hells Hole. This shoreline is a rather porous combination of sub-angular pebbles and cobbles with the most evident infauna being barnacles on the cobbles in the lower intertidal zone. The diesel formed a light "bath-tub ring" on this shoreline and only expressed itself on the water surface as an ephemeral silvery sheen when the shoreline sediments were disturbed (see photo). The state SCAT members were concerned that this sheen might have deleterious effects on birds; however, after consultation with Jacqui Michel, Gary Shigenaka, Alan Mearns and Heidi Stout (Tri-State Bird Rescue Center) those fears were allayed. As the diesel was decreasing daily, it was decided to just let Mother Nature take care of removing the minor amount of diesel in this short beach section. A second area, in and on both sides of a salmon stream, of slightly more contaminated beach gravel, was also closely examined and debated. However, it was decided that the net environmental benefit between an intrusive remediation technique and doing nothing weighed in favor of again letting Mother Nature take care of the situation with tidal pumping, wind and wave energy. This completed the SCAT assessment and the team was disbanded on Friday evening, July 27, 2007. Meanwhile the RP was preparing towing, decontamination, and waste disposal plans. Since the Nordic Viking had incurred engine damage during the grounding, a plan was developed to tow it to Seward, Alaska, to a dry dock facility for repairs (see photos). On the final evening of Friday, July 27, the NOAA SSC participated in a review and "hot wash" of the entire incident along with the Unified Command. The major points that resulted were: 1.) contingency plans by the Coast Guard and the State need to be developed to immediately utilize a portion of the vast response resources available at Alyeska/SERVS for non-TAPS spills in PWS; had these resources been brought into play very earlier in the scenario, it probably would have made a positive difference in the outcome and effects of the spill; 2.) more information needs to be developed regarding on-water and shoreline clean-up techniques for diesel spills since those are the most common in PWS and Alaska (much time was spent chasing after on-water oil in the rainbow to metallic thicknesses range) ; 3.) on a spill where there is no stipulation for a Qualified Individual (like for a fishing boat spill), the Coast Guard needs to be more proactive in expeditiously guiding the RP into the best and most appropriate response actions; and 4.) the Unified Command needs to develop and enforce unanimity of action instead of having one or more parties acting unilaterally. The Nordic Viking spill response was closed down late Friday night, July 27, and the NOAA SSC journeyed back to Anchorage on Saturday morning. It has remained that way through Wednesday, June 25. The NOAA SSC was contacted Sunday morning by the Valdez Coast Guard and was told that everything was under control and that there was no need for his presence in Valdez or on -scene. As a result, the Coast Guard was provided with an ADIOS diesel weathering output which showed that under these very calm conditions, roughly half the diesel would have evaporated in a day and one-half. The USCG, ADEC, and the RP established an Incident Management Team at the Marine Safety Unit in Valdez. Reportedly the mechanical skimming of this spilled diesel was not particularly effective. The commercial salmon fishery for Port Gravina remained closed. As of Tuesday night, July 24, all the diesel fuel was removed from the vessel and the Nordic Viking had been re- floated with response crews continuing to maintain containment boom around the vessel and are using sorbents to recover small amounts of oils that are being released from the vessel. Two additional ADEC responders are traveling to the spill area to begin the shoreline cleanup assessment. The PRP has contracted Polaris Applied Sciences, Inc to assist with this assessment. Oil released over the next 24 hours could reach as far up-river as the Newport News side of the James River Bridge, and as far downriver as Old Point Comfort. 3) Weathering and Fate Diesel Light refined products, such as diesel (or Fuel Oil No 2), typically have very high evaporation rates and do not tend to create persistent slicks. However, the terminology for refined products is not standardized, and, sometimes, heavier intermediate fuel oils are referred to as 'marine diesel'. These heavier products are much less volatile than normal Fuel Oil #2 and can form a more persistent slick. When spilled, the diesel spreads quickly into thin films, often forming patches of rainbow and silver sheens. If the sheens reach the shoreline in a few hours, a slight staining, or greasy film-like bathtub ring is common. These oils usually do not form a stable emulsion and, as a result, do not form a heavy or sticky residual to clean up. Note that lighter refined products do have a relatively high concentration of light aromatic compounds and tend to be more soluble and more toxic than heavier oils. These oils do not generally present an involved cleanup problem. However, they can result in an initial toxic shock to biota and can persist as a biological threat in low energy marine environments. [SEP] Tugboat spills fuel in river NEWPORT NEWS -- A tugboat ran aground Friday morning near the Newport News Small Boat Harbor, spilling an unknown amount of its diesel fuel. The Coast Guard was on the scene throughout the day, trying to contain and clean up the spill. The tug was carrying 34,000 gallons of marine diesel at the time of the accident, but it's unknown how much spilled, said Jerry Crooks, chief of investigations for the Coast Guard's Portsmouth station. The harbor is near the Monitor-Merrimac Memorial Bridge-Tunnel. A sheen - spotted by a Coast Guard plane near the north island of the bridge-tunnel - measured about a quarter-mile long by 200 yards wide, Crooks said. Crooks said small-craft boaters should stay away from the clean-up site, but the spill did not pose a great threat to human health. It's not clear why the Russell B. Murray, a 104-foot vessel owned by Express Marine Inc., ran aground, Crooks said. Right now the Coast Guard is focusing on responding to the accident, and will investigate later, he said. The grounding opened a 6-inch hole in the vessel, which took on water. The vessel also spilled some waste oil from its bilge pump, Crooks said. The Coast Guard and cleaning contractors responded by floating a containment boom around the ship and by applying what are called "hydrophobic" fabrics to the spill. The hydrophobics repel water but soak up contaminants. Of the fuel that escaped to create the visible sheen, Crooks said that in hot weather like we have now it evaporates faster than it can be contained and cleaned up. As of Friday afternoon, the plan was to drain the remaining fuel from the tug and apply a temporary patch to the opening in the hull. The ship would then be towed to a local shipyard and taken out of the water for investigation and repair, Crooks said. Once the remaining fuel is siphoned, officials can calculate the amount spilled, Crooks said. [SEP] Tidal Currents [SEP] After running aground, the tugboat was towed to Lyon's Shipyard for repairs. [SEP] On Saturday, 23 June 2007, the regional NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator was notified of a slick offshore Louisiana. The slick was reported to cover a 20 square mile area, and was composed of sporadic sheen and observed emulsified oil. The nearest point to land was 21 nautical miles E of the Mississippi Delta. NOAA was requested to provide a trajectory analysis. The initial reports of oil in this area were early last week. The USCG began working the issue at that time, but the scale of the problem was much smaller than that observed on Friday afternoon. The Scientific Support Coordinator was notified at that time by email, but that email was not viewed until a follow up phone call the next morning. At that time, no RP had been identified. The NOAA trajectory provided is attached as a separate ResponseLink entry. Most of the oil slick was expected to break and dissipate, but chunks of the emulsified oil as tarballs and pancakes might make shore in the SE portion of the Delta by mid-week. On Sunday, an RP was identified through requested pressure checks of all of the pipelines in the area. The source of the leak was determined to be a flowline at the MP228 facility. The USCG stated that the RP had stated that as much as 214 bbls of oil per day may have been lost when the line was active (I have not seen this statement in writing). At present, the facility has requested to pressure the line up with gas to determine the leak location. The USCG required that a response plan be established and that resources be positioned to respond to a subsequent leak. Additional information to follow. [SEP] Updated Information On 24 June 2007, the USCG was informed that the unknown sheen that had been observed for the past week in the area of Main Pass 288 area was indeed coming from Stone Energy's MP288A facility. On 25 June, the entire platform was shut in upon discovery of the leak at around 1900 the night before. The leak was discovered when they went to pressure test the line and saw it bubbling (observed gas escaping to the surface). The plans on the 25th focused on evacuating the line and using dye to identify the leak locations. The line that was identified as the source of the leak is a 4-inch departing line that goes from MP288A to MP289B and the capacity of the line is 238.9 bbls. On the 25th, the USCG observed no recoverable oil in the area, but very light sheen was observed during the flight. On 26 June, 4 holes were identified in the first 960 feet of the line beginning at the MP288A Facility. These were marked for repair. The USCG had required that a response vessel capable of skimming be either on-scene or positioned to response during all activities that could result in addition oil spillage. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP as it would affect any trajectory implications. ______________________________________________________ 1) 48-hour Wind Forecast Today through tomorrow night, winds from the East at 10-15 knots are forecast. 2) Trajectory Coastal HF Radar from the Skidaway Institute of Oceanography shows this area to be inshore of the Gulf Stream, with weaker currents less than knot in variable directions. If oil spills during this forecast period, the forecast winds from the East would move the oil inshore within four hours toward Jekyll Island, Georgia, with some potential contact with the southern portion of St Simons Island. If the oil reached the area of St Simons Sound during a flood tide, some oil could be advected into the estuary. 3) Weathering and Fate Heavy Fuel Oils Heavy refined products, such as Intermediate Fuel Oils (IFO), Fuel Oil No. 6 and Bunker C, are more persistent than lighter refined products. The refining process has removed the lighter components and left them somewhat pre-weathered. As a result they can present quite persistent floating pollutant problems. These oils do occasionally form an emulsion, but usually only slowly, and after a period of days. These oils do not spread into very thin films and often simply break up into smaller patches and then tarballs. It is also common for these oils to lose enough of their light ends so that they do not rapidly form sheens and the resulting scattered tarball fields are very difficult to observe using visual, or remote sensing techniques. This, combined with the persistence of the tarballs, makes these kinds of spills quite likely to result in long range, and occasionally unexpected, beach impacts. Fuel Oil No. 6 has a much lower vapor pressure than diesel and will thus be less volatile. The proportion lost to evaporation will be small as will the amount permanently dispersed into the water column. Fuel Oil No. 6 can emulsify with a typical water content of around 30% but usually does so slowly. Oil Name = FUEL OIL NO.6 API = 12.3 Pour Point = 59 deg F Wind Speed = constant at 10 knots Wave Height = computed from winds Water Temperature = 65 deg F Time of Initial Release = June 25, 1100 hours Total Amount of Oil Released = 704 metric tonnes ______________________________________________________________________ Hours Into Released Evaporated Dispersed Remaining Spill metric ton percent percent percent 1 704 - 0 - 0 - 100 2 704 1 0 99 4 704 - 1 - 0 - 99 8 704 3 0 97 12 704 - 4 - 1 - 95 16 704 5 1 94 20 704 - 5 - 2 - 93 24 704 6 2 92 30 704 - 6 - 3 - 91 36 704 6 4 90 42 704 - 7 - 4 - 89 48 704 7 5 89 54 704 - 7 - 5 - 88 60 704 7 6 87 66 704 - 7 - 6 - 87 72 704 7 7 86 78 704 - 7 - 7 - 85 84 704 8 7 85 90 704 - 8 - 8 - 84 96 704 8 8 84 102 704 - 8 - 9 - 83 108 704 8 9 83 114 704 - 8 - 9 - 83 120 704 8 10 82 Lubricating Oils Lubricating oils are ubiquitous. They are used in all types of engines operating on land, at sea, or in the air. All lubricating oils are composed mainly of high-boiling point (>400 ??C) hydrocarbons containing 25 to 40 carbon atoms per molecule. Compound classes that impart undesirable qualities to a lubricant (waxes, polar compounds, and others) are removed in the refining processes. To meet the requirements of many different engine types and operating conditions, a multitude of oil products have been developed. These can be divided into two groups: 1) oils used in continuous service, such as turbine oils and 2) oils used in intermittent service, such as motor oils. Oils used in continuous service operate at a fairly constant temperature for prolonged periods without frequent shutdown or renewal. Stability is of prime importance. Oils used in intermittent service must show little viscosity change with temperature (high viscosity indices). These oils must also be changed at frequent intervals to remove particulates collected during service. Stability of these oils is, therefore, a secondary consideration. At present, the well is still being worked to restore full control, but was deemed safe for the planned activities. The rig currently on-site will be demobilized and addition equipment brought in to complete the well control operation. From an environmental prospective, the two primary concerns are the mud deposited into the canal itself and the mud deposited on the spoil bank and adjacent wetland habitat. It was impossible to assess the canal given the current operations; therefore, this site visit focused only on the adjacent spoil bank and marsh. The drilling structure is located at the end of a man-made, dead-end canal and just north of Vermillion Bay. The well blowout resulted in a large amount of drilling fluid (mud) being deposited on the rig, in the adjacent canal, and on the eastern-side spoil bank. The drilling fluid was reported to be composed of 56.5 to 57 percent by volume diesel fuel as a lubricant, 4.5 to 5 percent water, and 38.5% by volume solids (primarily barite, a natural clay mineral). At the time of the incident, the log reported that 439 bbls of drilling mud was in the drill stream and that a total of 3,728 bbls composed the entire circulating volume. It is presently unknown how much of this material was lost to the environment. Much of it was sprayed onto the rig and barge itself. In some places, the thickness was reported as 6 feet at the base of the derrick. It is unknown to what extent production water and produced condensate (light petroleum distillant from the gas reservoir) impacted the adjacent area. During the event, mud spray impacted an area estimated as between 2 and 3 acres by coving the surface with a thick coating of diesel-based mud up to 10 to 12 cm in thickness. During the site visit, the deposition was roughly characterized as trace, light (only a few mm), and heavy. The RP's Environmental Representative will prepare a rough composite map of the area assessed. Adjacent vegetation was killed to include several hackberry and black locust trees and various scrub plant species and adjacent marsh plants. Given that most of the area was exposed spoil bank prior to the incident, the vegetative coverage of the impacted area was small. A composite sample of the surface mud contamination was collected for analysis by NOAA. In the impacted area, multiple attempts to recolonize the area by fiddler crabs was evidenced, but none of the crab burrows were completed and several dead fiddler crabs were observed. No live crabs were observed in the impacted area. Such observations would suggest that some mitigation would be required, and that was generally stated by the USCG representatives. Final discussion was postponed until the analytical results were available. To complicate the cleanup or mitigation process, the RP reported that they were considering a proposal to widen the work area by widening the canal. The state and federal representatives on the site visit requested that during any removal activity that the contaminated mud and sediments be segregated for assessment and proper disposal. At present, none of the regulatory agency had been presented an actual proposal. The plan was only being assessed by the RP at this time. Also note that the canal did have some form of flapper gated access on the south end probably for water management purposes. At present, this has been sealed with concrete. This report characterizes the general observations of the NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator on-scene, and has not been reviewed or edited by the other members of the site assessment team. It will be provided to them for review, and the report may be edited in the future.

Following Hurricane Katrina, oil pollution was observed in the area of Garden Island Bay (part of the Louisiana Mississippi River Delta).  The initial response was included as one of more than one hundred small pollution cases investigated during the post-hurricane response under ESF-10.  Subsequently, this site was been identified as a chronic source of oil pollution that may be derived from some historical, subsurface oil spill incident that wasn't observed until after the hurricane eroded much of the marsh in SE Louisiana.  A possible source is a submerged pipeline.  The USCG has requested renewed assistance from NOAA in this investigation. [SEP] During the Hurricane Katrina response, oil pollution was first observed at the Garden Island Bay site. This site was one of more than a hundred small releases investigated during the post-hurricane response. This response is being added as a separate ResponseLink entry to track the current site investigations and response activities. NOAA has been requested to provide detailed analytical chemistry support as part of the current investigation. During follow-up investigations, it was determined that the source of the pollution was probably from an old release that was disturbed by erosion and land loss created by the hurricane. Some reports estimate that more than 100 square miles of coastal marsh and lands were lost in SE Louisiana from the storm. Pollution from the site was observed on multiple overflights during the months following Hurricane Katrina, and oil pollution is still being observed at the site. The area has been boomed is cleanup routinely by an OSRO. The site is a chronic source of oil pollution. The latitude and longitude of the center area of the Garden Island Bay site was reported as 29 degrees, 04 minutes, 21 seconds N Latitude and 089 degrees, 10 minutes, 44 seconds W Longitude. Goldking, the current site operator, conducted an investigation in 2006. Multiple sediment core samples were taken at site. Some areas had over 300,000 ppm oil/grease content. More than one core sample indicated that there was a concentration of over 5,000 ppm at a depth of 17 ft. Based on this investigation and the identification of an adjacent, subsurface pipeline operated by Shell Pipeline, the initial RP (Goldking) stated that the pollution was not sourced from any of their activities, but rather from Shell's. The investigation continued at this point with no clear RP. In 2006, the USCG issued Notice of Federal Interests to the two possible RPs, naming both companies as potential sources of the spill. Next, Sector New Orleans then examined USCG historical spill data/records, spill sample analyses, and other agency data to rule out several other potential sources (pits, flow lines, pipelines, wells, etc.) in the immediate area of the spill site. After examining all data and available evidence, the Coast Guard determined a 10-inch pipeline (last operated by Shell Pipeline) as the most probable source of the persistent sheening at the Garden Island Bay site. As part of the follow up investigation by Shell, a series of sediment samples were taken at the site. The USCG has requested that NOAA assist in their investigation by analyzing a subsample of the samples collected by Shell. The samples should arrive at Louisiana State University (NOAA's Chemistry Support Laboratory) on 31 May 2007. Additional Background Information The Coast Guard investigation included the following site information: Garden Island Bay is located in Plaquemines Parish, LA in the Pass A Loutre State Waterfowl Management Area. There is a history of land loss in the area. The area was impacted by Hurricane Katrina and Hurricane Rita. 55% of area converted to open water. Area is actively sheening and was designated a Hurricane Katrina minor spill (originally under Enervest). Goldking is currently leasing the land from the State. The field was initially developed by Texaco, sold to Enervest in 2000, and then sold to Goldking on 31 October 2005. Goldking has been conducting clean-up operations since the hurricane (OSRO - OilMop). Samples of the oil were taken after the hurricane by Enervest and additional samples were recently collected by CG personnel. The samples indicate that oil is relatively old due to the lack of light ends. The samples that the CG took were not a match with the oil that is currently found at Goldking. Goldking contracted Quatenary Resource Investigation, LLC to conduct coring and sampling at the site. They provided a detailed report of the findings. As per the T. Baker Smith survey, there is a cluster of flowlines that lead directly into the "problem area" (buried, cannot be seen when you go to the site) and a flowline that leads to a platform within the boomed area that are technically Goldking's. The flowlines were ruled out as probable sources since no USCG spill history was found for those flowlines. Additionally, they were also ruled out as a probable source due to the fact that the heaviest concentrations of oil were found well below the substrate's surface, as these flowlines are above ground sources. LDNR SONRIS records reflect no production pit in the vicinity of this area. No evidence was found to indicate that this site was a pit, but the idea has not been officially ruled out due to the circular appearance of the area and its proximity to wells/facilities. Pit regulations were implemented in the mid 1980's. Pits which were previously abandoned, filled and/or sunk would not be included in the DNR database. No records have been found documenting the existence of a pit. Additionally, there is no other physical evidence that a pit existence at this location. T. Baker Smith Engineering was hired by Goldking and Shell to survey the location of the pipeline, as shown above. Shell owns the 10-inch pipeline that runs directly through the affected area, at a depth of about 6-8 ft beneath the surface of the substrate. On scene, it is clear that the Shell pipeline runs directly through the affected area. Goldking's Core Sampling report indicates a higher concentration level in the vicinity of the Shell Pipeline. Additional information will be provided. NOAA's response posture on this incident is to provide technical and scientific support to the USCG. NOAA has been an active participant in the investigation previously, but the change in level of interest and participation warranted inclusion as part of the ResponseLink spill documentation. Lead Scientific Support Coordinator, Charlie Henry.

On 14 May 2007, two humpback whales (Megaptera novaeangliae) were observed within the Sacramento River upstream of Rio Vista, CA. NOAA's National Marine Fisheries Services, The Marine Mammal Center, the U.S. Coast Guard, California Department of Fish and Game, and the Governor's Office of Emergency Services responded and coordinated rescue operations. By 27MAY2007, the whales had moved downstream of the Rio Vista Bridge, lingered near the Benicia Bridge on 28MAY and continued on to the Pacific on 29MAY. [SEP] The dorsal fin and right side of the female cow, showing the skin lesions, taken on May 28, 2007. This photo was 48 hours after administration of antibiotics and 24 hours after the whales' return to more saline water. Photo by: Bob Wilson, The Marine Mammal Center. [SEP] Photo of the cow with blowhole showing skin lesions similar to calf, and partial view of the wound. Photo by Sarah Wilkin, NOAA/NMFS [SEP] Sunday May 20, 7:30 p.m. At approximately 2:30 p.m. today, the two humpback whales that have been swimming in the West Sacramento turning basin started moving down the Sacramento Channel. The whales' action may have been in response to two tugs moving down the channel to assist a commercial vessel docking at the Agrium dock just south of the port. Officials are moving quickly to try and take advantage of this unexpected development by rushing to the whales boats that will be used to help keep the animals from entering the sloughs and tributaries beginning at the river's delta near Rio Vista. The animals are being followed by various vessels from the of Coast Guard, Fish and Game and Yolo and Sacramento county sheriffs departments. The whales were 14.5 miles south of the Port of Sacramento at 7:00 p.m. [SEP] Update on the whale rescue efforts from the Joint Information Center: ********************************************************* On Wednesday, May 23rd, the rescue team attempted multiple strategies to try and help coax the whales out of the River and towards the ocean: * In the morning, the team deployed several vessels on the water and the team exposed the whales to sounds by banging on pipes and having a tug boat maneuver in the area. The whales did not respond as hoped, and they remained in the general area of the Rio Vista Bridge. * In the afternoon, the team employed a new strategy by playing different sounds to the whales: (1) recordings of humpback whales feeding in Monterey Bay, (2) recordings of killer whales attacking a gray whale cow/calf pair off the coast of California, and (3) synthesized tonal sounds generated in a laboratory (similar to a car alarm). The whales did not respond to these playbacks either. As a result, the plan for Thursday, May 24th is to continue the visual health assessments and behavioral observations to monitor the whale's condition. No sounds will be used. The veterinarians and biologists on site believe that the whales need a day without excessive stimuli. [SEP] Hi All, I just talked with Frances (4:25 PM Sunday). The whales decided to move on their own. They are 5 miles down the channel right now and still going the right direction. Frances is with about 8 small boats following along. They picked up the pipes a little while ago but have not had to use them yet. My understanding is they never even brought the big ship up into the harbor. We're thinking we might just press the animals throughout the night, but we'll see what happens as it starts to get dark. Hopefully they will continue downriver and we'll just pick them up as we go along. Maybe they might even swim all the way out without our help. Wouldn't that be nice. You know you can make the best plan in the world, and have the training sessions all set up, and then the animals are just going to do what they're going to do. Fortunately they are doing exactly the right thing right now. Laurie J. Gage, D.V.M. [SEP] Following is the press release issued by the Joint Information Center on Wednesday, May 30, 2007: ***************************************************** After 3-week Inland Journey Wandering Whales Return to the Sea After almost three weeks meandering through the Sacramento River Delta, the wayward mother humpback whale and her calf that have been the subject of intense concern and a dedicated rescue effort, have apparently passed safely under the Golden Gate Bridge and back out to the Pacific Ocean. "A number of firsts were made during this operation," said Dr. Frances Gulland, Director of Veterinary Science at The Marine Mammal Center in Sausalito, who was the lead veterinarian for the rescue team. "This was the first time antibiotics have been administered to free swimming whales in the wild, and was made possible by generous donations from Pfizer, Bayer and Grandpa's Compounding Pharmacy, and the development of a new custom made remote delivery device by PAXARMS to successfully administer the medicine. The antibiotics will help the animals fight infections and enhance their recovery from the wounds they sustained from a vessel collision." The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's (NOAA) National Marine Fisheries Service, The Marine Mammal Center in Sausalito, the U.S. Coast Guard (USCG), California Department of Fish and Game (DFG), and the Governor's Office of Emergency Services (OES) established a unified command to monitor and assist the whales, coordinate rescue operations, and ensure their safety and of the public and rescue team members. "We are extremely grateful for the tremendous outpouring of support that we received from our partners and the local communities from San Francisco to Sacramento who helped these whales," said Dr. Teri Rowles, Director of NOAA's Marine Mammal Health and Stranding Response Program. "A number of veterinarians and marine mammal biologist were on scene to provide their expertise and assistance, and we consulted with numerous experts around the world on this case. The strong partnerships between the federal, state and local authorities and non-profit organizations allowed us to not only assist these whales, but to also collect scientific information that will help support the conservation and recovery of marine mammals in California and elsewhere." Rescue operations included utilizing DFG, Solano County Sheriff's Department, NOAA's Southwest Regional Office, and USCG boats to maintain a 500-yard perimeter around the whales to minimize disturbance of the whales and potential collisions with the whales. In addition, a 1,000-foot temporary flight restriction was established to further prevent disturbance of the whales. Ferry, tug, and other vessel operators were provided up-to-date information on the whales' position throughout this event so that operators could travel safely through areas. Timeline May 13 -- Whales were first observed near Benicia. May 14 - Whales were spotted further inland in the Sacramento River Delta near Rio Vista. May 15 -- 19 -- Whales made their way up the shipping channel to the Port of Sacramento turning basin and circled in the area for several days. Scientists made efforts to lure the whales out toward the Pacific Ocean using underwater broadcasts of humpback whale feeding and socialization sounds. May 20 - Starting at 2:30 p.m. and extending for more than 6 hours, the whales traveled approximately 25 miles down the Sacramento Channel to the Rio Vista area. The whales started their trek down the river after two tugs moved down the channel to assist a commercial vessel. May 21 - 26 - The whales remained north of the Rio Vista Bridge for 5 days. Efforts were made to herd the whales using pipe-banging (Oikami) and other sounds. Scientists took a skin sample of the female whale. Because the animals were in fresh water for a long time, biologists became increasingly concerned about the health of the whales especially after observing deterioration of their skin condition and wounds. For these reasons, on Saturday, May 26, the animal care team administered antibiotics to both the mother whale and her calf. This was the first time antibiotics were administered to free-swimming large whales in the wild. May 27 - One week after the initial movement south, the whales passed under the Rio Vista bridge around 1:30 pm and traveled approximately 25 miles toward the ocean,

Dead  Right Whale found off Cape Hatteras.Question is where could it have come from [SEP] For information purposes, I am including the following information to illustrate how ERD's involvement in this incident assists other NOAA line offices: On April 20, the Marine Mammal Health and Stranding Response Program of NMFS asked Emergency Response Division (ERD) staff to apply trajectory model to perform a hindcast for a dead right whale, an animal born this year. A hindcast is a trajectory analysis ran in reverse used to forecast the probable area of a previous location. In this case, fisheries scientists predicted the juvenile right whale died 3-4 days before April 20. Based on the hindcast, the right whale was predicted to have died south of Cape Hatteras.
