NOAA was notified on 11 March 2007 of a tug striking a wellhead platform resulting in a 15 to 20 foot spray of oil.  Fortunately, the incident only involved a connecting flow line that was cut by the tug's prop and not a wild well blowout.  An employee of the company that manages the well observed the incident and was able to access the platform and secure the line by shutting in an isolation valve.  As a result, what could have been a much larger problem was quickly minimized to a small spill.  NOAA has provided consultation to the USCG on the fate and transport of the spilled oil. [SEP] Slick shown moving away from facility and toward the west (photo credit, USCG). [SEP] Reported location of wellhead incident (map generated by NOAA). [SEP] Initial Report Shortly after noon on Sunday, 11 March 2007, the regional NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator was notified of an oil spill in Little Lake, Louisiana. Sometime between 1000 and 1100 hrs (local time), a tug struck a 4-inch flow line coming off of a wellhead operated by Hilcorp Inc. The vessel, BJ 103, is reported to have struck the flow line with the blade of the prop. The damage to the flow line resulted in a 15-20 foot high spray of oil. The wellhead and incident were reported at the following position: 29?? 32.84' N Lat., 090?? 09.78' W Long. in Little Lake. This position places the incident just S of the Bayou Perot incident. The line was shut in shortly after the incident, which significantly reduced the amount of oil lost to the environment. Hilcorp employees witnessed the incident along with other mariners in the area. A Hilcorp employee was able to quickly turn off the valve to the flow line and the duration of the discharge was estimated at only about 15 minutes. The flow line was then bled down and shut in such that there would be no further potential of discharge until repaired. The RP estimates that only 3 bbls of oil was discharged. When OSRO arrived on-scene, they were unable to locate any recoverable oil. A USCG helicopter was diverted to take aerial photographs. During the USCG overflight, the winds were out of the E at 7 knots. The oil slick was observed moving toward the western shore of Little Lake. When first notified, the initial reports were of an uncontrolled well blowout as the result of a barge and tug striking a wellhead platform. D??j?? vu all over again; this was what happened at the wellhead just N of this location in Bayou Perot on 21 Jan. 2007. As is often the case, the initial reports were inaccurate. Initial reports often underestimate the potential threat or release, but for this case... on-scene industry personnel were resolving the problem faster than the communications were reporting the problem to the regulatory and response community. As more information became available, the threat of a major spill dissipated. That said, an unknown amount of oil was released and an investigation is continuing. While the OSRO Team reported no recoverable oil and the overall volume of oil released thought to be relatively low, the USCG plans to follow-up with a second overflight and investigation team. The USCG overflight photographs from earlier the same day exhibited oiling that might persistent through the evening and cause some shoreline impact. The condensate crude oils in this area are often difficult to see atop the dark colored water. The Scientific Support Coordinator worked with the Sector New Orleans to develop assessment tactics and a rough threat area for the follow-up assessment. Fog is expected in the morning, and the winds are expected to make a slight shift to the SE. At present, NOAA is only providing support via telephone and telecommunications. No on-scene deployment is expected. [SEP] Different colors of oil exhibited by the slick, but relatively thick slick or sheen may not be easily visible due to the color of the oil and the dark background color of the water (photo credit, USCG). [SEP] Initial Resources at Risk for Upper Little Lake, Louisiana Fate and Behavior of Spill Oil: Expected Behavior of the Spilled Material Condensate crude oil is the oil that is co-produced from a gas well. It is generally a very light crude oil with only minor amounts of the heavier components. The oil may be an emulsion at release due to formation water, however, the emulsion is likely unstable and will break down over time. Emulsified oil will persist as thick slicks that could accumulate against a shoreline in pools or patches After the emulsion breaks, the oil is expected to spread into thin sheens that could penetrate deeply into sparse marsh vegetation patches. Shoreline Resources at Risk: Most of the shoreline of the bayous is characterized as intermediate to brackish salinity marshes. All marsh habitat is sensitive to both oil pollution and collateral physical damage cause by a poorly managed cleanup. Biological Resources at Risk: Fish - A wide range of fish are present. Juvenile fish are usually present all year. In general, juvenile and larval fish are more sensitive to spilled oil than adults. Fish in shallow water areas are more likely to be impacted, due to the potential for a higher concentration of oil in the water column.  Shellfish - Shellfish present in the area include bay squid, blue crab, brown shrimp, pink shrimp, white shrimp, and Gulf stone crab. Juvenile stages of all of these shellfish may also be present in the area. Shellfish in shallow water areas are more likely to be impacted, due to the potential for a higher concentration of oil in the water column. There are oyster leases in Lower Little Lake.  Birds - It is the end of the migratory/overwintering season for waterfowl, but there may still be numerous waterfowl in the marshes and the waters associated with them. Species that may be present include coot, wigeon, gadwall, and ring-necked duck. There are always egrets and herons at the water's edge. In the marshes, there are marsh birds such as clapper rail and marsh wren. Mammals - Raccoon, mink, muskrat, river otter, and nutria may be found throughout the wetlands and inland waters of this area. Oiling of these animals may reduce buoyancy, water repellency, and insulation provided by the fur, and may result in death by drowning or hypothermia. Grooming of oiled fur may also result in ingestion of oil causing irritation, sickness, or death. The light oil may also cause irritation to organs such as the eyes as well as the mucous membranes. Reptiles - American alligator (federally threatened) is found throughout intermediate to freshwater marshes. With the warm temperatures this winter, they may be active. Oil may cause irritation and inflammation of the mucus membranes, especially around the eyes and nostrils, in all of these reptiles. Human-Use Resources at Risk: Jean Lafitte National Heritage Park and Preserve is located along Lake Salvador (north and east of the spill site). [SEP] The USCG reported that no oil was observed on the western and northwestern portion of Little Lake from both an on-water and aerial survey of the area. There are no known additional NOAA trustee issues that require follow-up related to the Emergency Response Division's role associated with this incident. This record constitutes the final entry for the response. [SEP] Source of oil spill. Hilcorp platform and wellhead (photo credit, USCG). [SEP] Initial Report, 6 March 2007 On the morning of 6 March 2007, the NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator was notified of an oil spill in South Pass Block 11. At that time, the report was of a 5 gallon spill from an 8 inch pipeline. The report was of a cut in the pipeline while divers were conducting repairs at approximately 0200 hrs the same morning. Subsequent overflights reported a larger incident then that initially reported. The pipeline is operated by Energy Partners Inc. The source was reported located at 29?? 2.32' N Lat. 089?? 16.72' W Long. Boom was deployed at the source. First Overflight Report, 0900 hrs The RPs Spill Management Team conducted an overflight an estimate a total of 9 BBLS discharged. The observer reported that the sheen split into two leading edges (like a fork in the road). First leading edge was at 28?? 53.79' N Lat. 089?? 19.54' W Long. The second leading edge was located at 28?? 54.29' N Lat. 089?? 18.69' W Long. The trailing edge was located at 29?? 01.51' N Lat. 089?? 16.14' W Long. The observer stated the sheen has 80% coverage in the affected area (75% to 80% was silver sheen). Second Overflight Report, 1315 hrs The afternoon overflight reported the leading edge at 28?? 45.33' N Lat. 089?? 33.34' W. Long. The heaviest Slick was reported at 28?? 57.81' N Lat. 089?? 21.84' W Long. The USCG has requested a trajectory analysis and is planning a follow-up overflight in the morning. A USCG Pollution Investigation team will also be onsite in the morning. This is all of the information that is currently available at the time the report was generated. [SEP] On 6 March, the USCG conducted an overflight of the South Pass 11 incident. At the source (29?? 02.43'N, 089?? 16.82'W), the USCG observers reported a Jack-up barge and hard boom containing a small pocket of oil. This was the location where the divers had cut into an 8" pipeline containing oil. An unconfirmed reported stated that the divers may have cut into the wrong line since there were two lines in the same area. The well and pipelines were reported shut in and pipe was isolated with blocking valves. The leading edge of the sheen was reported as 28?? 45.33'N Lat. 089?? 30.34' W Long. At the time of the overflight, the sheen was an estimated 19 miles long and about 1/2 to 3/4 of a mile wide. The USCG observers estimated a 65%-70% coverage. Approximately 90% of the slick was light to silver sheen, and the remaining slick, approximately 10%, was emulsified oil. These estimates are consistent with after another overflight conducted by the RP. Most of the oil and the sheen dimensions seemed to be following along the convergence zone. The USCG investigated what was thought could be oil at or near the shoreline. The observers reported no oil impacting the shoreline, but did observe a few pockets of emulsified oil floating about 300' off shore and along the shoreline (this was latter determined to be organic detrital material and not oil). During the morning hours the winds are expected to increase to be from the East at 15 knots by late morning. An overnight release under light wind conditions would move primarily with the currents, as far as 2 nm per tide cycle either toward Baltimore (flood tide) or out toward the entrance (ebb tide scenario). As the winds increase from the E and then SE, the winds will begin to dominate the oil's movement within the bay, causing the oil to beach on the western shore. Any oil released in the next 24 hours would be expected to beach within 6 nm in either direction from the grounding site on the western shore of the bay. If a release occurs, please contact your SSC immediately for a more detailed trajectory forecast. [SEP] MARCH 5, 2007 OPERATIONS UNDERWAY TO RE-FLOAT MONTROSE BALTIMORE - Operations are underway in an effort to re-float the 712-foot Liberian flagged cargo ship Montrose currently aground in the Chesapeake Bay, west of the Choptank River. Crews under the direction of the Unified Command began the process known as "lightering" Sunday afternoon at approximately 3 p.m. Since then, approximately 4,800 tons of coal have been transferred from the ship to an attached barge. If weather permits, crews on-scene anticipate having the coal of the Montrose transferred to nearby barges by Tuesday around 6 a.m. When the coal transfer evolution is complete, a process known as de-ballasting will begin. De-ballasting is the removal of water that was used to keep the ship stable during the lightering process. Attempts to re-float the Montrose are scheduled to begin at approximately 4 p.m. Tuesday, weather permitting. Once afloat, the ship will be taken to a safe anchorage where it will undergo an underwater dive inspection. The Unified Command consists of the Coast Guard, ECM Maritime Services, Resolve Marine Group, Maryland Natural Resources Police, Maryland Department of Natural Resources, Maryland Department of the Environment, and Motia Navigation who is the operator of the Montrose.

[SEP] As part of the Post-Hurricane Katrina USCG Salvage and Debris project, the USCG responded under FEMA funding to this discovery. A HAZMAT contractor was secured and the drums were removed and segregated. It would appear that a total of 475 Paraquat labeled drums were being used as additional floatation in the barge. All of the drums were marked Poison and Do Not Reuse. Once removed, most of the drums were also identified by paint stenciling as having been rinsed in the 1980's. To insure public safety and proper disposal, the drums were segregated into damaged and intact. Most of the intact drums contained some liquid residue. Approximately 20 drums were sampled and analyzed. The preliminary results indicated that all of the drums contained some level of Paraquat contamination, but the concentrations were below 1 ppm (most of the drums were in the low ppb). Once the final chemistry report is provided to the USCG, the NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator will assist in reviewing the data and coordinating final disposal plans. The preliminary plan is that the residue will be collected for treatment, and the drums will be shredded and disposed of in a regulated landfill. Given that all indications are that there is no significant environmental or public health threat identified at present, this entry will constitute the Final Report. The NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator will continue to assist the USCG as part of on-going support to the USCG Salvage and Debris Team. [SEP] Initial Report During the USCG managed, FEMA directed mission to remove debris and hazards from selected Commercially Navigated Waterways impacted by Hurricane Katrina, a barge was discovered containing drums identified as Paraquat near Port Eads. Louisiana. Port Eads is just off South Pass in the Mississippi Delta and adjacent to Pass A Loutre Wildlife Management Area. It is not known if the drums contain any chemical or if they were simply reused for floatation in the barge. Given the potential hazard and clear stamping on the containers that state that the drums are not to be rinsed or reused, the barge is being treated as a suspected HAZMAT threat. It is thought that there may be 30 or more drums in the wreaked barge. The NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator is working with the USCG to develop an assessment and disposal plan.  Paraquat is highly toxic to humans and animals and has serious and irreversible delayed effects if absorbed. As little as one teaspoonful of the active ingredient is fatal. Death occurs up to 30 days after ingestion. Absorbed paraquat is distributed via the bloodstream to practically all areas of the body. The lungs selectively accumulate paraquat, and therefore contain higher concentrations than other tissues. When in the lungs, paraquat develops into pulmonary oedema and other lung damage leading to fibrosis. Liver damage occurs and renal failure may follow as the kidneys remove absorbed paraquat. During the late 1960s, a controversial program sponsored by the US government sprayed paraquat on marijuana fields in South America creating concerns that smoking cannabis that has been sprayed with paraquat may cause "serious, sometimes irreversible lung damage. Although no longer available in the United States as a pure product, paraquat carries the greatest morbidity and mortality among ingested herbicides. Paraquat is still a major cause of death and disability in some countries, such as Australia, and it was responsible for at least four deaths from acute poisoning in the United States in 1996. Because paraquat is highly poisonous, the form of it that was commonly marketed in the United States is reported to have a blue dye added to keep it from being confused with a beverage. Paraquat from outside the United States may not have such safeguards. [SEP] Photograph of one of the paraquat drums (photo credit, USCG). The gas leak has forced authorities to close a portion of U.S. 1, the major route between Columbia and the Richmond County/Fayetteville area. The gas leak was reported about 5:30 a.m. near U.S. 1, about 2 miles northeast of the town of Bethune. That is about 60 miles southeast of Charlotte and about 15 miles south of Pageland, S.C. Authorities are advising residents in and near Bethune, especially on the north side of town, to remain indoors until the leak is repaired. Residents are advised to close their doors and windows and turn off heating systems. The sheriff's office in Kershaw County said no evacuations have been ordered so far this morning. No injuries were reported. A break in the line about two miles northeast of here was reported shortly after 5 a.m., said Tess Catoe, a supervisor at the Kershaw County communications center. A spokeswoman for South Carolina Electric & Gas Co. was gathering information about the incident early Friday. Active cleanup and mainenance complete, and any residual oil trapped in the vegetation was left to natural recovery. The NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator didn't participate in the final signoff phase, but was briefed by both the state and USCG. The Scientific Support Coordinator was able to make a follow up visit to the site on 17 July 2007. The water level was higher than during the response phase. Most of the area looked good and no residual oiling was observed at the shoreline, but the high water could have biased such observations on that day. Some oil sheen was created by the airboat in shallow water where there was heavy oil contamination during the response phase. This observation was not surprising. Photographs of the wellhead post rebuilding and a section of the marsh on 17 July are provided. This entry serves as the final ResponseLink Report for the Bayou Perot Oil Spill Response. [SEP] Update, 7 March 2007 The NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator was requested on-scene to participate in an overflight and field cleanup assessment at the Bayou Perot spill site on 6 March. The Operations Section had reported that the cleanup was reaching diminished returns and wanted to discuss endpoints and future cleanup options. Yesterday marked Day 45 of the spill response and cleanup. The first impressions from the floatplane overflight were that very little oil remained (relative to several weeks ago) and that the cleanup had, for the most part, produced minimal collateral damage in the oil-impacted marshes. This statement must be balanced against the large quantity of oil that stranded in these sensitive areas in January. Small pockets of oil were still visible from the air and some collateral impact was observable, but the area essentially looked as if there had only been a small oil spill with sporadic oiling of the marsh and mud flats. The opposite was in fact true. While the previous characterizations are generalizations, they do characterize the overflight portion of the field trip. A large accumulation of stranded oil was being worked by three cleanup teams in Zone 3A (photos are provided in ResponseLink). Sporadic teams were padding up oil in all three remaining cleanup zones, 3A, 3B, and 4. Once on the water and visiting sites by airboat, it was evident that oil pollution was still widely scattered in the spill zone, but most of the remaining oil was patchy distributions of the waxy emulsified yellow oil that had adhered to flats, scarps, and fringing vegetation. On warm days, with available water, some of this oil will mobilize and reoil flats and fringing vegetation. Larger accumulations were recovered (and continue to be recovered) using the Vacuum Recovery Systems. These systems operated from airboats have been highly effective. Given that some of the residual oil doesn't readily migrate from oiled vegetative areas, some oil will be left in the environment for natural recovery. As a side observation, much of the adjacent marsh has recently been burned. The marsh was actually burned during the response activities by the local land manager as part of their marsh management practice. Burned marsh areas restrict the use of airboat activity to prevent collateral damage. All of the marsh operations are being conducted using airboats. The drivers have done an excellent job staying primarily on water and mud flats. This statement is amplified by the fact that the recover team has been operating an average of 30 airboats per day for more than a month and a half. At times, the airboats would cross marsh habitat or rest on marsh for cleanup and recovery. Foot traffic collateral damage has been minimal. If the workers were required to access the marsh, plywood was used to provide a walkway unless the site was highly compacted and stable marsh. There were observations where the fringe of marsh habitat was physically injured and small clumps of exposed vegetation in open areas had been damaged (it would have been impossible to avoid all collateral damage). One negative impact noted, that was again unavoidable, was the incorporation of oil into the sediments by the physical movement of the airboats over mud flats with free scattered oil. The latter observation, along with any physical collateral damage, factors into the point of diminished return on the cleanup operation. As fewer and less contaminated pockets of oil remain, the collateral damage of access must be weighed against benefit. At present, two Vacuum Recovery Systems are working the only remaining large accumulation of oil in Grid M10. The third Vacuum Recovery System was demobed at the end of operations on 6 March. The rest of the teams are conducting recovery of smaller accumulations of oil using sorbents or maintaining passive recover sorbent booms. The present strategy is to continue these operations for the remainder of the week. It is hopeful that the weather may provide another high water event to assess changes in residual oil migration and accumulations before active cleanup is terminated. Either way, the current plan is to shift to a passive recover mode by the middle of next week. The Unified Command is planning to have a SCAT sign-off team make a pass through the area to confirm the strategy and identify any areas where hot-shot teams will be directed to pad up oil that should be recovered prior to the shift to either natural recovery (Stage 3) or passive recovery (Stage 2). The original spill volume was estimated at between 5000 and 6000 bbls once the full damage to the well was known. That value has now been increased to 8,500 bbls only to account for the mass balance of fluids recovered, 8,270 bbls. Given that the release was an uncontrolled wild well release, we will never know the true volume of oil released. In addition, the released oil was already emulsified to between 60 and 70% formation water upon release into the environment. [SEP] Incident Update, 18 Jan. 2007 The USCG reports (based on information provided by the RP's Cleanup Contractor) that they have more than 5,000 feet of hard containment boom deployed. The responders have also deployed absorbent boom by airboats. Bird deterrent scare cannons should have also been deployed by the end of the workday yesterday. The current response plan is to allow the marsh to bleed out and then collect the product with drum skimmers (the words of the cleanup contractor, not the NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator). The product will be collected into 55 gallon drums and transported from the site by Jon boats. The cleanup contractor currently has 23 people on site. The source of the spill was reported to be a small leak that was discovered over the weekend. The source of the leak has been secured. The cleanup effort has begun, but weather has slowed progress. The following areas are reported oiled and are in the process of being cleaned: 1. Immediately east of the Harvest, Grand Bay Tank Battery #1 there was a 10' x 10' x 3.5' hole in a spoil bank that was filled by both marsh water and oil (Cleanup Zone 1). Oil was noted in the Roseau Cane on the southwest and north sides of the hole. It was later noted that the oil located on the southwest side of the hole traveled to the south side of the Tank Battery #1, and the oil located on the north side of the hole traveled into Roseau Cane further north and into the pond located immediately northeast of the hole. A very minimal amount of oil was located in the dead-end canal leading to the hole in the spoil bank. 2. The vegetation and spoil bank located on the south side of the pond were impacted by residual oil (Zone 2). In Zone 2, it was noted that there were three areas where a decent collection of crude oil had stranded on the spoil bank. 3. The cleanup contractor noted that there was spilled crude oil located on the west side of the pond (Zone 3) stemming from Tank Battery #2 to Zone 1; however; due the shallow water depth in the pond, the work boat utilized for the visual assessment was unable to travel in these waters to investigate. 4. A very minimal amount of oil had also impacted the east side of the pond (Zone 4). 5. Crude oil was located in the Roseau Cane on the east side of the Tank Battery #1 and the west/southwest side of Zone 1 (Zone 5). A portion of this oil was migrating southwest toward the oil field access canal bordering Tank Battery #1. The spill site is located NW of the Delta Wildlife Refuge. Based on observations from a USCG overflight on the afternoon of 17 Jan., its is doubtful that the oil will migrate out of the immediate area of the spill. Cleanup operations will continue. The NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator is not on-scene, but working with the USCG by phone and telecommunications.

[SEP] Grounded Fishing Vessel Clean Up Completed HONOLULU -- Coast Guard personnel along with experts from the Pacific Environmental Corporation (PENCO) Wednesday completed clean up of oil and hazardous material from the fishing vessel Wahine Kepaloa II, which ran aground Dec. 29 on Ni'ihau. The Coast Guard Pacific Strike Team supervised clean up of diesel water, propane, batteries, refrigerant and other hazardous materials from the 44-foot fishing vessel, which was hard aground near the southeast point of Ni'ihau. The Coast Guard had air lifted two uninjured crewmembers Dec. 29. PENCO used a helicopter with a sling to move nine batteries, two refrigerant cylinders, a propane cylinder and almost 1,000 gallons of watery fuel to an off-shore barge. On the barge, a Coast Guard site safety supervisor ensured proper storage of the hazardous materials. The barrels of waste were labeled and stowed safely in the barge's holding tanks and the barge is due to arrive in Honolulu this afternoon at 5:15 p.m. The Coast Guard worked closely with the State of Hawaii Department of Health and the Robinson family on the recovery operation. The cause of the grounding is still under investigation. [SEP] NOAA consulted with USCG Pacific Strike Team responders on-scene with regard to concerns about potential generation of marine debris from the grounded vessel. USCG responders are aware of the risks and concerns. No fishing gear is apparent on or near the vessel. USCG will continue to include marine debris concerns in the response strategy and will continue to consult with the NOAA SSC about marine debris and other natural resource issues. [SEP] According to the attached press release, the spill volume has been increased to 1000 barrels from the previous report of 500 barrels USCG Press Release Date: Dec. 26, 2006 Contact: Coast Guard Public Affairs (832) 250-6667 Pat Diamond, Plains Pipeline (337) 802-6971 UPDATE: RUPTURED PIPELINE LEAKS OIL INTO THE GULF OF MEXICO HOUSTON - The light crude oil pipeline that ruptured 30 miles south east of Galveston, Texas, Sunday has continued to leak oil into the Gulf of Mexico. An overflight sent out by Plains Pipeline today to view the spill site spotted a light sheen, which is approximately two miles long and 100 yards wide. The flight confirmed that the current and wind are pushing the oil away from shore, and it is not interrupting any ship traffic. The pipeline is leaking from the platform side of the rupture at approximately 500 gallons a day. As of 4 p.m., an estimate of 42,000 gallons of oil has been leaked. Plains Pipeline is bringing in a dive ship, the American Victory, which is scheduled to arrive Wednesday morning. Once on scene the divers will survey the damage and plug the pipeline. A Unified Command is overseeing the operation, and consists of the Plains Pipeline LP, the Coast Guard and Texas General Land Office. [SEP] From Charlie Henry: Initial Report, 24 Dec. 2006 Christmas Eve MSU Galveston notified the NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator (SSC) of a reported 500 bbl spill of a medium-heavy crude oil spill offshore of SE Texas. The location is roughly 20 miles offshore. The spill was the result of a pipeline failure discovered at 0640 hrs local time. The pipeline was immediately shut in. Bad weather hampered an overflight to assess the release. At 1145 hrs a 6 mile long slick was observed. The oil was reported as brownish, and the sea state as very rough: waves between 8 and 12 feet were being reported and winds in excess of 18 knots. The conditions were too rough for any offshore recovery operations. The location of the slick was reported as 28?? 49.9' N Lat. 094?? 34.2' W Long., but there was no additional information as to what part of the slick or even if that was the source of the leak. The USCG was attempting a second overflight from Airstation Corpus Christi. The TABS current meters and the NOAA Marine Weather forecast was investigated to formulate a very rough trajectory. At least until Tuesday, the currents are moving down coast and the winds are blowing with a northern component (offshore). These conditions should keep the oil spill offshore and moving toward the SW. Once better overflight information is available, NOAA will produce a better trajectory. In general, a 500 bbl spill exposed to the sea state conditions offshore, will soon breakup and weather such that only emulsified oil as tarballs and tar patties remain. These will be hard to see by air, and any sheens would be quickly lost in the breaking waves. Once there is a sustained period of onshore winds, the scattered tarballs and patties could wash ashore. The remnants of the spill may even make it all the way to the Matagorda or Padre Island, but that would take some time. The longer the remnants of the slick persist at sea, the more spread out and scatter the oil will become. When it does come ashore, it would probably be observed as sporadic oiling over a fairly wide area. Given that natural seep oil also comes ashore in these areas, it might be blended into the background levels of oil tar. With the limited information, it is too early to guess what might really happen. Strong winds and large waves have made working conditions unsafe, forcing the dive ship American Victory and the skimmer Ampol Recovery to stop operations. The skimmer Brutis is remaining on scene to monitor the oil sheen. The divers sealed the shore side end of the breach by inflating rubber buoys inside the pipe at 11:20 p.m. Wednesday. Divers were unable to locate the platform end of the breach due to zero visibility caused by heavy silt conditions and deteriorating weather conditions. According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the waves are currently five to six feet high, and are expected to reach eight feet by the end of the day. The winds are currently at 17 knots, with occasional gusts to 20, and are expected to pick up to 20 knots with gusts to 27 by tonight. The weather is expected to worsen over the next two days; with pipeline repair efforts expected to resume one Sunday. The ruptured pipeline has leaked an estimated 43,000 gallons of oil, and it continues to leak at approximately 500 gallons per day, or 21 gallons per hour. The cause of the rupture is still under investigation. A Unified Command, consisting of Plains Pipeline LP, Coast Guard and Texas General Land Office personnel, is overseeing the operation. USCG contacted ERD regarding a barge collision near Baton Rouge, LA.  The incident resulted in the release of raffinate, a gasoline type substance.  The USCG requested assistance in determinining an appropriate safety zone for response to the incident [SEP] Initial Report, 6 Dec. 2006 AM The NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator (SSC) was notified of a barge incident on the Mississippi River near the Port Allen Locks (the west side of the river near Baton Rouge, Louisiana) on the morning of 6 December 2006. Apparently a barge carrying raffinate was carried into a raft of other barges during a maneuver to enter the locks. Raffinate is a light petroleum distillate that is highly flammable and is sometimes labeled petroleum naptha. The tank barge was the MMI 612, a 297 foot barge with a max capacity reported at 31,825 barrels. The barge was damaged at the #3 Port Wing Tank and #2 Port Cargo Tank. The initial report stated that the MMI 612 hit the starboard bow corner wrapper on the rake of a barge in fleet at Cargo Carriers at mm 227.5. There was significant damage to the top of the #3 Port Wing tank as well as an estimated 2 1/2 foot inset into the #2 Port Cargo Tank. There are two cargo tank ruptures in the #2 Port Cargo Tank, both of which are above the deck and in way of the upset. The cargo tank extends an estimated 5' above the deck. The lower rupture is just above the deck and is a fractured weld. The cargo was offloaded to MMI 611 such that the remaining product was below the fractures and there is no additional leaking. The source was secured at approximately 0915 hrs local time. Both ruptures have been plugged using soap. The offloaded product was placed on the MMI 611. There was no water in any of the voids on the MMI 611, and the most significant damage to the wing tank is above the waterline. The barge that was struck was loaded with rock. The spilled product is petroleum naptha (Exxon product name is UDEX Raffinate). An estimated amount spilled is still unknown, but is probably significantly less than 100 barrels initially reported. Some suggest that the actual value may only be a barrel, or a few barrels. Given the small volume believed spilled, it would be difficult to make an accurate mass balance determination based on the volume of product remaining on the two barges. An OSRO responded on scene. The pollution team reported to the USCG that as soon as product hit the water it dissipated so there is likely little to anything to clean up. In truth, it didn't dissipate immediately. By the time OSRO arrived on scene, a small volume such as that reported spilled would have evaporated. A Safety Zone was established and is still in place. After we confirm that all clean up has been completed, and have a plan to move the damaged barge the Safety Zone will be cancelled. The proposed RP plan is to transit the barge to Pasenda, TX for offload. The USCG will not allow such a transit until a detailed damage survey of the cargo tank and integrity of the vessel is complete. At a minimum, the damaged cargo tank will be completed offloaded and a survey done of the remainder of the tanks to ensure there is no damage there for any transit. The NOAA SSC will follow-up with the USCG, but it would appear that there are few issues left to address. [SEP] Photograph of Barge MMI 612 (photograph provided by USCG). Ice Conditions on the Lake: This section of the lake is not expected to freeze over in the near future. Due to the predominant NW winds during the winter, the SE corner of Lake Superior has a lot of vertical mixing which would inhibit a layer of surface ice from forming. In a typical year, shore fast ice may form in late February or early March when the Lake temperature is much colder. An atypical cold period could result is ice formation earlier in the winter but at this time, this is not expected to happen. Given the maximum potential release of 2,000 gallons of diesel, there are no conditions predicted that would result in a sheen larger than 1 - 2 miles. Any shoreline impacts that do occur would be staining from the diesel similar to a "bathtub ring" effect. Long term persistant oil contamination to the shoreline is not predicted. These predictions are for contingency planning purposes, should operations begin that increase the likelyhood of an actual spill, or if an actual spill occurs, the NOAA SSC should be contacted to assess the situation in more detail using the actual on-scene conditions at the time. Trajectory Possibilities from Tug Seneca with no ice cover on the lake. For onshore winds  Wind speed of 20 - 30 knots Spotty shoreline staining within 1/2 mile of the vessel. Expect more impacts to the east of the vessel. Persistence of a visible sheen in the water, less than 6 hours  Wind speed of 10 - 20 knots Shoreline staining within 1- 1.5 miles of the vessel. Expect more impacts to the east of the vessel. Persistence of a visible sheen in the water, less than 24 hours For offshore winds ... no shoreline impacts expected  Wind speed of 20 - 30 knots A visible sheen extending for 1/4 - 1 mile persisting for less than 12 hours  Wind speed of 10 - 20 knots A visible sheen extending for 1 - 2 miles persisting for less than 24 hours What would happen if 2000 gallons of diesel spilled with significant ice cover? If the vessel was surrounded in ice and spilled 2000 gallons of diesel fuel, we would expect a noticeable staining on the ice with some oil being incorporated into the ice. We do not expect any oil on the ice or in the ice to move until the ice melted. Any oil spilled into the water under the ice, could move move with currents under the ice. However, there is no reason to expect strong currents under the ice in this nearshore environment. Therefore, we would not expect significant movement of the oil. A reasonable estimate of how far the oil could move would be 1 - 2 miles per day or less. If this should occur, we would expect the concentration of the oil to diminish over time as the oil spread under the ice. Note that this area of the Lake is not expected to freeze until late February if at all. ADIOS II Oil Fate estimates for Diesel Fuel Oil with no ice cover. Little information was initially known. An industry overflight conducted that afternoon reported a slick originating at 29?? 33.91' N Lat. 089?? 20.25' W Long. and extending more than two miles over open water. The winds were from the N at 10 to 20 mph and the slick was breaking up past that point. The USCG was initiating an investigation, but the weather was inhibiting an on-scene response. Breton Island, a Federal Wildlife Refuge, was located some 15 miles to the SE of this location. Because of the N wind and high sea state, the oil was moving S, not persisting, and not threatening the refuge. NOAA has been working with the USCG on this incident since the initial report, and the USFWS was notified. [SEP] The photograph shows the location where the oil pollution is surfacing. [SEP] Update, 21 Nov. 2006 AM An overfight was conducted at 0900 of the Boisd'Arc facility at Main Pass 21 on 20 November. Oil appeared to be leaking at about the same rate as previously reported (1 bbl, maybe more, per hour). At the time of the overflight, there was a strong N wind at 15 to 20 knots. The oil collecting in the boom in the boom was entraining and splashing over. The overflight tracked the sheen from the source, and estimated the size as about 100 yards wide and 2 miles long with ribbons of crude oil 5 to10 feet wide by a half a mile long coming off the boom. After that, the released oil was breaking up into sheen. The direction the sheen was moving was on a heading of 190 degrees, and the nearest land in that direction was about 9 miles to the south (29?? 23.40' N Lat., 089?? 22.56' W Long.). Suspected sources are still being investigated. Boisd'Arc stated they had a 3 inch sales line that ran into a 20 inch Chevron pipeline, and that this 3 inch line is under a sunken barge. Boisd'Arc stated that that line was capped and is 20 feet away from the barge. Boisd'Arc are not sure if the 3 inch line was shut in by chevron were it connects to the 20 inch pipe. There are also some old flow lines that the barge may be resting on, but they surveyed those lines about 6 months ago and they are not currently connected into anything. Boisd'Arc also stated that it is possible they might have missed some lines in the survey. Another possibility being investigated is a Harvest Oil 4 inch sales line coming out of Breton Sound 32 that is tied into Boisd'Arc's 3 inch line, which could be causing the leak (still under investigation). Harvest oil has been running that line for about two weeks and they have not noticed any pressure changes, and are unsure (they do not think) the Harvest Oil 4" inch line ties into the Boisd'Arc 3 inch line. Again, the source is still under investigation and will require a dive survey to confirm. The work barge and dive team was unable to make a survey on 20 November due to weather, but should be out today to attempt a survey. The Clean Gulf vessel Grand Bay is on stand by in Venice, and will be on scene when the weather starts to break. The Grand Bay is a 40 foot skimming vessel, and should be able to handle the amount of oil that is being released. [SEP] It was determined that the source of the oil spill was a three-inch connection line that was thought to have been isolated from the system. Once Harvest oil shut in a connecting flowline on 22 November, the discharged ceased. Bois d'Arc Resources has plugged the line and is in the process of removing it completely. No additional spill response support has been requested. In summary, the mystery slick was finally traced to a known source and secured. An unknown quantity of oil was released from a connection pipeline that has since been secured. Previous reports outline the observed sheens. During the duration of the event, strong winds contributed to a high rate of natural dispersion. No oil was reported to have been recovered due in part to heavy seas and sea-state that didn't allow for on-water recovery operations. [SEP] Final Report The last action that NOAA was asked to provide the USCG on this incident was a post-incident assessment of where the oil may have come from. The assessment is attached as a separate report. No other support has been request, but there were several lesson learned that would require follow-up through the Area Contingency Planning (ACP) process. One item identified was how to assess potential third party oyster lease claims when there is no Responsible Party and the damage claims will be filed against OPA90 Liability Funds. In summary, the mystery spill in Adams bay was responded to by the USCG as a Federal Project. The incident was first reported on 18 October 2006. The spill volume was initially thought to be 100 to 200 gallons. Once the recovery operations began, more than 900 gallons was collected near the Empire Floodgate, and the oil volume estimated was increased to 3000 gallons (estimate only). No RP has been identified. A map has been provided the highlights the areas impacted by the spill. There are many reasons for this, the characteristics of the slick, the lack of observed land impacts further to the south, and the oceanographic features and observations describe below. This region of where the slick was observed is in generally shallow water near the Mississippi River Delta. In this region, we expect any floating oil to be primarily moved by the winds with, in light wind conditions, some movement by tidal currents. The measured wind records from the Grand Isle C-MAN station for that time period indicate winds were generally from the south on the 18th and early 19th of October. On the 18th, the winds were fairly light, consistent with floating oil staying in approximately the same region, with some movement from the tides. There was an ebb tide in the late morning and afternoon on the 18th. This ebb tide, combined with the light winds could have moved the oil to the south, to the southern most observation by Hilcorp at: 29??18.31'N - 089??36.93'W. Around 2130 on the night of the 18th, the winds became stronger and more from the west. This would have moved any floating oil to the north and east, consistent with the oil found beached near the Empire Flood Gates. It is unlikely that the source of the oil was anywhere north of the Empire Flood Gates. The source was most likely in the region of initial observations. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP, as it would affect any trajectory implications. _______________________________________________________ 1) WINDS: At the end of October and the first few weeks of November, the prevailing winds vary in strength from about 4 to 16 knots, with an average of about 10 knots. The wind direction is from the southern quadrant (blowing toward shore) about 40% of the time, and from the northern quadrant (blowing away from shore) about 40% of the time. 2) TRAJECTORY: Data from TABS Buoy B (offshore of Galveston) indicate that the currents in the region at this time of year tend to move mostly down coast (toward Texas) at velocities up to 1 knot, but primarily less than 0.5 knots. Given the winds and the currents in the region, any released oil is most likely to move down coast toward Texas, and toward shore about 40% of the time, and away from shore 40% of the time. Thus, about 60% of the time, the oil will not approach land for a substantial period of time. Diesel fuel is volatile, and will not persist for long. However, if the winds and waves are low at the time of the release, a sheen could be visible for as long as about 10 miles. If the winds are stronger, the visible sheen will be smaller. In any case, it is highly unlikely that a noticeable amount will reach shore. The lube oil will be more persistent (see below) but will likely be broken up and dispersed before any land contact is made. In addition, toxicity is generally low to moderate, so we don't expect it to be a substantial environmental threat in an open water environment the expected quantities. 3) OIL FATE: NOAA's ADIOS 2 Oil Weathering Model indicates that less that 10% of the Diesel Fuel will persist on the surface for longer than 24 hours after a release in the average wind conditions of 10 knots. Diesel Fuel: Light refined products, such as diesel (or Fuel Oil No 2), typically have very high evaporation rates and do not tend to create persistent slicks. However, the terminology for refined products is not standardized, and, sometimes, heavier intermediate fuel oils are referred to as "marine diesel". These heavier products are much less volatile than normal Fuel Oil no 2 and can form a more persistent slick. When spilled, the diesel spreads quickly into thin films often forming patches of rainbow and silver sheens. If the sheens reach the shoreline in a few hours, a slight staining, or greasy film-like bathtub ring is common. These oils usually do not form a stable emulsion and, as a result, do not form a heavy or sticky residual to clean up. Note that lighter refined products do have a relatively high concentration of light aromatic compounds and tend to be more soluble and more toxic than heavier oils. These oils do not generally present an involved cleanup problem. However, they can result in an initial toxic shock to biota and can persist as a biological threat in low energy marine environments. Lubricating Oils Lubricating oils are ubiquitous. They are used in all types of engines operating on land, at sea, or in the air. All lubricating oils are composed mainly of high-boiling point (>400 degC) hydrocarbons containing 25 to 40 carbon atoms per molecule. Compound classes that impart undesirable qualities to a lubricant (waxes, polar compounds, and others) are removed in the refining processes. To meet the requirements of many different engine types and operating conditions, a multitude of oil products have been developed. These can be divided into two groups: 1) oils used in continuous service, such as turbine oils and 2) oils used in intermittent service, such as motor oils. Oils used in continuous service operate at a fairly constant temperature for prolonged periods without frequent shutdown or renewal. Stability is of prime importance. Oils used in intermittent service must show little viscosity change with temperature (high viscosity indices). These oils must also be changed at frequent intervals to remove particulates collected during service. Stability of these oils is, therefore, a secondary consideration. Additives Additives are used to improve or impart various properties to the highly refined lubricating base oil. Automotive engine oils can contain a wide variety of additives including metallic detergents or ashless dispersants for controlling deposits, oxidation inhibitors, corrosion inhibitors, anti-wear additives, low temperature flow improvers, viscosity and friction modifiers. Railway locomotive diesel engine oils and marine diesel engine oils typically contain ashless dispersants and metallic detergents. Zinc-free detergents and silver lubricity agents are used where silver bearings are present. Environmental Behavior Lubricating oils, for all their differences in formulation, have many similarities. When spilled into a lake, river, or ocean they will spread rapidly to a thin slick. They will not evaporate, and they will disperse fairly readily in high-energy conditions without the addition of chemical dispersants. In general, lubricating oils will be of low to moderate aquatic toxicity. While the base oils used in the production of lubricating oils are generally of extremely low toxicity to aquatic organisms, the large number of different additives, in varying amounts, make it impossible to issue more specific statements, unless details of the composition (usually proprietary) are known. [SEP] The barge is still being maintained and held in position while lightering is conducted. Lightering operations are continuing on the No. 2 Tank. Storage capacity for the transferred oil and water is a problem. The tank barge has a capacity of 546,000 gallons and is full. In order to continue current operations, the salvage team will either need a second barge or find a way to decant or transfer the contents. A vacuum truck is being used on the No.4 Tank. The product from the No.4 tank is being pumped into a tanks on the shore. There is roughly 250,000 gallons (5,952 BBL'S) of capacity left in the fractionation tanks that have been stage on scene. The next step is to enhance the transfer of the sludge and oil by cutting into the tanks for better access. To accomplish this, the tanks must be inerted. The tentative plan is to use dry ice to inert the tanks. Storage capacity options are still explored. The purpose of lightering is to remove the water, oil, and oil sludge such that the barge can then be loaded onto a deck barge. [SEP] Bucket with tank sludge [SEP] Diagram of water process [SEP] Update, 28 Nov. 2006 If you have been wondering what happened with this barge, this short update will provide an update. Over the last few weeks the salvage contractor has completely reconfigured the lift technique to employ harness plates rather than cables or cables and chaffing plates to lift the barge. These plates are shown in attached photographs. The change was time consuming and costly, but was the viewed as having the least risk of barge failure and additional spills during the recovery. Remember, there are three drinking water intakes located down-stream from the salvage operation. While the closest is 25 river miles away, the operations posed a threat given the characteristics of the oil sludge. During this reconfiguring process, several additional hot-tap connections were made to attempt to pump-off as much residual oil and sludge as possible. Given that the residual doesn't easily flow, this attempt to remove the pollution threat was only partially successful. At present, the NOAA SSC doesn't have a good estimate of the amount of bulk product removed. Far more water than oil was removed during this process, but there was some mitigation. On the morning of 28 November, the lightering barge to receive contaminated water and oil arrived on scene and the lift began using three cranes. By midmorning, the barge had been righted to an angle, or list of approximately 15 degrees and lifted to surface. Pollution response personnel were on-scene during the operation. Once the barge was at the surface, small spills of floating oil did escape the barge and was contained adjacent to the barge. The amount of oil released was not large, and was probably less than 10 bbls. At this point, the cranes could only hold the barge in position because the lift was at near maximum for the smaller of the crane barges (the Ajax Barge, located furtherest from shore). The next step was to begin lightering the barge to create buoyancy so that the cranes can be reconfigured for final lightering and lifting the entire barge onto a deck barge that has been configured specifically for this purpose. When the NOAA SSC departed the scene on 28 November, the initial lightering process was being configured between the sunken barge and the lightering barge. Operations were planned through the night. Once the MOR171 (the barge currently being salvaged) is complete. There is a second sunken barge that must be salvaged and residual non-floating oil pollution at the site evaluated for recovery operations. Additional updates will follow. On September 6, 2006 an oil spill was discovered at the Conoco Phillips Bayway Refinery, Carteret, New Jersey. The source was a 6 inch pipeline which hadn't been used in 15 years. It appears that the pipeline failure was due to corrosion. USCG and Conoco Phillips estimates that between 2,000-3,000 gallons of residual No. 6 oil spilled into a small freshwater pond that is located on the refinery's property. The pond is connected to Morris's Mill Creek which is tidal and eventually discharges into the Arthur Kill. Some oil did flow from the pond into the creek, but it was contained by fence boom, no oil made its way into the Arthur Kill. [SEP] Photo of decaying pipes and supports(Csulak Photo) [SEP] Photo of skimming devices (Csulak Photo) [SEP] Photo of pipeline(Csulak Photo) [SEP] On May 17, 2007 officials from USCG (LePouttre, Breimer), USEPA (Harrington) and NOAA (Csulak) met with Conoco Phillips(CP)at the spill site for the purpose of conducting a final site assessment and closing out this response activity. CP showed the new sheet piling and concrete wall that was constructed to isolate the pond water where the spill occurred from entering Morses Creek which downstream flows into the Arthur Kill. The man-made pond was formed as a result of dredged material being disposed there from on- site maintenance of Morses Creek. The spill area is also part of a large ongoing Exxon Mobile remediation site. Back in the early 1980's there was a liquid asphalt spill at this same location and there still remains a significant amount of residual asphalt in the sediment below the surface and adhered to several above ground and below ground pipes (not in service) and a culvert that previouly allowed water to drain from the pond into Morses Creek. Now that the pilings and concrete wall has been installed, there is no water exchange between the pond and the creek, thereby preventing any oily residue from entering the creek. A vac truck regularly inspects the culvert area and removes any oily residue that accumulates on the pond side of the new wall. We did a visual assessment of the pond where the spill occurred and found minimal sheen (mostly organic matter)and staining. The vegetation surrounding the pond has for the most part fully recovered, including a significant amount of new growth. We observed several different bird species feeding in or near the pond. Other than continued maintenance of the culvet area with the vac truck on an as need basis, the agencies agreed that no further response actions were necessary. We also conducted a visual inspection at the most downstream dam/culvert on site before Morses Creek enters the Arthur Kill and did not observe any sheening. [SEP] Prepared by Frank Csulak: On September 6, 2006, an oil spill was discovered at the Conoco Phillips Bayway Refinery, Carteret, New Jersey. The source was a 6 inch pipeline which hadn't been used in 15 years. It appears that the pipeline failure was due to corrosion. USCG and Conoco Phillips estimates that between 2,000-3,000 gallons of residual No. 6 oil spilled into a small freshwater pond that is located on the refinery's property. The pond is connected to Morris's Mill Creek which is tidal and eventually discharges into the Arthur Kill. Some oil did flow from the pond into the creek, but it was contained by fence boom, no oil made its way into the Arthur Kill. On September 8, the USCG contacted the NOAA SSC and requested assistance with recommending appropriate response actions. On September 10th, the NOAA SSC met with the NJDEP OSC, the USCG OSC, and Conoco Phillips response unit to view the spill site and discuss remedial options. Shoreline clean up around the pond and was underway with the use of vac trucks and floating disc skimmers. Several dozen contractors were cutting and removing oiled fragmitties and other debris along the pond's shoreline. NOAA SSC made recommendation to employ the use of snare to collect and remove oil in the very shallow areas of the pond . The snare proved to be very effective . In addition, SSC made recoomendation to use high volume, low pressure flushing to move oil from shoreline into the pond where vac trucks and skimmers can recovery oil.. This was implemented and was also working very effectively. As of 9/11, Conoco Phillips recovered about 500 gallons of oil. Tri-State was brought in over the weekend. Three oiled birds ( 2 mallards and 1 sandpiper) were caught and are undergoing rehab at Tri-State's facility in Delaware. On 9/11 the SSC met with NJDEP, USCG, and Conoco Phillips to review status of incident and plans for continuing response actions. Objective is to remove as much recoverable oil from pond, and continue to boom creek to prevent any oil from reaching Arthur Kill. Once recoverable oil has been removed, focus will be on removing any remaining oiled vegeation and debris along the shoreline. [SEP] Date: 1600 EDT September 6, 2006 To: NOAA SSC Steve Lehmann  FROM: NOAA/Hazardous Materials Response Division Modeling and Simulation Studies Seattle, WA 98115  SUBJECT: M/V Toro, St Lawrence Seaway, NY FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION, PLEASE CONTACT CJ Beegle-Krause MODELING AND SIMULATION STUDIES, NOAA, SEATTLE, WA 98115. PHONE (206) 526-4911. ______________________________________________________ We have looked at the issue of fate and transport from a potential release of heavy fuel oil from a grounded vessel. These notes are based on the following information: The M/V Toro is reported grounded at the bow but not leaking. The vessel is located on the US and Canadian border at 45 deg N, 074 deg 40'W off the southeast side of Cornwall Island in the St Lawrence Seaway. The vessel is taking on water at the focsle, but considered stable. HAZMAT has been requested to provide a trajectory for 10,000 gallons of #6 fuel oil while the response team awaits further information on the fuel type and amount on board. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP as it would affect any trajectory implications. ______________________________________________________ 1) 24-hour Wind Forecast Winds are forecast to be from the NE at 5-10 knots until midmorning Thursday, then SW 5-10 knots through Friday. 2) Trajectory The currents through the St Lawrence Seaway are controlled by the outflow from Lake Ontario. Under such light forecast wind conditions the oil would move mostly with the currents, with the wind potentially biasing shoreline impacts. Based on the St Lawrence Seaway Commission estimates of flow for this week of 7060 m3/sec, we estimate that the currents in the deeper channel near the vessel grounding are between 2 -- 3 knots. Oil released from the vessel could go 50-70 nm downstream in a 24-hours period toward Montreal. The winds from the NE today and tomorrow morning indicate that north facing shorelines would be more likely to be contacted by oil than southward facing shorelines. 3) Oil Weathering and Fate Heavy Refined Products Heavy refined products, such as Intermediate Fuel Oils (IFO), Fuel Oil No. 6 and Bunker C, are more persistent than lighter refined products. The refining process has removed the lighter components and left them somewhat pre-weathered. As a result they can present quite persistent floating pollutant problems. These oils do occasionally form an emulsion, but usually only slowly, and after a period of days. These oils do not spread into very thin films and often simply break up into smaller patches and then tarballs. It is also common for these oils to lose enough of their light ends so that they do not rapidly form sheens and the resulting scattered tarball fields are very difficult to observe using visual, or remote sensing techniques. This, combined with the persistence of the tarballs, makes these kinds of spills quite likely to result in long range, and occasionally unexpected, beach impacts. Fuel Oil No. 6 has a much lower vapor pressure than diesel and will thus be less volatile. The proportion lost to evaporation will be small as will the amount permanently dispersed into the water column. Fuel Oil No. 6 can emulsify with a typical water content of around 30% but usually does so slowly. A final note that may be of interest: A survey form was prepared for the 22 largest tanks on the island. The ground survey data was then coded into an alphanumeric string for ease of radio transmission. Each tank has the following data: Tank#/Damage/Spill/Follow-up/Sounded/Photographed, using the following codes: Location: O=original, U=Unknown, M=Moved, (location known) Damage: U=Undamaged, L=Light, M=Moderate, S=severe Spill: N=no spill, P= Potential, 0= spill occurred, G= Seepage, S= currently spilling Follow-up: N=Not required, D= Delayed, I= immediate Sounded: N=Not Sounded, otherwise % full Photographed: N=no, otherwise # is count of images. For example, Tank One was in its original location, undamaged, no follow-up required, 0% (empty), with 2 photographs taken was coded as 01/O/U/N/N/0/2 Using these codes allowed the SCAT team to easily transmit the status of all of the tanks in a short paragraph radio transmission. NOAA was provided copies of the survey forms and results if needed. [SEP] Landing craft in small boat harbor were undamaged. Small fuel tank in bottom of picture was not moved. The three crewmembers attempted to swim to shore but only one survived and was rescued. The USCG located the floating, yet overturned vessel and noted sheen and floating debris nearby. A self-locating data buoy was attached to the hull and the vessel's drift was tracked to a location near the shoreline of Chinese Harbor, Santa Cruz Island (34deg 01.02'N, 119deg 37.33'W).  When interviewed, the owner claimed that the vessel had a maximum fuel capacity of 400 gallons but estimated approximately 200 gallons of diesel were aboard at the time of the mishap. Because the vessel's condition and potential pollution threat are currently unknown, a patrol boat has been dispatched and a helicopter overflight is scheduled for tomorrow at first light. Based on the morning scene assessment, removal alternatives will be evaluated by USCG, the State of California, Channel Islands NMS and Channel Islands NP. WX support was requested by the USCG. Jordan Stout, SSC California [SEP] Drifting Vessel F/V Five Gs 0000 PDT, Thursday, July 13, 2006  NOTE: This is a site specific forecast from the National Weather Service generated specifically for this incident region. Action items for this team include -a better assessment of the impact area -a formal cleanup plan -better communications with SOSC and FOSC Surveys On 22 June, EM arranged for a survey of the impacted sites with the stated goal of signing off many of the locations. Unfortunately, the survey was by boat and direct shoreline access was difficult due to draft in most locations. In the one location where the team could access the shoreline, the oiling was heavier than first thought. Oil had penetrated the riprap to 12 inches and cleanup efforts had been less effective than hoped. The result of the survey was agreement that one, lightly oiled site would be signed off due to safety considerations, but the other required a future foot survey. On 27 June, a foot survey was conducted of the heaviest impacted areas. The survey included FOSC, NOAA and RP (SOSC was unavailable, but briefed with photos later in the day). Among the discoveries, oil is subsurface at several locations (see photos) and heavy under riprap in others. While the geographic extent is not great, access and working conditions are difficult. Fortunately, most of the impact area is on man-made materials (urban/industrial conditions, degraded environment) and there is virtually no access available to the public. Future Actions: EM has requested the use of Corexit 9580, an NCP listed shoreline cleaning agent. The NOAA SSC is coordinating the concurrence network of the RRT for judgment on the plan. The area covered by the plan is less than 10,000 square feet. EM proposes to apply the chemical, low pressure/high volume flush and recover with skimmers and sorbents. Steve Lehmann NOAA SSC On-scene
On May 17, 2006, the bulk carrier MV Spar Orion ran aground near Port Everglades, FL. The cargo is unknown at this time. The vessel is reported to have 480 MT of a heavy fuel oil. The incident occurred at approximately 0630 hours EST. The vessel is reported to be aground on a reef one mile off shore of Port Everglades, FL. The vessels location is 026-07.35N and 080-05.22W. The location of this grounding is similar to that of the FEDERAL PESCADORIS , a cement carrier, grounded around 2004 at the Western edge of the ancorage. [SEP] Resources at Risk for Bulk Carrier Spar Orion Grounding, Port Everglades, Florida I. Spill Source Information This report was prepared at 1200 EDT on 17 May 2006. Information in this report is based on the assumption that the bulk carrier Spar Orion is aground on a reef one mile offshore of Port Everglades (26&#8734; 06.7' N, 80&#8734; 05.5' W). The vessel is reported to contain 480 MT of a heavy fuel oil. No releases have been reported at this time. II. Geographic Region Covered This report covers an area approximately 2 miles north and 10 miles south of the reported grounding site. This area does not necessarily correspond to actual or potential oil locations or oil impact. Consult other Hotline reports for oil location information. III. Expected Behavior of the Spilled Material Heavy fuel oil may coat shorelines and biological resources using the shoreline or water surface. Due to relatively low concentrations of water soluble and acutely toxic compounds, impacts to water column resources are likely to be small. Heavy fuel oil is highly adhesive, making it difficult to clean up. It forms thick slicks that eventually break up into tarballs that are very persistent, posing significant risks to waterbirds and shorelines. IV. Shoreline Resources at Risk The outer coast shoreline in the area is primarily composed of coarse-grained sand beaches. There are a few areas of mixed sand and gravel beach to the south of the grounding site, and some riprap along inlets. The shoreline at Port Everglades (approximately 1 mile west of the reported grounding location) is predominantly sheltered, solid, man-made structures, with some riprap, mixed sand and gravel beaches, and sheltered marshes and/or mangroves approximately a mile south of the inlet. The most sensitive habitats in the area are marshes and mangroves. The heavy oil will readily adhere to and coat wetland vegetation. Heavily coated vegetation could experience sub-lethal effects, including die-back of the aboveground vegetation. In some cases the vegetation could experience lethal impacts, especially if oil becomes mixed into the sediments and root zone. Where wetland sediments are muddy and soft, it is important to prevent excessive disturbance and further mixing of oil into the substrate by foot traffic during cleanup activities, as this could result in more severe and long-term impacts to the marshes. On sheltered, solid man-made structures, heavy fuel oil may form bands or "bath-tub" rings at the water line. Heavy oils tend to form a thick band or "bath-tub" ring at the high water line on these solid structures. On riprap, oil may penetrate into the cavities between the boulders and adhere to the rough boulder surfaces, making it difficult to remove. Chronic sheening problems are possible, especially in sheltered areas. On beaches, the heavy fuel oil may form thick accumulations at the high-tide line. For coarse-grained sand and gravel beaches, oil penetration into the sediment may be up to 25 cm, and burial may be up to depths of 20 cm. If oil does strand on the beaches, it will be important to track the sediment erosion/deposition patterns as the winds change. There can be rapid burial of the oiled layer, making cleanup more difficult. Care should be taken not to mix oil deeper into the sediments through physical activity during cleanup. Direct oiling or concentrations of oil in nearshore waters may affect organisms on the beaches. V. Biological Resources at Risk Birds Least tern (state threatened) may be nesting within a half mile of the inlet and along the beach further south. Wilson's plover may be nesting 3 miles south of the inlet. Diving birds and wading birds may be nesting more inland near North Miami Beach. Migratory and resident shorebirds may be present in high numbers (over 1000 birds) along sand beaches and inside the Port Everglades inlet. Brown pelicans and double-crested cormorants may present in high concentrations in the area. Diving birds may be severely impacted from an oil spill because of the length of time they spend on the water's surface. Oil can adhere to the feathers reducing insulation, water buoyancy, and water repellency. These symptoms can quickly lead to death from hypothermia and/or drowning. Preening of oiled feathers can cause sickness or death in birds due to ingested oil. Fish and Invertebrates Numerous fish and invertebrates are potentially present in the area, including: bay scallop, American oyster, hard clam, pink shrimp (spawning), blue crab (spawning), spiny lobster (spawning), stone crab, gray snapper, pinfish, spotted seatrout, spot, Spanish mackerel, and gulf flounder. Heavy oils do not pose a large, direct impact to water-column resources because they have a low water-soluble fraction. The larval and juvenile stages are at a greater risk from oil spills because of the shallow water habitats they occupy and their sensitivity to the toxic compounds. Reptiles Green sea turtles (state/federally endangered), hawksbill sea turtles (state/federally endangered), leatherback sea turtles (state/federally endangered), and loggerhead sea turtles (state/federally threatened) may be present along sand beaches and in nearshore waters. All species are likely present in low concentrations, excluding loggerheads that may be present in moderate concentrations. Green, leatherback, and loggerhead sea turtles may be nesting (hawksbill begin nesting in June) and hatchlings may be present. Oil on the shoreline can coat the adult turtles as they come out of the water to nest, and may be transferred to the eggs. Research shows that the eggs have low survival rate and increased deformities when oiled. Also, bands of oil can coat the hatchlings as they travel to the ocean. Direct effects of oil exposure on adult turtles may include: oiling of sensory organs, reddening and sloughing off of the skin, dysfunction of the salt gland, uptake of oil in the gastrointestinal system, and disturbed diving and respiration patterns. Sea turtles may ingest tarballs resulting in sickness or death. Floating tarballs can coat the flippers, and the mouth can become coated as the turtle attempts to clean its flippers. Large quantities of tar have been known to immobilize smaller turtles. Low concentrations of crocodiles (state/federally endangered) may be present in wetlands. Marine Mammals Manatees (state/federally endangered) may be present in high concentrations in nearshore areas. Oil may cause irritation of skin and mucous membrane surfaces. Inhaling vapors may cause irritation of the lungs. Injuries to these animals are possible if increased small boat traffic occurs during the response effort. VI. Human-Use Resources at Risk Recreational beaches are heavily used in this area. This area is also used for recreational diving, particularly north of the reported grounding site. There are several marinas, boat ramps, the John U. Lloyd State Recreation Area, and the Hugh Taylor Birch State Recreation Area in the vicinity. There are several historical sites in the area. Port Everglades is an important commercial port, and both commercial and recreational vessel traffic in the area is likely. (206) 526-4911. _______________________________________________________ The reported scenario: A car carrying vessel, the M/V Ambassador has been adrift since 0900 EDT. It is 510' and fully loaded. Reported positions with times: 1615 EDT 25deg 24.146' N by 080deg 03.218' W 1647 EDT 25deg 23.143' N by 080deg 04.240' W 1722 EDT 25deg 23.500' N by 080deg 04.210' W These locations are about 7.5 nm from the outer barrier island off Biscayne Bay. Between 1615 and 1647 the vessel moved to the SSE about 1 nm. Between 1647 and 1722 the vessel moved to the N about 0.4 nm. Onscene conditions are seas 4 - 6 feet and winds from 030deg True at 17 knots A tug is expected to reach the vessel in about 3 hours. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP as it would affect any trajectory implications. _______________________________________________________ 1) Weather Forecast Winds are expected to be from the NE at 15-20 knots into the evening. 2) Ship Drift Analysis The vessel is located along the western boundary of the Gulf Stream. HF Radar measured currents in the area from the Univ. of Miami site, http://iwave.rsmas.miami.edu/wera/ indicates that currents are moving to the north between 1 and 1.5 knots. Car carrying vessels typically sit high in the water and have a significant amount of downwind sail effect. Typical 'windage' is about 5-10% of the wind speed. It appears that the wind, blowing the vessel to the south and the currents pushing the vessel to the north are almost at a standoff. Small variations in the winds, currents, or vessel orientation will result in the vessel moving either to the north or to the south over short periods of time. We do not think that the vessel will move significantly in either direction over the next few hours. Whatever movement there is will be primarily in the north - south direction. Therefore we do not expect the vessel to ground before the tug arrives onscene. Coast Guard investigators stationed in San Juan are looking for any signs of oil leakage, Coast Guard Petty Officer Dana Warr said. ''There are no signs of pollution, and [the team is] scheduling aircraft flight over the area,'' Warr said. The tanker -- known as the Margara -- ran aground at 1:15 a.m. It originated from Cartagena, Colombia. It was a few miles away from its destination, Tallaboa, Puerto Rico, when it ran into trouble. Investigators must first determine if there's an oil leak. If one isn't found, then they can remove the ship ''without creating any damage to the ship or creating a spill by actually moving the ship off the ground,'' Warr said. Its 28 crew members appear to be safe. [SEP] Trajectory 3/17/06 1830 [SEP] Sheen reported in Seattle's Elliott Bay Full story: http://seattletimes.nwsource.com/html/localnews/2002871824_websheen17.html By Seattle Times staff SEATTLE - About 15 gallons of oil spread over one square mile of Seattle's Elliott Bay today, most likely from a source on or near Harbor Island, the Coast Guard said. Petty Officer Kurt Fredrickson said the oil was too thinly spread to be removed by absorbent pads, but booms were placed around an area on the west side of Harbor Island after investigators found a heavier concentration of the spilled substance in this contaminated area. The source of the pollution had not been determined. Harbor Island is an industrial area on the south side of Elliott Bay. "It looks a lot worse than it is because it spread out," Fredrickson said, explaining that one quart of oil could spread out to cover the area of two football fields. Fredrickson called the leaked substance a "weathered oil product," and said it was heavier than diesel. He said it would take the Department of Ecology a few days to determine the petroleum product's exact makeup. The sheen was spotted by a tug boat on the north side of the bay and reported to the Coast Guard at 7:10 a.m., Coast Guard Petty Officer Jeff Pollinger said. It also was reported by four planes that flew over the bay on a landing approach to Boeing Field. The sheen spread between Smith Cove and Pier 70, said Ecology Department spokesman Larry Altose. "Hopefully we got it soon enough to get it stopped," Altose said. The Coast Guard sent a 41-foot boat and a helicopter to try to identify the cause, and others patrolled the shore on foot. Ecology also chartered a helicopter to fly over the area so investigators could get a better look at the sheen, Altose said. There was no sign of damage to wildlife from the sheen, Pollinger said, nor did it appear to have reached the shore. [SEP] Trajectory 3/17/06 1230
