PHONE (206) 526-4911. _______________________________________________________ Per your request, we have looked at the trajectory implications of a spill of Cumene from a barge on the Ohio River at Lock and Dam 52, near Brookport, Illinois. These notes are based on the following information: A barge had an accident near Lock and Damn 52. It is currently tied up at the lock wall. It has been reported that about 3700 gallons of Cumene may have spilled into the void space of the barge. It is unknown if any product has been released into the river. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP, as it would affect any trajectory implications. _______________________________________________________ 1) River Flow: The river is currently flowing fairly high. The locks are currently open. There is a moderate amount of sediment in the river at this time. Flow is estimated today by the NOAA River Forecast Center at 415,000 cfs. The flow is expected to increase moderately throughout the week. The mean velocity at the spill location is estimated to be about 2.6 to 2.7 mph. 2) TRAJECTORY: Any product that gets in the water will tend to move downstream and mix with the river water. As the product mixes, the maximum concentration will go down at it moves downstream. Given the estimated flow velocity, any product in the river will reach the junction of the Missouri River about 40 miles away approximately 15-20 hours after the release. We have run NOAA's river dilution calculator to provide estimates of the maximum concentration likely to be observed as any contaminant spilled moves downstream. This calculation assumes that 3700 gallons of product is spilled all at once, and that all of that product dissolves in the river. It is likely that less than all the product will dissolve. In addition, some of the product is likely to adsorb to the sediment in the river, which has not been taken into account in this calculation. Thus these estimates are conservative. There are no published drinking water standards for Cumene. However, it is likely that the toxicity is similar to that of Ethyl Benzene, which has a standard of 0.7ppm. An estimate of the median toxicity to fresh water aquatic organisms is about 10ppm. We estimate the maximum concentration will reach about 0.7ppm about 33 miles downstream of the spill. Monitoring is recommend for any drinking water intakes between the spill location and the junction with the Mississippi River at Cairo. Concentrations of concern to aquatic organisms are expected to be reached a similar distance downstream. If 3700 gallons or less of Cumene is released, we do not expect concentrations toxic to either humans or aquatic organisms to be seen in the Mississippi River below the junction with the Ohio River. [SEP] Based on local weather conditions from the NWS, we looked at a worst case release of 100% of 3700 gallons to the river. Cumene is lighter than water so would float and has a relatively low vapor pressure. The water temperature is low (in the mid 40's) so the expected evaporation rate would be small. ALOHA estimated a TEEL1 maximum distance of 100 yards. TEEL1 is defined as the maximum concentration in air below which it is believed nearly all individuals could be exposed without experiencing other than mild transient adverse health effects or perceiving a clearly defined objectionable odor. The TEEL2 and TEEL3 threat zone estimates were below the minimum distance ALOHA requires (due to near field effects and concentration patchiness near the release) so serious health effects would be a very local concern (10s of yards) Cumene's odor threshold is very low (0.1 ppm) so you could expect the odor zone to extend for a long distance from the release. For a 100% release this could be miles. Some physical property data for Cumene: Flash Point: 96.0 ?? On January 26, 2006, a runaway barge "M-53" loaded with 19,500 barrels of asphalt allided against a railroad bridge on the Ohio River in Louisville, Kentucky. The tug M/V Kelly Lee was heading down river with 3 asphalt barges when the breakaway occurred. Two of the barges were recovered, but one barge is trapped against the K&I Railroad Bridge at river mile 607.4. The USCG reports that the barge is lying on its side with the bottom of the barge against the bridge. The barge was also carrying 15,000 gallons of diesel used to keep the asphalt heated. An unknown amount of asphalt and diesel fuel has been released into the Ohio River. The river is closed to commercial traffic until the situation is resolved. The barge M-53 is owned by Magnolia Marine Transportation. [SEP] Resources at Risk for Ohio River Barge I. Spill Source Information This report was prepared at 12:00 EDT on January 27, 2006. Information in the report is based on a report of a barge carrying 15,000 gallons of diesel and 19,500 bbls of asphalt collided with a bridge at river mile 605 on the Ohio River at Louisville, Kentucky. Is is suspected that 15,000 gallons of diesel and up to 4,000 bbls of asphalt may have been released. II. Geographic Region Covered The area covered by this report is from Louisville downstream to Brandenburg, KY. This area does not necessarily correspond to actual or potential oil locations. Consult other Hotline reports for oil location information. III. Expected Behavior of the Spilled Material With the strong currents (reported at 4 knots) it is expected that the diesel fuel will mix into the water column and impact animals in the water column. Some product may accumulate along sheltered areas of the shoreline. Assuming the asphalt is heavier than water, it will sink to the bottom and possibly be transported by the currents, coating benthic habitats and possibly effecting benthic organisms. There would be very little risk of shoreline impact from sinking asphalt. IV. Shoreline Resources at Risk The shorelines from the bridge just above river mile 605 to the lock and dam are seawalls and riprap. Downstream of the lock the shorelines are predominately vegetated banks and unconsolidated sediments (sand, gravel, and mixed sand and gravel) with some short sections of riprap. V. Biological Resources at Risk Fish There are numerous species of fish in the Ohio River, including, but no limited to, catfish (channel, blue, and flathead), bluegill, bass (smallmouth, largemouth, spotted, and yellow), and crappie (blue and white), many of which could potential be in the spill area. The diesel fuel may impact some of the fish closer to the water surface. However with the volume of diesel spilled and strong currents, the water column concentrations are not expected to be high enough to cause mortality in the fish. The catfish and any other benthic feeding fish may have their gills coated by sinking asphalt and may also ingest it while feeding. This might result in mortality to some of these fish. Shellfish Various species of clams and mussels may be present in the river. However there are no records of any threatened or endangered species in this area. The mussels and clams may be coated by the asphalt Birds Waterfowl present may include Canada geese, green-winged teal, blue-winged teal, American coot, mergansers, scaup, wood ducks, American black duck, redhead, pintail, and canvasback. Waterfowl may be impacted from an oil spill because of the length of time they spend on the water's surface. Oil can adhere to the feathers reducing insulation, water buoyancy, and water repellency. These symptoms can quickly lead to death from hypothermia and/or drowning. Preening of oiled feathers can cause sickness or death in birds due to ingested oil. Mammals Semi-aquatic fur-bearing mammals, such as river otters, muskrat, and raccoons could occur in the area. Fur-bearing species may be found along the shorelines or within the waters of the river. Fur can become oiled from swimming through oil slicks or contacting oiled vegetation. Matting of the fur due to oiling results in impacts similar to those described for birds. Grooming of contaminated fur can also result in sickness or death depending on the amount of oil ingested. Vegetation There are several species of rare plants on the banks of the Ohio River just below McAlpine dam. Please contact the Kentucky State Nature Preserves Commission at (502) 573-2885 for more details. VI. Human-Use Resources at Risk The accident occurred just upstream of the McAlpine Locks and Dam. This is also the location of Falls of the Ohio State Park in Indiana and Falls of the Ohio NWCA. About 25 miles downstream from the incident is Fort Knox Military Reservation. MMT and salvers attached jumpers between the port and starboard heating coils on the # 3 cargo tanks in preparation for heating the asphalt. They are using heating oil from the MM 54 to run the system in those compartments with undamaged coils. As of 26 Feb., the asphalt in #3 starboard was almost at a pumpable temperature (>200??F). This morning salvage crews noticed that leaking was occurring around the cargo hatch, releasing asphalt into the river. This release was controlled, as well as possible, by the use of sorbent boom (see photos) in order to contain the asphalt (it attaches itself well to the boom while hot) long enough to cool the oil and allow it to sink in the immediate front (upriver side) of the barge. The asphalt is piling up in this area and reports indicate that the oil is not migrating around the barge in a significant way. This leak is now under control and lightering continues. In addition, this morning crews noticed a leak from a 2 1/2 inch pressure vacuum valve, emitting a stream of hot asphalt into the river. This, too, appeared to remaining in the deposit of oil in the front of the barge. By noon, the lightering to levels below the valve had caused this leak to stop. The lightering of this tank should be finished within the day or by tomorrow. Each tank will follow the same procedure (access, assessing heating pipes for use or installing new, flexible pipes, heating the asphalt, lightering, venting and securing the tank). [SEP] To: NOAA SSC Brad Benggio From: NOAA/Hazardous Materials Response Division Modeling and Simulation Studies Seattle, WA 98115 SUBJECT: F/V Captain Chance DATE: January 17, 2006, 1430 EST FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION, PLEASE CONTACT Chris Barker MODELING AND SIMULATION STUDIES, NOAA, SEATTLE, WA 98115. PHONE (206) 526-4911. _______________________________________________________ Per your request, we have looked at trajectory implications of a diesel fuel release from the F/V Captain Chance. These notes are based on the following information: On January 17, 2006, at approx 0900 EST, the 72 foot wood shrimp vessel F/V Captain Chance ran aground at location: 28??-09???€?N, 082??-49.9???€?W. This location is about two miles off Tarpon Springs, FL in St. Joseph Sound. The vessel is carrying up to 1,000 gal diesel fuel and about 50 gal. lube oils. It is currently slowly leaking diesel fuel through the vents. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP, as it would affect any trajectory implications. _______________________________________________________ 1) WEATHER: Today, winds are expected to be from the S at 20-25 knots, with gusts to 30 knots, shifting to be from the SW tonight. After midnight, the winds will shift to be from the NW at 20-25 knots, shifting to be from the N Wednesday morning. 2) TRAJECTORY: Diesel fuel released slowly from the vessel will result in a small sheen nearby and downwind, the sheen will evaporate and disperse quickly, and will likely be no longer visible after a short distance downwind. In addition, it can be hard to see any sheen in rough conditions. If there is a catastrophic release of the entire cargo, a larger sheen will result, perhaps as large as a mile. The movement of a surface sheen will be dominated by the local winds, until the oil evaporates and disperses and is no longer visible. The tidal currents in that region move primarily North and South, with a maximum velocity of about 0.5 knots. How large the sheen will be, how far it travels, and its persistence is a function of the wind, wave conditions and tidal cycle at the time of release. If the release occurs under the strong winds forecast for today and tomorrow, the sheen will likely be visible for less than a mile. The lube oils will be more persistent, but are in much smaller quantities. A release of all the lube oils at once might result in a small sheen, or be mixed with the diesel oil, and create a slightly more persistent sheen. We don???€?t expect substantial shoreline impacts from the diesel, but there may be some from the lube oil. If the release occurs today, the impacts could be the region of the mouth of the channel to Tarpon Springs. If a release occurs after midnight tonight, then there is a chance of some impact to Three Rooker Bar. If the release occurs during the ebb tide on Wed, it???€?s possible that some small impacts would be seen on North Pt. on Honeymoon Island. If a release occurs, this trajectory can be refined when the time of release is known. 3) WRECKAGE TRAJECTORY: If the ship breaks up, the currents and the wind will move the floating wreckage similarly to the oil. Different parts of the wreckage will float higher in the water, catching the wind more than others, spreading the wreckage out over a larger area. Depending on when the break-up occurs, the wreckage could end up near the mouth of the Tarpon Springs channel, or along the East shore of St. Joseph Sound as far South as Palm Harbor. Some wreckage might be found on Honeymoon Island if there is more of an easterly component to the wind than forecast. 3) OIL FATE: Light refined products, such as diesel (or Fuel Oil No 2), typically have very high evaporation rates and do not tend to create persistent slicks. However, the terminology for refined products is not standardized, and sometimes, heavier intermediate fuel oils are referred to as ???€?marine diesel???€?. These heavier products are much less volatile than normal Fuel Oil no 2 and can form a more persistent slick. When spilled, the diesel spreads quickly into thin films often forming patches of rainbow and silver sheens. Note that lighter refined products do have a relatively high concentration of light aromatic compounds and tend to be more soluble and more toxic than heavier oils. [SEP] Overflight photo taken by NOAA SSC Charlie Henry, Jan 13, 2006 [SEP] Overflight photo taken by NOAA SSC Charlie Henry, Jan 13, 2006 [SEP] Overflight photo taken by NOAA SSC Charlie Henry, Jan 13, 2006 [SEP] Overflight photo taken by NOAA SSC Charlie Henry, Jan 13, 2006 [SEP] On the morning of 13 January 2006, the NOAA SSC was informed of a fire at the Southern Scrap Facility near the Industrial Canal in the extreme western section of St. Bernard Parish. The fire had apparently begun the night before. The SSC was immediately tasked to coordinate and conduct an aerial overflight to assess the source, magnitude, and plume behavior for the ESF-10 Incident Command. An OSC was sent to support the State of Louisiana???€?s Department of Environmental Quality and the New Orleans Parish Fire Department. Due to inclement weather, the overflight began at 1000 hrs. The source of the fire was a 200 x 300 x 40 foot pile of scrapped refrigerators, air conditioners, and other white goods (post-hurricane Katrina debris) that had already been processed to remove Freon at the facility. At he time of the overflight, the fire evolved an area of approximately one half of a football field. Earlier, before the rain and segregation efforts by workers at the facility, the fire had been reported much larger. Strong NW winds in excess of 25 mph tended to force the plume near the ground, and plume height never exceeded 1000 feet. The plume traveled downwind over St. Bernard Parish passing very near the Murphy Oil site before crossing the Mississippi River. The plume extended at least 12 miles from the source. The area downwind remains largely evacuated due to hurricane Katrina and subsequent flooding. Later in the day, the U.S. EPA flew the ASPECT aircraft to assess pollutants in the plume. NOAA HAZMAT???€?s home team in Seattle, WA contacted IMAAC to run a plume trajectory model to support field and air sampling operations. The forecast suggest that condition would remain relatively constant throughout the daylight hours. The firefighting effort was hampered by a lack of water pressure and the nature of the fire itself. The plan evolved to essentially let the fire burn itself out. Crews worked to segregate the debris. Once power was restored to the facility, the scrape metal was processed, some of it still burning, through a metal shredder, sprayed with water, and loaded as chunks of hot scrape metal into an adjacent hopper barge. On 14 January, the fire was completely exhausted. The cause of the fire remains unknown. The Environmental Unit is currently reviewing air-monitoring data. This report will serve as both the initial and final report for this incident.

The forecast winds are from the Southeast and South for the next 12-16 hrs, which will move the oil toward shore. In addition, the coastal current in the region is expected to be moving downcoast, to the west, at about 1/4 to maybe as much as 1/2 knot. At the highest forecast wind speed, the sheen could move as much as 8 miles toward shore before the forecast shift in the winds Friday afternoon starts to move the sheen offshore again. In this time, the currents could move the sheen 4 to 8 miles downcoast. We do not expect the sheen to impact the shoreline.  3) OIL FATE: Without knowing what the product is, we can't forecast its persistence. If it is a light product, like a diesel fuel, it could be no longer visible in as little as 10-12 hrs. A heavier product could last a great deal longer, but will eventually break up into scattered sheen and small tarballs. The strong winds predicted for Friday afternoon and night are likely to break up the sheen if it persists that long.

It is currently 95% submerged at location: 40??-51???€?N, 72??-29???€?W. The vessel is carrying approx. 6,000 gal diesel fuel, and is not known to be leaking at this time. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP, as it would affect any trajectory implications. _______________________________________________________ 1) WEATHER: Today through Tonight, the winds are predicted to be from the NE at 25-30 knots. Wednesday, the winds are expected to be from the N at 20-25 knots. 2) TRAJECTORY: The currents in Shinnecock Bay are dominated by tides. Depending on when in the tidal cycle any release occurs, the oil could be carried as far as 1/2 miles East of Shinnecock Inlet to the East, or 1/2 mile West of the Ponquogue Bridge to the west. The strong NE and N winds forecast for the next couple days will tend to move the oil to the South and Southwest, so that shorelines affected will most likely be the Warner Islands and the North side of the barrier islands on either side of Shinnecock Inlet. Under these strong winds, beach impacts could occur in as little as one hour after a release. When small diesel spills strand on the shoreline, the oil tends to be washed off quickly by waves and tidal flushing If Fuel is released during an ebb tide, some of the diesel could be carried out of Shinnecock Inlet by the tidal currents. Any oil carried outside the inlet will then be moved by the winds as a sheen, to the South, away from shore. It is unlikely that this fuel will impact the shoreline on the south side of the barrier islands. 3) OIL FATE: Light refined products, such as diesel (or Fuel Oil No 2), typically have very high evaporation rates and do not tend to create persistent slicks. However, the terminology for refined products is not standardized, and sometimes, heavier intermediate fuel oils are referred to as ???€?marine diesel???€?. These heavier products are much less volatile than normal Fuel Oil no 2 and can form a more persistent slick. When spilled, the diesel spreads quickly into thin films often forming patches of rainbow and silver sheens. Note that lighter refined products do have a relatively high concentration of light aromatic compounds and tend to be more soluble and more toxic than heavier oils. These notes are based on the following information: Two Mobile Offshore Drilling Units (MODUs) were lost during the period of Hurricane Rita???€?s passage through the area, presumably from the hurricane conditions: the Rowan Halifax (28 deg 04???€? 26???€?N, 092 deg 41???€? 56???€?W) and the Rowan Fort Worth (28 deg 14???€? 33???€?, 092 deg 00???€? 40???€?W). MODUs are designed similarly to ships and therefore can float. Emergency procedures aboard the MODUs require the crew to make the platform watertight before evacuating by ???€?dogging???€? all the doors and hatches. The MODUs were sheared off from their legs, leaving the legs at the original location. The legs of the Rowan Halifax are currently directed due WSW, and the legs of the Rowan Fort Worth are directed W to WNW. The area from 260 ???€? 010 deg T (clockwise) has been searched out as far as 12 nm from the original location using side scan sonar. A MODU in between these two, the Rowan Louisiana, was found on the beach 83 nm away at a heading of 350 deg from the original location. The legs from the Rowan Louisiana were tilted 35 deg off the bottom in a NW direction similar to the ultimate resting location of the MODU. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP as it would affect any trajectory implications. ______________________________________________________ Background Hurricane Rita is estimated to have passed directly over the Rowan Halifax, and to the SW of the Rowan Louisiana and Rowan Fort Worth. The Rowan Louisiana???€?s final location on the shoreline indicates that these MODUs can float for a significant period of time. Therefore our discussions (one for each missing MODU) will reflect two different scenarios. The first is the short time-scale of the MODU shearing off and sinking within six hours. The second is a longer-term trajectory assuming the MODU remained afloat without sinking. NOAA HAZMAT has information regarding the locations where other drifting MODUs were found in the Gulf of Mexico. See attached graphic showing a summary of the initial and final locations for these other MODUs. We expect that these MODUs did not take a straight-line path from their original to the final locations as the lines on the graphic depict. Recently published data from Hurricane Ivan shows current speed and direction, and significant wave height from instruments located along the hurricane track. We think these data are useful in considering what may have happened to the Rowan Halifax as Hurricane Rita passed directly over. Along the Hurricane Ivan track the significant wave height peaked approximately six hours before the passage of the eye, with currents decreasing from approx 1.2 ???€? 0 m/s and varying in direction between WSW and W over that six hour period. These directions are 120-100 degree counterclockwise from the storm track during that six-hour period. NOAA National Data Buoy Center buoy 42040 was located just to the ???€?left???€? of the hurricane track, and the buoy broke free from its mooring during the passage of the hurricane eye. The initial drift of this buoy was in the SW direction approx 145 deg counterclockwise from the storm track. Case 1 ???€? Rowan Halifax From the above information we estimate that the search area for the Rowan Halifax would be between 140 deg to 270 deg T (clockwise) out as far as 15 nm from the original location of the MODU. If this MODU remained afloat, it would be very near the eye of the hurricane track and experience winds quite different from the Rowan Louisiana on the ???€?right???€? side of the hurricane track. The Rowan Halifax is likely to have moved offshore toward the shelf break where it could get caught up in the upcoast (Texas -> Louisiana) recirculation along the outer shelf or be picked up by the Loop Current depending on how far offshore it traveled. Case 2 ???€? Rowan Fort Worth The Rowan Fort Worth was further outside the ???€?right???€? side of the hurricane track than the Rowan Louisiana, so we would expect it to behave similarly with relatively weaker currents and winds. If the Rowan Fort Worth sank within six hours of breaking free, we recommend a search area of 270 ???€? 030 deg T (clockwise) out to about 12 nm. If the MODU floated for a significant amount of time, we expect that it would have drifted similarly to other MODUs that separated during the hurricane. Below is a table showing information about the platform trajectories shown in the graphic. We have listed (1) the platform name, (2) the minimum distance from the original platform location to the Hurricane Rita track, (3) the total distance traveled by the platforms (except for the missing MODUs), (4) the angle of the overall trajectory of the platform relative to the hurricane track, and (5) notes. Our hypothesis is that the platforms of similar distances from the eye of the hurricane would experience similar winds and have similar trajectories. The table is sorted from greatest to shortest distance from the hurricane track. Note that there is a rough trend for smaller angles with greater distances from the hurricane track. We expect the Rowan Fort Worth would have an overall trajectory toward the shoreline between 15 and 45 deg (clockwise) relative to the hurricane track, which translates to 325 ???€? 355 deg T (clockwise). The Deep Nautilus and the Noble Therald Martin have shorter tracks than the others. Since we believe the real trajectories traveled an arc initially more to the ???€?left???€?, we think these do fit with our analysis. Thus the search area for the Rowan Fort Worth would be in the general direction of 325 ???€? 355 deg T (clockwise) with the long boundaries skewed somewhat to the left as shown in the graphic. At approximately 0800 hours on December 16, 2005 a leaking valve was first observed at the Conoco-Phillips Rahway River Tank Field, adjacent to the Rahway River, New Jersey.  The valve was immediately replaced and the discharge of oil/water was stopped.  The product was primarily discharged off site at the edge of the property where it slopes down to the perimeter of the closed Linden Landfill.  The released product was a mixture of No. 2 heating oil (red dyed) and water.  Data from tank guages indicate 1,950 barrels of oil/water are unaccounted for.  Clean-up response includes vacuum trucks and deflection/exclusion booming operations in the Rahway River. Habitats at risk include wetlands, mudflats and river/estuary.  Oiled wildlife has been reported. [SEP] Photo from EPA OSC of the Conoco Philips spill area. The photo is date stamped the 12/16/2005 but is believed to be from 12/17/2005 [SEP] Tidal Heights - Rahway River [SEP] From Frank Csulak, 12/18/05 Description of Incident On Friday, 12/16/05 at 0800 hours Conoco Phillips discovered that an oil spill took place at their Rahway River Tank Field located in Linden, NJ. It is believed that the cause of the spill was due to a frozen pipeline valve that cracked due to frozen water in the line. The pipe, which burst at the valve, empties 18 above ground oil storage tanks. Conoco Phillips, US EPA, and NJDEP has estimated that 84,000 gallons of a heating fuel oil (No. 2 oil) and water mix was released. The oil then flowed into a nearby wetland area, the Rahway River and the Arthur Kill waterway. Officials estimate that maybe as much as 10,000 gallons of oil entered the water. Conoco Phillipps Bayway Refinery, which owns the refinery and pipelines has assumed the role of the Responsible Party. Linden, NJ is a mixed use of commercial, residential, and industrial uses. Newark International Airport is located just to the north of the spill site and the NJ Turnpike is located to the just to the west of the spill site. Staten Island, NY is located on the eastern side of the Arthur Kill. The primary areas of concern include the Rahway River, the Arthur Kill and it associated tributaries, Pralls Island, and several wetland restoration sites located along both the NJ and Staten Island, NY shorelines. Description of Cleanup Response Ed Levine, NOAA???€?s SSC has provided both on-scene and off-scene scientific support to the FOSC and SOSC, including aerial overflight support, mapping, trajectory information and information on the spilled oil. As of today the following Federal, State and local agencies and organizations have responded to the incident, including USEPA, USCG, NYDEC, NJDEP, NJ State Police, City of Linden, Union County Emergency Management, Tri-State Bird and Rescue, and NOAA. The USEPA is serving as FOSC. An Incident Action Plan and Site Safety Plans have been prepared and made available to all responders. Approximately 200 contractors have been brought in to clean up the spill. A number of skimmer vessels and vacuume trucks are working the area. Several lines of booms have been placed across the Rahway River. Clean-up contractors are also on-scene including Miller Marine and Clean Harbors. I have not been able to obtain any information on amount of product recovered. The Command Center is located at the Conoco Phillips Refinery, Linden, NJ. Trajectory The oil within Arthur Kill has been primarily moving with the tides, while the winds are expected to keep the oil to the eastern (Staten Island) side of the Kill. The northern extent of the oil has moved north to the Goethals Bridge and the southern extent to the Outer Bridge Crossing, with the southern extent possibly moving as far downstream as the Raritan River. Description of Damage Assessment Response NOAA is the only trustee on-scene, although I have communicated with John Sacco from NJDEP???€?s Office of Natural Resource Damages. I have not seen anyone from NYSDEC, NYC Parks or DOI???€?s FWS for NRDA purposes. Neither NOAA GC or RC have been involved with the response. Plan is to coordinate with NYSDEC, NYC Parks and USFWS as required. Conoco Phillips has contracted with ENTRIX and Shaw Environmental Services for NRDA support. I have informally invited the RP to conduct a cooperative assessment and they have agreed. The RP has provided NOAA with overflights and access to their contractors. Source oil sample has been collected and split with one sample for NOAA and one for the RP. Water and sediment samples have been collected at numerous locations in the Rahway River, Arthur Kill and associated wetland and shoreline area for both reference and impact areas. All samples are being maintained and stored. No arrangements have been made for analysis at this time. Photographs of spill area have been taken of the affected areas. Potential for Damage Assessment NOAA trustee resources potentially at risk include wetlands, shorelines, finfish, shellfish, benthic habitat and water column. Due to the time of year finfish and shellfish are not in great abundant, although there are several fish species that over winter in the local waterways, including perch, striped bass, and flounder. Impacts to recreational activities such as boating would be expected to be minimal, if at all because of the time of year and lack of recreational activities taking place in this area. There haven???€?t been any navigational, fishery, or park closures reported. No T&E species concerns to my knowledge. Other trustee resources potentially at risk include several bird groups including waterfowl, geese, and gulls, although very few have been observed. Several oiled geese have been observed and at least one was captured for rehabilitation by Tri-State but died. One oiled rabbit has also died despite heroic efforts to save it. At a minimum it is expected that there will be wetland impacts. There are Red Maple, fragmitties and spartina wetlands along the Rahway River that have been exposed to the oil. There have also been spartina wetlands along the Arthur Kill that have been exposed to the oil. In total an estimated 5-10 acres of wetlands have been oiled. Terrapin habitat may also been exposed to the oil based on ESI maps. Significant Events for the Next 24 Hours Need to coordinate with NJDEP, NYSDEC, NYC Parks, and USFWS for the purposes of bringing the trustees up to date on the incident and discuss future plans. Need to coordinate with NOAA HAZMAT, DAC, RC and GC programs. Continue collecting water and sediment samples as needed. Continue to coordinate with RP and co-trustees. The 68-foot fishing vessel SKY SUN ran aground on the eastern shore of the Big Island.  The longline fishing vessel is loaded with 3,000 gallons of diesel and has 4 tons of fish on board. Position reported at 37 deg 24.2???€?N, 077 deg 23.6???€? W. By 0915 EST the leak was reported subsided, but a later report at 1036 EST observed more product escaping. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP as it would affect any trajectory implications. ______________________________________________________ 1) 24-hour Wind Forecast Today through Tonight, the winds are predicted to be from the S to SE at 10-15 knots with gust to 22 knots. Tuesday, the winds are forecast to be from the S at 15-20 knots shifting in the afternoon with the passage of a cold front to be from the NW at 10-15 knots. Rain Tuesday may raise the river as much as 5-6 feet (still below flood stage). 2) TRAJECTORY Oil released is expected to sink to the bottom. Movement of oil on the bottom depends on how the oil behaves as it cools in the water of the James River. If the oil is soft, and sticky it may stay on the bottom locally where it was spilled. If the oil breaks into solid tarballs, we expect these could roll around on the bottom with the bottom currents. Tides over the next few days have a maximum current of 1.1 knots leading to a tidal excursion of 3-4 nm. The freshet of water associated with tomorrow???€?s rains could wash the oil further downriver, as much as 10 nm during the even. [SEP] Evening Report 25 November 2005 This morning the NOAA SSC met with representatives of the PR DNRA, EQB, underwater archeologist, and rangers to conduct an underwater survey of the grounding site. After several attempts we were able to locate the position of the ship where it was sitting on the bottom. We marked an area approximately 600???€? X 75???€? (17?? 57.613???€? N / 066?? 46.138???€? W & 17?? 57.524???€? N / 066?? 46.122???€? W). Preliminary survey indicates the area was flattened by the tanker and was not as barren as first surmised. The bottom had spur and groove bottom topography that was fairly level. There was evidence of a benthic community consisting of hard coral (brain and staghorn), soft coral, sea fans, sponges, and algae on the bottom. The DNRA staked the area and took some initial photographs. They plan to return next week to do a more in-depth survey. The site is in approximately 30 (+/-) feet of water. The local NOAA NMFS Enforcement officer has been notified. The impact site is within three nautical miles of the coast (within state territorial waters). From this initial survey it appears that the DNRA should have the lead on any damage assessment and NOAA should be available to support this assessment as necessary. During a morning conference call with the USCG and all interested parties the COTP announced that the vessel was cleared to depart since the bottom survey showed no significant damage. All boom will be removed from the water today. The investigation into the cause of the incident continues. [SEP] Sector Portland reported that at approximately 1400 Friday November 11 the 60 foot crabbing vessel F/ V Bold Contender was floating upside down about 2 nm offshore of Depoe Bay at Cape Foulweather with a potential of 6000 gallons of diesel and 300 gallons of hydraulic oil onboard. Reported coordinates were 44 45.98 N and 124 07.0 W. A light sheen was observed in the vicinity of the vessel. Based on the weather forecast, NOAA ORR estimated that the vessel, if it remained afloat, would ground to the north somewhere between Cascade Head and Cape Lookout before noon on Saturday November 12. Model results indicated all but approximately 15% of the diesel fuel would evaporate and disperse within 4 hours of a catastrophic release under current weather conditions. [SEP] Frame grab from the video of the submerged oil in the scour trench at the eastern end of the scour trench [SEP] Situation Update 01 January 2006 Recovery and discovery operations continue. The heaviest concentrations of oil observed thus far are in the vicinity of the pipeline located about 1 ?? NM west of the former barge location, although exhaustive surveys have yet to be completed further west and east of this location. Diver assisted recovery has led to the collection of approximately 1900 Bbls of oil as of 1300 01/01/06. The process is slow and involves two divers using shop vac hose attachments, crawling along the bottom, and sucking in the oil while controlling flow with a quarter turn ball valve. Very little sediment and relatively little water is collected using this method. However, a diver can expect to only cover about 100 square feet of oiled bottom in an hour on the bottom. There is on average one diver down at a time. Visibility has been low and has limited ROV operation efficiency and effectiveness. The bottom seems to be stirred up and in motion even with low surface activity (3ft 7sec swells). As a result of this motion, oil mats appear to be breaking into smaller snake like pieces aligned with the bottom sand ripples (see FTP:// video from 12-31). Finding another, more capable ROV is ongoing. The long term monitoring plan has been implemented. Snare filled crab pots are being deployed and checked in accordance with the plan agreed to by the unified command. No hits have been observed beyond those previously reported (seven miles west). NOAA Fisheries has issued a fishery advisory for the area. This advisory remains in effect. Several shrimping boats have been observed within the safety zone over the past few days. A side scan sonar will re-arrive on scene tomorrow. Its primary purpose will be to map the debris field where the barge salvage operations occurred. Its secondary purpose will be to investigate its oil detection abilities and possibly map out the distribution field. A test is planned. On November 6 a citizen reported observing pools of mercury in the surf zone on the beach approximately one half mile north of the jetty at the Siuslaw River entrance.  Approximate dimensions reported were 3 x 11 feet.  A sample was collected by the citizen and later confirmed to be mercury after analysis by NRC. An extensive survey was conducted of the location where the citizen reported the mercury but no mercury was found. [SEP] The shoreline area in Florence, Oregon where mercury pools had been reported by a citizen on Sunday was surveyed again today for any indication of mercury contamination. Pits dug along a survey grid in the area were examined visually and monitored with a Jerome mercury vapor analyzer. No mercury was detected. Sand samples from the immediate area were collected for laboratory chemical analysis. All contaminated sand collected by the cleanup crew yesterday was found in the upland dune, where a sample of the mercury collected in the surf zone by the reporting citizen on Sunday had been carried and later spilled. Unable to find any indication of remaining mercury contamination after two days of surveying and monitoring during the low tide, the Unified Command reopened the beach and demobilized the command post by the end of the day. NOAA personnel on-scene (departing Wednesday morning): Ruth Yender, Scientific Support Coordinator Jim Farr, Chemist [SEP] A hotline has been opened for a mercury release near Florence on the central Oregon coast. [SEP] On November 6, 2005 a citizen reported observing pools of mercury in the surf zone on the beach approximately one half mile north of the jetty at the Siuslaw River entrance. The SSC was contacted Oct 17 at 1100 am concerning an mystery slick on the Maumee River In Toledo, Ohio. The oil appeared to be waste oil and was seen floating between the Martin Luther King Bridge and the I 280 Bridge. The volume was estimated to be between 500 - 5000 gallons. Early reports indicated no shoreline or wildlife impacts, although there were reports of oiled vessels. The oil did not match any vessels in the area during the spill. A sewer outfall on the eastern shore near the MLK bridge was indicated as a possible source. An overflight showed heavy sheens and free product from the MLK bridge to the CSX railroad bridge. Scattered pockets of oil were seen on both banks. Shoreline impacts seem to be mostly in areas of riprap. A marina south of the MLK bridge on the east bank acted as a natural collection point. There were no known impacts to wildlife. A local clean up contractor recovered oil along an area of riprap. Information in the report is based on a spill of approximately 500 to 5,000 gallons of unknown product (reported as sheen) released in the Maumee River between the I-280 and Martin Luther King, Jr. Bridge, approximately 3 miles above its confluence with Lake Erie. II. Geographic Region Covered The area covered by this report includes the Maumee River, from the Martin Luther King, Jr. Bridge to the confluence of the river and Lake Erie, and Maumee Bay in Lake Erie from the Ohio/Michigan border east to South Shore Park. This area does not necessarily correspond to actual or potential oil locations. Consult other Hotline reports for oil location information. III. Shoreline Resources at Risk The shoreline along the Maumee River is highly developed and is composed primarily of riprap, solid man-made structures, and shelving bedrock shores. Grassy Island and the soil disposal areas adjacent to the mouth of the river, as well as the Bay shoreline to the northwest of the river mouth, are also primarily riprap and solid man-made structures. A few small wetland areas are present near the mouth of river, primarily in Otter Creek and behind Bay View Park. There are a few, small, sand beaches backed with low banks interspersed with riprap and solid man-made structures in the eastern portion of Maumee Bay. The small islands in Maumee Bay along the ship channel are shelving bedrock shores backed by mixed sand-and-gravel beaches. The most sensitive habitats in the area are wetlands, which are often highly productive, serving as important wildlife habitat and nursery areas for fish. Marsh vegetation can experience severe stress or mortality if it becomes oiled, especially if oil penetrates or becomes mixed into the sediments. Where wetland sediments are muddy and soft, it is important to prevent excessive disturbance and further mixing of oil into the substrate by foot traffic during cleanup activities, as this could result in more severe and long-term impacts to the marshes. In general, gasoline, diesel or other lighter products form thin slicks and are unlikely to accumulate in large amounts against the shoreline. Heavier or more persistent oil may adhere to piers or other harbor structures and penetrate between riprap boulders. Chronic sheening problems are possible for riprap and other permeable manmade shoreline types, especially in sheltered areas. On sandy beaches, burial of oil is possible, but penetration is unlikely. Penetration is possible on sand-and-gravel beaches. Depending on the stickiness of the oil, it is possible that it may also adhere to surfaces on exposed, shelving bedrock shores. IV. Biological Resources at Risk Fish Several species of commercial and recreational value may be present in the Maumee River and western Lake Erie, including: alewife, chinook and coho salmon, rainbow smelt, brown trout, northern pike, bluegill, white crappie, black crappie, yellow perch, largemouth and smallmouth bass, rock bass, pumpkinseed, walleye, white bass, channel catfish, brook trout (state threatened), fathead minnow, shorthead redhorse, white sucker, brown bullhead, green sunfish, grass pickerel, sauger, freshwater drum, and lake sturgeon (state threatened). Acute toxicity to water column organisms may be possible, particularly for gasoline, diesel or other lighter products with larger proportions of water-soluble components. Larval and juvenile fish inhabiting shallow waters, or wetland areas could be the most vulnerable to spill impacts. Birds Several species of shorebirds, wading birds, diving birds, waterfowl, raptors, gulls and terns are present throughout the area during the fall. State listed birds that may be present in the area include peregrine falcon (state endangered), bald eagle (state endangered, federally threatened) American bittern (state endangered), least bittern (state threatened), black-crowned night heron (state threatened), great egret (state species of concern), king rail (state endangered), Virginia rail (state species of concern), sora rail (state species of concern), and upland sandpiper (state threatened). Waterfowl may be in fall migration at this time of year, and may be passing through the area. Concentrations of herring and ring-billed gulls, and common terns (state endangered) are typically present in the spoil disposal areas near the mouth of the river during the spring and summer and may remain in the area. Waterfowl are usually at high risk during oil spills because they spend nearly all their time on the water surface. Wading birds, gulls, terns, and raptors can also be severely impacted by oil in some cases. Waterfowl and wading birds may be directly oiled and can become oiled on the upper body and feathers by coming in contact with oiled vegetation or wrack. Direct oiling of birds reduces the buoyancy, water repellency, and insulation provided by feathers, and may result in death by drowning or hypothermia. Preening of oiled feathers may also result in ingestion of oil resulting in irritation, sickness, or death. Bird oiling, particularly waterfowl and wading birds, may continue even after the floating oil slicks have been removed, depending on the extent of oiled vegetation. Mammals Muskrats may be present in wetland habitats throughout the area. These species can be severely impacted by swimming through oil slicks or contacting oiled marsh vegetation. Matting of the fur due to oiling results in impacts similar to those described for birds. Grooming of contaminated fur can also result in sickness or death depending on the amount of oil ingested. V. Human-Use Resources at Risk The coast of Lake Erie is a high-use recreational area. Activities include use of recreational beaches, fishing, hunting, boating, and other water activities. Several boat ramps, marinas, and hoists occur in the Maumee River and near the river mouth. The area had been subject to mystery spills before, but not to the point where cleanup was initiated. The responders cleaned approximately 200 yards of shoreline along the southern end of the bridge and the small cove south of the spill site. Three dead oiled birds were collected. Responders estimated that the spill consisted of 2-5 barrels of oil fresh oil and noted an equivalent amount of weathered oil that had stained the rip-rap along the shoreline. After the initial gross oil was removed, the responders noticed heavy staining of sediments in the intertidal, small tarballs surfacing and spreading into sheens, and oil oozing from the shoreline. Upon further inspection, the TGLO and USCG noticed heavy asphalt pavement in the area, both above and below the high tide line. The TGLO suspected that Hurricane Rita may have eroded the shoreline and exposed a historic spill site or industrial operation, and began researching the industrial history of the site. The bridge was built in the 50???€?s. The 1-2 acre parcel of land to the west of the bridge was isolated by the bridge construction. The site is owned by Union Pacific Railroad. The railroad initial had larger holdings in the area but sold them, and reported believed they had also sold the shoreside parcel. However, TGLO determined that UP continues to own the site and has been paying the taxes. TGLO and USCG both consider UP to be the responsible party for the site and UP unhappily has accepted preliminary responsibility for the cleanup and site investigation. The USCG initially opened the pollution response under Hurricane Rita ESF-10 funding, but has now notified the RP that the case will be pursued under OPA since the hurricane did not cause the spill but just exposed the incident. The TGLO found that the site was used as a shipyard during World War II, under the name Kane Shipping. At that time, the site had a small tank battery of fuel oil tanks. The TGLO believes that shoreline erosion from Hurricane Rita has exposed the historic footprint of at least one of these tanks. No tanks are present at the site now, but circular depressions are visible. The USCG requested NOAA???€?s assistance in determining how far to clean the site. Additionally, the USCG would like assistance in reviewing and overseeing the RP???€?s site investigation. Thus far, the site investigation has been very preliminary. The RP???€?s consultants have dug multiple cores for visual inspection. Oil has been found up to 5 feet below the surface. This initial scoping effort will be used to design a more thorough investigation. The TGLO has requested that meeting with the RP be held at 11:00 am on Friday, October 14, at the USCG Marine Safety Unit in Galveston to discuss further steps at the site. NOAA is invited and encouraged to participate. [SEP] There were no follow-up requests for support made to the NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator on this incident. On October 3, 2005, a fatal crash between a SUV and gasoline tank truck on theSeven Mile Bridge near Marathon, FL, resulted in a large fire and release ofgasoline and fire fighting foam into the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary. The burning fuel truck was extinguished using Aqueous Fire Fighting Foam(AFFF).  NOAA HAZMAT was requested to provide information on the potential fateof the spilled gasoline and AFFF.  Given the relatively small volumes involved,we believe that discernible impacts are unlikely.  However, recent concernsregarding the environmental impacts from AFFF suggest that sampling of bivalvesand corals adjacent to the bridge might be prudent. The accident resulted in a large fire and release of gasoline and fire fighting foam into the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary [SEP] Gasoline Tank Truck Accident- 7 Mile Bridge, Florida Keys. Summary: On October 3, 2005, a fatal crash between a SUV and gasoline tank truck on the Seven Mile Bridge near Marathon, FL, resulted in a large fire and release of gasoline and fire fighting foam into the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary. The burning fuel truck was extinguished using Aqueous Fire Fighting Foam (AFFF). NOAA HAZMAT was requested to provide information on the potential fate of the spilled gasoline and AFFF. Given the relatively small volumes involved, we believe that discernible impacts are unlikely. However, recent concerns regarding the environmental impacts from AFFF suggest that sampling of bivalves and corals adjacent to the bridge might be prudent. Background The situation as described by the USCG and FDEP suggest that relatively small amounts of unburned gasoline entered the waterway during this incident. Reportedly, 35 gallons of the firefighting agent AFFF were expended in extinguishing the fire. The most water soluble fractions (WSFs) of gasoline are the monoaromatic hydrocarbons, and include benzene, toluene and the xylene isomers. These are all in significant concentration in gasoline. However, these compounds have high vapor pressures and are likely to pose no major contamination problems in the water column. Studies at the Naval Supply Station Laboratory, Calif. have shown benzene/toluene concentrations in saltwater over a 24 hour period to be less than 1mg/L (1ppm) for both contaminants. Observations from the scene of this incident suggest that very little gasoline entered the saltwater environment; hence???€?based on this information???€?we believe the environmental consequences of the gasoline release will be minimal. Personnel from NAS Key West were reported to have used 35 gallons of AFFF foam to fight the fire. AFFF has been the primary firefighting agent used in aviation settings. However, concerns about "PBT," or persistence, bioaccumulation, and toxicity led the 3M Corporation, a major producer of AFFF, to announce in 2000 that it intended to cease manufacture of these and other fluorocarbon-based surfactant products. The specific chemical of environmental concern is the product of biological degradation of AFFF constituents called perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS). PFOS is persistent and is not known to degrade under natural conditions, and it has been shown to bioaccumulate. A 3M study showed that elevated doses of PFOS administered to adult rats caused toxic reactions in offspring. Low levels of PFOS have been found in fish and birds including those from remote oceanic locations. Use of PFOS precursors has been so widespread, and the chemical is so persistent that every person in the U.S. may be carrying low levels in his/her body. Human toxicology studies show that PFOS is absorbed orally and then distributes in serum and in the liver. Human toxic levels are believed to manifest themselves at concentrations two orders of magnitude higher than exposed 3M workers and four orders of magnitude higher than levels found in the general population; however, toxicity effects of PFOS are considered significant. Although acute environmental toxicity results are few, LC50 concentrations for test organisms like fathead minnow, rainbow trout, bluegill, and water flea fall into a similar range between 200 and 1500 parts per million. Because of the persistence of the degradation products in AFFF, if there are coral reef resources in the immediate vicinity of the incident, it may be prudent to monitor levels of PFOS in the environment to determine if there is any cause for concern or a need for further monitoring.

[SEP] Lake Calcasieu coastal RAR: Resources at Risk for Louisiana Coast from Calcasieu Lake to White Lake I. Spill Source Information This report was prepared at 4:00 pm EDT on October 3, 2005. Information in the report is a general overview of the resources in the area. II. Geographic Region Covered The area covered by this report is the shoreline from Calcasieu Lake to White Lake. This area does not necessarily correspond to actual or potential oil locations. Consult other Hotline reports for oil location information. III. Expected Behavior of the Spilled Material This report is not based on any particular product but a general overview of the resources in the area. IV. Shoreline Resources at Risk The predominant shoreline from Calcesieu Lake to White Lake are sand beaches (including fine, medium-, and coarse-grained, and mixed sand and gravel) backed by marshes. At the eastern end of this section of shoreline the sand beaches have been replaced by exposed tidal flats. All the wetland areas behind the beaches are marshes. The inlets to Calcasieu Lake and Mud Lake are protected by riprap groins. V. Biological Resources at Risk Included are general statements about the effects of oil on the various biological resources. The effects may vary based on the type of contaminant, since the behavior, toxicity, and availability of the material can vary from product to product. Fish - Fish present in the lakes and inland waters include, but are not limited to, Atlantic croaker, bay anchovy (spawning), gulf menhaden, pinfish, red drum (spawning), striped mullet, gray snapper, sheepshead, silver perch, and spotted seatrout (spawning). In the Gulf of Mexico waters gulf sturgeon (federally threatened) may also be present in low concentrations. Juvenile fish are usually present all year. In general, juvenile and larval fish are more sensitive to spilled oil than adults. Fish in shallow water areas are more likely to be impacted, due to the potential for a higher concentration of oil in the water column. Surface slicks usually do not have much of an impact on fish. Shellfish - Shellfish present in the area include blue crab, brown shrimp, pink shrimp, white shrimp, and Gulf stone crab. There also low concentrations of bay squid in the lakes and other inland waters. Oyster lease beds are present in Calcasieu Lake. Juvenile stages of all of these shellfish may also be present in the area. Shellfish in shallow water areas are more likely to be impacted, due to the potential for a higher concentration of oil in the water column. Surface slicks usually do not have much of an impact on crabs and shrimp. Crabs, oysters, and other benthic invertebrates may be contaminated by a heavy sinking oil. Birds - October is the beginning of the migratory/overwintering season for waterfowl, so there may be numerous waterfowl in the marshes. Scaup are present in open waters of the lakes and in the nearshore gulf waters. Piping plover (federally threatened) and other shorebirds are on the sand beaches of the gulf shoreline. Wading birds (roseate spoonbill and egrets) may be on some of the shorelines around the lakes. Least terns are also present in the area. Waterfowl are usually at greatest risk during oil spills, because they spend nearly all of their time on the water surface. Waterfowl and wading birds may be directly oiled and can become oiled on the upper body and feathers by coming in contact with oiled vegetation or wrack. Shorebirds usually avoid oil, but may be impacted by loss of feeding areas or intertidal prey, particularly during migration periods. Terns may be at risk because they are often attracted to and will prey on sick or injured prey which may result in oiling of feathers and the ingestion of oil. Oiling of birds reduces the buoyancy, water repellency, and insulation provided by feathers, and may result in death by drowning or hypothermia. Preening of oiled feathers may also result in ingestion of oil causing irritation, sickness, or death. Bird oiling, particularly for waterfowl and wading birds, may continue even after floating oil slicks have been removed, depending on the extent of oiled vegetation. Mammals - Raccoon, mink, muskrat, river otter, and nutria may be found throughout the wetlands and inland waters of this area. As with birds, oiling of these animals may reduce buoyancy, water repellency, and insulation provided by the fur, and may result in death by drowning or hypothermia. Grooming of oiled fur may also result in ingestion of oil causing irritation, sickness, or death. The spilled material may also cause irritation to organs such as the eyes as well as the mucous membranes. Reptiles - American alligator (federally threatened) is found throughout brackish to freshwater marshes. The diamondback terrapin are also in some of the wetland areas. There may be sea turtles in the coastal waters of the Gulf of Mexico. Oil may cause irritation and inflammation of the mucus membranes, especially around the eyes and nostrils, in all of these reptiles. Habitats - There are rare wetland plants throughout the coastal area. Louisiana Natural Heritage Program (Phone: 225-765-2821) can be contacted to obtain exact information on species and location of these plants. VI. Human-Use Resources at Risk Cameron Prairie National Wildlife Refuge is on the south and east sides of Calcasieu Lake. Rockefeller State Wildlife Refuge covers the coastal zone from about 92 55???€? East to 92 30???€? East.. [SEP] MODIS Sept 25, 2005 NOAA Coastwatch [SEP] SLOSH Model run for Hurricane Rita, produced from NHC advisory #25: 4:00pm CDT, Friday, Sept 23, 2005 This image is the result of a run of the SLOSH (Sea, Lake and Overland Surges from Hurricanes) model. SLOSH is a computerized model run by the National Hurricane Center (NHC) to estimate storm surge heights and winds resulting from predicted hurricanes by taking into account Pressure, Size, Forward speed, Track, and Winds. The colors correspond to the maximum predicted elevation of the water surface at each location as the storm passes over the coastline. Perhaps most useful, however, is not the predicted height, but the predicted extent of flooding. The image gives a quick estiime of the area likely to be flooded. These predictions are derived from the latest NHC forecast storm track at the time of the model run. As there is uncertainty in the forecast for the storm track, there is also uncertainty in the estimates for storm surge. The maximum surge could be either to the east or west of the predicted location. For more information about SLOSH, see: http://www.nhc.noaa.gov/HAW2/english/surge/slosh.shtml [SEP] This deck barge was washed ashore into a residential front yard. Photo taken 10/03/05. However, most of the fish are pushed along the south bank (not visible because of tree shadow). Fish kills were reported in a number of the East Texas/West Louisiana inland waters following Hurricanes Rita and Katrina. Hurricanes and tropical storms commonly cause low dissolved oxygen levels in shallow bays and estuaries. Oxygen levels can drop for a variety of storm-induced reasons, including nutrient buildup followed by algae blooms. Also, storms can drive oxygen-depleted water from marshes into fish habitats. The exact causes of the fish kills that have followed Hurricane Rita aren't yet known for sure. Photo taken 09/30/05. NOAA. [SEP] Resources at Risk for Jourdan River, Mississippi I. Spill Source Information This report was prepared at 10:30 am EDT on September 14, 2005. Information in the report is a general overview of the resources in the area. II. Geographic Region Covered The area covered by this report is Jourdan River. This area does not necessarily correspond to actual or potential spill locations. Consult other Hotline reports for location information. III. Expected Behavior of the Spilled Material This report is not based on a spill of any specific product but does provide a general overview of the resources in the area. IV. Shoreline Resources at Risk The shoreline of Jourdan River is mostly salt marsh. Shorelines associated with the canals are sheltered solid man-made structures. V. Biological Resources at Risk Included are general statements about the effects of oil on the various biological resources. The effects may vary based on the type of contaminant, since the behavior, toxicity, and availability of the material can vary from product to product. Fish - Numerous species of fish are present at this time of year including, but not limited to, Atlantic croaker (spawning), bay anchovy (spawning), catfish, gulf menhaden, silversides (spawning), red drum (spawning), silver perch, southern kingfish, spot, sand seatrout, spotted seatrout, stripped mullet, southern flounder, and threadfin shad. In general juvenile and larval fish are most sensitive to spilled oil. Fish in shallow water areas are more likely to be impacted, since there is likely to be a higher concentration of oil in the water column. Surface slicks usually do not have much of an impact on fish. Shellfish - Shellfish in the area include blue crab (spawning), Brown shrimp, pink shrimp (spawning), and white shrimp (spawning). There are oyster beds in Saint Louis Bay at the mouth of the Jourdan River. Juvenile and larval life stages of all of these shellfish are also present in the area. Shellfish in shallow water areas are more likely to be impacted, since it is more probable that there is a higher concentration of oil in the water column. Surface slicks usually do not have much of an impact on crabs and shrimp. Crabs and oysters may be contaminated by a heavy sinking oil. Birds - Present in the area are numerous species of shorebirds, wading birds, osprey, white pelican, brown pelican (federally endangered), bald eagle (federally threatened), peregrine falcon, osprey, mottled duck, terns, double-crested cormorant, common loon, and gulls. October is the beginning of the migratory and overwintering season for waterfowl. Large numbers of waterfowl may be in the area starting in October. Diving birds (pelicans, cormorants) and waterfowl are usually at greatest risk during oil spills, because they spend nearly all their time on the water surface. Waterfowl and wading birds may be directly oiled, and can become oiled on the upper body and feathers by coming in contact with oiled vegetation or wrack. Shorebirds usually avoid oil, but may be impacted by loss of feeding areas or intertidal prey, particularly during migration periods. Gulls, terns, and raptors may be at risk because they are often attracted to and will prey on sick or injured prey. This behavior may result in oiling of feathers and the ingestion of oil. Oiling of birds reduces the buoyancy, water repellency, and insulation provided by feathers, and may result in death by drowning or hypothermia. Preening of oiled feathers may also result in ingestion of oil resulting in irritation, sickness, or death. Bird oiling, particularly for waterfowl and wading birds, may continue even after the floating oil slicks have been removed, depending on the extent of oiled vegetation. Mammals - Beaver, mink, muskrat, raccoon, nutria, river otter, and wild hogs may be found throughout the wetlands and waterways of this area. As with the birds oiling of these animals may reduce buoyancy, water repellency, and insulation provided by the fur, and may result in death by drowning or hypothermia. Grooming of oiled fur may also result in ingestion of oil which may subsequently lead to irritation, sickness, or death. The spilled material may also cause irritation to organs such as the eyes as well as the mucous membranes. Reptiles - American alligator (federally threatened), Gulf salt marsh snake, and Mississippi diamondback terrapin are present in these waters at this time. The terrapins are nesting and hatching at this time of year. Oil may cause irritation and inflammation of the mucus membranes, especially around the eyes and nostrils, in all of these reptiles. VI. Human-Use Resources at Risk There are several boat ramps and marinas located near the mouth of Jourdan River. Also along the shorelines are numerous archaeological sites. [SEP] This photo is a ground-level view of some of the larger vessels that our survey team saw from the air. Owners of vessels of this size and value typically have the resources to work with salvage contractors and develop salvage plans. A process has been established to have their salvage plans reviewed by "Trustees." Trustees are those organizations in Government who have been assigned by law the responsibility of protecting specific natural resources for the American public. Notice the size of the vessel with 40-foot containers and cars. These shipments have been delayed. Crude oil spill into the Mississippi River from two damaged storage tanks at Bass Enterprises. Location is near mile marker 35 in Plaquemines Parish, LA. Each tank measures 16' high and 290' in diameter.  About 88,000 to 90,000 bbl have been released, with 10,000 bbl remaining in the tanks.  A large amount of oil is contained in the berm, but a significant amount of oil was lost to both the river and adjacent marsh.  Much of the oil ended up on the downriver side of the facility.  Cleanup in these areas was intense and in-situ burninig took place.  Stage 1 cleanup efforts were finished by 20DEC05.  All zones were in Stage 3 on 09FEB06. Refer to current Oil Budget and Resource Summary for details. *1) Total volume of recovered oil revised ???€? Daily quantities of oil recovered are based on the number/capacity of vacuum trucks discharging each day. This volume was reconciled based on measurements of the volume of oil and water contained in the Recovered Oil Tank (150-2). The total volume was increased by 175 bbls. 2) Total volume evaporated ???€? The volume of oil evaporated was originally estimated at 40% of the amount spilled using the ADIOS 2 model. The estimated amount evaporated had been reduced to 30% because we believe the ADIOS model will overstate the amount evaporated because it is designed to estimate evaporation of spills from open water. The oil spilled was contained in deeper pools than would occur with an open water spill due to the containment areas and canals in which most of the oil collected. The evaporation estimate has further been reduced to 28%. 3) Onshore volume revised ???€? The volume of oil remaining onshore has been reduced to reflect shoreline washing operations conducted this week. 4) Floating, Contained volume revised ???€? The volume of oil estimated to be floating, contained was revised based on the volume changes to the other categories.* [SEP] INCIDENT: MURPHY OIL Location: Meraux, LA. Mile Marker 87. [SEP] Date: 1400 EDT September 2, 2005 To: NOAA SSC Brad Benggio  FROM: NOAA/Hazardous Materials Response Division Modeling and Simulation Studies Seattle, WA 98115  SUBJECT: F/V Mr Natural, adrift offshore Sarasota Bay, FL FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION, PLEASE CONTACT CJ Beegle-Krause MODELING AND SIMULATION STUDIES, NOAA, SEATTLE, WA 98115. PHONE (206) 526-4911. ______________________________________________________ We have looked at the trajectory implications of a drifting vessel offshore Sarasota Bay FL. These notes are based on the following information: The F/V Mr Natural was reported adrift since 26 August 2005 30 nm south of Cape Romano. On 31 August 1950 hours the vessel was reported at 27o 17.8???€?N, 082 o 59.6???€?W; today at 0830 hours the vessel was reported at 27o 12.416???€?N, 082 o 53.367???€?W. Maximum potential fuel onboard is reported to be 4,000 gallons of diesel. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP, as it would affect any trajectory implications. ______________________________________________________ 1) 24-hour Wind Forecast Today through Tonight, the winds are predicted to be from the NE at 10-15 knots. Saturday, the winds are expected to continue from the NE at 10-15 knots. 2) TRAJECTORY The vessel is currently drifting at slightly more than 0.2 knots downcoast. We expect the vessel to continue to move downcoast, covering about 5.2 nm per day, and staying outside the 10 fathom isobath. If the fuel were lost from the vessel, a sheen extending downwind and downcurrent could be visible for at most 1/2 nm. Any fuel lost is not expected to reach the coast. 3) OIL FATE Diesel Light refined products, such as diesel (or Fuel Oil No 2), typically have very high evaporation rates and do not tend to create persistent slicks. However, the terminology for refined products is not standardized, and, sometimes, heavier intermediate fuel oils are referred to as ???€?marine diesel???€?. These heavier products are much less volatile than normal Fuel Oil no 2 and can form a more persistent slick. When spilled, the diesel spreads quickly into thin films often forming patches of rainbow and silver sheens. Note that lighter refined products do have a relatively high concentration of light aromatic compounds and tend to be more soluble and more toxic than heavier oils. At 0715 on Monday, August 15, well head in the Pass A Loutre Wildlife ManagementArea blew out, spewing crude oil and natural gas into the surrounding freshwatermarsh.  The spill, from Enervest Well #501, is located at 29d 05'45"N, 089d10'09"W released approximately 50 bbls of oil.  Some sheen moved from the immediate area and outthrough Dennis Pass into the Gulf of Mexico, but most of the oil was contained inthe marsh, much of it in two different pockets approximately 200 yards by 150'. Some of the oil stuck in the bordering Roseau cane.  2000' of boom was on-scene as well as 5 skimmers were on-scene.  No wildlife injuries were reported were. [SEP] On Tuesday during cleanup operations it was acknowledged that there was much more oil then initially reported. The current estimate was increased to at least 175 barrels of oil in the water. At the Tuesday evening brief, a SCAT plan was developed for the next day. Today two boats with members of USCG, NOAA, LADEQ, and representatives for the RP covered the spill area to the south and west of the spill source. There are some areas where some emulsified oil has accumulated, but most of the roseau cane seen was either slightly stained or unaffected. The areas further south and west had some sheen in the water, but appeared to be unaffected. The tides appear to be playing a large role in the spill, with two foot tidal changes adjusting the location of the boom. The tidal change also formed a strong current that helped flush out spilled out and sheen. Most of the oil is contained in the containment boom in two different zones, but some sheen is actually moving far enough down Dennis Pass that sheen and water hyasinth is drifting down out into the Gulf of Mexico. There have been no impacts observed along the land from this sheen. SCAT will continue tomorrow, and once completed a detailed map describing the impacted areas will be drawn up. Over 150 barrels of liquid have been recovered on scene from skimmers. Hazing canons were placed on scene this morning and there have been no reported wildlife injuries. The NOAA SSC continues to work the incident. [SEP] As of 1000 Tuesday, the well was under control.
