[SEP] Resources at Risk for Pass a Loutre Wildlife Management Area, LA I. Spill Source Information This report was prepared on 15 August 2005. Information in this report is based on the assumption that an estimated 50 bbl of a condensate/crude oil mix was released into Dennis Pass (29&#8734;05???€?45???€? N, 89&#8734;10???€?09???€?W). II. Geographic Region Covered This report covers Pass a Loutre Wildlife Management Area in the vicinity of Dennis Pass. This report does not necessarily correspond to actual or potential spill locations. Consult other Hotline reports for spill location information. III. Shoreline Resources at Risk Habitats in the area are predominantly freshwater marsh. There are four small sand beach islands in Garden Island Bay, and a few other sand beaches, wave-cut platforms in clay, and sheltered tidal flats along Garden Island Bay. III. Biological Resources at Risk Threatened and Endangered Species Piping plover (federally threatened) may be present approximately 4 miles from the release site on beaches in Garden Island Bay and East Pass. These islands are within the Designated Critical Habitat boundaries as defined by the USFWS. Loggerhead (federally and state threatened) and Kemp???€?s ridley (federally and endangered) sea turtles may be present in Gulf waters in low concentrations. Gulf sturgeon (federally and state threatened) may be present in inland waters.  Other Birds Three colonial waterbird rookeries containing egrets, herons, and ibises occur approximately 2-3 miles from the release site. Nesting activities for most species have likely concluded by August, but young may be present in the area. Mottled duck (3-18 ind/mi2) may be nesting in freshwater marshes. Shorebirds may be migrating through the area. Fish Largemouth bass are present in low concentrations (spawning adults, eggs, larvae, and juveniles) in freshwater marshes. Atlantic croaker (larvae and juveniles, abundant), black drum (larvae and juveniles, common), gulf menhaden (juveniles, highly abundant), red drum (larvae and juveniles, common), sand seatrout (juveniles, abundant), sheepshead (juveniles, common), silver perch (juveniles, common), southern flounder (juveniles, common), spot (juveniles, highly abundant), spotted seatrout (juveniles, common) are present in inland waters in August. Larvae and juveniles are particularly sensitive to the toxic components of oil. Inverts Blue crab (eggs, larvae, and juveniles, highly abundant), brown shrimp (larvae and juveniles, abundant), gulf stone crab (juveniles, common), pink shrimp (larvae and juveniles, common), and white shrimp (larvae and juveniles, common) are present in inland waters in August. Gulf of Mexico estuaries provide Essential Fish Habitat (EFH) for brown shrimp, white shrimp, red drum, Spanish mackerel, cobia, and bluefish. Reptiles and Terrestrial Mammals Alligators may be nesting and hatching in freshwater marshes. Small furbearers are present in marshes. Marine Mammals Bottlenose dolphins may be present in the area. IV. Human-Use The release site is within Pass a Loutre Wildlife Management Area. [SEP] sections of water hyacinth in the marsh with recoverable oil.
The NOAA SSC was contacted in regards to a 4000-gallon spill of calciumchlorides 32% solution.   The solution was spilled in to a storm water sewerdrain.  The drain was approximately 2 miles from Lake Michigan.     The USCGFOSC wanted information on the potential impacts from dilute calcium chloridesolution on the biota in Lake Michigan.    The local fire department waspreparing to flush the storm drain with copious amounts of water.The local fire department ultimately flushed the drain with 3000 gallons ofwater per minute for 3 hours.    The flushing water entered the drain at threedifferent locations on the run to the lake.   The drain entered the lake in anopen area, which would allow for maximum dilution.The USCG reported no impacts from the flushing of the CaCl to Lake Michigan. [SEP] Lake Michigan pipe release of Calcium chloride Storm drain with Calcium chloride (CaCl2) in 35% solution (350,000 ppm): The specific gravity of the calcium chloride solution (35%) is 1.35 relative to freshwater, so the product will sink (on the order of minutes) as it is released from the pipe. Resources at Risk: Freshwater species, including perch. Resources at risk will be those that are in the deeper areas of the Lake. Aquatic toxicity of Calcium Chloride for freshwater species include: &#8721; juvenile bluegill 96 hr LC50 is 8 ppt (8,000 ppm)(ECOTOX). &#8721; freshwater snails 48 hr LC50 3 ppt. (3,000 ppm) Recommendations: The product in the pipe should be diluted before discharge, if possible. To dilute the 4,000 gallons to below an action level of 3 parts per thousand would require that the concentrated solution be diluted and mixed with greater than 400,000 gallons of water. Injection of freshwater should occur at as many points along the route of the storm drain as possible to help the final dilution out the end of the storm drain pipe into the lake. This would help mix and dilute the salt and reduce the concentration measured at the outfall to the lake and minimize exposure of wildlife to high salt concentrations. An underwater diffuser pipe at the end of the discharge would further dilute the solution. If the only means of removing the product is by releasing it to the environment at its original strength, any efforts to increase the rate of mixing once the solution reaches the lake would be helpful. [SEP] At 1230 the NOAA SSC was contacted in regards to a 4000-gallon spill of calcium chlorides 32% solution. The solution was spilled in to a storm water sewer drain. The drain was approximately 2 miles from Lake Michigan. The USCG FOSC wanted information on the potential impacts from dilute calcium chloride solution on the biota in Lake Michigan. The local fire department was preparing to flush the storm drain with copious amounts of water. See the CaCl Michigan document provided by Seattle HAZMAT for information on the impacts to biota. The local fire department ultimately flushed the drain with 3000 gallons of water per minute for 3 hours. The flushing water entered the drain at three different locations on the run to the lake. The drain entered the lake in an open area, which would allow for maximum dilution. A follow-up call was placed to the USCG on Tuesday. The USCG reported no impacts from the flushing of the CaCl to Lake Michigan. [SEP] A hotline has been opened for a calcium chloride spill into a storm drain that flows into Lake Michigan near Kenosha, Wisconsin
On, or before 26 July 2005, the F/V Shirley Girl struck an object in OysterBayou (a small bayou that connects to the Gulf of Mexico in coastal Louisiana)causing it to sink and ground on an oyster reef. The USCG requested NOAA assistance to assessresponse trade-offs. [SEP] The NOAA SSC attended a meeting with the RP and the USCG. The result was a decision to develop a salvage plan. There was no additional support requested by the USCG, and there was no follow up information provided by the USCG. This entry constitutes the Final Report for this incident. [SEP] Resources at Risk (RAR) Near Oyster Bayou, Louisiana Last Updated: August 2, 2005 Area of Interest The F/V Shirley Girl was reported holed and grounded within Oyster Bayou, Louisiana. Active oyster lease sites are reported in the area, and the vessel is thought to be resting on a hard oyster-reef structure. Shoreline and Coastal Resources The shoreline habitat west of the Oyster Bayou consists of predominately gravel (shell-hash) beaches along with mixed sand and shell beaches. The shoreline east of the bayou consists of mixed sand and shell-hash beaches, exposed wave-cut platforms, scarps and steep slopes in clay. On the east side of the inlet to the bayou there is an area of sheltered tidal flats and vegetated low banks. The coastal habitat is almost entirely salt marsh; approximately 1.5 miles east of the Oyster Bayou, there is brackish marsh on Point Au Fer Island. Biological Resources Bird Species The lesser scaup may be found in the GOM October through March. Along the shoreline the gull-billed and the least tern (Mar. ???€? Oct.) may be present. In the salt marsh the following species may be found: American coot (Oct. - Mar.); American wigeon and gadwall (Oct. through Apr.); blue-winged teal (Sep. - Jun.); canvasback, lesser scaup, red-necked duck and hooded merganser (Nov. - Mar.); green-winged teal and northern shoveler (Sep. - Apr.); and northern pintail (Sep. - Mar.). The mottled duck may be found year round. Fish, Reptile and Invertebrate Species There are numerous oyster reef/leases in Oyster Bayou and the southern portion of Fourleague Bay. In the GOM adjacent to the site, the following fish species may be found: black drum, Florida pompano, Gulf menhaden, red drum, sheepshead, southern flounder, Spanish mackerel, spotted seatrout, striped mullet and tarpon. The Gulf sturgeon, a federally endangered specie, may also be found. Brown, pink and white shrimp as well as blue, Florida, and Gulf stone crab are invertebrate species that may be present. In addition to the fish species found in the GOM, the following species may be found in the inland waters of Oyster Bayou: Atlantic croacker, bay anchovy, crevalle jack, gizzard shad, gray snapper, sand seatrout, and silver perch. Also in the inland waters the following invertebrates may be present: bay squid, blue crab and Gulf stone crab, and brown, pink and white shrimp. The American alligator may be found in the salt marshes. Mammals The common raccoon, mink, muskrat, northern river otter, and nutria may all be found present in adjacent salt marsh and inland waters. [SEP] Initial Report (21 July 2005) At least two shrimp boats have been reported in distress or have grounded off the South Texas Coast in the wake of Hurricane Emily. The GOLDEN DRAGON was in-tow, but had to be abandoned due to increasing winds and heavy waves the night of 19 July. An anchor was set before the vessel was abandoned, but the line parted during the night or next morning. At 1300 hrs on 20 July, the GOLDEN DRAGON reported adrift approximately 1.5 miles off the Padre Island National Seashore, and was expected to strand on the shoreline that evening. The GOLDEN DRAGON, a steel hulled fishing vessel, was reported to be carrying 20,000 gallons of diesel. At that time, not much could have been done given the post tropical storm sea state (plus 10 foot seas and 25 knot winds), but the USCG was monitoring the situation and had planned a response when conditions allowed. That was yesterday afternoon. Last evening, the GOLDEN DRAGON stranded aground just off the beach and between two nearshore bars along the North Beach of Padre Island National Seashore. At present, the vessel is not leaking any fuel. When the sea state lessens, the current plan would lighter 15,000 gallons of the 20,000 gallons of diesel from shore. The hope is that the owner will be able to restart the engines and salvage her with a little help. To achieve that, they may have to hydraulically flush sand from around the hull and cut through one of the nearshore bars. Given the dynamic changes that are constantly occurring on such sand beaches, the effects would be very limited and any scaring would quickly fill in. There are no sea grass beads or reef structures at this location. Given that the sea state and surf are not expected to subside to working conditions until Saturday, the response plan may require changes as conditions change. The NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator has also provided scientific support consultation to the Chief Ranger of the National Seashore. This information will be updated as the situation changes. [SEP] Update (21 July 2005 PM) Comments and recommendations provided to the Chief Ranger, Padre Island National Seashore associated with the salvage of the GOLDEN DRAGON: The disturbed area should be kept to a minimum area and depth. Continue to watch out for the presence of sea turtles or marine mammals in the area. If sea turtles are observed, take appropriate precautions. Removing as much fuel as possible both lightens the vessel and reduces the risk from pollution. Dispersed fresh diesel is highly toxic to marine environment. Plans are to begin lightering this evening if conditions allow. Salvage may not began until the weekend. Potential for Damage to Nearshore Subtidal Sand Habitats from the Removal of Grounded Vessels off the Gulf of Mexico (Provided by Dr. Jacqui Michel, RPI Inc under contract to NOAA) Offshore sand habitats are highly dynamic, particularly the nearshore bars. During storms, sand is eroded from the beach and deposited in offshore bars, then returned to the beach in the post-storm recovery period. There are usually three bars off Padre Island, with the outer bars being more stable, compared to the inner bars. These nearshore bar habitats are important areas for certain types of fish and shellfish. Fish feed in between the bars where the sediments are more stable and have higher concentrations of infauna. Sea turtle juveniles may be present. Dredging of sand from around the vessel will have direct impacts where the sand and any associated infauna are disturbed. Recovery rates for infauna in these environments are high, particularly in offshore areas where there are large sources of recruitment. Recovery of estuarine sand benthos after dredging is usually within one year. Offshore, and during flushing rather than dredging, the recovery rate should be even faster. There should be no significant changes to sediment transport processes or patterns. If the flushing does create a break in the outermost offshore bar, it should fill quickly (within days). A break in the landward bar might cause some short-term beach erosion where higher waves could break directly on the beach. N, 93&#8734;49.34???€? W off of Sabine Pass. II. Geographic Region Covered This report covers the Gulf coast from Texas Point to the western edge of McFaddin NWR and offshore approximately two nautical miles. This area does not necessarily correspond to actual oil locations. Please consult other Hotline reports for current information. III. Shoreline Resources at Risk The shoreline in the area is primarily composed of scarps and steep slopes in clay near Texas Point NWR and mixed sand and gravel beach near McFaddin NWR with smaller areas of tidal flats, exposed riprap (the jetties), salt and brackish marsh, and fine-grained sand beach throughout the area. IV. Biological Resources at Risk Threatened and Endangered Species Loggerhead (state endangered and federally threatened) and Kemp???€?s ridley (state and federally endangered) sea turtles may be present in low concentrations in Gulf waters. Brown pelicans (federally endangered) are nesting along the shoreline and are present in Gulf waters. Osprey (state species of special concern) are present in McFaddin NWR. Other Birds Mottled duck, least tern, black skimmer, and clapper rail may be nesting in Texas Point NWR. Additional species present in the wildlife refuges at this time of year include wading birds, cormorants, gulls, and terns. Migratory shorebirds begin arriving in August. Along the shoreline south of Salt and Fence Lakes and in McFaddin NWR, nesting species include: clapper rail, sandwich tern, least tern, willet, and royal tern. Fish and Invertebrates Adults, and in some cases larvae and juveniles, of the following species are present in the area: gulf menhaden, sheepshead (larvae/juveniles), sand seatrout (larvae/juveniles), gafftopsail catfish (spawning adults/larvae/juveniles), hardhead catfish (spawning adults/larvae/juveniles), Spanish mackerel, silver seatrout, Atlantic croaker (larvae/juveniles), spot, Florida pompano, red drum, spotted seatrout (spawning adults/larvae/juveniles), gulf kingfish, white mullet, tarpon, sharks, southern kingfish, blue crab (spawning adults/larvae/juveniles), brown shrimp, and white shrimp (spawning adults/larvae/juveniles). Larvae and juveniles are particularly sensitive to the toxic components of light oil. Essential fish habitat (EFH) occurs in the area for brown shrimp, white shrimp, red drum, Spanish mackerel, cobia, and bluefish. Marine Mammals Bottlenose dolphins are present, mating, and calving in the area. V. Human-Use Resources Texas Point and McFaddin National Wildlife Refuges are present along the shoreline. There is a beach access point near Sea Rim Estates and a heliport in McFaddin NWR. The night of July 2, 2005 a 145 foot NOAA chartered vessel, the M/V Casitas, ran aground in the Northwest Hawaiian islands. The Casitas is hard aground on the northeast side of Pearl and Hermes Atoll at coordinates 2757.694 N and 17546.282 W. Sea conditions are 4-6 foot south swell with 15-20 knot winds. The vessel is carrying 16 marine debris divers plus crew for a Marine Debris recovery mission. All passengers and crew are reported safe with no injuries. The vessel contains approximately 30,000 gallons of diesel fuel, 3000 gallons of gasoline, and 200 gallons of lube oil aboard. A morning overflight by the USCG C-130 Hercules observed rainbow sheen from the aft portion of the vessel moving southwest, approximately a half nautical mile long by 200 feet wide. [SEP] Crews aboard the M/V Casitas have completed the lightering of the gasoline, using Option No. 3 of the approved Lightering Annex to the SSWP. The transfer of the product was carried out successfully without incident. The vessel is being prepared for removal from the reef, with the revised extraction date now given as 04 August at high tide (1600 hours local). The vessel will be towed by the M/V American Quest to the emergency disposition site approved by Unified Command, should the need arise to utilize this location. All loose materials, trash and related are being stowed below decks and will be secured prior to the extraction of the vessel. All remaining equipment on the deck will be stowed and secured prior to extraction on Thursday. The vessel will be uniformly de-ballasted near low tide with tow made up for the extraction. Once the tow is secured to the M/V American Quest, the vessel will be removed from the reef at, or near high tide, Thursday afternoon. The RP will try to schedule a charter to begin demobilizing personnel from Midway Saturday afternoon. The charter, if finalized, will have the capability of seating up to 12 people for the pre-assessment trip to Midway (where the M/V Condor will meet the investigation team) on Saturday morning, should this agree with everyone's respective schedules. If successful with the charter, the RP will email the Unified Command to apprise them of the time and location. NOAA Weather Service continues to provide site-specific weather forecasts, with special attention to swell conditions. NOAA ORR continues to provide remote support and to participate in plannning damage preassessment activities. During the evening of June 9, 2005 the M/V Sea Astride, a 150 foot Haitian coastal freighter was adrift with no power and taking on water 3/4 miles off Cabo Rojo, Puerto Rico. The vessel grounded at 17-59.04N, 067-13.365W in 12-15 feet of water. The vessel remained firmly aground and water entered the vessel's engine room. The vessel is a coastal freighter that is grounded ? mile to 1 mile offshore west of Bahia de Boqueron. II. Geographic Region Covered The area covered by this report is Bahia de Boqueron and the surrounding coastal areas. This area does not necessarily correspond to actual or potential oil locations. Consult other Hotline reports for oil location information. III. Expected Behavior of the Spilled Material Diesel is a light oil product that contains water-soluble and acutely toxic components that could impact water column resources. It is moderately volatile and has a rapid evaporation rate which helps to dissipate the product. Water column impacts would be more likely if diesel is stranded in large amounts near shallow water areas. Water column contamination could potentially be toxic to fish and aquatic invertebrates that reside in the shallow water areas. Diesel oil can spread rapidly into thin slicks, with the possibility of contaminating large areas. Wildlife using the water surface may be at risk of oil contamination. Lubricating oils have low toxicity and are mildly viscous. This oil will smother and coat rather than penetrate substrates. It will be degraded over time by microbes but may accumulate heavily in some areas if trapped by debris. Lubricating oils will likely float on the water surface, unless mixed into the water column from high-energy wave action. This may cause potential impacts to water column and benthic animals, although not severely due to its low toxicity. IV. Shoreline Resources at Risk The shorelines of Bahia de Boqueron are predominantly composed of coarse-grained sand beaches and mangroves. There are also areas of sheltered solid man made structures within the bay. To the north of Bahia de Boqueron, the shoreline consists of mixed sand and gravel beaches and wave-cut platforms. South of Bahia de Boqueron, towards Bahia Salinas, the shoreline consists of fine to medium-grained sand beaches with some pockets of coarse-grained sand beaches, rocky cliffs and/or solid man made structures. The most sensitive habitats in the area are mangroves. Mangroves are highly productive, serving as nursery habitat for many fish and invertebrates, and feeding, nesting, and general-use habitats for wildlife. Marine diesel fuels have high acute toxicity to mangroves, and impacts (yellowing of the leaves) are evident within days to weeks. Mortality of mangrove trees could occur if large amounts of light oils penetrate the sediments. Light fuels may concentrate at the high-tide line where they can penetrate into sediments or wrack/litter. This oil will weather more slowly and could be a source of sheening. V. Biological Resources at Risk Benthic Habitats Seagrass beds are present along the shorelines and shallows within the bay. Seagrass beds in shallow subtidal or intertidal zones could become affected. While there is potential for above ground die-off, it is likely that the plants will recover, as long as oil is not mixed into the sediments. It is possible that fauna hiding or living in the grass will be exposed to and impacted by the oil. There are extensive coral reefs outside of the bay entrance in the intertidal and subtidal areas along the outer coast. Shallow, protected coral reefs may be adversely impacted by diesel. There may be large concentrations of fish and invertebrates associated with these habitats. Fish Numerous species of fish are present throughout the bay and nearshore coastal waters. Reef fish which may be inhabiting the coral reefs surrounding Bahia de Boqueron include: Squirrelfish, trumpetfish, pipefish, scorpionfish, seabass, grouper, tilefish, jack, snapper, grunt, porgy, drum, angelfish, wrasse, parrotfish, and many other assemblages. Several assemblages of pelagic fish may be present in the nearshore waters including: mackerel, barracuda, dolphin, jack, wahoo, tuna, swordfish, billfish, and shark. The mangrove areas within Bahia de Boqueron serve as nursery grounds for several species of fish including snook and tarpon. Impacts to fish from the diesel are expected to be minor unless the diesel accumulates in shallow areas and mixes into the water column. In heavy seas, it is possible that the oil may be mixed into the water column along the outer coast. Fish mortality and sublethal impacts are possible under these conditions. Larval and juvenile fish inhabiting shallow waters, seagrass beds, rocky reefs, or mangrove areas could be vulnerable to spill impacts. Invertebrates Octopus, spiny lobster, and queen conch are common throughout the nearshore waters. Blue land crab and spiny lobster may be present in mangrove areas and/or in the surrounding estuarine waters. Larval and juvenile crabs and lobsters in shallow water areas of the spill zone may experience sublethal and lethal impacts. Birds Birds potentially present in and around Bahia de Boqueron include brown pelican (endangered), seabirds, terns, and various other species. Pelicans are usually at high risk during oil spills, because they spend nearly all their time on the water surface. The threatened least tern may be nesting on beaches in the eastern portions of the bay at this time. In the mangroves, several species of waterfowl and wading birds may be present including: American coot, blue-winged teal, brown pelican (endangered), Caribbean coot (threatened), common moorhen, least grebe (threatened), magnificent frigate bird, pied-billed grebe, ruddy ducks (threatened), white cheeked pintail, yellow-breasted crake. In addition, the endangered yellow-shouldered blackbird is also present within the mangroves and may be nesting at this time. Critical habitat for the yellow-shouldered blackbird exists in the eastern portion of the bay. Other birds such as waterfowl, wading birds, terns, and shorebirds can also be severely impacted by oil in some cases. Waterfowl and wading birds may be directly oiled, and can become oiled on the upper body by coming in contact with oiled vegetation or wrack. Terns may be oiled while capturing fish. Direct oiling of birds reduces the buoyancy, water repellency, and insulation provided by feathers, and may result in death by drowning or hypothermia. Preening of oiled feathers may also result in ingestion of oil resulting in irritation, sickness, or death. Mammals Whales and dolphins are present throughout the coastal waters of the area. Manatees are also present throughout Bahia de Boqueron. The oil could cause irritation to the skin and mucous membranes of marine mammals, and inhalation of vapors may cause irritation of the lungs, as well as have toxic effects. Manatees could accidentally ingest oil trapped within or adhered to submerged vegetation, resulting in sickness or injury. [SEP] Incident Summary: On the afternoon of 8 May the T/B Vane Brothers (VB) 53 reported hitting a submerged object and released an estimated 25-30 bbls of diesel fuel into the James River. By the morning of 9 May the vessel was stabilized and transfer of the product from #1 and #2 port tanks that were damaged in the grounding continued. NOAA SSC Support Activities: MSO Hampton Roads requested information as to resources at risk with particular attention to the route of the barge from the site of the grounding to the potential offload and repair facility in Kinder-Morgan up-river 5 miles in Richmond, VA. In addition, MSO Hampton Roads requested support for long-range weather forecasts, coordination with Resource Trustees, and analysis of cleanup endpoints for the marsh areas east of the grounding site described as the 'gravel pit' where much of the diesel oil had collected. The NOAA resource at risk summary that was provided generally described potential impacts to a number of spawning / larval species and habitat in the area of the grounding. However, discussions with representatives of Virginia Department of Game and Inland Fisheries and Virginia Marine Resources staff suggested that there were no special environmental areas that would be at increased risk if the T/ B VB 53 was moved up-river 5 miles to the off-load and repair facility. SPECIAL NOTE: VA DGIF reports a bald eagle nest located in between the site of the grounding and the repair location. This nest is located at the following coordinates 37,25,42.4 and 77,24,26.3. This information will be passed to operations staff as part of the planning considerations when the T/B is moved. The NOAA extended forecast for Wednesday is for SE winds at 10 knots, mostly cloudy skies, and chance of thunderstorms during the day. On Thursday N winds at 15 knots, mostly cloudy skies, and chance of showers are forecast. SSC Coordination with Trustees: The NOAA SST developed a number of information and status reports, developed location maps for the areas of the grounding and proposed area to which the T/B would be taken for off-load and repair, and posted several clear digital photos of the site of the grounding and the location where most of the oil had been contained in an area called the 'gravel pit.' An instantaneous release of this oil in the surf zone would be expected to influence less than one nm from the vessel. If the oil were released under onshore wind conditions, we would expect that the oil would experience significant dispersion within the surface, and may be visible less than 1 nm downwind. If the oil were released under wind conditions with an offshore wind component, we would expect oil sheens to be visible less than 1 nm downwind. 3) OIL FATE Diesel Light refined products, such as diesel (or Fuel Oil No 2), typically have very high evaporation rates and do not tend to create persistent slicks. However, the terminology for refined products is not standardized, and, sometimes, heavier intermediate fuel oils are referred to as ???€?marine diesel???€?. These heavier products are much less volatile than normal Fuel Oil no 2 and can form a more persistent slick. When spilled, the diesel spreads quickly into thin films often forming patches of rainbow and silver sheens. If the sheens reach the shoreline in a few hours, a slight staining, or greasy film-like bathtub ring is common. These oils usually do not form a stable emulsion and, as a result, do not form a heavy or sticky residual to clean up. Note that lighter refined products do have a relatively high concentration of light aromatic compounds and tend to be more soluble and more toxic then heavier oils. These oils do not generally present an involved cleanup problem. However, they can result in an initial toxic shock to biota and can persist as a biological threat in low energy marine environments. On 28 April 2005 at approximately 1530 the USCG Activities NY was notified of a release of gasoline from the barge B-35. The barge was moored at the Dynergy facility in Roseton, NY. It reported slight sheen around it and believed the damage was to the #1 and #2 port tanks (each containing 7,500 barrels of gasoline). ACTNY requested NOAA support for weather and trajectory information. The barge initially had 75,145 bbls of gasoline. Using the figures provided by the RP the amount lost would be 683 bbls or 28,686 gallons. The amount of product and water combined is 89,823 bbls which means that during the several times they lightered they took on an additional 7,803 bbls of water (the barges total capacity is only 82,020 bbls). The barge was single hulled and they believed it sustained an impact with the bottom near Diamond Reef (NE of buoy #56) while heading up river. Weather at time of incident was winds 12 knots from the SW, air temperature 41F, and visibility 10NM. The waterway remained open to all traffic with a Safety Broadcast for no-wake speed in the vicinity of the incident. The contractor conducted air monitoring of LEL and benzene levels. None were detected. Protective boom was deployed at the mouth of Wappinger Creek. If the total volume on the barge were released, less than 10% would remain after about 8 hrs. Gasoline is a light refined product with a specific gravity that can range from 0.76 to 0.70 at 15??C (54 to 70 API). The product typically has a very high evaporation rate and does not tend to create persistent slicks. When spilled, the gasoline spreads quickly into thin films by forming patches of rainbow and silver sheens. If the sheens reach the shoreline in a few hours, a slight staining, or greasy film is common. Normally, this type of release does not become an involved cleanup problem. There is a high flammability hazard associated with gasoline spills. Specifically, if a spill is kept from spreading freely by natural or man-made structures the gasoline slick might be thick enough to support ignition. In addition, vapor concentrations near the source of spill or vapors collected in sheltered areas can present an explosion hazard. Please note that gasoline does have a relatively high concentration of light aromatic compounds and tends to be more soluble and more toxic than heavier oils. In high-energy environments, the gasoline is likely to disperse as small droplets in the water column. Gasoline spills can result in an initial toxic shock to biota and persist as a biological threat, particularly in low energy marine environments such as shallow bays and inlets. 4) TRAJECTORY With the tidally dominated currents, the originally reported spill could make it as far upriver from the spill site as 2 nautical miles, and as far downriver as 4 miles within the first 12 hrs. If there were another release tonight or tomorrow, it could travel as far as 4 miles upriver and 5 miles downriver before evaporating. The current winds are gusty and variable in direction, making it hard to predict where the oil might beach. Tonight, the West winds will tend to move the oil toward the Eastern shore, but the river Valley may channel the winds to be more from the south. Tomorrow, the SW and S winds will help to move the oil northward, but could result in shoreline impacts on either shore. [SEP] At 1313 hrs (CDT) on 28 April 2005, the NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator was notified by the USCG of a collision between an outbound tanker and an Offshore Supply Vessel (OSV) in the Sabine Ship Channel just N of the jetties. The cause of the incident is still under investigation, but the consequence was that the OSV Rene 1 sank. All of the crew were accounted for, but the status of injuries is unknown. Initially, a small sheen was observed threatening Louisiana Point. That sheen quickly dissipated and no addition release was observed. At present, the OSV is capsized and sunk in the channel with only the bow above water. The reported position is 29?? 42.71???€? N Lat. 093?? 50.77???€? W Long. This position places the vessel just N of the jetties and in Sabine Lake. An estimated 4500 gallons of diesel remain on board. Salvage plans are being developed and protection booming is being deployed at Lighthouse Bayou, Texas Bayou, and Louisiana Bayou (a small cut near Louisiana Point). A trajectory analysis is attached. The SSC is on-scene and will continue to support response efforts including coordination of environmental issues during the salvage. Additional information to follow. The crew boat is reported to have 5,000 gallons of diesel fuel and 800-1,000 gallons of lube oil onboard. The last reported position of the crew boat is 29&#730; 42.102???€?N, 093&#730; 50.7???€?W. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP as it would affect any trajectory implications. ______________________________________________________ 1) 24-hour Wind Forecast Today, the winds are expected to be from the south at 10-14 knots. Tonight, S-SW winds at 15 knots are predicted. Friday, S-SW winds at 15 knots with gusts to 20 knots are forecast. 2) TRAJECTORY We expect any oil released this afternoon to move into Sabine Pass on the flood tide with the onshore winds. Oil could reach as far as Mesquite Point by early this evening. Because of the wind direction, we expect oil to be more likely to contact the eastern side of Sabine Pass rather than the western shore. As the tide turns late this afternoon, oil continuing to leak from the vessel could move out through the jetties and upcoast in the coastal current. The TABS Buoy R currently shows a weak upcoast coastal flow of 20 cm/s. By tomorrow with the onshore winds and a persistent upcoast flow we expect shoreline contact within 1.5 nm upcoast from the jetties to be the highest probability area. Beached oil could be found as far at 10 nm upcoast from oil that moved into the coastal current. 3) OIL FATE Diesel Light refined products, such as diesel (or Fuel Oil No 2), typically have very high evaporation rates and do not tend to create persistent slicks. However, the terminology for refined products is not standardized, and, sometimes, heavier intermediate fuel oils are referred to as ???€?marine diesel???€?. These heavier products are much less volatile than normal Fuel Oil no 2 and can form a more persistent slick. When spilled, the diesel spreads quickly into thin films often forming patches of rainbow and silver sheens. If the sheens reach the shoreline in a few hours, a slight staining, or greasy film-like bathtub ring is common. These oils usually do not form a stable emulsion and, as a result, do not form a heavy or sticky residual to clean up. Note that lighter refined products do have a relatively high concentration of light aromatic compounds and tend to be more soluble and more toxic than heavier oils. These oils do not generally present an involved cleanup problem. However, they can result in an initial toxic shock to biota and can persist as a biological threat in low energy marine environments. [SEP] On Saturday evening, the OSV Rene 1 was lifted from the Sabine Ship Channel and transported to the Sabine Anchorage. The fuel tanks had been plugged prior to this operation, but the large gash in the engine room still presented a pollution threat for oil escapement. Field operations were halted during most of the day due to strong winds that subsided late that afternoon. During the initial lift, only a small amount of diesel (probably slop from the engine room) was lost from the engine room, and only small sheen during the transfer (the sheen were thought to only represent a few gallons of oil). The spilled diesel was blown across the pass toward a small cut and marsh near the Sabine Pilot Station. This area had been boom in anticipation of such a trajectory and minimal impact was observed. Most of the diesel evaporated and naturally dispersed before reaching the shoreline. Approximately a half a bale of saturated pads were collected both on water and at the Pilot Station. Salvage operations will continue with the goal of rotating the capsized vessel pumping water from the vessel and placing it on a barge for final disposition. A containment boom has been configured around the vessel to mitigate additional pollution. Sadly, the Captain of the Rene 1 died of injuries on Saturday. The NOAA SSC demobilized from the scene on Sunday morning since the navigational channel was now open and a sound protection strategy was in place. Photographs will be provided. This is consistant with the predominantly southerly winds. The leak source was clamped and is secure. So far this response has been a joint effort by MSO New Orleans and MSO Morgan City, with NO in the FOSC seat. The reason for this is that the spill is on the NO side, but the oil is actually moving into the Morgan City zone. The USCG is discussing future shoreline impacts and the possibilities of switching the regulating MSO. There is approximately 16,000 feet of boom deployed. Some of the boom closer to the source and in areas where it is less affected is being moved to the north in an effort to collect oil and prevent it from reaching the northern edges of Creole Bay. There are no reported wildlife injuries. An aerial wildlife survey is scheduled for this afternoon. Barataria Pass was recently opened, though vessel traffic is restricted to the channel only. [SEP] Situation on evening of 4/20/05 [SEP] As was mentioned in the previous posting (Continuing Operations) it was decided by the Environmental Unit (EU) that the clean up and demobilizing of operations can continuewith limited involvement on the EU's behalf. This is due to the fact that what was observed by the SCAT teams in the field and by the previous overflights shows that the response was conducted in an appropriate manner and level and can continue to be monitored and demobilized in the same way. After the meeting with SCAT teams and the operationally focused EU members agreed on the revised future booming strategies the trustees met and discussed future action. Following their meeting, the trustees met with representatives of the RP to talk about future plans. Most feedback from the trustees was positive on the issue of them arriving on scene earlier and working alongside SCAT teams in their initial field assessment. Though the actual SCAT that was required from this spill was limited, this situation brought about an opportunity to bring the two groups together to share information. Future plans for operations consist of a once or twice a week visit by members of LADEQ, USCG, or NOAA to check on progress made in the clean-up effort. Passive recovery and demobilization will be the focus for the rest of the spill event. With regards to NOAA personel on-scene, Troy Baker (representing the trustees) was making a field trip with members of the RP out on-scene this morning, but Jim Johnsonne and the SSC departed the spill site last evening. An on-site field trip for next week is being planned. No other requests of the NOAA Scientific Support Team have been made at this time. [SEP] Response Guidelines for Barataria Bay Pipeline Spill 21 April 2005 These guidelines establish practical target end-points for cleanup. The guidelines do not constitute shoreline restoration or full recovery criteria, which will be further addressed through longer-term assessments. The objective of the cleanup criteria is to reduce the risk of environmental injury to the best extent practicable as judged by the professional judgment of the Environmental Unit, approved through Unified Command such that excessive treatment or cleanup may have no net environmental benefit and may delay, rather than accelerate, recovery of the shoreline habitats. General Criteria: ???€? Oiled shorelines shall be free of bulk oil and not produce appreciable sheen under all weather conditions. ???€? There shall be no appreciable floating oiled debris that can be removed by hand. ???€? Oil stain or sporadic coat on vegetation and large immobile debris that does not produce sheen and is not an appreciable contact risk to wildlife may be allowed to weather and degrade naturally. ???€? Some oil stain or coat may still be present if best professional judgment of the Environmental Unit/SCAT determines that further treatment will not produce environmental benefit. Specific Target Cleanup End-Points Fine-Grain Sand Beaches ???€? Oiled shorelines shall be free of bulk oil and not produce appreciable sheen. ???€? Light oil stain or sporadic oil coat on sediment that does not produce sheen and is not likely to result in ???€?asphalt-like conditions???€? may be allowed to weather and degrade naturally. ???€? Some oil stain may still be present at the end of active cleanup if best professional judgment is that further treatment will not produce environmental benefit. Sand beaches are one of the easiest shorelines to clean. Sand removal must be minimized. Material to be removed should be limited to oil, oiled sand, and oiled debris. Do not remove unoiled wrack. Access to upland areas must be restricted to prevent collateral damage. Cleaning by hand, scraping with a shovel and rakes are recommended. Snare and sorbant booms for additional passive recovery is also encouraged. Shell and Mixed Sand & Shell Shorelines ???€? Oiled shorelines shall be free of bulk oil and not produce appreciable sheen under all weather conditions. ???€? Oil stain or sporadic patchy coat on sediment that does not produce sheen and is not likely to result in ???€?asphalt-like conditions???€? may be allowed to weather and degrade naturally. ???€? Some oil stain may still be present, but the best professional judgment is that further treatment will not produce environmental benefit. Consider low pressure, high volume flushing onto free oil from shell into snare and containment boom. Snare should be maintained until the shoreline doesn???€?t create sheen. Minimize any shell removal since these area are primarily fill to fortify shoreline and facility structures. Marshes ???€? The area shall be free of free floating and potentially mobile oil, including oiled debris and wrack on fringe marsh. ???€? There shall be no appreciable sheens released from marsh. ???€? Oil stained and coated vegetation that doesn???€?t create sheen or appreciable wildlife threats may be left to natural recovery. Areas of light oiling will recover naturally. Aggressive cleanup may actually cause greater long-term damage. There shall be no physical cleanup activities in marsh areas unless in a specific area or situation agreed upon by the Environmental Unit and Unified Command. This is to prevent collateral damage to marsh vegetation and entrainment or entrapment of oil product into sediments. Sorbant boom or snare should be staked along the front edge of oiled marsh for passive recovery of sheens. These snares must be inspected and replaced routinely. Best professional judgment by the Unified Command, with input from the Environmental Unit/SCAT groups should be used to determine if further treatment or cleanup would have no environmental benefit and may delay, rather than accelerate, recovery of the vegetation. This judgment should be based on fact, past studies or data from previous oil spills. The vessel MV Sea Cloud, a 132 foot container ship grounded on coral or hardbottom on the south central coast of St Croix at approximately 0745 local onSaturday 26 March 2005.  CG reported the grounded position is 17-40.7N;064-45.9W. This position is at the Alucroix port channel near the Hovensafacility.  Water depths were reported as 9-4 fathoms, but this is unconfirmed.CG reported they believe the vessel is aground on coral.Fuel on board was initially reported as 500 metric tons of #6 fuel oil.  Thisinformation was later updated to be 180 metric tons of #6 and an unknownquantity of diesel fuel.  The diesel fuel was being transfered to inside tanksfor added security. NOAA provided contingency trajectory information and weather forecasts to the USCG MSD in St Croix.  After lightering the majority of fuel, the vessel was successfully re-floated without incident the morning of March 28 and taken into dock for hull inspection.  There was no significant damage to the hull.NOAA DAC coordiantied with co-trustees to assess damage to the reef grounding site. The Motiva facility is near the southern end of the Arthur Kill, a navigation channel between New Jersey and Staten Island. The barge was loaded with 966,000 gallons of #2 fuel and the damaged tank held approximately 99,000 gallons. After the crew from the tug Delta Tide realized they had hit something, they quickly returned to the Motiva facility where the vessel was boomed and the remaining fuel from the damaged tank was offloaded. The Coast Guard reports that the discharge from the barge has been stopped and the majority of the spilled fuel is held within an oil containment boom. The spill size is currently estimated at 13,000 gallons, but tank gauging is incomplete and the exact size of the spill is unknown. Pollution response contractors are on scene recovering the fuel and deploying boom to environmentally sensitive areas in the Arthur Kill Waterway and Raritan Bay, including Woodbridge, Smith, and Mill Creeks. At approximately 2330 March 20, 2005 a spill of 6000 to 7000 BBL (250,000-300,000 gallons) of #6 fuel oil was lost from a ruptured pipeline at the Commonwealth Oil Refining Company, Guayanilla Bay, PR. (NRC report 753234). The oil spill occured during a transfer operation when the pipeline supplying fuel to a vessel apparently ruptured due to corrosion. The rupture occured 5000 yards inland. An estimated 50 gallons of oil entered the waterway. The remainder of the release (7000 Bbls or 294,000 gallons) was mostly contained on land in a containment area of pipes and an adjacent ditch. USCG D7 requested NOAA develop weather forecast, tide and current predictions, and resources at risk information in the event of a significant release into the waterway. Recovery operations were effective, and little oil entered the waterway and the oil has remained effectively contained primarily in a land ditch. The only wildlife impacts reported were one egret oiled, but mangrove habitat along the ditch was oiled. I. Spill Source Information This report was prepared at 17:00 EST on March 21, 2005 Information in the report is based on a release of 7,000 bbls of No. 6 fuel oil. II. Geographic Region Covered The area covered by this report is Bah???€?a de Guaynilla and the shoreline and waters east and west of the bay. This area does not necessarily correspond to actual or potential oil locations. Consult other Hotline reports for oil location information. III. Expected Behavior of the Spilled Material No. 6 fuel oil is a heavy, viscous oil that may persist for a long time in the environment. There is a very low water soluble component to this oil. The majority of the impacts would be to the intertidal zone of the shoreline and animals on the water surface. IV. Shoreline Resources at Risk The shorelines on the southern portion of Bah???€?a de Guayanilla are predominately mangroves. The shorelines on the northern portion of the bay are a mix of fine- to medium-grained sand beaches, riprap, and sheltered seawalls. The outer coast to the west of the bay is exposed rocky cliffs and wave-cut platforms, mixed sand and gravel beaches on the outer shorelines; and mangroves and fine- to medium-grained sand beaches in the bays and coves. To the east of the bay the shoreline is a mix of mangroves, sheltered seawalls, riprap, and sand beaches. Corals are scattered along the shoreline east and west of the bay. For this type of oil mangrove shorelines are the most sensitive habitat present. The oil may coat the mangroves and mangrove prop roots, interfering with the normal respiration process of the plant. This coating may cause stress and even mortality in the trees. The oil may form a band at the high tide line on the sand beaches. In areas of heavy accumulation the entire intertidal zone may be coated with oil. Penetration into the sediment may be as much as 10 to 15 cm. There is also potential for the oil to be buried by sediment on these beaches, but probably not more the 30 cm. The riprap may be coated in the intertidal zone with pooling of the oil in the interstial spaces. This pooled oil may result in chronic sheening. Oil may form a band on the seawalls at the high tide line. Under heavy accumulation this band may cover most of the intertidal zone and smother any attached biota. V. Biological Resources at Risk Fish ?? Numerous species of pelagic and reef fish are present throughout this area. Impacts are expected to be minimal to the adult fish. Larval and juvenile fish near the water surface may be impacted by this spill. Shellfish ?? Caribbean spiny lobster, queen conch, and octopus are present throughout these waters. Since these animals are benthic there would be very little impact to them. Any animals, especially queen conchs, on intertidal flats may be coated by the oil during low tides. In areas of heavy accumulation there may be some sublethal impacts to the animals in the intertidal and shallow subtidal areas. Birds ?? On an island at the mouth of Bah???€?a de Guayanilla is a nesting concentration of least terns (state threatened), roseate terns (state endangered and federally threatened) and sandwich terns. Nesting season starts in April for the least tern and May for the other two species. Also present on the island are American oystercatcher, seabirds, and shorebirds. On Cayo Mar???€?a Langa are brown pelicans (state and federally endangered). Brown pelicans, wading birds, and waterfowl are found throughout Puerto de Guayanilla. Brown pelicans are found along the coast east and west of the bay. Waterfowl and diving birds (pelicans), are usually at greatest risk during oil spills because they spend nearly all their time on the water surface. Waterfowl can also become oiled through contact with oiled vegetation. Wading birds primarily become oiled on the legs while wading for prey. They may also become oiled on the upper body and feathers by coming in contact with oiled vegetation. Shorebirds usually avoid oil, but may be impacted by loss of feeding areas or intertidal prey, particularly during migration periods. Terns may be at risk because they feed on animals in the water. This behavior may result in oiling of feathers and the ingestion of oil. Oiling of birds reduces the buoyancy, water repellency, and insulation provided by feathers, and may result in death by drowning or hypothermia. Preening of oiled feathers may also result in ingestion of oil resulting in irritation, sickness, or death. Bird oiling, particularly of waterfowl and wading birds, may continue even after the floating oil slicks have been removed, depending on the extent of oiled vegetation. Mammals ?? West Indian manatees (state and federally endangered) are present in Bah???€?a de Guayanilla. Impacts of the oil on this species are not well known. However, it is assumed that oil and/or fumes may be inhaled by the animal. This could lead to respiratory distress. Also the oil may cause irritation of the eyes, nostrils, and mouth. Other mammals present in the nearshore and offshore waters include whales and dolphins. Few impacts are expected to these animals since they are very mobile and are not likely to spend any significant amount of time in the vicinity of the oil slicks. Reptiles ?? Green, hawksbill, and leatherback sea turtles (state

The 100 foot yacht TV ran aground at approximately 2200 EST on 16 March 2005at the entrance to Port Everglades on the north jetty.  The position of thegrounding is 26-05.671N; 080-06.222W as reported by USCG.  The vessel had 7000gallons of diesel oil onboard at time of grounding.  Hull damage has occurredand the engine room is flooded with free communication with the sea.  Lighteringof the fuel took place using vac trucks on the shore.Some water in the flooded engine room mixed with engine oil and lube oils.A conference call was held with the incident specific RRT to discuss decantingand discharge of the oily engine room water if necessary during a refloatoperation.  The RRT agreed to this operational tradeoff if necessary.  CoastGuard agreed that attempts to lighter all fuel and the oily seawater would beconducted prior to a refloat attempt.If decanting and discharge of the oily water becomes necessary, the dischargewould be directed into a containment boom with sorbent materials for recovery ofany oil sheens.  Pump rates would be controlled to eliminate or minimize anysheens into the water.Protection measures for sensitive areas inside the cut have been reviewed andboom and sorbents will be ready for deployment at turtle nesting sites to thenorth and to protect mangroves and Whiskey Creek to the south.The potential use of special solidifier products are being considered to removesheen from the engine room and as a filter for the oily water discharge.The M/V TV was successfully refloated at 1430 EST, March 18th.  Once refloated, the vessel did not appear completely stable, so the Coast Guard decided to direct the vessel to a nearby facility at the Dania cutoff canal rather than the planned facility further away in the New River.  The vessel made it safely to the facility without incident. No spill or even visible sheening was reported during the entire refloat and movement operation.  The vessel damage will be further assesed and repaired enough to continue to the New River facility or removed from the water by sling at the Dania location. Tides and Currents/Trajectory Info: Max flood current is at 1103 this morning and is predicted to be 0.3 knots in the cut. If a spill occurs during this time, trajectory analyses indicate that product would move west into the port along the cut. Once the oil gets into the open area inside the jetties, wind would move oil predominately to the south and east near or into the sensitive mangoves and Whiskey Creek area. Considerations: The fuel on board is estimated to be a small amount (300 gallons total). Visible sheens are likely if a release occurs during refloating, although these sheens should not persist beyond 1.5 miles from the release point. The best option enviromentally, is to conduct the refloat at slack high tide at 1400 so that any spill would be carried out to sea vs inside the port area. If this option is considered, then beach goers near the area may need to be advised of possible light sheens along or near the jetty entrance. [SEP] On the morning of Monday March 14, 2005 the NOAA Gulf region SSC was notified of a pipeline leak occurring in Main Pass block 69 off the Mississippi Delta in Louisiana. A 6???€? pipeline was observed leaking and the USCG MSO New Orleans was informed of the situation at 1530 on Saturday, March 12, 2005. An overflight on Sunday revealed an estimated 20 mile sheen with 2 miles of a darker/black ribbon strip of oil coming from the source in the area 29d 16???€?26???€?N 089d 01???€?28???€?W. The estimated release amount provided by the RP was less then 10 bbls with a total max pipeline capacity of 1284 bbls of south Louisiana crude oil. The pipeline was shut in and divers were ordered on-scene. Due to rough seas (3-6???€?) on-scene recovery was limited. Much of the escaping oil was sheening and the wind and waves helped increase natural dispersion. Because of a concern with a passing weather front which would shift the winds out of the east possibly pushing the oil onshore, the NOAA Scientific Support team devised an oil spill trajectory model for what it deemed a possible worst-case scenario, a continuous leak of 10/bbl per hour from the source. This trajectory showed that by the evening of March 14th the oil would move south and be directly off Pass-A-Loutre. The evening overflight conducted at that time matched the trajectory. The sheen at the time of the overflight was roughly 4 miles long and much less oil was being emitted from the source. On Tuesday, March 15 at 0930 the leaking pipeline was successfully patched by divers in the water. The morning overflight revealed a light sheen in some areas with no visible oil on any beaches. Seas were still rough and weather conditions forecasted rain and wind. At the time there has been no more assistance requested of the NOAA Scientific Support Team by USCG MSO New Orleans. Burn [SEP] Photo by CH [SEP] A Hotline has been opened to capture information related to the Pipeline Spill, Delta Farms, LA incident. [SEP] Photo by CH [SEP] Photo by CH [SEP] Today members from the USCG, NOAA, LA DEQ, and representatives from the RP met to initiate an ISB on the small spill located near Bayou Perot, LA. The area to be burned was approximately 1.6 acres in size on the SE side of a 96 acre spartina marsh island. Weather conditions were as predicted. Winds were ideal at 10-15 knots from the NNE, with the flags on the cane poles blowing in the exact direction that the burn needed to move. After the USCG Gulf Strike team had placed air monitoring stations in several locations the burn was lit. In about 15 minutes the burn had covered the length of the area and arrived at the water. After a slower start, the larger pools of oily mud were burning along with the spartina marsh. Black smoke rose approximately 150???€? off the 30???€? flames and was carried to the south as it rapidly dispersed. After 45 minutes most of the area where the burn was going to cover had burned and two airboats started to extinguish the perimeter areas by blowing down the smaller sporatic flames. A second section was lit after that. This was the south east corner of the plot and some of it was missed by the first initial burn. This second burn moved quickly towards the water and then slowly to the west with the help of the NNE breeze. After roughly an hour and a half the burn was completed with success. There was no collateral damage or unplanned upwind burning. There was some residual oil left, specifically sections of emulsified oil. Recovery is expected to begin rather soon, as fresh green shoots were appearing in the marsh. Results from the USCG Strike team air monitoring stations are pending. No further assistance has been requested by the Coast Guard. The spill was located on the southern side of a 96 acre island. The marsh consists mostly of Spartina with some young grasses just starting to green up with most grasses between 1-2m in height. The RP submitted an in-situ burn proposal on Tuesday, Feb 15, 2004 and a conference call was held to discuss the possibility. On 1/26/05 (Wednesday), a pipeline broke and spilled an estimated 63,000 gallons of light crude oil into the Kentucky River near Carrollton, KY. NOAA SSC assistance has been requested. Feb 14 2005 the FOSC made a boat survey from the Kentucky River past Louisville and saw no evidence of oil. Feb 15 2005 he made an overflight of the same area and saw no sheen. It appears that the high water on the Ohio River has removed any sign of oil. [SEP] Thursday afternoon the SSC was contacted by the EPA FOSC about a pipeline spill near Carrollton KY. Mid-Valley Pipeline owns the pipeline. The break occurred about 15 feet from the Kentucky River and released 63,000 gallons of a light crude oil /gas condensate mixture. The break occurred on January 26 and was secured and purged Friday. A series of boom was placed on the Kentucky River about 5 miles from the confluence of the Ohio River, and has been very effective. Large amounts of oil are collecting behind this boom. The spill contractors have recovered 30,800 gallons of OIL using drum skimmers. However, some oil has been seen downstream. The Ohio River Valley Water Sanitation Commission (ORSANCO) conducted a series of water sampling stations along the Ohio River to determine BTEX levels. On January 27th and the morning of the 28th BTEX levels of up to 8ppb were found 60 miles downstream of the spill site. By the afternoon of the 28th the levels had fallen to less than 1ppb. It appears that one ???€?slug???€? of oil escaped the Kentucky River before boom could be installed. The ORSANCO representative stated that background levels of BTEX on the Ohio River are at non-detect levels. ORSANCO plans on continuing the monitoring program at all municipal water intakes all the way to Paducah KY. The state of Kentucky has requested that the RP conduct a robust water-sampling program in the Kentucky and the Ohio Rivers, in addition to ORSANCO???€?s program. Today a mobile lab arrived on scene to process these samples. The lab is set up to test for volatiles, total TPH, semi-volatiles, and PAHs. Turn around time for the tests will be under 1 hour. The majority of the oil has been collected in three locations. The largest collection is in the downstream boom. The other two are the mouths of small tributaries that empty into the Kentucky River. The prevailing winds pushed the oil into the tributaries. Booms have been placed to keep the oil from remobilizing. SSC Activities: The original request from the FOSC was for SSC support in the SCAT process. Today a preliminary SCAT survey of the area was undertaken. Due to heavy snow cover little of the shoreline could be seen. However, important information on the area was learned. The main river and the tributaries are deeply incised. The banks are anywhere from 10-15 feet high. They are composed of a very fine, water soaked sediment with a consistency of frosting. The shoreline is to steep and soft to support shoreside cleanup activities. Also a cut was made in the bank at a heavily oil location, and no oil was detected 2 inches in. It appears that the sediment is to fine and wet to allow oil penetration. Three habitats are at risk from this spill. The steep unconsolidated banks, exposed tree root balls, and submerged trees. The only area that showed any indications of oiling was the submerged trees. Oil and floating detritus had collected in the branches and along the trunks of these trees. The SSC began developing cleanup strategies and endpoints with the RP and the EPA for these three habitats. Two of the folks from DEP were students from lat springs Fresh Water SOS class and had high praise for NOAA HAZMAT. This confidence allowed the SSC to work as a liaison between the USEPA and the State of Kentucky. [SEP] Large amounts of oil continue to collect behind boom. The size of gash is unknown at this time. The tug is located just north of pelican island at 27? 49' 46?N - 97?09' 42?W. The affected tank was holding approximately 6500 gallons of diesel. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP as it would affect any trajectory implications. ______________________________________________________ 1) 24-hour Wind Forecast Today, winds are expected to be from the NE at 10-15 knots with seas expected to be slightly choppy. Tonight, the winds are expected to be NE at 5-10 knots with smooth to slightly choppy seas. 2)TRAJECTORY The spill location is just north of Pelican Island, near the shipping channel. The tidal currents in the area have a max velocity of 0.7 knots. Any spilled oil will move mostly downwind to the SW, primarily reaching Pelican Island. Some fuel could be carried by the tidal currents as far east as Point of Mustang and as far west as the spoil island to the west of Pelican Island. Any fuel that is moved by the wind through the channels into Corpus Christi Bay should move to the SW while evaporating and dispersing before reaching shore. If there is a large release, during the strongest tidal current, and the winds are from the N or NW, rather than the predicted NE, then there could be some small impacts to Mustang Island, between Point of Mustang and Shamrock Island. Diesel fuel is not highly persistent. Much of the oil will be lost through evaporation and natural dispersion. Any shoreline impacts should only result in a ?bathtub ring? stain to the shoreline. 3) OIL FATE Light refined products, such as diesel (or Fuel Oil No 2), typically have very high evaporation rates and do not tend to create persistent slicks. However, the terminology for refined products is not standardized, and, sometimes, heavier intermediate fuel oils are referred to as 'marine diesel'. These heavier products are less volatile than normal Fuel Oil no 2 and can form a more persistent slick. When spilled, the diesel spreads quickly into thin films often forming patches of rainbow and silver sheens. If the sheens reach the shoreline in a few hours, a slight staining, or greasy film-like bathtub ring is common. These oils usually do not form a stable emulsion and, as a result, do not form a heavy or sticky residual to clean up. Note that lighter refined products do have a relatively high concentration of light aromatic compounds and tend to be more soluble and more toxic than heavier oils. These oils do not generally present an involved cleanup problem. However they can result in an initial toxic shock to biota and can persist as a biological threat problem in low energy marine environments. [SEP] Situation Update OSPR and OWCN had wildlife recovery crews out on beaches in Ventura and Los Angeles Counties through the weekend and today. On 15JAN, captured bird counts were 768 live oiled birds and 96 dead oiled birds - of these most were either Western or Clark's grebes and 2 were Brown Pelicans. On 16JAN, the total number of live captured oiled birds was up to 949 and a total of 155 dead oiled birds - of which 7 live oiled Brown Pelicans were captured. The numbers of birds captured on 17JAN were up to 1019 live oiled and 185 dead oiled, showing a slight decline in the daily collection. The Brown Pelicans are being held in a stabilization center in Ventura Harbor or at Point Mugu and will likely be transported to a rehabilitation facility at Sea World in San Diego sometime tomorrow. OSPR also conducted daily overflights in the area using their fixed-wing aircraft on FRI, SAT and SUN. Reports indicate that the large patch of sheen near Platform Holly was still present, but it's size appeared to be decreasing each successive day. A sheen was also observed in Santa Monica Bay, near an area known for natural seeps. Over the weekend, OSPR also sent several oil samples to their lab to be fingerprinted. Sample sources included oiled bird feathers, oil from a buoy just offshore of the Santa Clara River mouth and oil taken from the large sheen near Platform Holly on FRI. All three samples were identified as Monterey Formation Crude, however the oil from the buoy and the feathers was heavily weathered showing no light ends, unlike the fairly fresh fingerprint of the plaform oil. This would indicate that the birds whose feathers have been sampled most likely were not oiled by the sheen near Platform Holly, but rather were oiled by the same source that oiled the buoy outside Santa Clara River. One possible thought is that natural oil seeps in the upland, canyon regions of this river are impounded - either in natural low-lying areas, or in abandonned wells and pits - and during a heavy storm these impoundments were released into the river and out into the coastal region where nearshore birds became impacted. In the Wheeler Canyon region, along the Santa Clara River, there are some such abandonned wells or pits that were cemented over years ago but are currently being looked at as a potential source. The NOAA SSC had a teleconference today with the Channel Islands National Marine Sanctuary regarding the potential for any of the Sanctuaries resources to be impacted and whether NOAA had any potential NRDA issues. At this time there does not appear to be any damage to NOAA resources from this incident. Additionally, the NOAA SSC discussed setting up some sort of monitoring plan through the rest of the winter in anticipation of additional heavy storms and possibly more oiled bird or wildlife events. Further discussions on setting up this plan are to follow. The NOAA SSC also briefed the Chief of Port Ops in MSO LALB about this incident details. At this time, the USCG is not directly involved in the wildlife recovery efforts as the likely source of this oil appears to be natural causes, thereby not an OPA90 event. Today the Regional Response Team (RRT) Region IX had a conference call to be briefed on the incident. NOAA Hazmat helped prepare a briefing package for the RRTIX and the NOAA SSC provided briefings and answered questions. (The base map for the area will be attached in another Hotline entry). Future Plans At this time, OSPR continues its wildlife recovery and rehabilitation operations, as well as its investigation into the source. USCG remains in close contact with OSPR and will support their efforts as appropriate. These notes are based on the following information: An oil company reported 60 bbls of oil lost during the Ventura mudslide overnight last Sunday (January 9-10). This released oil would most likely have entered the Pacific Ocean via the Ventura or Santa Clara Rivers. NOAA/HAZMAT was notified of oiled bird reports on January 13th. 90% of the oiled birds were reported as western grebes, which generally stay within 1 nm of shore. USCG has requested an opinion on the possibility that this oil is related to the oiled bird reports. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP as it would affect any trajectory implications. ______________________________________________________ 1) WIND TIME HISTORY Between January 8-12th, the local wind record show winds with a westerly or southerly component for all time periods except the morning of January 12th. Winds were primarily either from SW quadrant (W, WSW, SW, S) with some SE winds. 2) TRAJECTORY During the heaviest runoff period (late January 8th through January 10th), the Ventura and Santa Clara rivers were running very high. Normal flow for the Ventura River is less than 10 cubic feet/second (cfs), while during this period flow rates were recorded over 100,000 cfs. Satellite imagery from the University of Wisconsin-Madison shows a large plume extending from the mainland shore in Ventura County to the eastern Santa Barbara Channel Islands. The area of the Ventura and Santa Barbara River mouths show dark brown runoff close to the shore. Considering the onshore winds, extensive flooding and reported oil release, the reported oil could be the source of the oil on the western grebes. The lower Ventura River is an area of active oil development, and other businesses may have had small oil releases during the flooding and landslide. The oil also could have come from another unreported area damaged by the flooding and landslide. [SEP] Initial Report On THU, 13JAN, the NOAA SSC was contacted by MSO Los Angeles/Long Beach re numerous oiled birds that had been washing ashore for the last 2 days. On an overflight in the Ventura Harbor area their team observed large patches of brown, floating material heavily strewn with debris. They sent the photos to NOAA Hazmat for examination. They also reported that 500 oiled birds had been observed by the 4 wildlife recovery teams working in the area, with about 170 Western Grebes captured as well as a few pelicans (mainly nearshore species). NOAA Hazmat examined the photos and determined, based on the amount of debris included in what looked like floating oil, that if this were oil it could have come from oil in the upland formations where the recent landslides and heavy runoff due to extensive storm activity have occured (La Conchita region). It is possible that if oil were released into the coastal region from the landslides and runoffs that this could be the source of oil that impacted the nearshore bird species seen over the last few days. On 15JAN (THU) the NOAA SSC was notified by the RRTIX DOC rep that there was an oil slick seen in the vicinity of Platform Holly, just offshore of Santa Barbara. This report came from observations from an OSPR bird survey flight done at about 1645 on THU, 13JAN. The SSC suggested the DOC rep contact the CINMS personnel, and then contacted USCG MSD Santa Barbara directly. The SSC spoke with both Channel Island Marine Sanctuary staff today (FRI) as well as USCG Marine Safety Detachment and received requests for trajectory modeling.
