Spill Source Information This report was prepared on 10 January 2005. Information in this report is based on the assumption that an estimated 100 bbl of crude oil was released near Joseph Bayou and East Bay (29&#8734;05???€?18???€? N, 89&#8734;16???€?37???€? W) on 8 January. This report does not necessarily correspond to actual or potential spill locations. Consult other Hotline reports for spill location information. II. Shoreline Resources at Risk Habitats are predominantly intermediate marsh along the East Bay sides of Southwest Pass and South Pass. Joseph Bayou is a freshwater marsh. Outer shorelines along the barrier islands of Southwest Pass are fine to medium grained sand beaches. The shorelines of the small islands immediately west of South Pass in East Bay are composed of fine-medium grained sand beaches, exposed tidal flats, sheltered tidal flats, and intermediate marshes. III. Biological Resources at Risk Threatened and Endangered Species Piping plover (federally threatened) may be wintering along the barrier islands west of South Pass in East Bay in the Pass a Loutre Wildlife Management Area. A brown pelican (federally endangered) rookery (estimated three nesting individuals) occurs off of the southwest tip of South Pass. Nesting activities likely occur from November-July. Loggerhead (state endangered, federally threatened) and Kemp???€?s ridley (state and federally endangered) sea turtles may be present in Gulf waters in low concentrations. Other Birds Five colonial waterbird rookeries containing egrets, herons, and ibises occur in and west of Joseph Bayou. Two black skimmer and Forster???€?s tern colonies occurs along Southwest Pass. Nine gull, tern, and skimmer colonies occur along the barrier islands in East Bay. Nesting activities are not expected to be occurring at this time of year for any of the species in the colonies, although birds may be present and nesting begins in February for some species. Lesser scaup are wintering in flocks on open water in East Bay. Several species of waterfowl are wintering in freshwater and intermediate marshes in the area, including: American coot, American wigeon, blue-winged teal, canvasback, gadwall, green-winged teal, hooded merganser, lesser scaup, mallard, mottled duck, northern pintail, northern shoveler, and ring-necked duck. Coot, wigeon, and gadwall, in particular, may be present in high concentrations. Fish and Invertebrates Species present in East Bay in January include: Atlantic croaker (larvae and juveniles, highly abundant), black drum (larvae and juveniles, common), gulf menhaden (juveniles, highly abundant), red drum (larvae, juveniles, common), sand seatrout (juveniles, common), sheepshead (juveniles, common), silver perch (juveniles, common), southern flounder (juveniles, common), spot (juveniles, highly abundant), and spotted seatrout (juveniles, common). Largemouth bass are present in low numbers in freshwater marshes (spawning adults, eggs, larvae, and juveniles). Blue crab (eggs, larvae, and juveniles, abundant), brown shrimp (larvae and juveniles, common), gulf stone crab (juveniles, common), pink shrimp (juveniles, common), and white shrimp (juveniles, common) are present in East Bay in January. Essential fish habitat (EFH) occurs in Gulf of Mexico estuaries for brown shrimp, white shrimp, red drum, Spanish mackerel, cobia, and bluefish. Other Reptiles and Aquatic/Marine Mammals Juvenile and adult alligators and several furbearer species (e.g. raccoon, mink, muskrat, otter, and nutria) are present in freshwater and intermediate marshes. Bottlenose dolphins are also present in the area. IV. Human-Use Resources Management Areas The Pass a Loutre Wildlife Management Area occurs along South Pass. [SEP] The Tug Wally Blessey was reported grounded and leaking in Corpus Christ Bay, TX at 1900 CST today and is reported located at 27&#730; 49.3???€?N, 097&#730; 17.7???€?W. The tug is reported to be carrying 9100 gallons of diesel and some lube and hydraulic oils. 1) 24-hour Wind Forecast Winds this evening are expected to be S at about 15 knots. Tonight, from 2000 to 0300, the winds will shift to be from the NW at 15-20 knots, until tomorrow morning. Tomorrow, the winds will then die down in the afternoon to light and variable the rest of the day. 2) TRAJECTORY Past spills in Corpus Christi Bay under strong wind conditions have moved down wind. Current winds are from the south and are forecast to change to be from the northwest overnight. We expect oil leaked in the first few hours after 2100 CST would head toward the north side of the bay potentially contacting the shoreline between Indian Point and the exposed shoreline of the island opposite La Quinta Channel. If oil continues to leak overnight from the vessel, oil could contact the shoreline counterclockwise around the bay as far south as University Heights. Diesel fuel is not highly persistant. Under the current conditions, much of the oil will be lost through evaporation and natural dispersion. The potential for oil impacting the shoreline is strongly dependant on the release rate: diesel on the surface from a small discharge rate will likely not make shoreline, but a large discharge rate could result in some degree of shoreline impact. 3) OIL FATE Light refined products, such as diesel (or Fuel Oil No 2), typically have very high evaporation rates and do not tend to create persistent slicks. However, the terminology for refined products is not standardized, and, sometimes, heavier intermediate fuel oils are referred to as ???€?marine diesel???€?. These heavier products are less volatile than normal Fuel Oil no 2 and can form a more persistent slick. When spilled, the diesel spreads quickly into thin films often forming patches of rainbow and silver sheens. If the sheens reach the shoreline in a few hours, a slight staining, or greasy film-like bathtub ring is common. These oils usually do not form a stable emulsion

A fuel-oil tanker ran aground in the East River. It was first feared that some of the 446-foot long barge's 130,000 barrels of home-heating oil on board had spilled.  But by daybreak divers determined not a drop had leaked. The barge was towed to the docks under the Whitestone Bridge, and divers were in the water just after 6:30 a.m. to look at the extent of the damage. The tugboat hauling that barge ran aground around 7:20 p.m. Thursday near the Hell's Gate Bride. A Staten Island transportation company owns the tugboat. The captain was tested for drugs and alcohol and tests came back negative. The barge is now being assessed for stability. NOAA provide trajectory and weather information. On 19 December 2004 a spill estimated at 100-150Bbls was reported near an abandoned tank battery near Galveston, TX. As the RP was unknown, the incident was federalized and sediment removal occured. In situ burning was considered for treatment. The incident was eventually transfered to the EPA. [SEP] Photograph of boardwalk installed to access the hot tub, a natural small pond in Zone B2 (photo provided by NOAA). [SEP] Source of spill is a small tank battery. The largest of the three storage tanks with a capacity estimated at 500 bbls failed. picture by CH [SEP] Status Update: On 28 December 2004, the response posture began the transition from an active oil recovery and cleanup to a passive recovery and maintenance phase. Gross oil contamination remains at the site, but active oil recovery had reached a point of diminished return. The bulk of what oil that could be effectively removed without additional environmental injury had been removed. As always, the cleanup goal is to do no more harm to the environment than the oil itself. Drum skimming and vacuum truck operations were being replaced by passive recovery using sorbent materials. Daily on-scene activities were being replaced with periodic maintenance activities. These changes represent the normal transition in a spill cleanup. Evaluations of long-term remedial activities are to be passed to the EPA for management. To that end, the USCG, TGLO, NOAA, and TPW met with an EPA OSC on Monday, 27 December, to begin the transition. The recommendation of the SSC was that the adjacent marsh area be left for natural recovery or consideration of some form of bioremediation of marsh habitat. Through the transition, NOAA requested to remain as a consultant on all activities affecting the marsh habitat. Formal transition to an EPA lead response was planned for 3 January. The NOAA SSC returned home on 28 December, but will remain in communication with both the USCG and the EPA. Background: On Saturday, 18 December 2004, oil was observed in Highland Bayou near Bayou Vista, Texas (a small community NW of Galveston). The source of the spill was determined to be an abandoned tank battery located at 29?? 20.141???€? N Lat. 094?? 57.408???€? W Long. Initial reports suggested that the spill volume may have been 50 bbl, but this value was later increased to 200 bbls. The actual cause of the leak was a corrosion failure of a support arm on a 500 bbl storage tank. When the arm failed, a ???€?shotgun pipe???€? rotated to the ground releasing the oil contained in the tank. The 200 bbl estimate was derived from what appeared as the level of the tank once a man way cover was removed and the tank investigated. The true volume will never be known since the original volume of oil in the tank was only an estimate. Since there was no active RP, the incident was federalized, and the SSC was requested on-scene as part of the Federal-State (USCG-TGLO) spill management team. Oil released escaped the poorly maintained containment berm and entered an adjacent marsh. Some oil eventually enter Highland Bayou and contaminated the adjacent shoreline bracketed by Interstate 45, Highway 6, and the community of Bayou Vista. The linear amount of shoreline impact was crudely estimated at 5 miles, but most of that impact was from sheens. Stranded oil was observed in natural collection points and as stranded oil on tidal flats. Total shoreline habitat where visible oil was observed was less than the 5 mile estimate, and was estimated at between 1 to 2 liner miles. TGLO, working with NOAA, will prepare a final shoreline oiling map (due to holiday travel, several key observers during the initial response phase had left the site for vacation before a final map could be prepared). The bulk of the released oil appeared to have been contained in the marsh immediately adjacent to the tank battery. The area of heavy marsh impact was estimated at 1 acre. The marsh adjacent to the tank battery was of the ???€?high marsh???€? variety. The characterization of high marsh reflects that most of the marsh was infrequently flooded by tides. The habitat had been significantly altered by anthropogenic activities prior to the spill event. The tank battery and an active wellhead were obvious as was a large water impoundment in the center of the marsh site. Less obvious were the ditches cut in the marsh and the multiple abandoned pipelines and associated scares that littered the entire area. The area as a whole was functioning as a marsh, but the topography and hydrology had been altered by past practices. The vegetative cover was diverse and included Distichlis spicata (saltgrass), Spartina pattens (wire grass), Juncus roemerianus (black needle rush), Scirpus sp. (leafy three-square and three corner grass), Spartina alternaflora (smooth cord grass), Borrichia frutescens (sea oxeye daisy), and Iva frutescens (marsh-elder). Given the extent of past activities at the site and that the foundation of the marsh substrate was highly compacted allowing foot traffic without sinking deep into sediments, a more aggressive (more aggressive than normal) active spill response was allowed to remove gross oil contamination. At the peak of the response, a small army of cleanup workers, vacuum trucks, skimmers, pumps, and flushing equipment was deployed. The spill zone was divided into three major divisions: Divisions A and C were outside the marsh and Division B represented the tank battery and marsh (see photomap). Activities in Division B were further divided into Zones B1, B2, and B3. Some locations within Division B developed unique nicknames such as the Ditch, the Hot Tub, and the Duck Pond. The primary cleanup strategy was to contain the bulk oil as close to the source as possible and access natural collection points for bulk oil recovery using vacuum and skimming techniques. Board walkways were constructed using plywood to reduce trampling. A limited amount of trenching and digging of sumps was allowed to enhance oil recovery. A solidifier agent was evaluated as a possible replacement for sorbent pads during the cleanup. In general, the solidifier worked well, but the use of solidifiers never progressed passed the evaluation phase. Additional technique development might be required to enhance the use of solidifiers during response. At the end of the active response, more than 270 bbls of emulsified oil was removed from the marsh by mechanical recovery and an unknown quantity of oil by sorbents. Of the 270 bbls of emulsified oil, the true oil volume might have been only 20% to 25%, or 50 to 60 bbls (a guess only). Such light oils generally lose 30 to 50% by simple evaporation. If we assume that an additional 10 bbls were recovered by sorbents (only a guess), the total oil recovery might have been as high as 70bbl. Discounting evaporative loss of approximately 80 bbls, only 50 bbls would remain unaccounted for at the end of active cleanup. Of the 50 bbls unaccounted, maybe 25 bbls were lost to Highland Bayou. The remaining 25 bbls would represent the residual oil contamination left in the marsh. Such a mass balance given the uncertainty in available information should be considered only a best guess. For prospective only, approximately 60% of the spilled oil was recovered. For a marsh spill, this would be considered a very good recovery rate. The fate of the remaining oil will largely be left to natural recovery (natural biodegradation). Given the porosity of the marsh sediment, residual subsurface contamination exists. There has been some discussion of collecting marsh cores to evaluate the depth and degree of subsurface contamination, but any such follow up must be coordinated with the EPA. The NOAA SSC departed the scene on 28 December 2004. Unless additional response issues are identified, this entry will represent a final response update. [SEP] Photograph of the Duck Pond area. During the night of 15 December 2004, the chemical tanker IEVOLI SPLENDORcollided with a barge resulting in damage to a tank and spilled some 20 to 40bbls of heavy fuel oil (IFO-180) in the Houston Shipping Channel, closing the channel. The Responsible Party's spill management team proposed that PES-51 spray and wipe technique be applied (chemical cleaning agent). [SEP] Photograph provided by USCG. [SEP] Photograph provided by USCG. [SEP] Evening Report At approximately 2130 hrs (local time) on 15 December 2004, the 544 foot chemical tanker M/V IEVOLI SPLENDOR struck an empty barge while attempting to dock. The allision resulted in a 10 inch by 2 inch gash on the aft port side of the vessel and the release of 23 bbls of heavy fuel oil (IFO-180) into the Houston Ship Channel. The oil was reported contained in the industrial portion of the upper ship channel. An early report estimated that at least 5 miles of the river had been oiled to some degree. The VOPAK and CARE dock area, several tugs, barges, and at least one deep draft vessel have been reported oiled. Initially, the Houston ship channel was closed, but was reopened by midday on 16 December. In anticipation of a request to use PES-51 by the cleanup contractors to enhance the effectiveness and efficiency of demobilizing the oiled vessels, MSO Houston contacted the NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator to assist in evaluating and requesting Regional Response Team VI (RRT6) approval. As part of the process, NOAA consulted with both the state and local NOAA habitat managers related to the potential use of surface washing agents. On 16 December, RRT6 meet by conference and approved the use of surface washing agents on vessels if convention flushing was shown to be ineffective. At approximately 2300 hrs, the USCG contacted the NOAA SSC to jointly review a plan to use PES-51 and to review the conditions for use approved by RRT6. The argument from the cleanup contractors to use the chemical cleaner was in part due the cold temperature conditions that made conventional flushing ineffective (the predicted low was 38?? and the high temperature for next day was forecasted as 58??). As part of the review, the need to justify use due to the inefficiencies of conventional methodologies was emphasized as a requirement. The Responsible Party???€?s (RP???€?s) spill management team proposed that PES-51 using the ???€?spray and wipe???€? technique be used on several vessels in the VOPAK and CARE port area. During the review of the plan, the need for proper worker safety and personnel protection was emphasized as well proper containment and recovery of any oil run-off from the vessels. NOAA has not respond on-scene, but continues to provide the USCG verbal support and will continue to monitor the situation. On-scene plans reported to the SSC include continued vessel cleaning and shoreline assessment to identify a strategy for environmental cleanup. [SEP] Initial Report At 0415 hrs this AM, the Barge MMI605 was involved in a collision in the Houston Ship Channel near MM 28. The vessel was holed and at least 1000 bbls of Alkylate was released. Alkylate is a petroleum product much like Naphtha and is highly flammable. The barge was carrying between 20 and 25 thousand bbls of Alkylate. NOAA has been notified and the SSC is providing support to USCG MSU Galveston. First cut estimate of persistence based on ADIOS Model: As a starting point, I used a 250 bbl/hour release rate for 4 hours with 10 mph winds. In short, the model predicts that approximately 20% may persist for at least 24 hours (long enough to make landfall). At present, the currents are outbound through at least noon and the winds have a strong north component, which will also move the spilled product south. We???€?re still tuning the trajectory to the most likely impact areas. Also, the winds are expected to increase which will enhance natural dispersion and help dissipate the surface slick (if the winds are strong enough, shoreline impacts will be marginal if at all). The product is highly flammable. There is also an inhalation human health concern to both responders and the public near the source and if the product should be pooled such as in a boom. The product is not very persistent, so exposure concerns will likely be of a short duration. Likewise, there are wildlife risks. A trajectory and natural resources at risk analysis will follow shortly. Assuming that the spill occurred between 0400 and 0800 CST, most of the product will be flushed out of the Bay by the end of the ebb. With the offshore wind predicted to increase to 15 - 20 knots later today we expect very little of the alkylate to come back into the Galveston Bay on flood. The TABS buoys indicate weak downcoast flow which is consistent with the winds. We expect this condition to continue into tomorrow. As a result, the main force moving the slick will be the winds. The product should move offshore and slightly downcoast. 3) OIL FATE The persistence of the product will depend upon the exact chemical makeup. Alkylates can come in different flavors. ADIOS II oil fate model predicts that the product should persist between 6 and 24 hours depending upon the exact nature of the product. The information included is based on the report of a potential release of 25,000 bbls of alkylate naphtha from a barge located at MM28 in the Houston Ship Channel (29&#8734; 22.319???€?N and 94&#8734; 47.213???€? W). II. Geographic Region Covered The area covered by this report includes the Houston Ship Channel and the west end of Bolivar Peninsula, Pelican Island, and eastern Galveston Island. This area does not necessarily correspond to actual or potential oil locations. Consult other Hotline reports for oil location information. III. Expected Behavior of the Spilled Material Alkylate naphtha has low solubility, is volatile, and is extremely flammable. Exposure to skin, mucous membranes, lungs, or the gastrointestinal tract may lead to toxic effects for birds, reptiles and marine mammals. This product may be highly toxic to aquatic fish and invertebrates. Lethal effects on freshwater eels were observed in less than 9 hours at concentrations of 1000 ug/L for a similar product (http://www.epa.gov/cgi-bin/ecotox_quick_search). Spilled alkylate naphtha may penetrate substrates. IV. Shoreline Resources at Risk The shorelines along the western tip of the Bolivar Peninsula are composed of coarse-grained sand beaches, fine-grained sand beaches, exposed man-made structures, exposed riprap, and salt and brackish marshes. Shorelines along the northern and southern shores of the Bolivar Peninsula are primarily fine-grained sand beaches with portions of salt/brackish marshes. The North and South Jetties and the Texas City Dike are composed of exposed riprap structures. Northeastern Pelican Island is composed primarily of coarse-grained sand beaches. Southeastern Pelican Island is composed of coarse-grained and fine-grained sand beaches with some exposed riprap, exposed solid structures, and sheltered, solid man-made structures. The western shoreline of Pelican Island and the small spoil/marsh island to the west is primarily salt/brackish marsh and scarps/steep slopes in clay with some fine-grained sand beach. The shoreline along Galveston Channel is primarily exposed, solid man-made structures with some exposed riprap and sheltered, solid, man-made structures. The Lagoon is a salt and brackish marsh. The shoreline adjacent to Bolivar Roads and the Gulf of Mexico on Galveston Island is primarily fine-grained sand beach. V. Biological Resources at Risk Threatened/Endangered Birds/Reptiles Common loon (state species of special concern) may be present in Galveston Bay. Reddist egret (state threatened) may be present at the western edge of Bolivar Peninsula. Piping plover (state/federally threatened) may be present in high concentrations and peregrine falcon (federally endangered) may be present in low concentrations at Bolivar Flats. Other T/E species potentially present at Bolivar Flats include: long-billed curlew (state species of special concern), reddish egret, and brown pelican (federally endangered). Brown pelican, reddish egret, and white-faced ibis (state threatened) may be present on the marsh/spoil island west of Pelican Island. Brown pelican may be present on Pelican Island and in Gulf/Bay waters. Species potentially present on eastern Galveston Island include: brown pelican, piping plover, and reddish egret. Designated Critical Habitat for wintering piping plover occurs near Big Reef (Galveston Island) and Bolivar Flats. Loggerhead (state endangered/federally threatened) and Kemp???€?s ridley (state/federally endangered) sea turtles may be present in low concentrations in Gulf waters. A Natural Gas Pipeline failed releasing gas and condensate in Galveston Bay, Texas. The Coast Guard set up an exclusion zone based upon air monitoring data. [SEP] Initial Report, 9 December 2004 PM On Thursday evening, 9 December 2004, the NOAA SSC was notified by MSO Houston of a natural gas release at a platform in Galveston Bay, Texas. The reported location is approximately 1 mile off Eagle Point at the following position 29?? 31.33???€? N Latitude, 094?? 54.14???€? W Latitude. The source of the release was reported as a ???€?silver dollar-size???€? hole in a 12???€? pipeline at the platform. The line normally operates at 5000 p.s.i., but may have been as high as 7,500 p.s.i. at the time of the failure. The material released was characterized as natural gas and water with very little condensate or light petroleum distillates. The greatest immediate threat would be an explosion due to an ignition source such as a ship or boat accidentally coming too close to the release. Natural gas is not highly toxic, but is extremely flammable. The release point is less than one mile from the Houston Ship Channel. In support of the response, NOAA provided a site-specific weather forecast to confirm the local forecast and an assessment of a possible fire/explosion safety zone. The latter is a very difficult value to estimate given the uncertainty associated with such releases. From a tactical prospective, air monitoring was being deployed to aid in delineating and establishing (or verifying the safety zone). Given the uncertainty in source strength information, field monitoring data is invaluable. A first order approximation based on the limited information available suggested that a 300 to 500 yd zone would probably be acceptable if the pressure of the line had in fact dropped and the size of the hole was no larger than estimated. To be conservative, the level of concern used in this estimate was 1/10th the LEL or 5000 ppm. If the pressure remained high and the hole was actually larger, the estimate would increase to 700 to 1000 yds. This same information was verbally passed to the USCG and is roughly consistent with the ERG guideline of 800 meters for a large release. Note, neither the model or the ERG was designed specifically for this type of release in part due to the water and condensate combined with the natural gas. That said, both the model and the ERG are generally conservative. From an environmental pollution prospective, sheens formed from released condensate were reported to be small and dissipate rapidly. A second attempt to shut in the line is planned for first light. At present, the NOAA SSC is standing by. [SEP] A Hotline has been opened for the Natural Gas Release, Eagle Point, Galveston, TX incident. [SEP] Update (10 Dec. 2004) The source of the release, a hole in a 12???€? natural gas pipeline, couldn???€?t be controlled by in-place valves (valve failure). A lift boat and repair team are expected on-scene in the morning to attempt to secure the source. On-scene monitoring continues and there has been a safety zone of 200 yds established and enforced by the USCG. The distance was decided based on actual monitoring data and an additional safety margin. No additional issues have been identified that would require NOAA support; therefore, the NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator is maintaining a stand-by posture on this response.
During early December of 2004, a huge storm drove the floundering M/V Selendang Ayu onto the rockly shoals on the west side of Unalaska Island, where the vessel broke in two releasing over 75%  (337,000 gallons) of its total petroleum fuel products of IFO-380 and marine diesel.   Nearly all the oil was driven onto the mostly rocky shorelines of Makushin and Skan Bays.  Within two weeks the bow section had sunk; however, the stern section remained afloat with the balance of the fuel.    From early January, 2005, until mid-February, 2006, a heavy lift helicopter was used to lighter this fuel from the stern section with over 70 round trips to Dutch Harbor, 25 miles away, and using a 2000 gallon steel sling-loaded cube.   Due to the potential for an additional release during this period, skimmers and dispersants (Corexit 9500) were maintained as standby response measures.   Reasonable weather during these operations allowed for reconnaisance SCAT evaluation and some modest manual shoreline cleanup. 2005 winter operations were halted around mid February due to deteoriating weather conditions.        In mid-April, 2005, SCAT and full shoreline cleanup teams returned to Unalaska Island and worked into October, 2005, until again winter weather shut down the operation with only a couple dozen of over one hundred shoreline segments needing further cleaning and/or inspection.   Modest SCAT personnel and shoreline cleanup folks returned in May, 2006, to complete the final shoreline cleanup and inspections.    Manual shoreline cleanup was the dominate technique utilized; however dry mechanical tilling and berm relocation were used quite successfully on the appropriate shorelines.      One of the key peripheral issues involved possible oiling of the commercial sea food harvest that is caught around and processed on Unalaska Island.  Heightened monitorning and inspections resulted in the finding of no oiled fish products.   Another issue was the oiling and tainting of traditional and subsistence food harvested by the Alaska natives who live on the island.   Task forces of federal, state,  local, and industry representatives were established to deal with these issues. [SEP] Soybeans Emulsion 1 12/28/04 [SEP] M/V Selendang Ayu Cleanup Operations Complete -June 20, 2006 This week marks the completion of cleanup from the M/V Selendang Ayu oil spill near Dutch Harbor, Alaska. The M/ V Selendang Ayu ran aground and broke apart near Unalaska Island between Skan Bay and Spray Cape approximately 25 miles southwest of Dutch Harbor on December 8, 2004. An estimated 321,000 gallons of intermediate fuel oil, 14,680 gallons of marine diesel, and the vessel's load of approximately 60 thousand tons of soybeans were released and contaminated miles of nearby beaches. Cleanup activities were conducted between May and September of 2005 and resumed in May 2006 for shorelines that did not reach cleanup endpoint criteria last year. Over the past 19 months, several NOAA ORR scientists have helped conduct shoreline surveys, make cleanup recommendations, and inspect shorelines after cleanup. Assessment of damage to natural resources and restoration planning continue. All activities have been conducted in cooperation with the U.S. Coast Guard, State of Alaska, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, the Alaska Department of Conservation, and the party responsible for the spill. On December 3, 2004, NOAA DAC was notified by the USFWS of a truckaccident along Route One near Woodbridge VA that resulted in a release ofpowdered lime into Powells Creek.  The truck was loaded with 27 tons of lime. The exact amount spilled into the Creek is unknown, but preliminary visualestimates suggest that up to 20 tons may have spilled into the Creek.  Powellscreek enters the Potomac River just south of Occuquan Bay, approximately 25miles downstream of Washington D.C.  The spilled lime is having a visible exothermic reaction in the creek and thewater is boiling near the release site.  In addition to the heat given off bythe reaction, there is concern regarding elevated pH.  NOAA has requestedchemistry support from LSU to evaluate the potential fates and behavior of thespilled lime.This portion of Powells Creek is tidally influenced and is an environmentallysensitive area.  NOAA resources, primarily anadromous and catadromous fishspecies, are present in this area and there are already reports of fish kills. [SEP] VA DEQ conducted a pH survey of Powell's Creek yesterday, December 7. As expected, following the rain, the pH levels have begun to decline in the creek. FWS and DEQ are in the field today to perform another pH survey. A call among the trustees is scheduled for tomorrow to discuss our findings and next steps. [SEP] At approximately 830 AM local time, NOAA was notified by the USFWS of a truck accident along Route One near Woodbridge VA that resulted in a release of powdered lime into Powells Creek. The truck was loaded with 27 tons of lime. The exact amount spilled into the Creek is unknown, but preliminary visual estimates suggest that up to 20 tons may have spilled into the Creek. Powells creek enters the Potomac River just south of Occuquan Bay, approximately 25 miles downstream of Washington D.C. The spilled lime is having a visible exothermic reaction in the creek and the water is boiling near the release site. In addition to the heat given off by the reaction, there is concern regarding elevated pH. NOAA has requested chemistry support from LSU to evaluate the potential fates and behavior of the spilled lime. This portion of Powells Creek is tidally influenced and is an environmentally sensitive area. NOAA resources, primarily anadromous and catadromous fish species, are present in this area and there are already reports of fish kills. Joe Steinbacher, NOAA ORR in Silver Spring is enroute to the spill site to collect additional information and coordinate with the State and USFWS regarding environmental impacts. The SSC has been notified but at the point ORR???€?s involvement is as a natural resource trustee. These notes are based on the following information: The Tanker Kristen Poling is grounded at coordinates: 40d 35.077???€?N, 73d 45.614???€?W on a sandy bottom just outside East Rockaway Inlet, NY. It is carrying 18,000 bbls of number 2 Fuel. We have been asked for to provide and estimate for a worst case scenario release from the vessel. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP, as it would affect the estimated trajectory. _______________________________________________________ 1) WEATHER: This afternoon through Tonight, the winds are expected to be from the W to NW at 15-20 knot with gust to 30 knots. Saturday, the winds are forecast to be from the W at 10-15 knots shifting in the afternoon to be from the SW at 15-20 knots. 2) TIDES: Strong tidal currents are predicted in the vicinity of the vessel, with max flood of almost 2 knots into East Rockaway Inlet at about 2239EST Dec 03, and 1040EST and 2320EST On Dec 4th. Ebb tides, also of about 2 knots are predicted for 0434EST and 1700EST on Dec 4th. 3) TRAJECTORY: The Worst case would be for the product to be released near the time of one of the flood tides. In this case, the oil would be moved by the flood tides and the West winds into East Rockaway Inlet, and could make it as far as Broad Channel. From there it could spread into the surrounding Marsh. If the product were released near an ebb tide, it could move more offshore, then be pushed by the west winds past Silver point, and impact the Western end of Long Beach, in the Atlantic Beach region. 4) OIL WEATHERING: An ADIOS computer model run predicts that up to 7% of the oil could evaporate, and 85% disperse into the water column, leaving less than 10% floating after 24 hours. However, this estimate is for fully developed seas outside the inlet. Inside the inlet, the dispersion will be substantially less. In this case, there could be about 10% of the oil remaining after 36-48 hours. [SEP] Here are the tidal currents [SEP] Here are the tide heights [SEP] Tide heights and tide currents. At approximately 9:30 p.m. on November 26, 2004, the M/T Athos I, a 750-foot tanker, hit one (or more) obstructions in the Delaware River near Philadelphia, PA. A 15-foot curved piece of pipe was ultimately found with the assistance of the NOAA Navigation Response Team. After further examination, the hull showed evidence that the ship may have hit more than one object. The tanker, registered in Cyprus, was carrying 325,000 barrels (13.6 million gallons) of heavy crude oil from Venezuela. The collision(s) created three holes, the largest a 6-foot by 2-foot tear in the hull that breached a center cargo tank and port side water ballast tank, releasing approximately 264,000 gallons. After the incident, a review of PORTS tide level recordings showed the collision(s) occurred at maximum spring low tide. The oil from the ruptured tank spread down river, ultimately oiling 57 miles of Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Delaware shorelines. The spill closed the Delaware River to commercial vessel traffic for over a week. Submerged oil resulted in contamination of water intakes and the closure of the Salem Nuclear Power Plant. The snare at the southern end of Tinicum Island was heavily oiled along the bottom 5 feet, the next 5 feet were clean, and the rest of the snare (35 ft) was very lightly oiled, with light oiling near surface. This information indicated the potential for significant amounts of submerged oil. Three additional ???€?snare water-column samplers???€? were deployed: 1) in the river near the mouth off Big Timber Creek; 2) near Mantua Creek; and 3) near the Logan Power Plant. The mechanisms of submergence that are being researched include: 1) some part of the oil initially sunk to the bottom at the collision site; and 2) the oil initially floated then stranded onshore, picked up sediment, then was eroded from the shoreline. A source sample is being sent for analysis of density, viscosity, distillation fractions, and density/ composition after evaporative weathering. Samples from oil from the bottom at a known submerged oil site (to be collected by divers under USCG supervision) will also be chemically analyzed to determine whether they sank initially or after stranding (e.g., show evidence of weathering dominated by evaporation or dissolution). Plans are being made to collect additional samples via grab samples, ???€?diaper drops???€? (e.g., sorbent pads on an anchor), and snare drag chains in the upper river, and more snare water column samples (particularly in the upper bay) over the next few days. On November 17, 2004, the M/V Fortune Epoch detected an oil sheen in its wake after it left the Savannah River. It then anchored and notified USCG. [SEP] Date: 1530 EST November 17, 2004 To: NOAA SSC Brad Benggio FROM: NOAA/Hazardous Materials Response Division Modeling and Simulation Studies Seattle, WA 98115 SUBJECT: MV Fortune Epoch FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION, PLEASE CONTACT CJ Beegle-Krause MODELING AND SIMULATION STUDIES, NOAA, SEATTLE, WA 98115. PHONE (206) 526-4911. ______________________________________________________ We have looked at the trajectory implications of a leaking vessel offshore of Savannah, Georgia. These notes are based on the following information: Today, NOAA HazMat was notified at 1045 PST (1345 EST) of a leaking vessel offshore of Savannah, Georgia. The MV Fortune Epoch was reported leaking diesel from a 37,250 gallon tank approximately 4 hours earlier. Approximately 1-1.5 hours earlier an overflight reported a 6 nm sheen oriented from the vessel toward shore. The vessel is currently anchored at 31&#730; 59???€?N, 080&#730; 41???€?W. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP as it would affect any trajectory implications. ______________________________________________________ 1) 24-hour Wind Forecast Today through tonight, the winds are expected to be from the N to NE at 10 knots. Thursday, variable winds at 5 knots are predicted. 2) TRAJECTORY For a tank leaking below the waterline, the product above waterline most likely leaked out quickly. The remaining oil below waterline would be leaking out slowly. The observed winds over the last 24 hours have been northerly at about 10 knots. With forecast light winds from the N to NE, weak currents downcoast, and rotary tides offshore, we expect a possibility of beach impacts on Little Tybee Island by tomorrow (depending on the oil type, see OIL FATE below). If the oil were to reach The Jones Island Range in the shipping channel when the tide was flooding, the oil could be brought in as far as 3 nm. 3) OIL FATE Diesel: Light refined products, such as diesel (or Fuel Oil No 2), typically have very high evaporation rates and do not tend to create persistent slicks. However, the terminology for refined products is not standardized, and, sometimes, heavier intermediate fuel oils (IFO) are referred to as ???€?marine diesel???€?. These heavier products are much less volatile than normal Fuel Oil no 2 and can form a more persistent slick. When spilled, the diesel spreads quickly into thin films often forming patches of rainbow and silver sheens. The most conservative estimate for the persistence of this oil is to use a marine diesel and IFO 180 to bracket the length of time the oil could be on the water. For a marine diesel, the fuel would evaporate significantly with 10% remaining after 20 hours. For an IFO 180, 75% of the oil would remain after 5 days. If the oil does not evaporate quickly, we should revisit the trajectory implications with the information from the next overflight. Gary Shigenaka prepared the following information. On January 4, 1999, the M/V Star Evviva was responsible for an incident involving substantial loon impacts off South Carolina. That incident has some similarities to the M/V Fortune Epoch. The initial release was reported as 17 gallons spilled, then <100 gals, ultimately estimated discharge of 25K gal 30 nm offshore even though almost no oil was reported on the water. CG Marine Safety Lab made positive match with the MV Star Evviva. >200 birds oiled, mostly loons, most died. Why loons? That one is fairly easy...in winter, common loons favor shallow salt-water areas close to shore. While they are solitary when feeding in winter, they also congregate in loose flocks at night. Therefore, overflights may not identify aggregations because the birds are dispersed during daylight hours. We are uncertain what accounts for the loon-only impacts...other birds don't favor the same impacted nearshore habitat? Loons are somehow more buoyant, hardier, and make it to shore more readily? Attached is information on the MS Star Evviva incident. The Damage Assessment and Restoration Plan prepared by the USFWS for the incident is available if necessary. (from Wildlife & Oil Spills, Vol. 8, No. 1) Star Evviva Spill - On January 16, oiled loons began washing ashore along the coast of North and South Carolina. The vessel Star Evviva spilled an undetermined amount of oil during a transfer operation while at sea. The oil contaminated loons that were wintering off the coast of the Carolinas. A total of 97 oiled birds were retrieved, the majority of which were loons. Because the birds were oiled off the coast and slowly drifted in to shore, they were in very poor condition when collected. Therefore, only 5 of the 97 oiled birds collected were successfully rehabilitated. NOAA assisted with multiple incidents on the Mississippi Delta in Louisiana resulting from Hurricane Ivan. [SEP] This spill, which occurs in the Breton National Wildlife Refuge along Raphael Pass consisted of 362 bbls of oil spilled into the marsh due to a leaking tank from the hurricane. On Sept 22nd, LA DEQ, USCG, USFWS, and NOAA met with the ES and H individual representing the RP. Most of the oil has naturally dispersed and moved due to the high water and wind (water at this time, thanks to east winds, was 2-3' above normal high tide). SCAT by boat was done by LA DEQ and NOAA. A good estimate of oil remaining couldn't be established, but most of the oil is gone. I'd estimate maybe 5-10 bbls are left. Most oil observed was sheening (silver and rainbow colored) with patches of black oil found in the reseau cane. The USFWS expressed concern for waterfowl and birds and wishes to have most of the cane that is oiled near the facility cut. The clean up method recommended for the rest of the area and the area surrounding the facility as well was a passive clean up utilizing sorbent boom. 1600' of it was brought out later that day. LA DEQ, USFWS, and USCG are returning Friday for another round of observations. Due to weather there are no ops today. [SEP] Yesterday afternoon there were differences in what the situation was on scene concerning how much oil was on the water. Estimates varied from 25 to 500 bbls. Because of this, response approaches, concerns, etc varied from the different groups. After Shell took over responsibility for the clean up (note, NOT the oil) they contacted the NOAA SSC expressing an interest to use dispersants. Phone calls were made to the appropriate parties for dispersant approval, and before the end of the day on Friday, Sept. 24th, clearances for dispersal application by boat (in depths greater then 20???€?) had been approved by all of the concerned parties except for the EPA (who had yet to respond). At the end of the day Friday, the big issues were the unknowns on what exactly was going on out on scene while the oil continued to leak. An evening overflight conducted by LA DEQ found the thicker oil heading south, with the southern tip estimated at 29d 12.5???€?N, 088d 58.55???€?W. Word from the first morning overflight on Saturday Sept. 25 by DEQ brought news of large amounts of oil in the areas of Lonesome Bayou, North Pass, Pass A Loutre, and Blind Bay. The Coast Guard RRT liason was then contacted and he contacted the EPA who approved the possible use of dispersants by boat or air, so the use of dispersants has been approved by the RRT. The NOAA Scientific Support Team arrived on scene to observe pictures from the morning overflight. There was significant oiling in the areas mentioned above, with oil streaking from the point of origin 29d 15.62???€?N, 089d 01.2???€?W south as far as 29d 09.8???€?N, 88d 01.25???€?W, approximately 6.8 miles from the spill site. The Louisiana Responder was on scene yesterday, the Mississippi Responder and Grand Bay arrived on scene this morning. Decanting has been approved. The plan for use of the skimmers is to have the Mississippi Responder stay close to the leaking source, with the Louisiana Responder behind catching the oil entrained by the Mississippi Responder. The noon overflight by with NOAA on board was similar. There are streaking slicks south from the source down from the edge of North Pass to the westward edge of Lonesome Bay. The oil is then moving thru a cut (that is boomed) down into Pass A Loutre and across a sandbar/marsh area into Blind Bay. Turns out this is possible because the bathymetry is almost W to E. The source is right along the slope and this means there is a current running west to east at the source. Obviously with the windage at about .6 knots, this means the current is gotta be at least 3/4 of the knot or more. I'm guessing as high at 1.5 knots because it is being fed by the strong persistent East winds that will bring water along the coast from the East and from whatever runoff is entering the Gulf from East of the Miss R. This is the only explanation for the oil moving into the wind. So we go with it until proven wrong. The bathymetry turns to the south at the end of Pass A Loutre, at about 6 - 7 miles from the source. This means the current will turn to the south and eventually to the SW. The oil too will turn south. After this happens, the E winds will be perpendicular to the currents and should start moving the oil toward shore. Most likely impacts would be between Blind Bay and Garden I Bay. If the oil is only a few thousand gallons of an API in the mid 30's or higher, it may not persist long enough to impact shore, unless it emulsifies. In the early morning hours Sept. 21, 2004, vandals severed the fuel hoses feeding into the Auke Bay marina releasing both diesel and gasoline into the marina. Barge Kirby 7304 had a stuck valve and leaked Isoprene. A .25 mile safety/exclusion zone was established near the town of Brusley, LA. The product was safely offloaded and flushed with inert gas. There were no injuries. [SEP] Hotline has been opened to capture information about the Kirby Barge #7304 in Brusley, LA reported to be leaking C5 distillate. [SEP] On 26 August 2004, the NOAA was notified of a barge releasing gases from a pressure relief/vent value (PV) that was apparently stuck in the open position. The barge, identified as Kirby 7304, was located at a fleeting area on the Mississippi River near the town of Brusley, Louisiana. Two elementary schools were evacuated and a safety/exclusion zone of 0.25 miles was established. The product was a mixture of very light distillates with an extremely narrow boiling point range around C5 (pentane). The most abundant chemical in the mixture was isoprene, and the product was reported to have an average boiling point of 85??F. The product was extremely flammable with a LEL of only 1.4%. In the hot summer afternoon, the barge temperature was clearly above the products boiling point resulting in excess pressure and venting. NOAA was request to provide on-scene scientific support to MSU Baton Rouge to include weather, chemistry consultation, and modeling. Two questions were identified. The first was to insure that the cause was a stuck valve and not a runaway polymerization problem. The second was to develop a strategy should the attempt to reset the valve fail. NOAA work with the USCG consulting the product manufactures representatives as to the potential for polymerization complicating the situation. It was determined that the barge was used solely for this product and that the product had been treated with an inhibitor to reduce the risk. The final conclusion from the experts was that the potential for a reaction to create or complicate the proposed response was low (as the RP???€?s chemist stated, never say never). If resetting the value failed, several options were investigated to mitigate the threat such as the application of a water spray during the evening hours. Fortunately, the HAZMAT team was able to make an entry and reseat the value at approximately 0630 hours. The barge was off-loaded at a near-by facility and inerted with nitrogen gas. The barge would require cleaning and gas freeing before inspection and repairs could be made. No addition support was requested from NOAA. There were no reported injuries or releases in the river. The Delta Star, a 72' Tug struck a buoy in the jetty entrance to Sabine Pass and released its fuel. No fuel was ever found. [SEP] Hotline has been opened to capture information about the Tug Delta Star that allided with a navigation buoy in Sabine Pass, TX. [SEP] Initial and Final Report At approximately 0650 hrs (CDT) on Sunday, 22 August 2004, the NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator (SSC) was notified that the Tug DELTA STAR had allied with a buoy within the jetty entrance to Sabine Pass due to a loss of steerage. The location of the accident was reported to be Buoy 21 or 22 (the buoys are across the pass from each other and do not represent mile markers); that position places the accident approximately 1 nautical mile off Louisiana Point, Louisiana. The DELTA STAR, a 72' vessel, was reported to have had 2,500 gallons of #2 Fuel Oil (diesel) on board at the time of the allision. Shortly after the accident, the vessel was towed into the pass and up the ship channel to a facility near Pleasure Island, Texas. The initial USCG investigation reported that essentially all of the fuel had been lost before the vessel arrived in port. Containment around the vessel was ordered as pumps were maintained to control flooding. Sheens were observed near the vessel. The SSC was requested to provide assistance as to the probable trajectory and fate of the spilled diesel fuel. By chance, the SSC was at a hotel across the street from the MSO and was able to respond on-scene immediately. Trajectory and Mass Balance The NOAA C-Man station at Sabine, Texas reported on-shore SSE winds at 16 to 18 kts at the time of the allision shifting to S at 17 to 19 kts at around 0400 hrs (CDT). ADIOS2, NOAA's oil weathering model, predicted, that if most of the oil was lost near the buoy, after six hours only 12% would remain on the surface (the rest being lost to evaporation and natural dispersion). Given that the winds were out of the SSE, the surface slick would move through the jetty, possibly toward Texas Point, Texas (a highly sensitive area). The predicted tides would have little effect on surface transport. The jetty, itself, would enhance dissipation of the surface slick by increasing diffusion and natural dispersion. It would be unlikely that any appreciable quantity of diesel would persist for more than 1 nautical mile from the release point (Texas Point is less than a nautical mile from Buoys 21 and 22). If oil continued to leak as the vessel was towed into the pass, the Louisiana Point and Lighthouse Bayou (both highly sensitive areas) would be at risk. Overflight Surveillance The USCG conducted an overflight of the scene between 0730 and 0815 hrs the same morning. No oil pollution was observed in the lower pass, but a small sheen was observed further up the ship channel and some sheen was observed around the vessel. The observers suspect that the observed sheen in the channel was unrelated to the DELTA STAR incident. Given that no residual surface oil pollution was observed, no addition additional support was requested. The NOAA SSC will follow-up with notifications to the NOAA Injury Assessment Coordinator for Texas and the NMFS Habitat Conservation Office in Galveston, Texas.
At 0530 on August 2, 2004, the NOAA Scientific Support Team was requested by MSOPort Arthur for an oil spill in the Natchez River in Texas. The T/V Torm Mary was struck by a fuel barge readying to load, leaving roughly a5'x 1' crack in the Torm Mary . [SEP] 100_0539.JPG - East of Bird Island 100_0545.JPG - Facility west of Port Neches Park 100_0547.JPG - Facility west of Port Neches Park 100_0548.JPG - Unocal pier 100_0549.JPG - Unocal pier [SEP] Overflight maps [SEP] Overflight map 08/04 0815 [SEP] Update (18 August) Spill response is often filled with defeated expectations; Tuesday, 17 August was one such day on the Neches River Spill. The Unified Command met at the Unocal facility for a final walk through that Tuesday morning. The expectations were that a few locations would require additional active cleanup, but the spill management team believed that most of the cleanup had progressed to the maintenance phase. Unfortunately, the conditions had changed (or were not nearly as complete as thought) and there was free floating oil and sheen along the entire shoreline at Unocal. The source of this new, or newly released, oil is thought to have been a combination of sources: oil under Unocal Dock #1, riprap cleaning, and a small marsh area east of Unocal where passive recover had been removed (prematurely). A deep draft vessel had recently docked and may have freed oil into the river combined with a lower than predicted morning tide. The response posture immediately changed back to containment and recovery around the Unocal facility. Clearly, too much containment was removed too early (hind-sight is always 20/20). The amount of oil lost from the site was not major, but beyond our expectation. On the afternoon of 17 August, SCAT resurveyed and segmented the Unocal facility, identify cleanup locations, developed a plan for additional cleanup, and will monitor operations. Twenty segments were created to monitor work progress. The NOAA SSC will remain on-scene until the maintenance plans are finalized. [SEP] 100_0507.JPG - T/V Torm Mary 100_0515.JPG - Rainbow Bridge looking into Sabine Lake 100_0516.JPG - Star Lake Canal 100_0519.JPG - South of Port Neches Park 100_0522.JPG - East of Unocal Facility 100_0523.JPG - Unocal Facility [SEP] Just after midnight tonight will mark Day 21 (three weeks) into the TORM MARY oil spill and response. Cleanup has progressed such that only one mile of shoreline remains in the active cleanup phase. That site, the Unocal facility on the S shore of the Neches River was one of the heaviest impacted areas. Most of the shoreline is armored with concrete riprap, and oil coated a 1 to 3 foot band along most of the facility property and the marsh immediately downstream. Oil not only covered the exposed surfaces, but also coated the unexposed underside surfaces and pooled oil was observed in between the crevices and loose gravel under the larger riprap structures. There are also numerous man-made structures such as moorings, piers, pilings, and a boat ramp at the Unocal facility that were also oiled and for a short period were sources of secondary pollution until the entire area was completely isolated using hard boom. Cleanup continues using a combination of a chemical shoreline cleaning agent (PES-51) with low pressure flushing, high-pressure hot water cleaning, and passive recovery. Most of the effort has reached a state of minimum return and only passive recovery was planned for the weekend before a reassessment on Monday or Tuesday (weather and tide dependant). The underside of the largest dock and pier remain a problem to cleanup efforts. While the dock platform is high enough to facilitate deep draft vessels, there is a lower series of platforms that are used to facilitate numerous pipelines making under-the-dock access nearly impossible except at extremely low tides. Multiple attempts at flushing seem to have removed the surface oil. The underside dock cobble shoreline has been cleaned twice, once with CytoSol and once with PES-51. Each cleaning results is acceptable levels of surface washing, but oil that had seep into the cobble continues to slowly leach out (possible enhanced by the effect of the chemical agents). ???€?It seems that every time we think that we make good progress under the dock, more free floating oil is observed and the cobble shoreline appears reoiled.???€? The NOAA SSC remains on-scene at the request of the FOSC to continue to monitor cleanup activities and assess progress. The Environmental unit has drafted a detailed plan to shift the operation from an active response into the maintenance phase early next week. The NOAA SSC has also participated in discussion with the Natural Resource Damage Assessment Trustees. A field trip with the trustees is planned for Wednesday, 25 August. NOAA is also been request to provide the Regional Response Team with written reports as to the testing and use of the different shoreline cleaning agents. The Clipper Odyessy unexpectedly grounded on an uncharted rock immediately west of the Baby Islands just east of Unalaska Island.  The grounding occurred at approximately 9:30 pm on July 31, 2004, rupturing only the forward fuel tank which contained about 5000 gallons of diesel, all of which was released.   At the time of the grounding, 196 passengers were on board the Clipper Odyssey.   These passengers were all evacuated via local fishing vessel, etc. from Dutch Harbor and transported back to Dutch Harbor.  With the assistance of two tugs, the salvor Magone Marine stabilized the vessel early morning of Aug. 1 after which it proceded to Dutch Harbor.  Oil containment boom was placed around the vessel upon arrival in Dutch Harbor.  Diesel fuel was reportedly leaking from the damaged #1 port tank immediately after the grounding and enroute to Dutch Harbor.  The response contractor, Chadux, was activated and pre-staged response equipment in Dutch Harbor.  The Baby Islands are part of the US Maritime National Wildlife Refuge and as such are loaded with a variety of birds.   No oiled birds were observed, however, the IBRRC was alerted.   NOAA provided support in the form of weather forecasts, tidal current information, trajectories of the diesel release, and resources at risk information.

[SEP] This morning(07/27) the SSC was notified of a barge grounding on the Saint Lawrence Seaway. The Canadian flagged, barge KTC-115 broke free from its tug during a steering failure. Before the tug could recover the KTC ???€? 115, it grounded on Frontenac Shoal in position 44?? 20.408' N 075?? 55.508' W near Alexander Bay NY. KTC-115 contained 35% calcium chloride solution. The barge sustained damage to the starboard tank, which contained 170,000 gallons. Over 12,000 gallons spilled from the tank before it reached equilibrium. The tank continues to take on approximately 1/8 inch of water per hour. Divers found three cracks near the starboard bow. Burlap wrapped wedges were placed in those cracks accessible to the divers. A lightering barge is expected to arrive on scene Friday morning. The USCG requested that NOAA HAZMAT determine the at worst case release of the total contents of the starboard tank. No further NOAA assistance is needed at this time. [SEP] Hotline has been opened to capture information about the grounded barge in the Saint Lawrence River. [SEP] St. Lawrence Seaway ???€? Barge aground on Frontenac Shoals The USCG estimated 12,000 gallons of Calcium chloride (CaCl2) in 35% solution leaked from a barge hard aground on the Frontenac Shoals, 44?? 20.04???€? N, 075?? 55.508???€? W. An estimated 158,000 gallons remain onboard. The USCG asked what would be the consequences of losing the rest of the cargo. The spill is located near the deep water channel of the St. Lawrence River. The specific gravity of the calcium chloride solution (35%) is 1.35 relative to freshwater, so the product will sink (on the order of minutes) as it leaks from the vessel. The estimated flow of the river is approximately 7600 m3/s (230,000 ft3/s) which will help mix and dilute the product. However, the product will move along the bottom of the river, and will hinder mixing and dilution. Resources at Risk: Water intakes: There are several water intakes in the spill area. The primary intake is the Alexandria Bay Municipal Drinking water intake is located at the spill site. There are several fish species expected in the area which will be acutely sensitive to high concentrations of the product. For example, the 96 hr LC50 for juvenile bluegill is 8 ppt (ECOTOX). For freshwater snails, the 48 hr LC50 is 3 ppt. Resources at risk will be those that are in the deeper areas of the river. In depressions in the channel, the product will be more persistent. Recommendations: The remaining product should be lightered, if possible. If the only means of removing the product is by releasing it to the environment, the pumping rate should be low enough to keep concentrations below 100 ppm on the bottom. This is an order of magnitude below toxicity endpoints in test species.

[SEP] Resources at Risk for Lake Grande Etaille, LA This report was prepared on 22 July 2004. Information in this report is based on the assumption that a pipeline release of approximately 50-100 bbls occurred in Lake Grande Etaille in northeast Barataria Bay (29&#8734; 23.5???€? N, 89&#8734; 47.55 W). This report does not necessarily correspond to actual or potential spill locations. Consult other Hotline reports for spill location information. Habitats Habitats in Lake Grande Etaille and northeast Barataria Bay are mostly salt marsh. Birds There are at least six colonial waterbird nesting colonies in the vicinity of Big Island in Barataria Bay (within 3 miles of assumed release site). Approximate counts of species nesting and feeding in the area are: black-crowned night-heron (22 birds), Forster???€?s tern (330 birds), great egret (62 birds), snowy egret (30 birds), tricolored heron (80 birds), little blue heron (8 birds), black skimmer (8 birds), and reddish egret (1 bird). July is the end of the breeding season for most species, so fledglings are likely present on and around the nests. Mottled duck may be nesting in marshes. Fish and Invertebrates Several species of fish may be present in the area. Very abundant species include: Atlantic croaker (spawning adults, eggs, larvae, juveniles), bay anchovy (spawning adults, eggs, larvae, and juveniles), gulf menhaden (juveniles), and spot (juveniles). Abundant species include: red drum (juveniles), sand seatrout (spawning adults, eggs, larvae, and juveniles), sheepshead (larvae and juveniles), southern flounder (juveniles), spotted seatrout (spawning adults, eggs, larvae, and juveniles), and striped mullet (juveniles). Very abundant invertebrate species present in the area include: blue crab (eggs, larvae, juveniles), brown shrimp (spawning adults, eggs, larvae, and juveniles), and white shrimp (spawning adults, eggs, larvae, and juveniles). Oyster lease sites occur in the area. Essential fish habitat (EFH) occurs in Gulf of Mexico estuaries for brown shrimp, white shrimp, red drum, Spanish mackerel, cobia, and bluefish. Reptiles and Aquatic Mammals Juvenile and adult alligators are transient in salt marshes, and several species of aquatic furbearers are residents (raccoon, mink, muskrat, river otter, and nutria). clean-up assessment, flush and vacuum products and cut heavily oiled plants [SEP] On the morning (0930) of 22 June 2004, the NOAA SSC was notified by the Ohio Spill Planning Prevention and Emergency Response Association (OSPPERA) that a truck and a van collision had resulted in both vehicles coming to rest in an arrowhead plant (Sagittaria sp.) dominated marsh. The truck fuel tanks and lube oils had leaked resulting in a 200 gallon spill. Ohio EPA and OSPPERA had requested information on the possibility of using insitu burning to remove the oil. The accident site was within the Magee Marsh Wildlife Area and the State wanted the oil removed. Due to the proximity to residences and the accessibility of the oil, burning was ruled out as an option. The SSC arrived on scene around 1200. Prior to the arrival, the decision had been made and the contractors had commenced to cut the oiled vegetation and vacuum the remaining floating product. Dr. Jacqui Michel of RPI was contacted to determine impacts of this strategy. It was her opinion that flushing should be attempted prior to cutting. If flushing was ineffective, only those plants heavily oiled should be removed. Although Arrowhead is a nearly indestructible perennial, some portion of the plant needs to remain above the water surface for oxygen exchange to ensure survival. Based on this input, the Ohio EPA rep. requested the cleanup crews flush as much product out as possible, cut only the heavily oiled plants and leave some of the plant material above the waterline. Absorbent booms will remain in place until the area no longer sheens. The SSC departed the scene at 1400 hours. No further NOAA support is needed at this time. [SEP] Hotline has been opened to capture information about the truck collision and spill, Magee Marsh, OH. A release on an ebb tide would move a slick to the southwest and into the western side of Iphigenia Bay (about 4 miles southeast of Warren Island). Any remaining oil would move northerly on the flood tide and, with the forecast westerly winds, likely threaten the northern tip of Heceta Island and the Davidson Inlet area. 2) Oil Weathering Diesel Oil Diesel products used in recreational vessels typically have very high evaporation rates and do not tend to create persistent slicks. When spilled, the diesel spreads quickly into thin films often forming patches of rainbow and silver sheens. If the sheens reach the shoreline in a few hours, a slight staining, or greasy film-like bathtub ring is common. These oils usually do not form a stable emulsion and, as a result, do not form a heavy or sticky residual to clean up. With the wind speeds greater than 10 knots and mixing due to strong tides, we would anticipate that 90% of the diesel would evaporate and disperse in the first 12 hours of a catastrophic release. Spill Source Information This report was prepared on 26 May 2004. Information in this report is based on the assumption that a double-hulled barge with 7,200 bbls of Oleum (sulfuric acid/sulfur trioxide) grounded near Port Arthur Texas at Buoy 69 (29&#8734; 58.7???€? N, 93&#8734;50.5???€?). II. Geographic Region Covered The area covered by this report is Sabine Lake and the surrounding area in the vicinity of Port Arthur, Texas. This report does not necessarily correspond to actual or potential spill locations. Consult other Hotline reports for spill location information. III. Expected Behavior of the Spilled Material Sulfuric acid/sulfur hydroxide is a strong acid that is heavier than water, very soluble, and is expected to have an energetic reaction when mixed with water. Where addition of acid changes the pH significantly, water-column and benthic organisms will be impacted. A pH value around 4.5 represents the approximate thresholds beyond which most life processes in natural waters are seriously impaired (Strumm and Morgan 1996). Rounding to the nearest whole pH unit, if added acid lowers pH to less than about 5, aquatic organisms will be impacted. The duration of exposure for this pH-related impact is on the scale of minutes to hours because the physiological functions of aquatic organisms depend so highly on charge balances in membranes and cells. A pH limit of 5 is close to results from bioassays in fresh water. Another risk of any release of oleum is mobilization of contaminants such as heavy metals from sediments where the concentrated plume comes in contact with bottom sediments. IV. Shoreline Resources at Risk The shoreline along Port Arthur is predominantly solid man-made structures and riprap. The Humble Island shoreline is predominantly composed of scarps and steep slopes in clay along the Neches River and salt/brackish marsh along Old River Cove. The Lower Neches Wildlife Refuge is almost exclusively marsh with some small coarse-grained sand and shell beaches. Sydney Island and Stewts Island shorelines are mostly mixed sand and shell beaches with areas of marsh (Stewts Island) and scarps and steep slopes in clay (Sydney Island). Large bayous surround Sabine Lake within 5 miles of the release site. Because the oleum is expected to sink, intertidal habitats are likely to be exposed to diluted concentrations. Little is known about pH impacts to salt marsh vegetation. In areas of very low pH, it is likely that above-ground vegetation could be affected, as well as the biota who live there. V. Biological Resources at Risk Fish and Invertebrates Species of commercial and recreational interest potentially present in Sabine Lake include: hardhead catfish (spawning), spotted seatrout (spawning/larvae and juveniles present) pinfish (spawing/larvae and juveniles), red drum, striped mullet, Atlantic croaker (juveniles), bay anchovy (spawning/larvae juveniles), gulf menhaden, southern flounder, brown shrimp (larvae/juveniles), blue crab (spawning/larvae and juveniles), and white shrimp (spawning/larvae and juveniles). American oyster are present in western portions of Sabine Lake (spawning/larvae and juveniles). Similar species of fish and invertebrates are present in surrounding rivers and bayous. High concentrations of red drum occur in the Lower Neches Wildlife Management Area (WMA). High concentrations of white shrimp (larvae/juveniles) occur near Blue Buck Pt. Essentially, there are lots of species present, and many sensitive early life stages present. Larvae and juveniles are less likely to avoid areas of low pH. Thus, impacts to both water-column and benthic fish and invertebrates may be severe where the pH exceeds 5. Birds A black skimmer colony (100 nests) occurs on Sydney Island. Skimmers may also be nesting on Stewts Island, and American white pelicans and rails may be present. Wading birds and rails are present in the Lower Neches WMA, Sabine National Wildlife Refuge (NWR) and other bayous and wetlands surrounding the lake. Diving birds may be present in open water. Impacts to birds may result from feeding on fish killed or incapacitated by exposure to low pH water, such as burning and irritation of tissues that come in contact with acid on the fish. Reptiles and Small Mammals Texas diamondback terrapins (candidate species for federal listing) may be present in shallow, open water, and alligators are present in bayous and wetlands. River otters are present in the Lower Neches WMA. Human-Use Resources A Gulf States Utilities Co. water intake occurs in Old River Cove, very close to the release site. Three water intakes occur along the Neches River (Texaco Chemical Co., Star Enterprise, and FINA Oil & Chemical Company). Three water intakes are present behind Pleasure Island along the Port Arthur Ship Channel. (Star Enterprise, Rice-Carden Corp., and Chevron U.S.A. Inc.). Boat ramps are present throughout the area. The Lower Neches WMA and Sabine NWR are adjacent to Sabine Lake. [SEP] Final Report: MSO Port Arthur reported that the grounded barge was refloated during the night of May 26. The barge was transferred to the Bean Fleet pier to allow inspectors to check the condition of the barge and cargo. By this morning, May 27, there were no problems noted and it was expected that the barge will continue on its voyage. No additional NOAA response support is expected. A release below the vessel waterline would result in a vigorous oleum water (hydrolysis) reaction. Sulfur trioxide gases may be generated around the area where the reaction is occurring resulting in white fuming acid vapors. PEOPLE WORKING IN THIS AREA SHOULD BE AWARE OF A POTENTIAL AIR HAZARD. The reaction converts sulfur trioxide to sulfuric acid. Since the sulfuric acid is much heavier than water, it will sink and the hydrolysis reaction will mix the acid into the water column.

The Alaska State Ferry, M/V LaConte, grounded in clear and calm weather on Cozian Reef at the north end of Peril Strait on Admiralty Island in SE Alaska on May 11, 2004. The vessel was hard aground and suffered significant damage, including multiple stress fractures. However, no oil (deisel) was released. Nevertheless, boom was deployed around the vessel and lightering commenced up to 3000 gallons remaining onboard as an operational supply. A substantial amount of response equipment was on-scene and a salvage barge was en route from Seattle. Potential harbors of refuge were evaluated in the vicinity of Cozian Reef. Arrangements were made for bird hazing in the event of an oil release impacting nearby tidal flats. Resource experts from both NOAA Fisheries and the US Fish and Wildlife Servcie were consulted and assisted in assessment of resources at risk. The LaConte was stabilized and anchored at Cozian Reef for the lightering and for temporary patches to the hull prior to towing the vessel to Ketchikan for permanent repairs in their drydock facility. The ferry was refloated and moved off the reef on May 17, and after confirming that the temporary patches were adequate, the vessel was towed to Ketchikan for repairs. However, the terminology for refined products is not standardized, and, sometimes, heavier intermediate fuel oils are referred to as ???€?marine diesel???€?. These heavier products are much less volatile than normal Fuel Oil no 2 and can form a more persistent slick. When spilled, the diesel spreads quickly into thin films often forming patches of rainbow and silver sheens. If the sheens reach the shoreline in a few hours, a slight staining, or greasy film-like bathtub ring (in the case of diesel) is common. These oils usually do not form a stable emulsion and, as a result, do not form a heavy or sticky residual to clean up. Note that lighter refined products do have a relatively high concentration of light aromatic compounds and tend to be more soluble and more toxic than heavier oils. Therefore these oils may not present an involved cleanup problem, however they can result in an initial toxic shock to biota and persist as a biological threat problem in low energy marine environments. [SEP] April 30, 2004 Evening Report: Suisun Slough Pipeline Spill The NOAA SSC, John Whitney, and a Seattle biological scientist, Amy Merten, reported to the Suisun Slough Duck Hunter???€?s Command Post early Friday morning, Apr 30. The response team including MSO San Francisco with FOSC CDR Williams; the California Fish and Game (OSPR Group); the RP, Kinder Morgan who was supported by several consultants including MSRC; and the USCG Pacific Strike Team. After orientation and discussion with onscene personnel, it was realized that the affected area is less than one-half square mile with the heavily impacted area less than 20 acres (Zone A). In addition it was evident that the size of the spill was less than 1 million gallons, an early figure that was floated. The NOAA Team immediately began pursuing two goals: 1) an overflight of the entire area, and 2) organization of multi-agency SCAT teams. The NOAA SSC joined an RP rep, who had flown the spill sight the day before, for an overflight. Only oil sheening was observed in some of the inner sloughs. Four SCAT teams covered the areas where oil had been identified or expected. In Zone A, actual pooled oil was detected by the ground SCAT, in small pools which weren???€?t sheening due to lack of water in the marsh. In other zones, small pools of product were also identified. The goal for tomorrow is to work with operations to successfully remove the oil from the marsh without doing more harm than good. On Wednesday, 28 April 2004, NOAA was notified of a hydrogen sulfide release from a barge located in a fleeting area near Baton Rouge, Louisiana. At that time, the identified problem, i.e., the failure of two gaskets, was repaired and no subsequent emissions were observed. During assessment activities, it was discovered that the product was "off-spec" and the barge was not certified for such a product. The NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator (SSC) worked with USCG Marine Safety Unit Baton Rouge to address concerns related to the stability of the barge product and plans to off-load the product to prevent subsequent releases that might threaten local communities. Off-loading of the cargo began at approximately 0914 hrs on 10 June after several small delays during final configuration of the modified scrubber. The NOAA SSC was on-scene to assist the USCG in operational oversight and air monitoring coordination. [SEP] The NOAA Scientific Support Team was notified today that the RP wished to change their design for the scrubbers on board FT-22. The hopes were to go from 3 individual scrubbers to one, larger scrubber. The Coast Guard's concerns were with the PVC and PVC cement the RP wished to use on the design, and if the amount of Calcium Hypochlorite that was to be used was adequate. The USCG received the following report: During the 05/17/2004 Barge FT-22 briefing the USCG Baton Rouge MSU recommended the use of a vapor scrubber system as a secondary containment measure to remove any H2S emitted from the barge. The RP suggested the use of a two-stage vapor scrubber system. LSU was asked to furnish the calculations for determining the amount of calcium hypochlorite required to effectively remove any H2S vapors from the barge. Volume figures from the USCG estimated the total volume of the three (3) tanks to be 60,600 cubic feet with a total headspace of 46,700 cubic feet (77%). It should be noted the RP estimated the total volume and headspace to be 141,000 and 94,000 cubic feet, respectively. All calculations are based on the volumes received from the USCG on a daily basis. A temperature increase from 75 F to 110 F would emit approx. 3070 cubic feet or 86 cubic meters. At a H2S conc. of 2800 mg/m3 (2000ppm), approx. 244,000 mg of H2S would be released through the scrubber system. Calcium hypochlorite reacts with H2S at a rate of 2.1 to 1, requiring 512,000 mg of Ca(OCl)2 to neutralize 244,000 mg H2S. Using tablets at 64% total Ca(OCl)2 , approx. 1.8 lbs. of tablets should be used per day. It should be noted the large tablets typically need to be submerged in flowing water for them to adequately dissolve. It may be beneficial to use a combination of granulated and small tablet Ca(OCl)2, instead of the larger tablets. Compatibility charts have shown that H2S and PVC piping are compatible.
