[SEP] Resources at Risk, Potash Mystery Spill This report was prepared on 27 April 2004. Information in this report is based on the assumption that a pipeline release of approximately 50 bbls occurred near the Mississippi River between Port Sulphur and Potash (29 28???€? 20???€?-50???€?N, 089 42???€?4???€?-40???€?W). This report does not necessarily correspond to actual or potential spill locations. Consult other Hotline reports for spill location information. Habitats Habitats in this area are predominantly salt and brackish marsh. Birds A rare raptor may be nesting along the river in the area. Colonial waterbirds may be nesting in salt marshes and bays near the river, but are not likely to be affected by a small spill in the mainstem river, as most nests are 8 or more miles from the estimated release site. Some holdover wintering waterfowl may be utilizing adjacent bays and wetlands, but most birds have departed by this time of year. Use of the river by waterfowl is less common than use of open water in bays. Fish and Invertebrates Several commercial and recreational fish may be present in the river, including freshwater (e.g. sunfish, crappie, carp, bass, perch, gar) and saltwater (e.g. croaker, drum, jack, sturgeon, flounder, spot, seatrout, tarpon) species. Atlantic croaker and bay anchovy may be highly abundant, and sensitive life stages (spawning, eggs, larvae) may occur at this time for both freshwater and saltwater species. Higher concentrations of sensitive life stages are expected in shallow water in sheltered nearshore areas. Gulf sturgeon (federally threatened) are present in the area. Oyster lease sites occur in adjacent bays. White river crawfish, river shrimp, brown shrimp, pink shrimp, white shrimp, and blue crab are present in the river at low to moderate abundances. Reptiles and Aquatic Mammals Juvenile and adult alligators and several species of aquatic furbearers (e.g. river otter, muskrat, mink, nutria, raccoon) are present in marshes and along the river. [SEP] Follow-up investigations by the USCG and pressure checks on three flow lines in the Potash Oil Field have resulted in identifying the source. It was one of the three lines. On Wednesday, 5 May 2004, the Assistant SSC participated with the NRDA trustees on a site visit to the spill site. Cleanup continues, but the primary efforts are only the maintenance of deployed sorbent materials for passive recovery. [SEP] 0133. Core sample collected. The picture shows a 4 inch core tube partially filled with sediment. [SEP] On 29 April 2004, the NOAA SSC participated in a field trip to the Potash Oil Spill site with the USCG. The purpose of the site visit was to assess the cleanup operations, roughly delineate the spill impact area, and further investigate possible sources of oil pollution. One previous observation of great interest during the site visit was a report of subsurface oil that could be liberated by disturbing the sediment with a pole. At present, there is no identified RP and all cleanup is under USCG direction. Additional Background Information The USCG was notified of the incident on 17 April. The current operator of the old Potash Oil Field stated that the oil was not from any of their operations, but they had originally initiated cleanup. Since there was no clear source identified, the USCG assumed the cleanup effort and began a through investigation to include securing samples of possible sources for detailed oil fingerprinting. At the time of the site visit, 12 days later, cleanup operations had shifted into the maintenance stage. Sorbent booms remain in most of the canals to recover oil liberated from the marsh during tidal exchanges. Site Visit Observations The first location investigated was near position 29?? 28???€? 37.4???€? N Lat. 089?? 42???€? 11.9???€? W Long. This is one of two sites where disturbing the subsurface sediments would liberate sheen and small droplet???€?s of black oil. The source of this pollution is unknown. Possible theories include a leaking subsurface pipeline or oil that may have become entrained in small burrows during a low tide. Probing with a small glass tube was used to investigate this observation, which was first observed by noticing oil surfacing after the airboat passed over the area. A core sample was also collected. During the site visit, many flow-lines were observed laid directly across the marsh and alongside canals. It is not known if there are any buried lines in the area. The marsh in this area shows evidence of residual oil contamination as a heavy band along the marsh edge. Vertically, the oil band measures from the sediment surface to approximately 12 to 15 inches on the vegetative stems and leaves. Oil contamination within the site is variable. Some areas are heavily oiled, whiles others are only lightly impacted by films and sheens. SAV is also present within the site. The extent of exposure to SAV is unknown. The site visit was just past low tide, and most of the SAV was not exposed. At one location, sheens were observed in the same area as SAV, but visible oiling, i.e., sorbed black oil, was not observed. A second site where subsurface oil was reported is located near position 29?? 28???€? 37.9???€? N Lat. 089?? 42???€? 08.2???€? W Long. It was actually easier to free oil at this location, but interestingly, marsh vegetation near this position was not heavily oiled. Stirring the sediments easily created heavy rainbow sheen and small oil droplets were observed. Using a stake, a portion of the sediment was brought to the surface; the sediment appeared to be saturated with oil. Again, the source of this pollution is unknown. Such locations are not common at the spill site, but at least two such locations have been identified. Future Plans The investigation continues. NOAA has been tasked with investigating winds and tides prior to the observation of the spill to investigate possible additional sources. Site photographs will be added when the SSC returns to the office. [SEP] Date: March 26, 2004 To: NOAA SSC Brad Benggio FROM: NOAA/Hazardous Materials Response Division Modeling and Simulation Studies Seattle, WA 98115 SUBJECT: Grounded Cargo Vessel, Fort Lauderdale FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION, PLEASE CONTACT Debra Simecek-Beatty, MODELING AND SIMULATION STUDIES, NOAA, SEATTLE, WA 98115. PHONE (206) 526-4911. _______________________________________________________ Per your request, we have looked at trajectory implications of the heavy fuel oil that may be released from a cargo vessel. These notes are based on the following information: A cargo vessel ran aground at 26?? 07.06???€?N, 80?? 5.57???€?W?? (about half a mile off Fort Lauderdale Beach) sometime overnight. The vessel is carrying approximately 280 metric tons (about 75, 000 gallons) of heavy fuel oil and 14.3 metric tons (4,300 gallons) of diesel. At this time, the vessel is grounded and not leaking product. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP as it would affect any trajectory implications. _______________________________________________________ 1) TRAJECTORY The weather forecast indicates winds will easterly at about 20 to 25 knots for the next 24-hours. If the vessel should leak product during this period, it is likely that within one hour of the release the bulk of the released product would move due west and onshore threatening the shoreline from the north jetty of the entrance to Port Everglades and northward to Birch Ocean Front. We would not anticipate oil moving through the jetties and into Port Everglades. However, long shore transport and associated rip currents could move small amounts of oil offshore. On-scene observations of the rip currents (return cells) would be needed to further assess the movement of any offshore oil behavior. Since a spill may occur in an area with sandy beaches and high surf, there is a possibility of oil droplets adhering to suspended sand particles in the water column. The combined oil-sediment particle can either remain suspended in the water column or slowly settle to the bottom when the water conditions become more quiescent. Also, any stranded oil that is transported off a sandy beach maybe transported subsurface. The high surf may result in buried oil on the shoreline and in offshore areas. 2) Oil Weathering Heavy Fuel Oil Heavy refined products, such as Intermediate Fuel Oils (IFO) are routinely made by mixing a diesel (Fuel Oil No. 2) with a heavy residual oil or with the residuum from the refining process itself. The exact composition of an IFO can vary depending on the properties of the constituents. However, IFO's are often sold as IFO180 and IFO380. These designations indicate the final product meets certain specifications. Both are viscous fluids, IFO180 has a viscosity of 180 centistokes (cSt) at 50??C and, IFO380 has a viscosity of 360 cSt at 50??C. However, the specific gravity or API of the final product for either designation can vary significantly between 0.99 - 0.95; API gravity 11.5.0-35. When spilled in the marine environment, the oil will change physical properties as it ages and may result in quite persistent floating pollutant problems. Up to one-third of the oil may evaporate in the first 24 hours of the spill but this is very much dependent on the amount of diesel in the IFO. These oils can occasionally form an emulsification or mousse, but usually only slowly, and after a period of days. Again, depending on the mixture, up to 30% of the mouse can be water. IFOs may not spread into very thin films and often simply break up in smaller patches and then tarballs. It is also common for these oils to lose enough of their light ends so that they do not rapidly form sheens and the resulting scattered tarball fields are very difficult to observe using visual, or remote sensing techniques. This, combined with the persistence of the tarballs, makes these kinds of spills quite likely to result in long range, and occasionally unexpected, beach impacts. Particularly if a small amount of product is moved off shore in a rip current. 3) Oil Weathering Diesel Oil Lighter refined products, such as diesel, typically have very high evaporation rates and do not tend to create persistent slicks. However, the terminology for refined products is not standardized, and, sometimes, heavier intermediate fuel oils are referred to as ???€?marine diesel???€?. These heavier products are much less volatile than normal Fuel Oil no 2 and form a more persistent slick. When spilled, the diesel spreads quickly into thin films often forming patches of rainbow and silver sheens. If the sheens reach the shoreline in a few hours, a slight staining, or greasy film-like bathtub ring (in the case of diesel) is common. These oils usually do not form a stable emulsion and, as a result, do not form a heavy or sticky residual to clean up. We would anticipate that much of the diesel would evaporate or disperse in the first four hours of the release. [SEP] Resources at Risk for Fort Lauderdale/Port Everglades I. Spill Source Information This report was prepared at 11:00 am EST on 26 March 2004. Information in this report is based on a spill of 244 metric tons of HFO. Presently, the dry bulk freighter Eastwind is aground off of the Fort Lauderdale coast. II. Geographic Region Covered This report covers the beaches several miles north and south of the grounding site. This area does not necessarily correspond to actual or potential oil locations. Consult other Hotline reports for oil location information. III. Expected Behavior of the Spilled Material With the relatively high east winds and associated wave activity, the oil is likely to be mixed into the water column near the shore. In addition there will be high suspended sediment loads, which may adhere to the oil. This could result in the oil becoming heavier than water and sinking. The oil is expected to have a low water soluble component, so there would be minimal impacts to animals that live in the water column. Once onshore, the oil would likely coat the intertidal zone of the shoreline. IV. Shoreline Resources at Risk All of the outer beaches in this area are coarse-grained sand beaches. The only inlet in the area is at Port Everglades. Inside the inlet, the shorelines at the inlet and to the north are all seawalls. The shorelines to the south of the inlet are sheltered marshes and mangroves, with some riprap. On the outer beaches the oil will leave a band of oil in the intertidal zone starting at the high tide line. The width of the band is dependent upon the amount of oil that comes ashore at a given location. The oil may penetrate 5- 10 cm into the sediment. There is also a risk of the oil being buried, if the wind shifts. On the seawalls a band of oil will form at the high tide line. Oil may coat the vegetation in marshes

It was reported that Navy divers have attempted to determine if any crewmembers are alive and trapped within the vessel using a sophisticated acoustic system, but no positive results were reported. The apparent loss of all five ship???€?s crew has created a somber atmosphere within the on-scene command post. Yesterday evening (day one of the response), one of the spill responders discovered a stranded hardhat adjacent to the stranded diesel fuel. The found hardhat was marked with the name of the sunken vessel. The hardhat currently rests within the command post providing a silent reminder of the tragic accident. Rainbow sheens continue to be released by the sunken vessel. There is no estimate as to the volume of fuel released to date or remaining fuel oil aboard. Containment and exclusion booms have been deployed and oil recovery efforts continue. The current cleanup strategy was to use a combination of low pressure flushing to move the oil out of the riprap followed by mechanical recovery using drum skimmers. By the end of the day, most of the accessible pooled and flushable diesel fuel had been recovered. There is oil still trapped in riprap. Additional hard boom and sorbent boom have been deployed to help mitigate the diesel still leaking from the vessel. The lower Mississippi river remains closed. A wildlife recovery team has been deployed and coordinated by USFWS. USFWS also provided a floatplane to support response operations. The USCG participated with USFWS to secure aerial photography to support response planning. At the time this report was written, no report of oiled or injured wildlife was available. A salvage plan has been submitted to the USCG for review. The NOAA SSC, working within the Unified Command and as part of the USCG response team, has been actively involved in providing input into the environmental protection plan. On Monday, the salvers plan a survey dive, but it may be several days before the actual salvage operation is conducted. It was reported that the divers would attempt to plug the fuel tank vents as part of the salvage effort. The NOAA SSC has departed the Lee III command post, but will return to the site as needed. Background Information Before daylight on the morning of 21 February 2004, the M/V ZIM MEXICO III and the OSV Lee III collided within Southwest Pass on the lower Mississippi Delta. The cause of the accident is under investigation. The OSV was reported to have sunk almost immediately with five crewmembers aboard. The outbound OSV was reported to have 30,000 gallons of diesel aboard at the time of the collision. The reported location of the sunken vessel was N29?? 03.070???€? Latitude W89?? 18.852???€? Longitude. This position places the vessel on the Mississippi Delta, approximately 8.8 miles below head of passes and within Southwest Pass. Saturday morning (yesterday), the NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator (SSC), along with USCG and Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality (LDEQ) representatives, was able to view the incident site and diesel pollution while on a Unified Command overflight to support the GENMAR ALEXANDRA spill response. At the time of the overflight, the Lee III was capsized and sunken at the stern: only the forward section of the bow remained visible above the water and an attached life raft served as a marker buoy. Diesel, in the form of sheens, was still leaking from the sunken vessel. Pools of red-dyed diesel was observed stranded in catchments along the Left Descending Bank (LDB) for approximately 1.5 miles down river, and on-water sheens were visible further down river, through the ???€?spillway cut???€? and to the end of the Southwest Pass. While observing the pollution problem, the members of the overflight also scanned the shoreline for possible survivors. Numerous migratory birds (primarily ducks) were observed in the area of the spill and this information was passed to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS). While the spill site was not within the boundaries of the State and Federal wildlife management areas, it is located adjacent to these refuges and does quality habitat for migratory waterfowl as well as many other bird species. The spill was reported as a result of a tug striking a well head in Terrebonne-Timbalier Bay before noon at position Lat. 29?? 06.236???€? and Long. 090?? 31.783???€? (see attached map). Given that the information available at present is limited, i.e., no known volume or reliable on-scene observations, the trajectory should be considered as preliminary in scope. At present, the winds are out of the N at 20 knots and are expected to remain from the N over the next 24 hours. The sea-state is rough. With strong N winds, the oil would have most likely impacted the western end of Timbalier Island on the bay side. Some oil might escape through the pass into the Gulf of Mexico. Note, if the release is significant, there may be threatened/endangered species in the area that might be at risk (see attached Natural Resources at Risk Analysis). It was reported later, that "an overflight indicated only sheens, and that they were heading out..." The spill may not be as big of an environmental concern as initially thought. The sea state is very rough in the area, and a small release of a light condensate oil would easily be naturally dispersed under such conditions. The current sea state would also preclude any on-water response activities. Unless there are further developments, no additional NOAA response support is expected.

If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP as it would affect any trajectory implications. ______________________________________________________ 1) 24-hour Wind Forecast Tonight, the winds are expected to be from the NW at 20-25 knots with gusts to 40 knots becoming 20-25 knots with gusts to 30 knots by the late evening hours. Friday, west winds at 15-20 knots are predicted to decrease to 10-15 knots by the afternoon hours. 2) TRAJECTORY Strong winds with a westerly component in the forecast indicate that most of the oil that does not naturally disperse will be transported across Arthur Kill to the western shore of Pralls Island. At the site of the accident, there may be gasoline trapped in natural collection zones or under piers that may result in an explosion hazard. 3) OIL FATE There is a high flammability hazard associated with gasoline spills. Specifically, if a spill is kept from spreading freely by natural or man-made structures the gasoline slick might be thick enough to support ignition. In addition, vapor concentrations near the source of spill or vapors collected in sheltered areas can present an explosion hazard (see Health and Safety Considerations). Gasoline is considered a light refined product with a specific gravity that can range from 0.76 to 0.70 at 15??C (54 to 70 API). The product typically has a very high evaporation rate and does not tend to create persistent slicks. For most releases smaller than 100 barrels in open water conditions and with wind speeds greater than 5 knots, 90% of the gasoline would be expected to evaporate within the first 1 to 2 hours of the initial release. When spilled, the gasoline spreads quickly into thin films by forming patches of rainbow and silver sheens. If the sheens reach the shoreline in a few hours, a slight staining, or greasy film is common. Normally, this type of release does not become an involved cleanup problem. Please note that gasoline does have a relatively high concentration of light aromatic compounds and tends to be more soluble and more toxic then heavier oils. In high energy environments, the gasoline will likely disperse as small droplets in the water column. Gasoline spills can result in an initial toxic shock to biota and persist as a biological threat particularly in low energy marine environments as often found in shallow bays and inlets. Barge grounded; 18K #2 pot; diesel; Wx/Verbal [SEP] Date: December 2, 2003 1900 EST To: NOAA SSC Ed Levine FROM: NOAA/Hazardous Materials Response Division Seattle, WA 98115 SUBJECT: Barge Kristen Poling FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION, PLEASE CONTACT Debra Simecek-Beatty, MODELING AND SIMULATION STUDIES, NOAA, SEATTLE, WA 98115. PHONE (206) 526-4911. _______________________________________________________________________ Per your request we have looked at trajectory implications of the potential Fuel Oil #2 spill. These notes are based on the following information: On December 2, 2003 at approximately 1700 EST, the barge Kristen Poling grounded at 40?? 35.1???€?N, 73?? 44.4???€?W (off Atlantic Beach, New York). The barge is carrying 18,000 barrels of Fuel Oil No. 2. At this time, the vessel is not leaking product. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP as it would affect any trajectory implications. ________________________________________________________________________ 1) WINDS Tonight, the winds are expected to be from the NW at 18 knots. Wednesday, NW winds at 10-15 knots are predicted. Wednesday night, NW winds at 8- 12 knots are forecast. 2) TRAJECTORY While the tidal currents at the entrance of East Rockaway Inlet are strong (about 2 knots), there are weak rotary currents along the outer coast and in the vicinity of the grounded vessel. As a result, we would not expect much net movement of the oil due to the tidal currents. The longshore currents are very much dependent on the strength and direction of the waves. Since the winds are strong from the northwest, the waves and the subsequent alongshore transport are likely weak. Therefore, the winds are likely to dominate oil transport rather than the current. Some oil will likely come ashore in the vicinity of the barge. However, oil is less likely to be transported around Silver Pt. and through East Rockaway Inlet due to the strong northwest winds. For the next 24-hours, much of the oil will probably move offshore and to the southeast. 3) OIL WEATHERING Lighter refined products, such as Fuel Oil No. 2 and diesel, typically have very high evaporation rates and do not create persistent slicks. When spilled, the oil spreads quickly into thin films, often forming patches of rainbow and silver sheens. The diesel, if spilled during the present high wind conditions, should disperse or evaporate within a day or a day and a half of the end of the spillage. A significant amount is expected to disperse into the water column. If the winds calm down, some resurfacing is likely with scattered local sheens. If the spill occurs during weaker wind conditions, the surface slicks will be more persistent. If the diesel reaches the shoreline, a soot-like bathtub ring is common. These oils don't usually form a stable emulsion and, as a result, don't produce a heavy or sticky residual to clean up. It should be noted that lighter refined products do have a relatively high concentration of light aromatic compounds and tend to be more soluble and more toxic than heavier oils. So, even though these oils may not present an involved cleanup problem, they can result in an initial toxic shock to biota and persist as a biological threat problem in low energy marine environments. Spill Source Information This report was prepared at 19:00 EST on 2 December 2003. Information in the report is based on a spill of 5,000 bbls of gasoline and 7,000 bbls of diesel fuel released in Mobile Bay at the intersection of the Mobile Ship Channel and Intercoastal Waterway. II. Geographic Region Covered The area covered by this spill is the southwestern portion of Mobile Bay, the entrance to the Mobile Bay, and the eastern end of Dauphin Island. This area does not necessarily correspond to actual or potential oil locations. Consult other Hotline reports for oil location information. III. Expected Behavior of the Spilled Material The gasoline is highly volatile and also has a relatively high water soluble component. Most of this product will evaporate fairly quickly. However with the volume spilled water column impacts may occur, especially in the vicinity of the release. Diesel fuel is more persistent and is likely to cause more impacts than the gasoline. The water soluble components of the diesel may impact animals in shallow water areas and intertidal zones. IV. Shoreline Resources at Risk The shoreline along Mobile Bay is mostly sand beaches, with some sections of riprap and seawalls. Marshes are the dominant shoreline in Dauphin Bay, Graveling Bay, and the northern side of Mississippi Sound. If the diesel is washed up into the marshes and trapped then it may penetrate into the sediments and could potentially kill the marsh vegetation. V. Biological Resources at Risk Shellfish ???€? There are major oyster beds in and around Grants Pass and Pas aux Herons (the passes between Mobile Bay and Mississippi Sound) and the portions of Mobile Bay adjoining those passes. With the shallow waters and the relatively high solubility of the products spilled it is possible that these oysters may become contaminated. Birds ???€? Piping plovers (Federally endangered) are present along the shorelines of Bon Secour National Wildlife Refuge, just west of the spill site. There may also be some rafts of overwintering waterfowl in the area. Mammals ???€? The Alabama beach mouse (Federally endangered) is present on Mobile Point. These animals are not likely to be impacted directly by the spill, but regarding any cleanup operations in the area USFWS should be consulted. Habitats ???€? There are scattered small patches of seagrass beds along the western shore of Mobile Bay as well as in Dauphin Bay and Heron Bay. VI. Human-Use Resources at Risk Bon Secour National Wildlife Refuge is on the eastern end of Dauphin Island. Fort Morgan State Park is at Mobile Point. At approximately 10:30 AM (local time), an estimated 50 bbl oil spill was observed in Barataria Bay, South Louisiana. The location was reported as N 29 deg 19.67' Lat. W 089 deg 58.67' Long. The source of the leak was initially unknown. Later the pipeline was identified and shut in, but not until a reported 350 bbl of crude oil was released. At the request of the USCG, NOAA provided a trajectory, a Resources and Risk analysis and on-scene support. [SEP] At present, containment and passive recovery efforts are continuing. The last time the Scientific Support Coordinator (SSC) visited the site was on 5 January 2004, but a field trip is planned for 21 January. Overflight reports provided by the RP continue to identify visible residual oil and mousse in one small section of E Racoon Island. Other than that location, no visible oil has been observed by aerial survey within the spill area. Notes from 5 January Field Trip: The NOAA SSC participated with the RP on both an overflight of Raccon Island and a beach survey of the shell beach located on the N side of E Racoon Island on Monday, 5 January 2004. A snapshot of those field observations follows: Marsh. Sheens were still visible within the containment area indicating that free oil was still trapped in the broken marsh, but the majority of the sheens were limited to just one section of the marsh, a zone identified as RE07. Very little sheen and emulsified oil was observed in RE01 and RE02. No oil was observed in the other areas of Racoon Island. Most of the deployed snare-type boom (pom-pom on a rope) had sunk and was ineffective. It was recommended that the pom-poms sorbents should be removed since they are providing little if any passive recovery, and that round sorbent boom be maintained and repositioned in key areas for continued passive recovery. Hard boom should be maintained to provide containment of the spill area (in particular the area identified as RE07), but may be removed in areas where it is no longer of containment value. Shell Beach. At the shell beach (N beach in section RE01), there was significant improvement from a month ago, but oil was still trapped in the soft middle intertidal zone composed of peat and soft sediment under a veneer of shell. It was soft along this zone, and your boots would sink 3 to 4 inches in most areas. Footprints created would show pooled oil droplets seeping into the depressions. In only one small area was visible sheen observed (and it was confined to a shallow depression). The harder packed upper tidal zone of the beach contained only oil stain and some lightly oiled wrack (a remnants from one of the past storms). The snare-type boom (pom-pom on a rope) that had been deployed along the front of the island had broken and washed ashore. Like the hard boom that was placed along the N shore previously, it did not survive storms given the direct exposure to N winds. It was recommended that the pom-pom sorbents be removed and the area left for natural recovery. Loose oiled wrack should be removed along the upper intertidal zone. Any actions to mechanically flush the oil out of the soft substrate would create physical damage and possibly enhance erosion. The net trade-off would suggest that natural reworking of the beach face by storms would have the least overall environmental impact. [SEP] Evening Report (4 December 2003) At approximately 4:00 PM (local time), most field operations were cancelled due to approaching weather. A cold front is currently passing through southern Louisiana with forecasted winds of 10 to 20 kts (and higher) for Thursday evening through Saturday. Such conditions will not allow safe small boat operations. NOAA weather support was important in planning response activities and assessing the approaching cold front relative to responder safety concerns. The spill was apparently caused by the failure of a 12???€? pipeline. A longitudinal split has been identified, and a repair plan is being developed. The total volume spilled was estimated at 365 bbl by the RP. At the end of the day, some 165 bbls of oil and emulsified oil have been recovered. More than 20,000???€? of containment boom and more than 10,000???€? of sorbent boom have been deployed in an effort to minimize the spread of the current spill. Much of the observed heavy oil accumulations are concentrated around Racoon Island, but additional marsh islands have observed oil impacts. Multiple wildlife impacts have been reported. A total of 12 birds were captured and returned to the wildlife rehabilitation center. There were probably a greater number of birds impacted, but the approaching weather combined with logistical problems limited the number of recovery teams and the recovery efforts. The expected high winds and cold weather conditions will significant limit any wildlife recovery efforts for the next two days. The approaching high wind and sea state conditions may defeat much of this effort. Overflight are planned to assess oil transport, delineate the special distribution of spilled oil, and develop a response strategy to be implemented when field conditions allow. This process is being described as an aerial SCAT survey, and will be followed up by a ground truth survey when the winds slacken. The NOAA SSC has consulted with USFWS as to their field surveys to enhance the planned SCAT strategy. In addition, NOAA participated in an evening overflight with the RP???€?s environmental representative and the USCG. Pictures from this overflight, taken by the NOAA biologist on-scene are attached. Maps identifying the extent of oiling will be provided after Friday???€?s aerial surveys. The NOAA Scientific Support Team will remain on-scene providing scientific support. The planned SCAT activities will aid in developing a continued response strategy and document oil observations. [SEP] On 21 November 2003, the NOAA SSC was notified of a small mystery spill that stranded an estimated 40 gallons of oil on the bayside of Isle Deniers, LA. Isle Deniers is a coastal barrier island on the southern edge of Terrebonne Bay. The SSC followed up this contact with consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife (USFWS) since the area is classified as Piping Plover Critical Habitat. Several small patches of oil were identified and cleaned by small crews using manual removal by shovels on 22 November. USFWS assisted in the response on-scene and identified two additional small areas that were also cleaned (NOAA did not respond on-scene). As follow-up, the USCG has asked the NOAA SSC to help consult on any consultations required by the Endangered Species Act and the MOU between USCG, DOI, and DOC. It is my understanding that no plovers were identified during the response effort, and the consultation will be directed at the habitat and cleanup actions. As requested, the SSC will provide whatever follow-up is required.
At 1100 PST on November 19, 2003, a US Coast Guard patrol boat report was received of a dark-colored slick 3nm by 10nm, two miles off Lopez Point, CA.  A subsequent flight by CG helo at 1300hrs located the oil about 15nm north of Pt Lopez, and about 15nm north of the originally reported position.  The oil was described as breaking up into smaller pieces and large tarballs, with associated sheening. [SEP] Situation Update, 20NOV03 On Thursday morning, 20NOV03, OSPR dispatched their fixed-wing aircraft to the vicinity of the slicks to determine their new location and search for oiled wildlife. During the flight, the slicks were not located and there were no signs of oiled wildlife. Additionally, there have been no reports to date of oiled wildlife from this incident, nor of oiled shoreline. Since no oil was observed from this OSPR overflight, the MSO decided not to launch one of their own. It was reported this morning that during yesterday's CG overflight a Data Marker Buoy (DMB) was dropped in the vicinity. Hazmat was told initially that this was the new type of DMB that can be tracked real time by satellite and more accurately follows surface currents. However, after some phone calls to the CG R&D center, it was determined that the DMB dropped yesterday was of the old type, which can only be monitored over a specific radio frequency and requires a CG platform on scene to collect positional data. Since the MSO decided not to deploy any further assets to the area, we were unable to get any positional data from this buoy. The SSC attempted to retrieve more detailed information about the position and original description of the slick from the CG patrol boat, however it was learned that this boat apparently did not log this observation and transcribed the wrong coordinates for the slick, resulting in no useful information for trajectory modeling. The MSO did ask Hazmat if it would be possible to hindcast from the positions obtained during the 19NOV overflight. We discussed potential start locations based on recent winds with them and they determined that since non-tank vessels that transit this region can come within 12nm of the coast, the source could very likely have been one of these transiting vessels. At this point, there is no further support requests from the MSO, but the SSC remains in close contact with them and we have prepared our model if they do request some modeling products. [SEP] Situation Update, 19NOV03 This morning around noon, the USCG Marine Safety Office San Francisco Bay contacted NOAA Hazmat for trajectory and weather support for a mystery slick observed off Point Lopez, CA (about 20nm south of Point Sur). This slick was observed by a USCG patrol boat and originally thought to cover an area of about 3nm by 10nm and was described as being "fresh". Crew members on the patrol boat did take a sample of the oil, however they collected and stored the sample in a plastic bottle. NOAA Hazmat contacted the National Weather Service and obtained a detailed forecast for the specific area. Based on the forecasted wind and available current information and the initial reported position of the slick, they produced an initial verbal trajectory (see report in this Hotline) that predicted the slick could move as far south as Ragged Point in the following 24 hrs. Since both the winds and currents in the area were most likely parallel to the coast, shoreline impacts were considered unlikely, but if they did occur would likely impact NW-facing beaches first. The MSO SF requested an overflight with a CG helo and at 1300 the flight got underway with two Pollution Investigators from the MSO onboard. Initial reports from the observers were that the oil was actually present in three smaller slicks of the following approximate areas: 50 x 20 yds, 200 x 500 yds, and 100 x 500 yds. These three slicks were spread out over an area with a northern most point of 36?? 11.6'N, 121?? 52.0'W and with a southern most point at 36?? 00.5'N, 121?? 36.2'W. These positions put the oil about 15nm north of Pt Lopez, and about 15nm north of the originally reported position. The oil was described as breaking up into smaller pieces and large tarballs, with associated sheening. The new, more accurate position of the slicks altered the trajectory somewhat. The new positions showed the slicks to be closer to the edge of the continental shelf. Currents in this shelf break region can often be very complex and difficult to predict. Also, this is the time of year when the currents transitsion from a fall to a winter regime, another feature that predicts instability and difficulty to forecast in the currents of this region. However, since the winds were forecast to continue from the N-NW and stay relatively strong, the overall south-southeasterly trend of the slicks from the initial trajectory forecast was still considered to be the most likely prediction. MSO San Francisco determined from this overflight that the product was unrecoverable, and did not require further trajectory updates from Hazmat. We also recommeded to the MSO that they transfer the oil sample collected earlier from onboard the patrol boat into a glass or non-plastic container as plastics contaminate the sample, making fingerprinting very difficult. Even though this sample did spend some time in contact with plastics and therefore was likely contaminated, we suggested they may still want to have it analysed for some descriptive information, especially given that their plans to send out a sampling team on Friday might prove unable to find the small slicks again. California Dept of Fish and Game's Office of Spill Prevention and Response (OSPR) has been engaged as well and has plans to launch their fixed-wing aircraft to perform a wildlife reconnaise and search for the slicks on Friday morning. [SEP] Date: October 3, 2003 To: NOAA SSC Steve Lehmann  FROM: NOAA/Hazardous Materials Response Division Modeling and Simulation Studies Seattle, WA 98115  SUBJECT: T/B Superior Endeavor FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION, PLEASE CONTACT Debra Simecek-Beatty, MODELING AND SIMULATION STUDIES, NOAA, SEATTLE, WA 98115. PHONE (206) 526-4911. _______________________________________________________ Per your request we have looked at trajectory implications of the diesel and lube oil from the grounding of the T/B Superior Endeavor. These notes are based on the following information: On October 3, 2003 at 0630 local time, the T/B Superior Endeavor grounded at 42?? 19???€? 22.3???€?N, 70?? 55???€? 07.9???€? W (Brewster Spit off George???€?s Island, Boston Harbor). The vessel is carrying 9, 000 gallons of diesel and 250 gallons of lube oil. At this time, the vessel is not leaking product. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP as it would affect any trajectory implications. _______________________________________________________ 1) TRAJECTORY Lighter refined products, such as diesel, typically have very high evaporation and dispersion rates and do not tend to form persistent slicks. When spilled, the oil spreads quickly into thin films often forming patches of rainbow and silver sheens. In the event of a catastrophic release of 9000 gallons of diesel on Brewster Spit off George???€?s Island, the tides and winds will transport the oil. Since the forecast winds are expected to clock around (from WNW to SE) in the next 24-hours and with the movement of the tide, there is a possibility of shoreline contact within a two mile radius of the T/B Superior Endeavor. Under these environmental conditions, we would expect 70 to 80% of the oil to evaporate and disperse within 9 to 12 hours of the initial release. If the sheens should contact the shoreline, the oiling would likely appear as a slight staining, or soot-like bathtub ring. Diesel doesn???€?t usually form a stable emulsion and, as a result, don't result a heavy or sticky residual to clean up. Lubricating oils tend to be more persistent in the marine environment. When spilled into the water, they will spread rapidly into a thin slick. They will not evaporate, and they will disperse fairly readily in high-energy conditions. If a lube oil release were to occur in the next 24-hours under the forecast wind conditions, approximately 10 to 25% of the oil would disperse in the first 12- hours of the release. Although lube oil is more persistent, the amount is very small and we would not expect significant concentrations of oil to be transported beyond a 2-mile radius of the grounding site. Shoreline cleanups of this type of product tend to be more involved than that of a diesel spill. [SEP] The jackup barge ???€?Superior Endeavor???€? was refloated at approximately 1745 on Oct. 03. As the tide fell during the day of the 3rd, the vessel extended her jackup ???€?legs???€? to relieve stress on the hull. The vessel refloated at just prior to evening high tide. It is worth noting that while the vessel grounded on the morning high, the evening high tide level was greater by almost a foot. The jackup barge ???€?Superior Endeavor???€? was transported to dry dock in Boston for repairs. Although there was no release of oil, she was holed in the forward ballast tank and lost a quantity of potable water. Her forward jackup leg was also damaged. Case closed. Dispersants have be evaluated as a contingency and resources have been identified, but their use and potential for effectiveness is limited by the type of oil and the expected oil spill trajectory: the oil will most likely move across a series of breakers and shallow shoals that are not within the preapproval guidelines and within an area that has observed manatees and reported sea turtles. Future plans will be directly determined by the effectiveness of tomorrows salvage operation and whether (or not) there is an oil release. Date: 9/9 9/10 9/11 9/12 9/13 Gauge(feet) 19.4 20.9 21.5 21.5 21.1 Flow(CFS) 512K 547K 564K 564K 547K [SEP] Methyl chloroform or more frequently called 1,1,1-trichloroethane is a widely used industrial solvent and used in a number of consumer products. It has a moderate toxicity rating of 3 in "Clinical Toxicity of Commercial Products". It primarily acts as a central nervous system depressant at rather high concentrations of above 350ppm. The ERG2 , the level thought to protect the general public, for this material is listed as 700ppm. These levels are difficult to sustain as the vapor pressure at Standard Temperature and Pressure is in the range of 4 mm Hg, which is rather low. Additionally, it is unlikely that enough of the chemical could pool up on a barge if a catastrophic event occurred and the compound was spilled or released from the barge tank. The compound has a density (>1.3) that would cause the material to sink rapidly to the bottom of the river. Travel downstream seeking low areas in the river bottom where it would pool. It's low solubility in water <1ppm dictates that rather low levels are expected to be found in the water column (probably low ppb range because the solubilized trichloroethane will be quickly diluted in the water column). The primary concern for this scenario, the close proximity of a fire to the barge of 1,1,1-trichloroethane, makes the threat of a BLEVE type of explosion a possibilty. The flash point for the compound is >200 deg. F. with explosion limits between 7-12%. The compound being a halogenated hydrocarbon makes it very difficult to ignite in a vapor, in fact this material is similar to many compounds that are routinely used as fire retardents, therefore, it is not a high flammability risk. However, with a fire impinging on a tank, and with that tanks sudden failure, a BLEVE explosion, rupture may result and with it all the collateral damage resulting from an explosive event. This is the reason for the evacuation distance in the ERG being 800 meters(please note this on the faxed sheet). [SEP] Posted below is an initial report from Charlie Henry, NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator, capturing information on the grounding of the M/V Peljesac near the Sabine Jetties. _______________________________ Initial Report On Sunday, 31 August 2003, the NOAA SSC was notified of a grounded freighter, M/V Peljesac, near the Sabine Jetties. The bow of the vessel was reported aground on soft sediments. The vessel was carrying 52,000 tons of petroleum coke. The SSC initially provided a brief hazard characterization of the cargo to aid the USCG responders in assessing the potential environmental concerns. This information is attached below. Initial response efforts failed free the vessel. On 5 September, the MSO Port Arthur requested an oil spill trajectory to further assess potential environmental concerns (the trajectory and weather are provided as separate documents). To reduce the potential of a heavy fuel oil spill impacting sensitive habitat some four miles NNW of the grounding site, the USCG directed the vessel owner to lighter the bulk of the heavy fuel oil and retain only enough diesel fuel to maintain operations. This operation was completed by 9 September. NOAA was also asked to provide a side-scan sonar survey given that a team was already in the area. At present, the plan is to off-load some 22,000 tons of coke using clam-shell buckets into open barges in an effort to remove the vessel from it???€?s current position. Since each barge is capable of holding approximately 1000 tons of product and the removal rate may be as slow as 1 barge load per day, this operation may take some time. Additional updates will follow. Additional Background: The freighter was reported aground near the Sabine Jetties. The cargo was reported as 52,000 tons of Petroleum Coke. Coke is classified as a nonhazardous material. Petroleum Coke is a residual product yielded during the refinery cracking process. While a residual waste product in crude oil refining, coke is used in various high temperature metal processing industries. It is generally a black fine powder to lumpy material. The product is insoluble in water, should not sheen (any sheening would be minor), and is only considered an inhalation occupational risk, as the fine particulates would be a minor irritant hazard. If the hold is breached, the material could be lost to the sea. Based on the reported bulk density (45-55 lb/ft3) most of it should float, but I believe much of the product would sink since the true specific gravity is probably greater seawater. What product that escapes a damaged hold would either sink, float, or be suspended in the water column. A combination of the three is likely with the larger lumps sinking and the finer particles suspended and floating. Brief Hazard Characterization: The environmental risk of the coke is minor (it is defined as a nonhazardous material). The suspended particles would present a minor risk to aquatic animals, but not from direct toxicity, but rather as suspended particulates or smothering effects. Any large accumulations of coke stranded on public use beaches should be removed. Whether any effort would be required to recover the sunken portion of the product, is impossible to predict at present (such a discussion would require input from various natural resource trustees). Based on the information provided, the greater environmental threat is the 200 tons of diesel and 1200 tons of heavy fuel oil on board. Given the on-shore winds from the passing tropical storm and the predicted higher than normal tides, the fuel oils would present a far greater hazard to coastal resources than the coke product. With the higher than normal water conditions, the fuel oils could be transported into much of the protected backmarsh habitat by overwashing. The currents in that area of the river are all down stream, despite the fact that there is about a 5.5 foot tidal range. The current runs about 0.3 knots. So, over a tidal cycle of 12 hours any released product could travel between 3 to 4 miles down river (depending on wind conditions). Showers are possible this afternoon and thunderstorms tonight. Wednesday it should be dry. Just a heads up, if there is a release of jet fuel the biggest threat would be any product collecting under pier, docks, etc. This could cause a highly flammable atmosphere (but you already knew that). Flushing would be the best response option. The jet fuel, if released in sufficient quantity, could cause a significant fishkill and also kill any river bank vegetation. On Wednesday, August 20, 2003, it was reported to Coast Guard MSOAnchorage that the F/V Donna Ann, a 50' wooden-hulled boat built in1947,  ran aground after dragging anchor in gale force winds from theNW.  The vessel was anchored in Tanglefoot Bay adjacent the community ofKarluk on the west side of Kodiak Island.   The vessel had 1000 gallonsof diesel and finally came to rest at position N57-34.4, W154-29.4 wherean on-scene observer reported surf crashing through the wheelhouse.Planned CG helo overflight for August 21 was canceled due to the helomechanical problems.  Instead the CG opened up the Liability Trust Fundand hired a fixed wing Beaver to fly from Kodiak and assess thesituation, the report from which won't be available until the morning ofAugust 22.   NOAA has provided support with weather and resources atrisk information.  By Thursday night, Aug. 21, the NW winds are expectedto drop to 5-15 kts, and by late Friday the wind should shift around tothe SW at 10-15 kts.   The grounding site is about one-half mile east ofCape Karluk, the site of a seabird rookery and about one mile west ofthe village of Karluk and the Karluk Lagoon which supports salmon runsMay through November.   The Lagoon is also the site of sea ducks,occasional sea otters, and occasional brown bear activity.PolRep 2 and final: Joint Coast Guard/ADEC team flew to Karluk on Thursday afternoon,August 21, and were able to board the F/V Donna Ann.  The wheelhouse hadbeen separated from the hull as a result of the prolonged beating by theheavy surf and the old wooden hull was in pretty bad shape.  It wasdetermined that all the diesel had been purged from the tanks and beendispersed in the large and turbulent seas. [SEP] Posted below is a report from John Whitney, NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator, capturing information on the August 20, 2003, grounding of the F/V Donna Ann in Tanglefoot Bay, Kodiak Island, Alaska. _______________________________ PolRep 1: On Wednesday, August 20, 2003, it was reported to Coast Guard MSO Anchorage that the F/V Donna Ann, a 50???€? wooden-hulled boat built in 1947, ran aground after dragging anchor in gale force winds from the NW. The vessel was anchored in Tanglefoot Bay adjacent the community of Karluk on the west side of Kodiak Island. The vessel had 1000 gallons of diesel and finally came to rest at position N57-34.4, W154-29.4 where an on-scene observer reported surf crashing through the wheelhouse. Planned CG helo overflight for August 21 was canceled due to the helo mechanical problems. Instead the CG opened up the Liability Trust Fund and hired a fixed wing Beaver to fly from Kodiak and assess the situation, the report from which won???€?t be available until the morning of August 22. NOAA has provided support with weather and resources at risk information. By Thursday night, Aug. 21, the NW winds are expected to drop to 5-15 kts, and by late Friday the wind should shift around to the SW at 10-15 kts. The grounding site is about one-half mile east of Cape Karluk, the site of a seabird rookery and about one mile west of the village of Karluk and the Karluk Lagoon which supports salmon runs May through November. The Lagoon is also the site of sea ducks, occasional sea otters, and occasional brown bear activity. PolRep 2 and final: Joint Coast Guard/ADEC team flew to Karluk on Thursday afternoon, August 21, and were able to board the F/V Donna Ann. The wheelhouse had been separated from the hull as a result of the prolonged beating by the heavy surf and the old wooden hull was in pretty bad shape. It was determined that all the diesel had been purged from the tanks and been dispersed in the large and turbulent seas. Case closed.
On August 19, 2003, it was reported to Coast Guard MSO Valdez that theskipper of the 54' long F/V Valiant Maid, hit a submerged rock and capsized in 45 feet of water on the NW side of Spike Island just offshore from the town of Cordova in Prince William Sound.   The location of the sunken vessel was N60-33.0, W145-46.3, and it went down with an estimated 500 gallons of diesel in an area of very strong tidal currents.  A long oil slick was noted on the surface, and it was believed that this was just the fuel emanating from the vents and that the two fuel tanks were intact.   Trying to beat some forecast heavy winds for the night of August 19, the owner immediately hired divers to plug the vents.  In so doing the divers noted that the starboard tank was empty of an estimated 200 gallons of diesel.   The next day, when the strong winds never materialized, divers again descended to the vessel to attempt to pump out the port fuel tank, but found it empty also.   Apparently all the fuel  had escaped the first day and been rapidly dispersed by the strong tidal currents, and there was probably less than 500 gallons of diesel on the vessel when in sank.  NOAA provided support to the CG with weather, tidal and resources at risk information.   Several sea otters and seabirds were in the vicinity, but a wildlife observer from the local Eyak native community noted no abnormal behavior. During the afternoon of 18 August 2003, the NOAA Scientific SupportCoordinator was notified by USCG MSU Galveston of a mystery slick offthe Texas Coast.  The slick was reported as "chocolate mousse-like" andextending some 5 miles with an approximate location of 29 deg 05 min N Lat.094 deg 36.4 min W Long., some 15 miles off the Texas coast.  Although theUSCG didn't suggest a possible source, the description of the slick andthe proximity to the vessel traffic lanes are consistent with a shiptransiting the area and pumping bilge. [SEP] Posted below is a report from Charlie Henry, NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator, capturing information on a Mystery Slick off Galveston Jetties, TX. _______________________________ Mystery Slick off Galveston Jetties Initial and Final report (19 August 2003) During the afternoon of 18 August 2003, the NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator was notified by USCG MSU Galveston of a mystery slick off the Texas Coast. The slick was reported as ???€?chocolate mousse-like???€? and extending some 5 miles with an approximate location of 29?? 05???€? N Lat. 094?? 36.4???€? W Long., some 15 miles off the Texas coast. Although the USCG didn???€?t suggest a possible source, the description of the slick and the proximity to the vessel traffic lanes are consistent with a ship transiting the area and pumping bilge. The USCG requested trajectory assistance. This time of the year, the surface current generally flows up coast (to the east). However, observations from the TABS array indicate the currents are weak and probably inertial (variable). The NWS predicted weak WSW winds becoming WNW but still weak on 19 August. With the weak winds and currents, it is likely the oil (or mystery substance) would remain a cohesive slick and stay offshore for the next 36-hours. Shoreline contact is possible late Wednesday (20 August) or early Thursday due to forecast southerly winds. Bottom line, the follow-up overflight, on the evening of 18 August by training observers, defined the mystery slick as being a debris line composed primarily of Sargasso weed. No additional response actions were required.
On Thursday afternoon, August 7, 2003, the Coast Guard was notified that the F/V Chichagof, an 81 foot wooden-hulled fishing tender, grounded in Alitak Bay, Kodiak Island with 15,000 gallons of diesel.   The vessel operator hit a rock, after which he intentionally grounded the vessel at position, 55-53.6N, 155-13.4W.  The grounding resulted in damage to the vessel's bow area, and the fuel tanks were not compromised during the incident.  Nevertheless, it was taking on water.  A Good Samaritan vessel delivered a pump to the F/V Chichagof, but that was unable to keep up with the flooding.   Not until a Coast Guard helo from station Kodiak delivered two additional pumps was the vessel able to control the flooding.  The next morning a welder and marine surveyor were on scene to assess  and repair the damaged bow with a patch over the roughly 1 foot X 1 foot hole.   By Saturday, August 9, the vessel was fully repaired and back fishing.  NOAA supported the Coast Guard in dealing with this incidence by providing detailed weather information and forecasts, tidal data, and resources at risk information. The approximate location is reported as 26?? 06' N by 080?? 05' W. No oil has been leaked. The vessel has no apparent damage and is sitting on a soft bottom. NOAA Damage Assessment reports that the ship has between 400 and 500 metric tons of #6 fuel oil onboard. This translates to 130,000 to 160,000 gallons. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP as it would affect any trajectory implications. ______________________________________________________ 1) 24-hour Wind Forecast Winds are expected to be from the SE at 10 - 15 knots this afternoon, becoming SE at 5 - 10 knots tonight. On Friday winds are expected to be in the 5 - 10 knot range from the SE. 2) TRAJECTORY The location of vessel is close to the inshore edge of the Gulf Stream. This along with the SE winds over the next few days will cause any oil spill to move to the NNW. If 160,000 gallons of #6 were to spill over a few hours under these conditions we would expect a slick which could extend from the vessel to the NNW for about 10 - 12 miles. Patches of sheen and dark oil could extend for an additional 5 - 10 miles to the north over the next 24 hours. The most probable areas of first impact would be along he outer coast between Ft. Lauderdale and Hillsboro Inlet within 5 - 7 hours from the first oil being lost. 3) OIL FATE Heavy refined products, such as Fuel Oil No. 6 and Bunker C, have been refined to remove the lighter components and as a result are somewhat pre- weathered. As a result they are usually persistent floating pollutant problems. These oils can occasionally form a mousse, but usually only slowly, and after a period of days. Fuel Oil No. 6 and Bunker C often will not spread into thin films, instead they often break up into smaller patches and then tarballs. The resulting scattered tarballs are very difficult to observe using visual, or remote sensing techniques. This combined with the persistence of the tarballs makes these kinds of spills likely to result in long range, and occasionally unexpected, beach impacts. FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION, PLEASE CONTACT Glen Watabayashi MODELING AND SIMULATION STUDIES, NOAA, SEATTLE, WA 98115. PHONE (206) 526-4911. ______________________________________________________ The reported scenario: The M/V Alam Senang, a 584' vessel, is aground about 1.5 miles off Port Everglades. The approximate location is reported as 26?? 06' N by 080?? 05' W. No oil has been leaked. The vessel has no apparent damage and is sitting on a soft bottom. It has between 400 and 500 metric tons of #2 fuel oil onboard. This translates to 130,000 to 160,000 gallons. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP as it would affect any trajectory implications. ______________________________________________________ 1) 24-hour Wind Forecast Winds are expected to be from the SE at 10 - 15 knots today, becoming SE at 5 - 10 knots tonight. 2) TRAJECTORY The location of vessel is close to the inshore edge of the Gulf Stream. This along with the SE winds over the next few days will cause any oil spill to move to the NNW. If 160,000 gallons of #2 were to spill over a few hours under these conditions we would expect a visible sheen which could extend from the vessel to the NNW for about 10 - 12 miles. A bathtub ring type beach staining should be expected to the NNW of the vessel within 4 - 6 hrs after the spill. The most probable areas of impact would be along the outer coast between Ft. Lauderdale and Hillsboro Inlet. 3) OIL FATE Lighter refined products, such as diesel, typically have very high evaporation rates and do not tend to create persistent slicks. However, the terminology for refined products is not standardized, and, sometimes, heavier intermediate fuel oils are referred to as ???€?marine diesel???€?. These heavier products are much less volatile than normal Fuel Oil no 2 and form a more persistent slick. When spilled, the diesel spreads quickly into thin films often forming patches of rainbow and silver sheens. If the sheens reach the shoreline in a few hours, a slight staining, or greasy film-like bathtub ring (in the case of diesel) is common. These oils usually do not form a stable emulsion and, as a result, do not form a heavy or sticky residual to clean up. Note that lighter refined products do have a relatively high concentration of light aromatic compounds and tend to be more soluble and more toxic then heavier oils. Therefore these oils may not present an involved cleanup problem, however they can result in an initial toxic shock to biota and persist as a biological threat problem in low energy marine environments. The initial report was a 2.5 mile x 2.5 mile ???€?black sheen.???€? Additional reports suggested that the observed sheen might not have been oil (?). The MSO requested trajectory support. The observed oil (or sheen) was observed less than five miles from the coast west of Marsh Island. A follow-up overflight reported sheen some 2miles by 2 miles in size moving to the NW. The sheen was reported to be light, mostly silver sheen with some rainbow. The source remained unknown. NOAA reported to the USCG that landfall would be expected given strong on-shore winds. Given the remoteness of this area, the lack of any observed recoverable oil, and the expected high degree of natural dissipation, no further support was requested by the MSO. Attached is the trajectory provided to the MSO. This short report represent the initial and final report on the mystery sheen reported on 8 July. Given this information, we would expect the sheens nearest the coast to begin contacting the shoreline this evening with the offshore oil continuing to move onshore into tomorrow afternoon. Our best estimate indicates the oil is likely to come ashore between Freshwater Bayou Channel eastward to 3 miles east of Cheniere au Tigre. Similarly, a stronger coastal flow than expected to the west could result in areas near Mulberry Island being threatened.

At approximately 5:30 pm on Sunday April 27, 2003, the US Coast Guard's Marine Safety Office in Providence, Rhode Island received a report of a discharge from the barge "B No. 120" owned by the Bouchard Transportation Company of Hicksville, NY. The barge grounded, outside of the shipping lanes, at the entrance to Buzzard Bay in southern Massachusetts. Following the grounding, the tug and barge continued to anchorage LIMA, where it officially reported the discharge to the USCG. The barge B-120 had a capacity of 97,000 barrels (4,074,000 gallons) and discharged approximately 2,333 barrels (98,000 gallons) of heavy number 6 fuel. Overall, more than 90 miles of coast line were impacted (40 miles of direct impact and 50 miles of tar ball impacts), 415 birds were killed, and the habitats for three endangered species (roseate tern, piping plover and NE tiger beetle) were oiled. Clean up costs exceeded $23 million. This plan will require approval by Army Corps of Engineers, the MDEP and the local Conservation Commission and such approval requests are in process. Currently, the plan calls for the removal and replacement of like material under the supervision of the state coastal geologist. A meeting with the Fairhaven Conservation Commission (the town in which most of the sediment replacement is needed) will take place tomorrow. Surface Washing Agent The RP has received approval for the testing and subsequent use of CytoSol (a NCP listed surface washing agent). The choice of CytoSol was made following a bench scale test in small pools of PES 51, Corexit 9580 and CytoSol. CytoSol was chosen based on its effectiveness in the bench scale test, its relatively low toxicity and its cost. The field test will take place tomorrow (today???€?s test was called due to rain) on a 30 ft X 30 ft section of oiled cobbles and boulders on Long Island. If it is determined that (1) the product lifts and floats the oil and (2) the refloated oil can be recovered by snare and sorbent sweep, then the product will be used operationally on selected areas. These areas will be along shoreline segments slated for sediment replacement and removal that cannot be removed due to access or sediment size. A report on the test and application will be forthcoming. Snare Traps The snare traps deployed off Barneys Joy and other location to determine where submerged oil may be moving have been regularly checked and replaced. To date, only the Barneys Joy traps have yielded (light) oiling. The traps in other areas will be redeployed tomorrow to encompass a wider scope around Barneys Joy in order to scale the problem. The conventional wisdom holds that oil-sand mixed tarballs are being liberated during the cleaning process at Barneys Joy and are impacting the snare traps. Nevertheless, we are endeavoring to prove that oil is not coming from some offshore source, yet undiscovered. These trap will be deployed with snare running along their buoy lines to determine if any oil is moving within the water column, unseen. Steve Lehmann NOAA SSC [SEP] Evening Report June 09-11, 2003 Surface Washing Agent Test CytoSol was used on a 45 ft wide by 15 ft deep section of heavily oiled cobble/boulder armored shoreline on Thursday (06/05/03) with mixed results. The section was sprayed with 5 gallons of the chemical one hour prior to flushing (the prescribed dose and soak time), using a hand-held wand sprayer. Hard boom was set in the water with sweep sorbent inside. Several barriers of sorbent snare were set and workers were standing by with sorbent pads. Half the section was flushed with ambient water using a two inch hose and trash pump along with a T-bar deluge. The other half used a high pressure ambient water spray with a T-bar deluge. Section One (low pressure flush & T-bar) The flush liberated oil from the cobbles and the oil was collected in the snare and pads. Clearly the pads worked better than the snare on this oil as it had been thinned by the CytoSol. The surface of the cobble/boulder was not visually improved and likely would not meet the strict standards established for shorelines used recreationally. Section Two (high pressure spray & T-bar) This procedure released more oil than the flush, cleaning the stone???€?s surface more completely. However, the addition of the chemical did not make an appreciable difference from the high pressure alone (observed in other locations in the spill impact zone). Conclusions While the team established by the U.C. to judge the technique were not adverse to the wider use of the CytoSol (under certain restrictions), the Operations Section felt it did not provide enough advantage to justify its use in anything but very selective areas. At the time of this writing there is no plan to employ CytoSol as a treatment. Personal Observations on the CytoSol Test I must rely on the Operation personnel when they say that is provides too little marginal benefit to justify its wider use, however, it is possible that if this product (or a similar product) had been used as a first order response technique, when the oil was much fresher, it may have taken the cobbles down to a light coat or even a stain. Clearly the oil during the test was heavily weathered and very sticky. High pressure washes remove the oil without CytoSol, but flushing does nothing. A test of CytoSol or other surface washing agents should be encouraged during the first days of a #6 oil spill in order to test this theory. Of course this would require pre-authorization well ahead of the spill. [SEP] Attached and posted below is a report from Charlie Henry, NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator, capturing information on an 25 April 2003, collision of the chemical tanker M/V Bow Lion, which occurred on the Mississippi River near mile marker 144 north of New Orleans, Louisiana. _______________________________ M/V Bow Lion Xylene Spill, Mississippi River Initial and Final Report Just after midnight on the morning of 25 April 2003, a chemical tanker collided with a towboat pushing 38 hopper-type grain barges on the Mississippi River near Garyville, Louisiana (near mile marker 144 and north of New Orleans). The collision resulted in a 75 foot by 1 foot gash to the starboard side of the chemical tanker M/V BOW LION and a chemical spill. The gash was located approximately 3 feet above the ships water line. Just before 2:00 AM on Friday, 25 April 2003, the NOAA HAZMAT Duty Officer notified the NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator (SSC) of the collision and chemical spill. The SSC contacted USCG Marine Safety Office New Orleans and began the preliminary hazard assessment for the reported products on-board the chemical carrier, which included acrylonitrile, chloroform, ethylene dichloride, and xylene. At the time of the initial notification, the actual chemical released was unknown. What was known was that workers near the accident were reporting a strong sweet odor and complaining of headaches and possible nausea. Significant public health concerns would be warranted should the spilled chemical be acrylonitrile since it has an IDLH of only 100 ppm by inhalation. Choroform and ethylene dichloride would sink into to the bottom and be transported downstream with just enough water solubility to create a potential risk to public water supplies. The least of the chemical hazards was the xylene product. The USCG requested the SSC to report to the Marine Safety Office in New Orleans. In route, the SSC was contacted and updated on the incident. One of the two tanks holed was empty; the other was filled with xylene. Xylene is a commercial mixture of three dimethylbenzene isomers and commonly used as a solvent (paint thinner). Xylene constituents are also a common components of gasoline and jet fuels, and like such products, will float on water and evaporate quickly. Some of the product would be lost to dissolution (the product is only slightly soluble in river water), most of the spilled product would evaporate in probably less than 6 hours (a conservative estimate based on profession judgment alone). Monitoring teams were being dispatched to assess the area. NOAA recommended that areas of debris accumulation on the river be investigated after first light as any unevaporated product might be trapped in those areas and present a more persistent hazard. Of the total volume reported in the hold of 294 Metric Tons, only 125 Metric Tons (or approximately 42,000 gallons) was spilled. Most measured values during the initial monitoring were below the TLV. By 10:00 AM all values were below detection limits. The New Orleans Sewage and Water Board were notified by the MSO. No follow-up issues were identified by the MSO that would require NOAA support.

These notes are based on the following information: On April 4, 2003, the F/V Leaker ran aground at 40?? 59???€?N, 72?? 04???€?W (off Napeague Beach, Long Island). The vessel is carrying 9,000 gallons of diesel and has not leaked any product at this time. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP as it would affect any trajectory implications. _______________________________________________________ 1) Weather Forecast Today, the winds are expected to be from the NE at 25 knots. Tonight, NE winds at 25-30 knots are predicted to decrease to 20 knots by the late evening hours. Saturday, winds are expected from the NE at 15-20 knots and decreasing to 10-15 knots by late afternoon hours. Saturday night, NW winds at 30-35 knots are expected. Sunday, the winds are expected to be from the NW at 30-35 knots shifting to be from the N at 10-15 knots by the late morning hours. Sunday evening, winds are expected from the SE at 10-15 knots. 2) Oil Weathering Lighter refined products, such as diesel, typically have very high evaporation rates and do not tend to create persistent slicks. When spilled, the diesel spreads quickly into thin films often forming patches of rainbow and silver sheens. These oils usually do not form a stable emulsion and, as a result, do not form a heavy or sticky residual to clean up. It should be noted that lighter refined products do have a relatively high concentration of light aromatic compounds and tend to be more soluble and more toxic then heavier oils. Therefore, these oils may not present an involved cleanup problem, however they can result in an initial toxic shock to biota and persist as a biological threat problem in low energy marine environments. 3) Trajectory Analysis The vessel is currently aground in the surf zone off Long Island. If a catastrophic release were to occur, we expect much of the oil to be dispersed into the water column. With the forecast winds from the northeast, any visible sheens will likely move down coast (to the southwest) and offshore. With forecast winds from the northwest, any visible sheens will likely move up coast (to the northeast) and offshore. If the sheens reach the shoreline in a few hours, a slight staining, or greasy film-like bathtub ring (in the case of diesel) is common. For a catastrophic release of 9, 000 gallons of diesel, a sheen extending 2 to 3 miles from the vessel is not uncommon. Since the forecast indicates winds 20 knots or greater, it is likely any visible sheen would be considerable smaller.
