[SEP] The following photographs were taken during the 27 March field survey (photo credit NOAA). [SEP] Update (24 March 2003) During a fixed wing overflight on 20 March, USFWS observed rainbow sheens derived from the unnamed marsh and moving N over Lake Grande Ecaille and emulsified oil in the broken marsh habitat (see attached photos). The USFWS observer characterized the sheens as significant and extending across the lake. Feeding pelicans were also observed in the area. Such sheening was not expected and suggests that either the sorbent booms were not being effective (due to placement or saturation with oil) or there was a greater volume of residual oil in the marsh than was observed during previous overflights. This has lead to speculation that the hard containment boom was removed prematurely, and the observations on 20 March would appear to support this argument. During a routine scheduled RP overflight on 21 March to assess maintenance activities, the RP also observed sheen and the emulsified oil, but stated that the sheens were not ???€?significant,???€? yet the conditions were different (two different days). A follow-up RP overflight is scheduled for Monday, 24 March (today), and if needed, an on-water field trip to assess residual clean issues is planned for Tomorrow. While the observed sheening on 20 March was greater than expected, the forecasted N-NE winds combined with an active sorbent maintenance schedule should have reduce the potential for such chronic sheening through last weekend. It is difficult to estimate how much oil was observed by the USFWS overflight on 20 March. To help put the volume of surface sheen in prospective, consider the following (SSC prospective only): contiguous light sheen over one square mile may represent 1 bbl of oil; contiguous bright rainbow sheen over the same area would represent approximately 5 bbl of oil. If the sheens observed covered five square miles of area, the sheens observed may represent between 5 and 25 bbl of oil. From the pictures provided, the volume is probably toward the lower of the two values, but also represents a continuous source given high water and southerly winds. Also of note, even the lower value should not be considered insignificant. One should also consider that there may have been small ???€?fragments???€? of weathered bulk oil in the observed sheen as such was observed in the broken marsh on 13 March. The term ???€?fragment???€? was used since much of the oil observed in the broken marsh had mixed with organic matter and did not easily form contiguous streamers. Natural oil degradation was expected to have continued since 13 March. Based on the observations of 20 March, there is speculation that more weathered oil was trapped in some of the more dense marsh just behind the north shore or trapped in wrack and organic depositional matter (locally termed ???€?coffee grounds???€? because of their appearance). If true, it would have contributed to the oil flushed during the event observed on 20 March. Either way, there is only a finite volume of residual oil remaining in the impacted marsh. Any strong winds with a southerly component combined with high water levels could create similar events if the current passive recovery strategy fails (as observed on 20 March), but future sheening events are expected to be of a lesser magnitude. Sheens that escape the Zone-1 North marsh island are not expected to persist based on observations of similar sheens observed during the first few days of the spill response - such speculation should be confirmed. The bottom-line, passive recovery is continuing and pollution clearly remains in Zone-1 North. The NOAA SSC will follow-up with the USCG and the RP to assess if any changes in response strategy are needed. [SEP] The following photographs were taken during the 27 March field survey (photo credit NOAA). [SEP] On Thursday, 27 March 2003, the NOAA SSC and two RP representatives conducted a field survey to assess residual oil contamination in the northern zone of the unnamed marsh island (known by the spill responders as Zone-1 North of Mardi Gras Island). Overall the cleanup has progressed well, but isolated pockets of residual oil contamination were identified along the wrack debris line and adjacent Spartina marsh. Clearly, these areas were in part responsible for the sheens observed on 20 March during the USFWS overflight. Most of the marsh within the northern zone that had been impacted some 25 days earlier was free of observable oil and sheen. Based on the field survey, some adjustments to sorbent boom placement were recommended to retard future sheening. Included in the recommendations was the placement of additional boom along the northern shore where additional oil pockets were observed. This report focus on characterizing the sources of residual oil contamination observed during the field survey and response recommendations from the NOAA SSC???€?s prospective. As previously stated, isolated pockets of free oil were observed along the northern shoreline. Most were in or adjacent to the wrack debris line. The oiling was not contiguous, but highly sporadic. Access to these areas is restricted and only possible by airboat. The dead wrack itself has acted as a natural sorbent and what free oil that was observed was thinly spread on overlaying water or trapped and adsorbed into the dead vegetation that constitutes the wrack itself. The ???€?thinness???€? of the surface oil contamination was observed while attempting to collect a representative sample for chemical analysis. While the surface oil is black, it is apparently a very thin slick. Removing the oiled wrack would be problematic given the difficultly in accessing the sites. Collateral damage to the adjacent vegetative marsh habitat would argue against physical removal. Oil adsorbed into the dead wrack is expected to degrade naturally, and the wrack matrix may actually enhance the rate of oil degradation. The NOAA SSC recommends that these areas be allowed to flush naturally and sorbent booms be maintained to collect oil and oil sheens released during high tides. Small pocket ???€?beaches???€? composed of organic detritus or coffee grounds are a natural feature along the northern shoreline. The coffee grounds are more than a foot deep at many locations. The shoreline itself is mostly composed of peat and is very soft; few of these areas will support a person standing. Most of these shoreline areas were observed to have been impacted early in the response. At present, most of the coffee ground depositional areas appear to pose little threat as a source of secondary sheens after 25 days of natural recovery. At one location, the SSC was able to exit from the airboat onto the shoreline to assess residual oil contamination. A pit was dug to below the water table: no oil sheen was observed. At another location, where coffee grounds were deposited adjacent to broken wrack and oiled marsh, visible oil contamination was observed. Like the oiled wrack, physical removal would be problematic due to access limitations: the environmental trade-off appears to be in favor of natural recovery with sorbent booms deployed to collect any secondary sheening during the natural recovery process. Pockets of highly emulsified oil mixed with organic detrital matter and algae were observed. From the air, these packets appear as brown emulsified oil, but from the ground they are clearly dominated by non-oil organic matter. The term scum is a better characterization than emulsified oil. While the oil scum does have a soapy feel, it doesn???€?t appear to sheen or pose a threat to adjacent vegetation or wildlife. Based on field observations, the NOAA SSC recommends that the scum be left in place and allowed to degrade naturally. In addition, it would be very difficult to recover this material manually since it will not easily adhere to sorbents and manual recovery using nets would be very difficult. A sample was collected for detailed chemical analysis to quantify and characterize any oil residuals in the scum matrix. A total of three samples were collected during the field survey for chemical analysis. Two samples of surface oil in wrack were collected at 29?? 21.205 Latitude 089?? 48.486 Longitude and 29?? 21.412 Latitude 089?? 48.821 Longitude. A sample of emulsified oil scum was collected near Flag 14. The field samples will be submitted to LSU for chemical analysis and comparison to the original reference oil. In summary, the field survey provided a better characterization of the sources of residual oil contamination. Sporadic pockets of thin surface oil were observed in wrack and broken marsh along the northern shoreline. Overall, few sheens were observed in interior of Zone-1 North (the northern section of the unnamed marsh island). Continued passive recovery was recommended, as was the placement of additional sorbent boom along the northern shore. [SEP] The

[SEP] Resources at Risk for M/V Genmar Alexandra, Mississippi River, LA This report was prepared on 20 February 2004. Information in this report is based on the assumption that an estimated 1000 bbl of #6 bunker oil was released into the Mississippi River near mile marker 125 (Hahnville) on 19 February 2004. This report covers the area from approximately River Mile 125 to River Mile 10. This report does not necessarily correspond to actual or potential spill locations. Consult other Hotline reports for spill location information. Endangered/Threatened Species An endangered fish may be present along the river (RM 125-120, RM 104-103). Threatened raptors may be nesting in Salvador WMA and marshes near RM 125-120 and RM 85-80. Juvenile gulf sturgeon (federally threatened) may be present near Phoenix (RM 60-50) and in the lower river (RM 25-10). A great egret rookery (average 13 individuals) occurs slightly south of Venice (RM 11-10). Rare bats and rare turtles occur near Gretna (RM 97-96). A rare seabird may be present near Poydras (RM 85-80). A rare raptor may be present near woodland (RM 55-50). Birds Colonial waterbirds may be nesting in wetlands along the river (RM 125-110). Wintering waterfowl may be present in wetlands throughout the area. Lesser scaup may be present on inland waterways near Gretna (RM 100-90). [SEP] Attached is a field report that documents the current cleanup issues at the Belair site. [SEP] At present, cleanup operations continue at two location on the Mississippi River: the Avondale Shipyard (mm 108) and the batture area adjacent to Belair (between mm 66 and 65). Good progress is being made at both locations. On 26 February, at the request of MSO New Orleans, the NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator (SSC) made a site visit to the Avondale Ship yard to assess both the current cleanup operation and a report of additional cleanup required at a second raft of logs and debris. The site visit was coordinated with representatives of the land owner, Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality, and the USCG (represented by the SSC). Active cleanup was on-going where heavily oiled debris had been previously identified. Some oil in the form of splotches of oil on logs and oil residue trapped within one small section was observed at the site in question. It was determined that the current cleanup was progressing effectively and that the second raft of logs and debris did not need to be removed to meet cleanup goals (see attached photographs and read below for additional information). Today (27 February), the NOAA SSC along with representatives from Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality and the RP???€?s spill management team conducted a site visit of the Belair site. More than 16 roll-off boxes of oil and contaminated debris have been removed, but the operation is only half complete. Tomorrow the NOAA SSC will conduct a second site visit to the Belair location with the expressed goal of developing a detailed site map to track cleanup progress (see attached photos). Additional Information Site Aerial Photograph 01 provides a snapshot overview of the Avondale area on 21 February. After four days, the current cleanup has progressed to the point where crews are manually removing the last of the oiled debris (see photo 01) by hand. Some additional cleanup is required to remove oiled debris lodged on the front side on the dock facility as agreed to in the original cleanup plan. The area in question was a raft or logs and debris located on the upriver side of the dock facility and is identified in the aerial photo. Clearly from the air, the upriver raft of logs appears ???€?clean???€? relative to the downriver raft where heavy oiling was observed. Land owner representatives requested that cleanup be conducted in this second area to remove oil contamination. The RP???€?s spill management team acknowledged that ???€?some???€? oil was present, but did not believe that cleanup was justified. In an effort to resolve the cleanup dispute, a meeting and site visit was conducted on 25 February that included representatives from the RP???€?s spill management team, land owner representatives, Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality, and the USCG (represented by the SSC). Photo 02 provides a ground-level snapshot of the site. The site visit confirmed the aerial assessment that the site was not heavy oiled. Splotches of oil were observed on some of the debris and one small area (maybe 2 feet by 3 feet) exhibited greater oil pollution than anywhere else within the second site (see photos 3 and 4). Adsorbent pads swished in the debris yielded only small particles of tar-like oil pollution (see photo 5). Land owner representatives stated that the amount of oil observed would not affect shipyard operation, but expressed concern that the residual oil would sheen during warmer weather conditions and that the Avondale site might be blamed as a polluter. The general consensus was that the small quantity of oil, combined with expected oil weathering, would not create a significant secondary pollution threat. Also, the site is a natural collection point for trash and debris as well as an industrial area and not considered a sensitive habitat. At the time of the site visit, there was organic foam and scum flowing into the site. That material was not thought to be oil nor was it believed to be related to the GENMAR ALEXANDRA incident. The land owner representatives did not fully support this opinion and requested that the site be cleaned. The SSC suggested that snare (pom-poms on a rope) be swashed in the small area of greater oil accumulation. If free oil, which could be a secondary pollution threat was present, the snare should readily pickup that oil and quickly become saturated. If it should be extremely difficult to recover the observed oil residue, the recovery effort would have confirmed that no significant quantities of free oil were present. [SEP] Initial Report On the evening of 19 February 2004, the NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator was notified by MSO New Orleans of an allision between the Freighter BRIGHT STATE and the Tanker GENMAR ALEXANDRA near mile marker (mm) 125 on the Mississippi River. This position placed the vessel some 30 miles up-river of New Orleans, Louisiana. The time of the accident was reported as 8:00 PM (local time). The amount of oil released was initially unknown but thought to be several thousand bbls (the spill volume was later estimated at 518 bbls). The cause of the accident remains under investigation. The impact resulted in several gashes into the port side of the tanker ship and damage to a heavy fuel oil tank. The SSC immediately responded on-scene at the request of the USCG and requested weather and trajectory modeling support from the NOAA HAZMAT ???€?Home Team.???€? At the time of the accident, the Mississippi River water level was high and rising. River currents were in excess of 3 knots (and even greater, 4 to 5 knots, near New Orleans). A USCG overflight using an infrared camera reported that within 3 hours of the incident, a 10 mile long slick could be observed back to the vessel, which was still releasing oil. NOAA predicted that the oil might travel as far as 45 river miles before morning if the oil remained in the center of the channel. The initial responders, the foundations for forming an incident command structure, developed a response strategy and deployment scheme to attack the oil spill at first light (unsafe river conditions precluded most night operations). Operations on the tanker established source control by 11:30 PM. The initial response plan was to stage equipment at seven locations down river and as far away as Belle Chase (mm 75, some 50 miles from the release point). Water intake issues were addressed and the locks down river were requested to be closed and remain closed. More than
The NOAA SSC was notified by the Hazmat Duty Officer on Friday morning (2/14) at approximately 0630 concerning the grounding of the T/B Energy 5501 about 2 miles south of Norwalk, CT. The USCG requested the SSC on scene. The Initially, it was unknown how much home heating oil was lose from the barge. The barge was loaded with 56,000 barrels (2,352,000 gallons) and had a draft of 17.9 feet. It struck a rock charted at 18 feet mean low water. Due to the stage of the moon, falling tide, and offshore winds the water depth over the rock was minimal. The tug was hugging the CT coast to stay in the lee of winds from the NW as it headed to its destination in Port Jefferson, NY. The barge was taken to a nearby location (41deg 02.6 N / 73deg 22.053 W) and anchored. The NOAA Scientific Support Team provided the USCG initial trajectory and oil weathering information, weather, tides, and resources at risk summary. At about 0800 the CT Department of Aquaculture closed the shellfish beds in all waters in the Norwalk, Darien, and Westport area until further notice. The divers survey discovered 14 cracks and holes in all six starboard tank bottoms. The original estimate of cargo loss by the naval architect was 450 barrels (18,900 gallons). Two morning overflights (0900 and 1200) by USCG personnel spotted an oil slick extending several miles from the barge. A relief barge arrived along side the holed barge at about 1400. At 1600 the SSC, RP rep and USCG FOSC went on an overflight in a helicopter. A sheen consisting of light rainbow to silver and gray was observed several miles from the barge. It measured about 3.5 miles long by 200 yards wide at the leading edge and 600 yards wide at the trailing end. The rest of LI Sound was search and not other oil was located. The overflight also mapped locations of ice along the LI coastline. A new trajectory model was developed based on the GPS positions of the slick. With the updated oil trajectory model showing land impacts on the northern Long Island coast plans were made to pre-position protective boom as several location near identified sensitive areas. By the evening meeting at 1800 the revised estimate of lost oil was downgraded to about 53 barrels (2,226 gallons). This estimate was within the range of oil observed on the afternoon overflight. Plans were made to begin over-the-top lightering operation during the first night, but due to logistics and operational constraints they were unable to begin until later the morning of the 15th. On 2/15 the morning overflight only spotted one small streamer of light silver and gray sheen within the area predicted by the trajectory model. The stern starboard quarter of the barge was seen to be awash. No oil was observed near the barge or anywhere near the LI coast. Almost all of the oil had evaporated and naturally dispersed. The NOAA modelers were requested to provide a ?Worst Case Discharge" trajectory for a possible release from the barge on Saturday evening or Sunday morning. The new model indicated potential land impacts on LI more westerly than the oil that was initially released. Based on the updated weather forecasts for significantly worsening weather, the Unified Command decided to move the barge into Bridgeport harbor for safe haven to make temporary repairs and off-load the cargo. At present, as of 1800 this evening (2/15) the barge is in route to Bridgeport. Travel time is anticipated to be about 5 hours at two knots. Contingency plans are prepared for the possibility of spills while enroute or in Bridgeport harbor. No additional oil was released during the transit. On the morning overflight the FOSC observed no sheens in the harbor or in the coastal area. As of this morning no lightering had begun. A barge was being positioned next to the Energy 5501 for offloading. The plan is to begin lightering oil from #6 starboard tank and then pump air into the tank to help raise the stern quarter out of the water. Currently there is 10 ? 12 inches of water on the deck. The barge is boomed at the dock and protection boom has been place in the creek in case of any additional discharge. Issues of Special Interest: ?In Time Delivery? The barge Energy 5501 was en route to Port Jefferson, NY for an ?in time delivery? to a storage and distribution facility. This means that without this cargo the facility would not have sufficient home heating oil to maintain its delivery schedules to local residents. This has become standard practice with the price of oil fluctuating at this time. The barge operators had to scramble to find a replacement delivery in order to keep the fuel flowing and avert people losing heat during this cold winter weather. Safe Haven Due to the condition of the barge (at least 14 holes and cracks in the bottom) and the impending severe weather, the FOSC requested that the barge be allowed to enter Bridgeport harbor. The state of Connecticut OSC agreed with the FOSC?s decision. Even though the barge was in CT waters it was destined for a NY port. The state of CT could have denied the initial request for Safe Haven. The FOSC began exploring the issue to see what the alternative would have been had CT denied the request, but since they did allow the barge in the questions were never answered. [SEP] Fifth Coast Guard District requested on 3 February that NOAA provide a trajectory assessment for a gasoline barge grounded in the Chesapeake Bay at 38-12N and 75-58.8 W. Observers on-scene had reported that the vessel was not leaking but was surrounded by broken ice. NOAA responded within one hour to the Coast Guard request with local weather and a written trajectory estimate if gasoline would have been released from the grounded barge. NOAA also provided a written assessment of the danger from explosion and the potential direction of the resulting smoke plume. Within several hours the barge was refloated and was moved to its destination without further incident. The underwater survey of the bottom of the barge was unable to detect damage as a result of the grounding. Case closed. [SEP] Date: February 3 2004 at 1400 EST To: NOAA SSC Gary Ott FROM: NOAA/Hazardous Materials Response Division Modeling and Simulation Studies Seattle, WA 98115 SUBJECT: Vane Brothers Fuel Barge Grounding FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION, PLEASE CONTACT Debra Simecek-Beatty, MODELING AND SIMULATION STUDIES, NOAA, SEATTLE, WA 98115. PHONE (206) 526-4911. _______________________________________________________ Per your request we have looked at trajectory implications of the gasoline that may be released from the fuel barge. These notes are based on the following information: A fuel barge carrying 26,000 barrels of gasoline has broken its tow and is currently located at 38??12???€?N, 75??58.8???€?W. Observers???€? on-scene report the vessel is not leaking but is surrounded by broken ice. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP as it would affect any trajectory implications. _______________________________________________________ 1) 36 Hour Weather Forecast: Today, the winds are expected to be from the south at 10-12 knots shifting to be from the west at 10-12 knots by the afternoon hours. Tonight, west winds at 10-12 knots are predicted. Wednesday, NW winds at 10-15 knots are forecast to decrease to 5-10 knots by the evening hours. 2) Oil Weathering and Trajectory There is a high flammability hazard associated with gasoline spills. Specifically, if a spill is kept from spreading freely by natural or man-made structures the gasoline slick might be thick enough to support ignition. In addition, vapor concentrations near the source of the spill, vapors collected in sheltered areas or partial to empty tanks that have not been inerted, can present an explosion hazard (see Health and Safety Considerations). If an explosion were to occur on the vessel, multiple fireballs may be produced with a black smoke cloud mushrooming several hundred feet into the air. After an explosion, the hull may be ruptured with the fire spreading to the other tanks. The smoke plume may be visible up to 12 miles and, with the forecast aloft winds (west at 10-15 knots at 1000 feet), likely drift to the east. Based on the Handbook of Chemical Hazard Analysis Procedures, a risk from fragment and thermal radiation could be as much as a half to one mile. Gasoline is considered a light refined product with a specific gravity that can range from 0.76 to 0.70 at 15??C (54 to 70 API). The product typically has a very high evaporation rate and does not tend to create persistent slicks. Even under the cold-water conditions of the spill, gasoline would be expected to retain a low viscosity. Depending on the oil/ice interaction and the ice undersurface roughness, the ice may act as a barrier to the spreading of the slick with some of the oil becoming trapped on the undersurface of the ice, leading to a secondary source of sheens as the ice breaks up or melts. If a release were to occur this afternoon under the forecast westerly winds, we would expect 90% of the gasoline to evaporate within 4 hours or less, provided there is sufficient open water for the gasoline to spread to a thin sheen. We would expect the ebb tide this afternoon to transport the gasoline to the south with westerly winds moving product onshore. This afternoon, the shoreline from Hall Pt. to Little Deal Island would likely be threatened. Gasoline impacts on the shorelines may be noticeable only by a slight staining at the high tide mark (i.e., bathtub ring) or by smell. It should be noted that gasoline does have a relatively high concentration of light aromatic compounds and tends to be more soluble and more toxic then heavier oils. In high-energy environments, the gasoline will likely disperse as small droplets in the water column. Gasoline spills can result in an initial toxic shock to biota and persist as a biological threat particularly in low energy marine environments as often found in shallow bays and inlets. [SEP] Our initial resources at risk summary provides detailed information on potential resources at risk as a result of a release of diesel fuel from the VB-53. Two particular points of concern to the resposne effort is summarized below: 1. There have been no reasons identified to not move the VB-53 from the point where she is grounded to a repair facility some 5 miles upriver at the Kinder-Morgan facility. No areas along this track have been identified that would require special preventative booming strategies to be implemented. 2. The separate resources at risk document clearly identifies a potential risk to spawning fish and habitat in the area of the grounding. The need to stabilize the barge and stopping any further leaks of oil before the barge is moved is a given. Reference direct discussions with VA DGIF staff. 3. The oyster spawn is normally expected in July and August. With almost no oil from this release expected to reach critical spawning areas in the lower James River, and with the spawning season expected much later in the year, no impact on oyster spawning from this incident is expected. Reference direct discussions with VMRC staff. [SEP] Evening Report: 30 January 2003 NOAA was notified by the USCG of a pipeline release in the NW corner of Terrebonne Bay. The 10 inch pipeline was reported to be carrying Eugene Island Crude. The location of the source is reported at 29?? 11' 57.5" N by 90?? 36' 6.6" W. A 6 mile sheen extending to the SW was reported. The actual release is, at present, unknown. The pipeline has been reported shut in, but the status of the pipeline is currently unknown. Divers have reported finding a small leak. Photographs provided by the USCG show oil impacting islands in lower Terrebone Bay that are well know bird habitat. The NOAA SSC has conferred with USFWS relative to resources at risk in the Lake Pelto and Terribonne Bay area. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP as it would affect any trajectory implications. _______________________________________________________ 1) Weather Forecast Winds are expected to be 20 - 30 knots from the NW tonight becoming 15 -20 knots tomorrow and tomorrow night. Light and variable winds are expected for Friday. 2) Ship Drift Trajectory When a vessel??s propulsion or steering device fails, a ship will drift due to the combined effects of the wind, waves, current, trim, and ballast. In general, vessels will drift at 2 to 10% of the wind speed. A ship does not generally drift straight downwind, but will show a drift angle to the wind. This drift angle can vary by 60 degrees or more to the right or left. Drift analysis of the ship's positions between Feb. 3rd and Feb. 6th indicate: Windage on the vessel has been between 8% and 10 % of the wind speed. The drift angle has been between 30 and 50 degrees. Estimated ship locations from analysis: Last reported location Feb. 6, 1100 EST : 31?? 47.8'N, 70?? 20.2' W Friday, Feb. 14 at 1200 EST : 60 - 100 miles from the Feb. 6 location, ESE to S of Feb. 6 location Sunday, Feb. 16 at 1200 EST: 65 - 110 miles from the Feb. 6 location, ESE to S of Feb. 6 location Tuesday, Feb. 18 at 1200 EST: 75 - 130 miles from the Feb. 6 location, E to SSE of Feb. 6 location 3) Oil fate and behavior If the vessel remains to the east of the Gulf Stream as expected, we would not expect any oil that might be lost, to make any noticeable shoreline impacts. Potential oil spill 14 January 2003.At 2300 on 14 January the NYSSC was notified of a potential oil releaseof 33,000 gallons of diesel oil. The bulk carrier Anthea Y ran agroundat approximately 1700 approaching its pier in Cementown, NY (on theHudson River north of Kingston). The Anthea Y is a 641 foot shipcarrying a cargo of salt. The ship berthed at the pier and was groundedthere. Four tanks were compromised during the grounding. Three of theholds were empty, one contained 33,000 gallons of diesel oil. The shipwas boomed in but no oil was reported released. The river containedabout 50% ice cover. A morning overflight detected no oil on the river.A salvage plan was implemented and oil removed from the vessel prior toattempts for refloating. The SSC provided ESI data and tide information. [SEP] Below is a report from Ed Levine, NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator, capturing information on a potential oil spill 14 January 2003. At 2300 on 14 January the NYSSC was notified of a potential oil release of 33,000 gallons of diesel oil. The bulk carrier Anthea Y ran aground at approximately 1700 approaching its pier in Cementown, NY (on the Hudson River north of Kingston). The Anthea Y is a 641 foot ship carrying a cargo of salt. The ship berthed at the pier and was grounded there. Four tanks were compromised during the grounding. Three of the holds were empty, one contained 33,000 gallons of diesel oil. The ship was boomed in but no oil was reported released. The river contained about 50% ice cover. A morning overflight detected no oil on the river. A salvage plan was implemented and oil removed from the vessel prior to attempts for refloating. The SSC provided ESI data and tide information.

No fuel has been lost and the bottom is sand. An attempt will be made to pull the vessel off at high tide today or tomorrow. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP as it would affect any trajectory and oil fate estimates. ______________________________________________________ 1) 24 hour Wind Forecast NE winds becoming E and SE today and tomorrow. 2) TRAJECTORY A spill of 4,000 gallons of diesel fuel in the high energy near shore region will result in a sheen that would extend between 1/2 to 1 1/2 miles depending upon the conditions at the time of the spill and how the spill occurs. If the spill should occur under the forecast NE -E and SE winds, we would not expect any shoreline impacts. Any oil spilled under these conditions will not persist long enough for any wind switch to bring it onshore. 3) OIL FATE ADIOS II predicts that under today???€?s 15 knot winds and sea conditions, a 4,000 gallons spill of diesel will be 90% evaporated and dispersed within 3 hours. Under the 5 knot winds expected tonight and tomorrow, 90% will be evaporated and dispersed within 6 hrs. See attached PDF file for more information concerning small diesel spills.

Jim Elliot FROM: NOAA/Hazardous Materials Response Division Modeling and Simulation Studies Seattle, WA 98115 SUBJECT: Grounded vessel Alouette Arrow FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION, PLEASE CONTACT Glen Watabayashi, MODELING AND SIMULATION STUDIES, NOAA, SEATTLE, WA 98115. PHONE (206) 526-4911. _______________________________________________________ Per your request, we have looked at trajectory implications of a possible release of oil from the grounded vessel Alouette Arrow. These notes are based on the following information: As of January 9, 2003 at 4:30pm local time, the 522' Freighter Alouette Arrow was hard aground on a soft bottom 8 miles east of Port Canaveral, FL (28?? 23.5???€?N, 80?? 25.6???€?W). The vessel was not leaking oil at this time. The vessel is carrying a cargo of wood and steel, and the following fuel oils: 111.2 metric tons (34,400 gal.) of marine diesel, 342.8 metric tons (105,700 gal.) of diesel, and 18.9 metric tons (5,300 gal.) of gas oil. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP, as it would affect any trajectory implications. ______________________________________________________ Wind forecast: Tonight, the winds are expected to be from the west at 15-20 knots increasing to 20 knots by the late evening hours. Friday, West winds at 20 knots are predicted. Friday night, West winds at 20 knots are forecast to shift and be from the NW at 15-20 knots by the late evening hours. Trajectory Analysis: The average current west of Cape Canaveral is not very strong, and is expected to be moving to the South. The predicted winds of 15-20 knots will dominate the movement of any spilled oil, moving it to the East, away from the shore. Oil fate: All three of the products listed above are fairly light and, with the predicted winds, will have a short persistence. In the event of a large release within the next 24 hours, a slick of up to 10 miles in diameter could form, but would persist for only about 24 hours, with 90% of the product either evaporated or dispersed into the water column within about 12 hours. On 26 December 2002 the M/V Kyowa Violet struck the northern side of the reef on the entrance to Yap Harbour. Upon discovery that the vessel had been holed, 3 nm later and 1 nm shy of the dock, the vessel turned around and headed to back to sea. Dispersants were considered. [SEP] Initial Report - M/V KYOWA VIOLET On 02 Jan 03, NOAA HAZMAT was notified by the Pacific Strike Team (PST) that the M/V KYOWA VIOLET had grounded in Yap at 0800 on 26 DEC 02. The grounding occurred in Yap Harbor near lighted beacon No. 14 on a reef but the vessel was able to free itself with damage & unknown loss of product (IFO 180) and head back out to sea. There was a request from the PST to give advice about a dispersant that the Kyowa company was planning to use to clean up some of the oil washed ashore and in the mangrove areas. They wanted to know if this was a safe chemical to use for the clean-up? The following is an excerpt from an e-mail which contains the request for information on the dispersant. ----------------------------------------------------- Kyowa did not notify EPA about the oil spill when it happened on or about the early morning hours of Thursday last week, December 26. Concerned Yapese who learned of the situation contacted EPA about the matter at about noon Thursday, hours after the spill. Based on the information our EPA office has at this point, it seems that the ship hit the northern side of the reef as it entered the mouth of the channel when entering our harbor. The ship then continued on its way to the dock, a distance of almost a mile, but realized (about over 3/4 of the way in) that it was spilling oil, so it turned around and went back and stayed miles off the reef. So, the oil probably spilled immediately after the hit and during its trip inside the harbor channel. Upon learning of the incident, EPA and other State agencies began a survey of the situation and cleaning up effort and I believe cleaning up started late Thursday, all day Friday and throughout the weekend. Our EPA have issued a clean- up order to Kyowa Friday on their immediate plan to clean up the mess and the representatives of Kyowa and other interested parties are now in Yap meeting with State agencies and assessing the situation. Survey and assessment of the damages began Thursday and have continued up to today as far as I know. Our EPA office doesn't have a clear picture yet as to the extent of the damages from the spill and amount of spill. The cleaning up effort by Yap agencies is temporary (contain and clean up whatever can be contained and cleaned up) pending Kyowa's plan and clean up work. The deadline given to Kyowa is January 2 to come up with a clean up plan. No charges have been filed yet, but it's probably best for the agencies to work with Kyowa first and see how good they handle the clean up while we are getting more accurate facts on the incident. Cleaning up, making sure that Kyowa, etc. follow the EPA order, and monitoring will continue to be done by the State agencies. Late this afternoon (Friday, 9 Feb. 2001) a US submarine collided with a 190ft Japanese Training Vessel approximately 8-10 miles south of Waikiki Beach, Honolulu, HI (21 03.7'N/157 51.8'W). The vessel had just refueled and was carrying at least 21000 gals of diesel fuel oil. It is believed that the sub surfaced under the vessel causing it to sink in 1800ft of water. Although its likely there was a release of oil focus right now is on search and rescue. There is fear that some passengers are missing. USCG district 14. These notes are based on the following information: On February 8, 2001, a submarine collided with a 190' cruise ship at approximately 8 miles of Waikiki, Hawaii (21?? 03.7'N, 157?? 51.8'W). The cruise ship sank in 1800' of water and was known to be carrying 21,000 gallons of diesel. At this time, it is not known if the cruise ship is leaking product. If any of this initial information is incorrect, please let us know ASAP as it would affect any trajectory implications. _______________________________________________________ 1) Weather Forecast Winds are forecast from east-southeast at 10 - 20 knots through tomorrow. 2) Trajectory Analysis The surface currents in the accident area generally flow east to west. Offshore eddies are also known to occur in this area. With southeast and east-southeast winds and a westward current, we would expect oil to be transported to the west-northwest. Lighter refined products, such as diesel, typically have very high evaporation rates and do not tend to create persistent slicks, particularly if the winds are greater than 10 knots. If a catastrophic release occurred, we would expect on-scene observers to report a slick extending 2 to 4 miles trending in a west-northwest direction. We would not anticipate shoreline contact from a diesel release. 3) Oil Weathering The terminology for refined products are not standardized, and, sometimes, heavier intermediate fuel oils are referred to as 'marine diesel'. These heavier products are much less volatile than normal Fuel Oil no 2 and form a more persistent slick. These oils don't usually form a stable emulsion. When spilled, the diesel spreads quickly into thin films often forming patches of rainbow and silver sheens. It is likely that 50 to 60% of the oil will evaporate in the first 12 hours of the release. Finally, lighter refined products do have a relatively high concentration of light aromatic compounds and tend to be more soluble and more toxic then heavier oils. So, even though these oils may not present an involved cleanup problem, they can result in an initial toxic shock to biota. At 0530 on the morning of 12 September 2000 the USNavy LST La Moure County struck a submerged rock near Pta Artigas, Bahia Lavata, Chile.  This Bay is near the village of Cifuncho.  An unknown volume of fuel was released at the grounding site and subsequent anchorages in the small bay near the village of Cifuncho.  The area is locally defined as Bahia Lavata.  The initial estimate was 40,000 gallons spilled, but it was later determined that a larger volume had been lost.  The best "guess" is between 80,000 and 120,000 gallons of fuel.  While marine diesel (DFM F-76) was the dominant product spilled, several of the damaged compartments also carried JP-5 and mogas (gasoline). NOAA had two scientists on-scene to assist the US Navy in developing a proactive response strategy. [SEP] PPT of NOAA efforts

A sample of the oil was obtained by MSO Hampton Roads and sent to the Institute for Environmental Studies at Louisiana State University (LSU.) LSU's report showed that this heavy fuel oil would remain floating after 24 hours of agitation and suggested that the oil tested would remain afloat if spilled into the James River. At approximately 3:15 AM on 24 Nov. 1999, a pipeline release occurred just east of East Grand Terre Island off Barataria Bay, Louisiana. The cause of the release is still under investigation. Between 850 and 1200 bbls of a deep well production oil was released. The oil was identified as MARS Blend, a relatively high sulfur, low asphaltene crude oil. The initial trajectory predicted the oil would move south of Four Bayous pass and sustained north winds would move most of the oil offshore. The winds were less than the forecast and the spill coincided with a spring tide (not the season Spring, but the description of the time in the tide cycle characterized by the greatest high and low tides, derived from spring up or rise). Much of the oil moved back into Four Bayous and Barataria Pass. The next morning. Heavy concentrations of oil were observed on shorelines and on water. The NOAA SSC participated in a morning overflight (pre-SCAT survey) on Thanksgiving morning to delineate oiled shorelines and surface oil. Heavy surface oil concentrations north of Grand Terre and south of Four Bayous Pass were identified and skimmers repositioned. Heavy oil was observed on the barrier islands of Barataria Bay. The barrier islands impacted were Elmer's Island, Grand Isle, Grand Terre, and East Grand Terre. The latter two were the heaviest impacted and the most remote (no road access). Stranded oil was heaviest near the passes and on the eastern end of each island. At least one marina at Grand Isle was impacted. By Friday (two days after the spill), overflights looked encouraging. Very little oil was visually observed on the beaches and on-water sheens were significantly reduced; unfortunately, most of the oil was buried by depositional sand and the lower tide level was preventing remobilization of stranded oil. The SCAT team used the aerial pre-SCAT survey to aid shoreline assessments since the heavily oiled beach areas were previously identified, but now mostly hidden by over-laying sand. SCAT was an essential element in the response and used by the Unified Command to define areas which required cleanup as well as monitoring cleanup activities to insure that the cleanup recommendations were both adequate and adhered to by field crews. More than 100 cleanup works were engaged in this response. Cleanup objectives and endpoints were developed within the SCAT organization. SCAT recommendations developed a balance between preserving beach sand (a valued state resource) and minimizing potential environmental threats. At the end of the day (Sunday, 28 Nov.), only five sites are still being cleaned. Of particular interest are a small marsh on the interior of East Grand Terre and a Gobi revetment (riprap) along the Conoco facility on the north side of Grand Isle (see Hotline #15 pictures, EGT and GIC, respectively). Both sites contain free oil. Both sites present unique cleanup problems. The interior marsh is highly isolated and composed of very soft sediments which restrict access without causing environmental injury. Each of the Gobi blocks is an Ïegg crate-like" structure with spaces which hold trapped fluid oil. USCG district 8. [SEP] Offshore Resources at Risk, Quatre Bayoux Pass Spill, LA Nearshore and offshore sensitive resources in the area include penaeid shrimp, blue crabs, and several finfish species. Major commercial harvests and some spawning sites for fisheries species occur in the area. Endangered sea turtles and bottlenose dolphins are also likely to occur in the area. Major year-round nursery areas for Kemp's ridley sea turtles occur within Barataria Bay and in nearshore waters, as well as along a large portion of the Gulf Coast. All the resources mentioned above are widespread along the coast, and are not specifically limited to marine waters off Barataria Bay. [SEP] Resources at Risk for Quatre Bayoux Pass, Louisiana I. Spill Source Information This report was prepared on November 24, 1999. Information in the report is based on the assumption that a pipeline spill of 850 bbls of an unknown crude oil occurred at a 29 21' 30" N latitude and 89 53' 32"W longitude in the Quatre Bayoux Pass in Barataria Bay. II. Geographic Region Covered The area covered by this report includes the immediate vicinity around the spill site in Quatre Bayoux Pass. This area does not necessarily correspond to actual or potential oil locations. Consult other Hotline reports for oil location information. III. Expected Behavior of the Spilled Material The spilled product is a medium-light crude oil. This oil would be expected to impact intertidal resources and biological organisms that occur on or at the water surface, primarily through physical fouling or coating. In addition, depending on wave conditions and the amount of spilled oil, acutely toxic water column impacts could also occur, especially, if large amounts of oil accumulate in shallow areas and/or areas with restricted water circulation. IV. Resources at Risk Salt marshes are the predominant shoreline type in the area. Small tidal flats may be present among the marshes. Outer coast shorelines along the exposed side of the barrier islands may contain some sand beach and overwash areas. Marshes are extremely sensitive to oil contamination. Marsh vegetation could experience severe stress or mortality if oiled, especially if oil penetrates or becomes mixed into the sediments. Any cleanup in marsh areas should avoid physical disturbance to the vegetation and substrate, especially any activities that could result in oil becoming mixed into the sediments, including foot traffic. Tidal mudflats are also very sensitive during spills. Numerous commercial and recreational fish are likely to be found throughout the spill area, including red drum (may be spawning), gulf menhaden, sheepshead, sand seatrout, spotted seatrout, spot, croaker, black drum, striped mullet, and southern flounder. Adults and/or juveniles of most species may be present during this time of year. Larvae and juveniles are most at risk to
At 0930, 18 November 1999, the cement carrier M/V Sergo Zakariadze ran aground at the entrance to San Juan Harbor, Puerto Rico. The actual amount of fuel and lube oil onboard is unknown, however the vessel's fuel oil capacity is 480,000 gallons and lube oil capacity is 30,000 gallons. The vessel is currently exposed to eight foot seas and is being pushed against the rocks. There are three tugs made fast at this time. USCG district 7. It is estimated that the hull is 2/3 grounded with the aft 1/3 of the ship floating free in shallow water. The stern of the ship is taking the brunt of the heavy seas and concern exist that significant structural damage could occur. The diesel fuel, stored in the aft section of the ship currently posses the greatest risk of spilling should the tanks in the aft section develop cracks. The engine room of the ship is flooding with sea water. As the ship's engine room continues to leak seawater, portable pumps are being used to transfer this water, which is contaminated with some oil into the #7 cargo hold. It is anticipated that eventually, this hold will be completely filled and the water will then have to be offloaded to allow continued dewatering of the engine room. Planning has been asked to evaluate the release of this contact water. Planning will coordinate with operations and request assistance from EPA for developing a plan for this, to focus on possibly pumping this water over the side. This issue will be discussed tomorrow during an RRT conference call. So far, the forward sections of the vessel appear to be intact with no leak in the IFO tanks or the holds containing the cement cargo. Samples of the diesel and IFO were taken from the vessel and shipped to LSU via airport counter to counter for characterization and dispersant effectiveness evaluation analysis. The NOAA SSC has been designated by the FOSC as the planning section chief for the ICS. Planning began preparing the CRRT Dispersant Use Checklist and developing a report for the RRT to consider approving the use of dispersants. Corexit 9500 has been ordered and should be on-scene by 2200 tonight (11/19). A dispersant application aircraft has been made available and will be on standby in the event of a large oil release. Smaller surgical use of dispersants using a ship' fire monitor or other similar delivery system is being evaluated in the event of a smaller release during planned lightering operations. Lightering operations are planned for tomorrow. A 3500 gallon capacity tug is to be used to begin offloading the IFO. At 0900 PST on February 4, 1999, the M/V New Carissa, a 639-foot bulk freight ship of Panamanian registry, went hard aground in heavy seas about 150 yards off a stretch of remote, undeveloped sandy beach three miles north of Coos Bay, Oregon. Heavy surf and high winds throughout the next several days made boarding the vessel difficult and dangerous. While the preferred option was to salvage the vessel with the oil on board, the Unified Command requested that contingency plans for vessel lightering, cleanup and pollution response be developed. The longer the ship remained grounded, the greater the risk of it leaking its load of nearly 400,000 gallons of fuel oil. Moreover, a small group of endangered snowy plover was located approximately 800 yards south of the vessel. In fact, on February 8, shipboard personnel observed oil burping out alongside the ship from a small crack in the hull and on the beach near the ship. On February 9, a tug tried to pull the ship off the beach. But by then winds and waves had driven the New Carissa approximately 600 feet further shoreward, beyond the operational reach of the salvage vessel and its ability to safely anchor near the surf zone. The bow section was towed and sunk on March 11, 1999 in 1,811 fathoms of water 282 nautical miles off the Oregon coast. 58 Federal, state, county, and local agencies took part in the month-long response. NOAA, Oregon Fish and Wildlife, Oregon Parks and Recreation, DOI Bureau of Land Management, U. S. Fish and Wildlife, U. S. Forest Service, Oregon Dunes National Recreation Area and South Slough National Estuarine Research Reserve identified and prioritized sensitive environments potentially at risk. A total of 537 birds died (239 oiled; no endangered snowy plovers), with 201 birds at the rehabilitation center (172 oiled; no snowy plovers) as of March 1999. Media interest remains high. Thirteen months after the spill, NOAA and the Coast Guard continue to maintain the following incident web sites, which contain public press release information, Coast Guard pollution reports, and digital photographs: http://www.uscg.mil/d13/units/grunbend/airstation/grounding http://www.uscg.mil/d13/dpa/news As of March 8, 2000, these web sites had totalled over 45,800 hits. On May 9, 1996, the 846-foot T/V Anitra, carrying 41.9 million gallons of crude oil, reported approximately 200 gallons of oil bubbling from below her waterline. The vessel was anchored at Big Stone Anchorage in Delaware Bay. The on-scene weather was light winds, air temperature 49?F, with overcast skies and calm seas. The DBRC's two skimmers, Del River and Del Bay, and the National Response Corporation (NRC) skimmer Patriot response vessels, dispatched to the scene, boomed off the vessel and began skimming operations. Initially, it was believed that the oil was leaking from the sea chest, indicating the possibility that cargo was leaking into the ballast water piping. Observers on an overflight the next morning reported a steady stream of product extending from the vessel's stern to sea in a south-southeast direction for 3.5 miles, followed by a 3.8-mile sheen. After the first day, the estimate of oil spilled was raised to approxiñmately 10,000 gallons; after 10 days the estimate was 42,000 gallons. Diver surveys were conducted to identify the source of the leak. Approximately 600 barrels of an oil/water mixture were recovered by skimmers. USCG district 5. Keyword: endangered species, shallow water recovery, skimmers, tourism losses, Tri-State Bird Rescue. [SEP] The effects of this spill to tourism and recreation areas were of high concern due to the proximity to the Memorial Day weekend. The New Jersey beach towns that were impacted are financially dependent on beach tourism for the majority of their income. Beaches were never closed during this incident. Wildlife impacts and rehabilitation were the other key issues faced by the Unified Command. Delaware Bay is a major migratory stop-off point for the spring migration (millions of birds arrive at the end of May) and the endangered piping plover and threatened least tern nest on New Jersey beaches. Tri-State Bird Rescue cleaned about 20 oiled piping plovers. There were no reports of dead wildlife. Effects to human health and safety were an issue for the workers due to heat stress. Some days the temperature was over 90 degrees. Work crews were monitored for heat stress. A test plow/tilling of a high tarball concentration area along the high-tide line in Ocean City, New Jersey was conducted. NOAA informed the Unified Command that this was a temporary solution, in that once the tide began to rise to the levels where the oil was laid down they may observe frothy oil/water and/or more tarballs. The tilling was done to remove the oil from the surface so birds and people would not come in contact with it and to attempt to increase natural degradation. Nevertheless, the oil would probably remain for weeks to months, unless physically removed. Media interest throughout the incident was very high. The Governor of New Jersey and the Commissioner of DEP held numerous press confer-ences with the COTP. The incident was covered by the television, radio, and newspapers. [SEP] Captain of the Port Philadelphia Area Contingency Plan [SEP] exposed fine-sand beaches, fine-sand beaches, marshes, salt marsh, saltwater marshes, sand/ gravel beaches, sheltered marshes [SEP] Once the oil was reported, the DBRC dispatched response vessels to boom the tanker and skim floating oil. The tanker performed inspections, diver surveys, and tests to determine the source of the leak. The sea valve was identified as the cause. Once this was remedied, the ship completed lightering, took on bunkers, and was allowed to depart the anchorage. The NRC Patriot followed Anitra to collect any oil released that may have clung to her. Unsuccessful attempts were made to boom several inlets on the New Jersey coast. Marshes and marinas inside the inlets had small amounts of oil migrate through them. Open-water recovery was performed by large skimming vessels inside Delaware Bay and by Lori skimmers in shallow water just off the New Jersey beaches. Shoreline cleanup was mostly manual with rakes and shovels. In some areas shop-vacs were used to vacuum oil from the sand beaches. Tilling was employed on several sections of upper beaches. Removed oily sand was disposed of in an asphalt plant. [SEP] On May 9, 1996, the 846-foot T/V Anitra, carrying 41.9 million gallons of crude oil, reported approximately 200 gallons of oil bubbling from below her waterline. The vessel was anchored at Big Stone Anchorage in Delaware Bay. The on-scene weather was light winds, air temperature 49??F, with overcast skies and calm seas. The DBRC's two skimmers, Del River and Del Bay, and the National Response Corporation (NRC) skimmer Patriot response vessels, dispatched to the scene, boomed off the vessel and began skimming operations. Initially, it was believed that the oil was leaking from the sea chest, indicating the possibility that cargo was leaking into the ballast water piping. Observers on an overflight the next morning reported a steady stream of product extending from the vessel's stern to sea in a south-southeast direction for 3.5 miles, followed by a 3.8-mile sheen. After the first day, the estimate of oil spilled was raised to approxi-mately 10,000 gallons; after 10 days the estimate was 42,000 gallons. Diver surveys were conducted to identify the source of the leak. Approximately 600 barrels of an oil/water mixture were recovered by skimmers. Shoreline impact inside Delaware Bay occurred on the New Jersey side (approximately two miles of Higby and Sunset beaches in Cape May) by the third day after release. The ocean beaches of New Jersey were impacted several days later, from Cape May to Atlantic City. The USCG COTP Philadelphia and New Jersey DEP formed a Unified Command with the RP. Media coverage was high (the Governor was present at press conferences) due to proximity to the Memorial Day weekend. Avoiding beach closures was a major goal of the response. The other concern for the response was protecting the endangered piping plover and threatened least tern that nest on the beaches. Major efforts were made to remove the oiled sand and sediment as rapidly as possible. At one point over 400 workers were employed. Cleanup consisted of manual raking and, in several instances, tilling. Workers used shop-vacs at a number of locations to vacuum up the tarballs from the sand. [SEP] Birds: diving coastal birds, waterfowl, shorebirds, wading birds, gulls, terns, raptors, rookeries, foraging areas, migration stopover areas, nesting beaches, migratory routes, critical forage areas Fish: anadromous fish, nursery areas, estuarine fish, demersal fish Mollusks: oysters, clams, seed beds, abundant beds, harvest areas, high-concentration sites Crustaceans: horseshoe crab high-concentration sites Recreation: beaches, marinas, boat ramps, high-use recreational boating and fishing areas, state parks Management Areas: wildlife preserves, reserves Resource Extraction: commercial fisheries, bivalve aquaculture sites [SEP] NOAA was notified of this incident on May 13, 1996, by COTP Philadelphia. The COTP sent samples of oil from the vessel and tarballs for analysis to determine weathering and toxicity. The two reference oils received on May 21, 1996, were very similar in composition. The Kabinda and the Nemba were both high-alkane (waxy) crude oils with a low abundance of aromatic hydrocarbons (AH). The high wax content made the oils readily susceptible to biodegradation. The tarball sample exhibited a significant reduction in the toxic AH components due to a combination of evaporation (weathering) and water-in-oil emulsification. NOAA delivered weather forecasts and provided the USCG with some warning of current reversals and possible areas of impacts. Trajectory analysis performed four days after the initial release indicated that oil had moved out of Delaware Bay and could possibly impact Cape May, New Jersey and Cape Henlopen, Delaware. The SSC provided a Tarball Information Sheet for use by the general public and media and participated in incident debriefs where the pros and cons of response options were discussed. The SSC supported this incident sporadically as needed by the USCG by telephone and fax. The response lasted 50 days. [SEP] tilling oil into sand [SEP] Both Nemba and Kabinda crude oils are light products having a 38.5 and 32.9 API, respectively. The oil initially spread into thin films as observed during the May 10 overflights. Over time, a combination of wind and waves weathered and tore the films into smaller patches (tarballs from pea- to marble-sized) that scattered over a much wider area. An increase in sea state tended to overwash the tarballs and break up any associated sheens. A lack of visible sheen associated with the tarball field is not an indication that the oil sank. Using both visual and remote sensing techniques, the resulting tarball field was difficult to track because the tarballs were widely dispersed. NOAA developed a trajectory analysis that indicated a necessarily large uncertainty due to the delay and limited nature of the information provided. This analysis indicated that the Seven Mile Beach area was threatened. The trajectory analysis uncertainty indicated for May 14, 1996, increased due to the changes in the weather since the last trajectory. Therefore, the tarballs were likely to be dispersed over a much wider area. Although climatological currents indicated a southerly flow outside Delaware Bay, shelf-waves transiting the area are not uncommon and would lead to local, non-climatological currents.
At 1430 Eastern Standard Time (EST) on January 19, 1996, MSO Providence received a call from Station Castle Hill that the tug Scandia was on fire. The tug Scandia was located some three miles south and west of Point Judith, Rhode Island towing the barge North Cape, which was carrying 94,000 barrels of #2 home heating fuel Weather was severe with sustained winds of more than 40 knots from the south-southeast and forecast to increase. The tug Scandia was abandoned and USCG Search and Rescue teams were dispatched to assist the crew. At approximately 2000 EST, a USCG helicopter reported that the barge North Cape was aground on Nebraska Shoals, directly adjacent to the Trustom Pond National Wildlife Refuge, owned and operated by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS). The helicopter further reported that the barge was releasing oil. The barge North Cape spilled oil in two separate releases. The first, released during the height of the initial storm, was 700,000 gallons and the second, less than a day later, was 125,000 gallons. The combination of the type of oil released and the energy of the storm caused great dispersion into the water column. As a result, in the days following the spill, great numbers of shellfish (mostly bivalves and juvenile lobsters) washed ashore. Subsequently, the Rhode Island Department of Health closed more than 200 square miles of commercial fishery in the area of the spill. This closure was coordinated with the EPA Region One and with NOAA's National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), which closed federal fishing grounds using the Magnuson Act. This is the first time federal fisheries have been closed due to oil contamination. The emergency phase of the response lasted seven days and the on-scene command post was demobilized following the removal of the barge North Cape from the beach. Active USCG spill response and assessment continued from the MSO, including re-survey of key impacted recreational and endangered piping plover nesting beaches. The full re-opening of the Rhode Island fishery was not complete until the middle of June. Organoleptic panels were established to certify that seafood, lobsters, and clams, in particular, were marketable. USCG district 1. Keyword: endangered species, ARTES. It should be in the hot line. - - Fuel Oil # 2 Spill - Health and Safety Considerations - - Below are health and safety considerations for fuel oil #2 spill: - - Toxicity - Fuel oil #2 is a mixture of volatile hydrocarbons. While exposure to low concentrations (several parts per million) of fuel oil #2 vapors is not a hazard to most people, inhalation of high concentration of fuel oil #2 vapors may cause dizziness, nausea, vomiting and eye irritation. Prolonged skin exposure may cause dermatitis, especially to sensitive individuals. Aspiration (intake of fuel oil #2 liquid into the lungs) is difficult to treat and may cause severe pneumonitis and pulmonary edema. - - Recommendations- Response Personnel - ???€? - Conduct air sampling and provide respiratory equipment if needed - ???€? - Provide protective clothing, gloves, and eye protection to all response personnel coming in contact with fuel oil #2 - ???€? - Educate workers on the risks they face and appropriate use of personal protective equipment (PPE) - ???€? - Monitor the working environment to make sure that safe work practices are being carried out. Hazards such as hypothermia, work near/on water, and other safety related problems may be more of a threat than chemical exposure. - - General Public - ???€? - Monitor possible exposure to the general public - ???€? - Provide a timely public advisory, and if needed advise of necessary steps to take (e.g., shelter in place) - ???€? - Provide a contact point for concerned citizens to call - - Flammability - Fuel oil #2 is a combustible liquid, with a flash point between 110 and 190 F (USCG). If ignited, a fuel oil #2 layer thicker than 3 mm on the water may burn. In addition, spilled fuel accumulated on the beach may burn as well, if ignited. Fire potential is especially serious in confined spaces. - - Recommendations: - ???€? - Measures should be taken to prevent accidental ignition of the spilled fuel - ???€? - Entry into confined spaces should always follow OSHA and USCG safety requirements, which include air sampling, ventilation, protective equipment, and standby rescue. - - Odor Vs. Threat - The odor threshold of fuel oil #2 is around 1 part per million (ppm). While an average person would detect fuel oil #2 vapors at this concentration, some people could actually smell it at much lower levels. At air concentration of 1 ppm fuel oil #2 vapors are rarely a hazard to the average person. However, sensitive individuals may be affected by the vapors even at this low levels, while others may perceive the odor as offensive and assume that they are overexposed. - - Recommendations: Provide timely information to both the general public and to health and emergency authorities. This step is crucial. Past experience has shown that the sooner the public and local authorities are informed of what has spilled, how much, what to expect, and what are the possible hazards, the lower the level of anxiety is and the easier it is to provide additional information later. - - Sampling for fuel oil #2 - Since fuel oil #2 is a mixture of hydrocarbons, precise sampling for it is difficult. Nevertheless, photoionization detectors, flame ionization detectors, calorimetric tubes, and other instruments may provide an approximate concentration of fuel oil #2 vapors in air. Use sampling instrumentation with the limitations and shortcomings of these instruments in mind. Hurricane Emily caused a number of small oil spills and one hazardous material spill near Cape Hatteras, NC on September 1, 1993. After the hurricane moved north past the North Carolina outer banks, MSO Hampton Roads launched an observation flight to assess the damage done to the island's infrastructure, homes, and environment. The overflight found three areas in need of immediate attention. Oden Dock Marina (loss of a 500-gallon waste oil tank), Pelican's Roost Texaco Station (loss of a 2,000- to 3,000-gallon #2 diesel tank) and a location near the Pilot House Restaurant (loss of a home heating oil tank estimated less than 100 gallons). After the initial on-site inspections, MSO Hampton Roads maintained a staff at the island's Emergency Operations Center (EOC) with other federal, state and local emergency response personnel for two weeks. The USCG surveyed the entire coast of Hatteras Island by helicopter and land-based Pollution Response teams (PRTs). There was very little oil spilled; eight spills were reported and only three of these required cleanup. By September 3 cleanup at Oden's Marina and the restaurant had been completed and the removal of oil from the damaged Texaco tanks was underway. About 2,500 gallons of oil were collected and removed. The emergency response activities from Hurricane Emily on Hatteras Island consumed the attention and resources of most of the emergency response staff and the island's residents. The actual oil cleanup was handled by the USCG and their contractor International Marine Services. USCG district 5. Keyword: containment boom, sorbent boom, vacuum trucks. [SEP] tidal marsh, sandy beach [SEP] The light oil from the various tanks on the island moved downstream into the marsh structures adjacent to each facility. The waste oil lost from the tank at Oden's Marina oiled marsh grasses next to the marina for a length of 100 yards with a black band of oil approximately 12 inches wide. A 150- by 500-yard pocket of oil was found behind Pelican's Roost Texaco, and a fairly heavy concentration of oil was found in a small inlet one-quarter mile east of the Pilot House Restaurant in Buxton, NC. The Coast Guard has surveyed the entire coast of Hatteras Island by both USCG helicopter and land based Pollution Response Teams. In general, there is very little oil spilled. However, oil spills were reported at eight different sites on Hatteras Island. Only three of these, Pelican's Roost Texaco, Oden's Marina, and a canal 1/4 mile east of Pilot House Restaurant have required cleanup. Over 2,500 gallons of diesel oil have been collected and removed. Limited numbers of dead fish have been observed washing up on shore at two locations. These fish kill locations are not located near any known oil pollution sites. No other injured or oiled wildlife have been observed near any oil pollution sites. On August 10, 1993, at approximately 0545, the freighter Balsa 37, the barge Ocean 255, and the barge Bouchard 155 collided in the shipping channel west of the Skyway Sunshine Bridge south of Mullet Key in Tampa Bay, FL. MSO Tampa closed the port to vessel traffic. This collision caused three separate emergencies: 1) the Balsa 37, which was carrying a cargo of phosphate rock, was severely damaged on the starboard side, was listing at an increasing rate, and was in danger of capsizing in the channel; 2) the Ocean 255, which was loaded with jet fuel, gasoline, and a small amount of diesel fuel was burning out of control just south of Mullet Key; and 3) the Bouchard 155 was holed at the port bow spilling approximately 8,000 barrels of #6 fuel oil into Tampa Bay. Stabilizing the vessels was the first priority of responders. By 2200 the Ocean 255 barge fire was extinguished and the GST was conducting cooling procedures and maintaining a fire watch. Lightering operations were well underway on the Bouchard 155 barge in preparation for moving it to dockage in the Port of Tampa where it would be cleaned before dry docking. The Balsa 37 was intentionally grounded outside the shipping channel to prevent it from capsizing and to open the channel for traffic while repairs and stability evaluations were conducted. August 10 overflight observations showed a three- to six-meter wide band of oil along the beaches. By the next day, this band appeared to be about half its original width. Systematic shoreline surveys were conducted and oil was found buried by two to eight inches of clean sand deposited during high tide. Cleanup crews focused on manually removing the band of surface oil high on the beach. A plan was developed to remove the subsurface oil without generating large volumes of sediment for handling, disposal, and replacement. The plan called for mechanical removal of the heavy buried layers, manual removal of moderately oiled sediments, and mechanically pushing stained sand onto the lower part of the beach for surf washing. Pompoms were strung along the surf zone to collect any oil refloated during the surf washing. By August 11 the status of the vessels had improved substantially. The response focus began to change from emergency issues to skimming operations, protection strategies, forecasts, and planning. Meanwhile, cleanup crews were contending with very thick oil that had been deposited around some mangrove islands. Tarmats formed when sediment was mixed with oil along the shallow flats surrounding the islands. Large thick mats coated mangrove roots, oyster and seagrass beds, and tidal mud flats. Most of this oil was vacuumed out using vacuum transfer units on grounded barges staged around the islands and shallow areas. Seawalls within the bay were being washed using high-pressure water heated to 110 degrees. The GST was onscene throughout the spill response. They provided support with the Vessel of Opportunity Skimming System as well as the fire fighting, monitoring, and lightering of the Ocean 255 barge. Roughly 14.5 miles of fine-grained sand beach from St. Petersburg Beach north to Redington Shores Beach were affected by this spill. Sand beaches on Egmont Key at the entrance to Tampa Bay were also oiled. Additionally, four mangrove islands inside the entrance to Boca Ciega Bay at Johns Pass and two small areas of Spartina marsh were oiled. Jetties, seawalls, and riprap within the bay and at Johns Pass and Blind Pass were also oiled to varying degrees. It is estimated that over 30 miles of residential seawalls were oiled within Boca Ciega Bay. Some impact also occurred on the northern side of Mullet Key at Bonne Fortune Key in fringing mangroves. Seawalls, jetties, walkways, and riprap were cleaned by high-pressure hot-water washes. PES-51 was considered for some of these cleaning needs, but after observing comparison tests performed by the manufacturer, the RP decided against its use. Cleanup of submerged tarmats offshore is ongoing. NOAA is working with the RRT, the GST, the Army Corps of Engineers, the FOSC, State officials, and various scientists and engineers to develop a sound method for dealing with the tarmats. Additional on-scene participation by NOAA is anticipated. USCG district 7. Keyword: sorbent pompoms, high-pressure warm-water washes, sorbent boom. [SEP] NOAA was notified of this incident on August 10, 1993, by MSO Tampa Bay. The MSO needed immediate support so a former SSC, now with NOAA Aircraft Operation in Tampa, went onscene to help until the Florida SSC arrived at 1230. The NOAA on-scene team consisted of representatives from NOAA HAZMAT Modeling and Simulation Studies Branch (MASS), and Biological Assessment Team (BAT), the SSC from Louisiana, and NOAA contractors. They were onscene through September 7. The NOAA team provided daily weather, tides, currents, trajectory updates, and cleanup tracking and monitoring reports. The team also participated in all RRT teleconference calls, served on the Shoreline Cleanup Technical Committee and the How Clean Is Clean Committee. They provided evaluation and observation reports on cleanup techniques and progress to the FOSC, worked closely with all the responding entities to develop sound approaches to cleanup and environmental issues, and provided support and information regarding several important health and safety issues.*&*&NOAA coordinated efforts focused at trajectories, weather, tides and current information, and environmental response and study issues among several academic, state and federal institutions. NOAA's Aircraft Operations Center, based at MacDill Air Force Base, provided helicopter support for overflights. They also provided temporary hanger storage for GST response equipment. The USCG DRAT environmental specialist worked with the NOAA team on environmental issues. The director and one faculty member from the University of Miami's newly formed South Florida Oil Spill Research Center spent several days with the NOAA team to increase their knowledge of spill responses. NOAA gave the FOSC a report addressing concerns, considerations, benefits, and liabilities of several possible techniques that could deal with removing the tarmats and submerged oil. The SSC expects to return onscene to help evaluate new cleanup operations when they begin. [SEP] oil burial on sand beaches, cleanup of buried oil, oil patches submerging and stabilizing around mangrove islands, stranded oil on oyster and seagrass beds and tidal flats, and chemical countermeasures [SEP] During the cleanup operations, a test demonstration of PES-51 for cleaning jetties, riprap, concrete walkways, and metal hand railings at the entrance to Johns Pass was conducted. PES-51 washes were performed twice. The effectiveness was compared to results from the high-pressure hot-water washes being used to clean the seawalls within the bay. The water washes generally did a better job on the rocks and rough surfaces; whereas, the PES-51 seemed to have a slight advantage on the smoother surfaces. After observing the tests, the RRT granted approval for the use of PES-51 on jetties, concrete and wooden walkways, and hand railings as needed. NOAA recommended using the water washes and then, if needed, use PES-51 to further clean the more heavily oiled and persistent areas. The RP chose not to use PES-51 for any of the cleaning. The Ocean 255 fire was a health and safety risk. The smoke plume presented a hazard as did the potential for explosions and burns. After the fire was out and during subsequent lightering operations, the possibility of flashbacks or explosions still existed. Heat stress became a problem for many of the responders and cleanup crews. The potential health risks to swimmers and users of oil-contaminated public beaches became an issue. The oil spilled has a high aromatic fraction and high levels of sulfur. Also addressed, was the use of public beaches while heavy equipment was in operation. Local weather was watched closely throughout the spill response. Tropical storms or localized thunderstorms could be a detriment to the response. One responder was struck by lightning. Representatives from the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) were brought onscene to address these issues and to monitor proper worker safety. NOAA, the USCG, and OSHA worked together closely while addressing these issues.*&*&The cooperation among all the parties involved in this response was exceptional. Local officials were supportive throughout the response and provided meaningful input to the process. The State of Florida assumed the role of lead trustee and did an excellent job of coordinating efforts for the response, while at the same time performing damage assessment duties. It was officially noted that the success of wildlife and bird rescue and treatment operations were unprecedented. Most of the birds affected by the spill were Brown Pelicans.
