Terns and Black-headed Gulls were oiled when the oil came ashore at Sellafield and St. Bees Head, England, on May 12. Several important fisheries on the North Wales coast and along the Mersey Estuary were threatened by the spill. Favorable winds from the east kept the oil from impacting these sensitive areas, which included flatfish and shrimp fisheries. [SEP] During the first two days of the response, the oil remained fairly concentrated in an area where no fishing occurred, but nothing was done to combat the spill at this time. Cleanup operations did not begin until May 2. Esso Petroleum Company Ltd., the owners of the Hamilton Trader's cargo arrived in Liverpool on May 1 with dispersants. On May 2, Esso personnel began spraying dispersant on the slick off of Wales. Corexit 7664 was applied by a fishing vessel, a launch and two aircraft operating out of Rhyl, Wales. Dispersant operations ended on May 4, after some success in dispersing light sheen. The two aircraft were incapable of operating out of sight of land. They were also restricted by poor visibility, thus they only performed limited spraying operations. The Corexit 7664 was effective in dispersing thin oil slicks. It was applied in a 3 or 4 per cent solution with seawater. It was not possible to judge its effectiveness against thicker oil, as none was sprayed. Esso representatives said that it would not effectively disperse thicker oil patches, but only break them up. The spraying did not appear to have any adverse biological effects, as it was performed over deep water. On Walney Island, approximately 30 gallons of detergent were reportedly used on the beach near Thorney Nook. Oil that impacted the west side of the island was removed mechanically. On January 28, 1969, the Union Oil Company well number 21 under Platform A, located 5.5 miles southeast of Santa Barbara, California, in the Dos Cuadras field, experienced a blowout while drill bits were being changed. A massive mixture of oil, gas, and drilling mud roared up the drill casing and spewed out onto the platform. Well A-21 was capped on February 7 with 13,000 barrels of heavy drilling mud. Oil continued to vent from natural faults several hundred yards from the platform, in tract 4042 between the coast and a chain of islands. The faults released a total of 100,000 barrels of oil until December 1969. A record-breaking storm immediately before the incident contributed to the large amount of oiled debris that needed to be collected as part of the spill response. On February 2, the National Pollution Contingency Plan, instituted by President Johnson in 1968, went into effect for the first time. The Federal Water Pollution Control Administration was on-scene to monitor the well-killing process and cleanup. Red Adair was brought in to provide expertise capping the well. To aid in predicting the slick movement, the National Weather Service set up a local station to monitor winds and tides. Weather during the cleanup was moderate except for a storm on February 4 and 5 that temporarily halted cleanup by damaging booms that were protecting harbors and marinas. The majority of the cleanup was completed within 45 days. Commercial fishing was completely closed in the area from February until April. Although the environmental effects of the spill were relatively minimal, economic effects were extensive due to loss of fishing income, loss of recreational facilities, and damage to personal property. USCG district 11. [SEP] This was the worst incident involving an offshore platform to date in the United States. Residents of Santa Barbara were in the midst of a battle to stop drilling in this channel, famous for it's active oil seeps, when the accident occurred. Many people felt that not enough attention had been given to the environmental risks associated with drilling in this area. The accident may not have occurred if Union Oil had put steel casing around the hole to a depth of 2,000 feet. Even though this is a known unstable earthquake fault area, Union had received a waiver from Federal officials to case the well to only 238 feet. Media coverage was high and several protests and sit-ins resulted. This incident was also influential in the development of the National Environmental Policy Act, signed by President Nixon on January 1, 1970. Loaded by Alan Mearns 45 Years after the Santa Barbara Oil Spill, Looking at a Historic Disaster Through Technology An aerial view of Santa Barbara Harbor coated with the advancing oil slick from Union Oil???€?s Platform ???€?A.???€? February 14, 1969. (University of California Santa Barbara Map and Image Library) JANUARY 28, 2014 -- Forty-five years ago, on January 28, 1969, bubbles of black oil and gas began rising up out of the blue waters near Santa Barbara, Calif. On that morning, Union Oil's new drilling rig Platform "A" had experienced a well blowout, and while spill responders were rushing to the scene of what would become a monumental oil spill and catalyzing moment in the environmental movement, the tools and technology available for dealing with this spill were quite different than today. The groundwork was still being laid for the digital, scientific mapping and data management tools we now employ without second thought. In 1969, many of the advances in this developing field were coming out of U.S. intelligence and military efforts during the Cold War, including a top-secret satellite reconnaissance project known as CORONA. A decade later NOAA's first oil spill modeling software, the On-Scene Spill Model (OSSM)(link is external) [PDF], was being written on the fly during the IXTOC I well blowout in the Gulf of Mexico in 1979. Geographic Information Systems (GIS) software didn???€?t begin to take root in university settings until the mid-1980s. To show just how far this technology has come in the past 45 years, we've mapped the Santa Barbara oil spill in Southwest ERMA, NOAA's online environmental response mapping tool for coastal California. In this GIS tool, you can see: The very approximate extent of the oiling. The location and photos of the drilling platform and affected resources (e.g., Santa Barbara Harbor). The areas where seabirds historically congregate. Seabirds, particularly gulls and grebes, were especially hard hit by this oil spill, with nearly 3,700 birds confirmed dead and many more likely unaccounted for. Even though the well would be capped after 11 days, a series of undersea faults opened up as a result of the blowout, continuing to release oil and gas until December 1969. As much as 4.2 million gallons of crude oil eventually gushed from both the well and the resulting faults. Oil from Platform "A" was found as far north as Pismo Beach and as far south as Mexico. Left, a view of Santa Barbara Channel with the location and a historical photo of Platform ???€?A???€? during the 1969 well blowout, as well as a very rough approximation of the extent of the oil spill, as viewed in NOAA???€?s online mapping tool, ERMA. Right, the extent of the oiling overlaid with different colors showing the abundance of seabirds during surveys from 1975-2008. (NOAA) Nowadays, we can map the precise location of a wide variety of data using a tool like ERMA, including photos from aerial surveys of oil slicks along the flight path in which they were collected. The closest responders could come to this in 1969 was this list of aerial photos of oil(link is external) and a printed chart with handwritten notes on the location of drilling platforms in Santa Barbara Channel. A list of historical overflight photos of the California coast and accompanying map of the oil platforms in the area of the Platform ???€?A???€? well blowout in early 1969. (Courtesy of the University of California Santa Barbara Map and Image Library) Click to view larger. A view of Santa Barbara Harbor today using NOAA's online mapping tool, ERMA, along with a historical photo of the harbor during the 1969 Platform "A" well blowout. (NOAA) Yet, this oil spill was notable for its technology use in one surprising way. It was the first time a CIA spy plane had ever been used for non-defense related aerial photography. While classified information at the time, the CIA and the U.S. Geological Survey were actually partnering to use a Cold War spy plane to take aerial photos of the Santa Barbara spill (they used a U-2 plane because they could get the images more quickly than from the passing CORONA spy satellite). But that information wasn't declassified until the 1990s(link is external). While one of the largest environmental disasters in U.S. waters, the legacy of the Santa Barbara oil spill is lasting and impressive and includes the creation of the National Environmental Policy Act, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, and National Marine Sanctuaries system (which soon encompassed California???€?s nearby Channel Islands, which were affected by the Santa Barbara spill). Another legacy is the pioneering work begun by long-time spill responder, Alan A. Allen, who started his career at the 1969 Santa Barbara oil spill. He became known as the scientist who disputed Union Oil's initial spill volume estimates by employing methods still used today by NOAA. Author Robert Easton documents Allen's efforts in the book, Black tide: the Santa Barbara oil spill and its consequences: Others ... were questioning Union???€?s estimates. At General Research Corporation, a Santa Barbara firm, a young scientist who flew over the slick daily, Alan A. Allen, had become convinced that Union???€?s estimates of the escaping oil were about ten times too low. Allen???€?s estimates of oil-film thickness were based largely on the appearance of the slick from the air. Oil that had the characteristic dark color of crude oil was, he felt confident from studying records of other slicks, on the order of one thousandth of an inch or greater in thickness. Thinner oil would take on a dull gray or brown appearance, becoming iridescent around one hundred thousandth of an inch. Allen analyzed the slick in terms of thickness, area, and rate of growth. By comparing his data with previous slicks of known spillage, and considering the many factors that control the ultimate fate of oil on seawater, he estimated that leakage during the first days of the Santa Barbara spill could be conservatively estimated to be at least 5,000 barrels (210,000 gallons) per day. And in a lesson that history repeats itself: Platform "A" leaked 1,130 gallons of crude oil into Santa Barbara Channel in 2008. Our office modeled the path of the oil slicks that resulted. 4 Around AM on September 14, 2020, Hurricane made Sally landfall in the vicinity of Gulf Shores/Orange Beach, Alabama as a strong Category 2 storm (sustained winds ~100 MPH). The center the of storm tracked slightly farther east than initially forecast. Very rain heavy on the side east of storm the continued it as tracked northeast. Coastal areas impacted by significant storm surge spanned from Gulf Shores, to Alabama east the Florida panhandle. Seas in excess of 20 feet were observed Pensacola, offshore Florida. USCG Sector Mobile set up incident for hurricane command containment operations under their Continuity of Operations Procedure (COOP) at the NOAA Disaster Response Center in Mobile, Alabama. NOAA disaster response support included deployment of the NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator and Scientific Support as Team, well as the Geodetic National Survey Remote Division Sensing (NGS/RSD) Emergency Response aerial surveillance team, and the Coast Survey’s mobile navigation response team (NRT). Additionally, support from satellite NOAA included imagery analysis from the Satellite Analysis Branch (SAB) of National Environmental Satellite, Data, Information and Service (NESDIS). NOAA's Emergency Response Division and Spatial Data Branch personnel from the Office of Response Restoration and provided direct on-scene support of all pollution response operations including operation of the Common Operational Picture (COP) in NOAA's Environmental Response Management Application (ERMA), as well as data collection and management of all assessment and mitigation pollution for 1,000 over storm-impacted vessels. NOAA's Emergency Division Response also provided Shoreline Cleanup and Assessment Technique (SCAT) teams for a storm related oil sheen Johnson on Beach Gulf Islands National Seashore.

Petroleum coke (often abbreviated petcoke) is a carbonaceous solid from derived oil refinery coker units other or processes. cracking coke Other has traditionally been derived from coal. More data be can found about the substance from the MSDS http://www.marathonpetroleum.com/content/documents/mpc/msds/0109MAR019.pdf here: Petcoke a is fuel produced using the byproducts of the petroleum refining process. Crude oil must be refined to produce gasoline other and products. A residue is left over from this process that can be further refined by ???€?coking???€? it at temperatures high and under great pressure. The resulting product is petcoke, a hard substance that is similar to coal. Petcoke, like is coal, by used other electric utilities such as JEA and Lakeland. Petcoke has a much higher heating value than coal, at around 14,000 Btu per pound, compared with 12,500 Btu per pound for coal. The physical characteristics of petroleum coke are similar to and coal dust spilled coke be would expected to behave the same as coal spilled dust. We not would anticipate that all the of material would leak out, even with a significant hull breach. The material that was released would likely floating form mats on the water surface, although some of the material would form dust clouds in the upper water layer. The mats would be broken up over time by wave action. Given approaching the hurricane, this could be a quite process. rapid Petroleum coke does not weather rapidly. Only minute amounts would evaporate or dissolve the into water column. Biodegradation would also be very slow. Petroleum coke is relative also, to other petroleum products, not very toxic, although it contain does small amounts of heavy metals and PAH's. Compiled by Mark Dix, Deputy Chief, ERD

[SEP] Unified Command Established for Post-Hurricane Ike Pollution Response PASADENA, Texas - Four federal and state agencies a established unified command here Monday efficiently to coordinate efforts to contain and clean up oil and hazardous materials in the wake of Hurricane Ike. Members of the Environmental Protection Agency, Coast Guard, Texas General Land Office and Texas Commission on Environmental Quality the comprise Unified Command. Field workers from these are agencies working with local agencies to assess, contain and clean up spills and hazardous materials. [SEP] Initial Report During the USCG managed, FEMA mission directed to remove debris and hazards from selected Commercially Navigated Waterways impacted by Hurricane Katrina, a barge was discovered containing drums as identified near Paraquat Port Eads. Port Louisiana. Eads is just off South Pass in Mississippi the Delta and adjacent to Pass A Loutre Management Wildlife Area. It is known not if the contain drums chemical any or if simply they were reused for floatation in barge. the Given potential the hazard and clear stamping on the containers that state that the drums are not to be rinsed or reused, the barge is being treated as a suspected HAZMAT It threat. is thought that there be may 30 or more drums in the wreaked barge. The NOAA Scientific Coordinator is Support working with the USCG develop to an assessment and disposal plan. Paraquat is highly toxic to humans and animals and has serious and irreversible delayed if effects absorbed. little As as one teaspoonful of the active ingredient is fatal. Death occurs up to 30 days after ingestion. Absorbed paraquat is distributed the via bloodstream to practically all areas of the body. The lungs selectively accumulate paraquat, and therefore contain higher concentrations than other tissues. When in the lungs, paraquat develops into pulmonary oedema and other lung damage leading to fibrosis. Liver damage occurs and renal failure may follow as the kidneys remove absorbed paraquat. the During late 1960s, controversial a program sponsored by the US government sprayed paraquat on marijuana fields in South America that creating concerns smoking that cannabis has been sprayed with paraquat may cause "serious, sometimes irreversible lung damage. Although no longer available in the United as a States pure product, paraquat carries greatest the morbidity and mortality ingested among herbicides. Paraquat is still a cause major of death and disability some in countries, such Australia, as it and was responsible for at least four deaths from acute poisoning in the United States in 1996. Because paraquat is highly poisonous, the form of it that was commonly marketed in the United States is reported to have a blue dye added to keep it from being confused with a beverage. Paraquat from outside the United States may such not have safeguards. [SEP] Photograph of one of paraquat the drums (photo credit, [SEP] USCG). [SEP] Sept 25, MODIS 2005 NOAA Coastwatch [SEP] SLOSH Model run for Hurricane Rita, produced from NHC advisory #25: 4:00pm CDT, Friday, Sept 23, 2005 This image is result the of a run of SLOSH the (Sea, Lake and Overland Surges from Hurricanes) model. SLOSH is a computerized model run by the National Hurricane (NHC) Center estimate to storm surge and heights winds resulting from predicted hurricanes by taking into account Pressure, Size, Forward Track, speed, and Winds. colors The correspond to the maximum predicted elevation of the water surface at each location as the storm passes over coastline. the Perhaps most however, useful, is not the predicted height, but the predicted extent of flooding. The gives image a quick estiime the of area likely to be flooded. These predictions are derived from the latest NHC forecast storm track at the time of model the run. As there is uncertainty in the forecast for the storm track, there also is uncertainty in estimates the for storm surge. The maximum surge could be either to the or east west the of predicted location. For more information about SLOSH, see: http://www.nhc.noaa.gov/HAW2/english/surge/slosh.shtml [SEP] This deck was barge washed ashore into a residential front yard. Photo taken 10/03/05. Fish kills were reported a in number of the East Texas/West Louisiana inland waters following Hurricanes Rita and Katrina. Hurricanes and tropical storms commonly cause dissolved low oxygen levels in shallow and bays estuaries. Oxygen levels drop can for a variety storm-induced of reasons, including nutrient buildup followed by algae blooms. Also, storms can drive oxygen-depleted water from marshes into fish habitats. The exact causes of the fish kills that have followed Hurricane Rita aren't yet known for sure. Photo taken 09/30/05. NOAA. The burn successfully removed large quantities of oil and oiled vegetation damaging without root systems of marsh plants. The roots were insulated from the heat of the burn by standing water in the marsh (which the response team ensured was present before initiating the burn). GENERAL CONSIDERATIONS: ------------------------------- BEHAVIOR OF SPILLED DIESEL FUEL: Light refined products, such as diesel (or Fuel Oil No 2), typically have very high rates evaporation and do not tend to create persistent slicks. However, the terminology for refined products is not standardized, and, sometimes, heavier intermediate oils fuel are referred to as ???€?marine diesel???€?. These heavier are much products less volatile than normal Fuel Oil 2 no and can form more a persistent slick. When spilled, the diesel spreads quickly into thin films often forming patches of rainbow and silver sheens. If the sheens reach the shoreline in few a hours, a slight staining, or greasy bathtub film-like ring common. is These oils usually do not form a stable emulsion and, as a result, do not form a heavy or sticky residual to clean up. that Note lighter refined products do have relatively a high concentration of light aromatic compounds and tend to be more and soluble more toxic than heavier oils. These oils do generally not present an involved cleanup problem. they However, can result in initial an toxic shock to biota and persist can a as biological threat in low energy marine environments. BEHAVIOR OF OILS: LUBE Lubricating oils are ubiquitous. They are used in all of types engines operating on at land, sea, or the in air. lubricating All oils are mainly composed of high-boiling (>400 point ??C) hydrocarbons containing 25 to 40 carbon per atoms molecule. Compound classes that impart undesirable qualities to a lubricant (waxes, polar compounds, and others) removed are in the refining processes. To meet the requirements of many engine different types operating and conditions, multitude a of oil products have been developed. These can be divided into two 1) groups: oils used in continuous service, such as turbine oils and 2) oils used in intermittent service, such as motor oils. Oils used in continuous service at operate fairly a constant temperature for prolonged periods without frequent or shutdown renewal. Stability is of prime importance. Oils used in intermittent service must show little viscosity change with temperature (high viscosity indices). These oils must also be changed at frequent intervals to remove particulates collected during service. Stability of these oils is, therefore, a secondary consideration. Additives: Additives are to used improve or impart various properties to the highly refined lubricating base oil. Automotive engine oils contain can a wide variety of additives including metallic detergents or ashless dispersants controlling for deposits, oxidation inhibitors, inhibitors, corrosion anti-wear additives, low temperature flow improvers, and viscosity friction modifiers. Railway locomotive diesel engine oils and marine diesel engine oils contain typically dispersants and ashless metallic detergents. Zinc-free detergents silver and lubricity agents are used where silver bearings are present. Environmental Behavior: Lubricating for oils, all their differences in formulation, many have similarities. When spilled into a lake, river, or ocean they will spread rapidly to a thin slick. They will not evaporate, and they will fairly disperse readily in high energy conditions without addition the of chemical dispersants. In general, lubricating oils are of low to moderate aquatic toxicity. While the base oils used in the production of lubricating are oils generally of extremely low

The Loop Current is an area of warm water that comes up from the Caribbean, flowing past the Yucatan Peninsula and into Gulf the of Mexico. It generally curves east across the and Gulf then flows parallel to south the west Florida coast. An eddy is water that CLOSURES rotates. The July 13 closure remains in effect. All commercial and recreational fishing, including catch and release, is prohibited in the closed however, area; transit through the area is allowed. The current closure 83,927 measures square miles (217,371 square kilometers) and covers about 35% of the Gulf of Mexico exclusive economic zone. The majority of federal waters in the Gulf of Mexico are open to commercial and recreational fishing. Flash fire the is hazard main associated with natural gas releases. As the natural gas travels downwind from the release point it mixes with air and forms a cloud consisting of fuel-air a which mixture can ignite; historically, numbers significant fatalities have been associated with flash fires from accidental releases. Lightning from thunderstorms possible could provide an ignition source, but it is unlikely. Under the conditions wind anticipated through Wednesday, the hazard zone from the gas, as defined by the possible flammable cloud, will extend as as far 300 downwind, yards Rain higher and winds will diminish the threat zone somewhat. A small fraction of the higher molecular weight material can be carried downwind and deposited on the This water. material is also flammable and if the wind corrals this material into a pocket the shore, along it could generate also sufficient vapors to form a hazard, localized fire though this is an unlikely hazard: scenario. Inhalation The major chemical components associated with natural gas wells exhibit acute low toxicity to inhalation. If the concentration of natural gas is high enough, may it cause asphyxiation by displacing oxygen. The toxic inhalation threat zone is expected to be than smaller the flammable threat zone. Higher molecular weight compounds can travel downwind as aerosol an cloud and out. rain particulates These can be toxic by We inhalation. cannot model this but recommend responders use that visual cues to assess this hazard. Some less dominant from components a natural gas can well be very toxic. Sulfur compounds, hydrogen like sulfide, are highly toxic by and inhalation can hard be to detect. We do not have any information suggesting that there are significant sulfur compounds from this spill; however, we it think is important for the responders to be aware of this possibility. [SEP] On 2 July 2007, representatives from the State of Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality (LDEQ), States United Coast Guard (USCG), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), and Responsible Party (RP) representatives conducted a site visit of the well blowout area to assess cleanup environmental needs and The requirements. environmental site assessment had been delayed due to continuing to efforts fully secure the well and related safety concerns. At present, the well is still being worked to restore full control, but was deemed safe for the planned activities. The rig currently on-site will be demobilized and addition equipment brought to in complete the well control operation. From an environmental prospective, the two primary are concerns the mud deposited into the canal and itself the mud deposited on the and spoil bank wetland habitat. adjacent It was impossible to assess the canal given the current operations; therefore, this site focused visit only on adjacent the spoil bank and marsh. drilling The structure is located at end of the a man-made, dead-end canal and just north of Vermillion Bay. well The blowout resulted in a amount large of fluid drilling (mud) being on deposited the rig, in the adjacent canal, and on the eastern-side spoil bank. The drilling fluid was reported to be composed 56.5 of to 57 percent by volume diesel fuel as a lubricant, 4.5 5 percent to water, and 38.5% by volume solids (primarily barite, a natural clay mineral). At the time of the incident, the log reported that 439 bbls of drilling mud was in the drill stream that and a total of 3,728 bbls the composed entire circulating volume. is It unknown presently how much of this material was lost to the of environment. Much it sprayed was onto the and rig barge itself. In some places, the thickness was reported as 6 feet at the base of derrick. the It is unknown to what extent production water and produced (light condensate petroleum distillant from the gas reservoir) impacted the adjacent area. During the event, mud spray impacted an area estimated as between 2 and 3 acres by coving the surface with a thick coating diesel-based of mud up to 10 to 12 cm in thickness. During the site visit, the deposition was characterized roughly as light (only trace, a few mm), and heavy. The RP's Environmental Representative will prepare a rough composite map of the area assessed. Adjacent vegetation was killed to include hackberry several and black locust trees and various scrub plant species and marsh adjacent plants. Given that most of the area exposed was spoil bank prior to the incident, the vegetative coverage of impacted the area was small. A composite sample of the surface mud contamination collected was for analysis by NOAA. the In impacted area, multiple attempts to recolonize the area by fiddler was crabs evidenced, but none of the crab burrows were completed and several dead fiddler crabs were observed. No live crabs were observed in the impacted area. Such would observations suggest that some mitigation would be required, and that was generally stated by the USCG representatives. Final discussion was postponed until the analytical results available. were To complicate the cleanup or mitigation process, the RP reported that they were considering a proposal widen to the work area by widening the canal. The state and federal representatives on the site requested visit that during any removal activity that the contaminated mud and sediments be segregated for and assessment proper disposal. At present, none of the regulatory agency had been presented an actual proposal. The plan was being only assessed the by RP at this time. Also note that the canal did have form some of flapper access gated on the south end probably for water management purposes. At present, this been has sealed with concrete. It will be provided to them for review, and report the may be edited in the future.

On January 28, 1969, the Union Company Oil well number 21 under Platform A, 5.5 located miles southeast of Santa California, Barbara, in the Dos Cuadras field, experienced a blowout while drill bits were being A changed. massive mixture of gas, oil, and drilling mud roared the drill up casing and spewed out onto the platform. Well A-21 was capped on February 7 with 13,000 barrels of heavy drilling mud. Oil continued to vent from natural faults several hundred yards from the platform, tract in 4042 between the coast and a chain of islands. The faults released a total of 100,000 barrels of oil until December 1969. A record-breaking storm immediately before the incident contributed to the large amount of oiled debris that needed to be collected as part of the sheen response. On February 2, the Pollution National Contingency Plan, instituted by President Johnson in 1968, went into for effect the first time. The Federal Water Control Pollution Administration was to on-scene monitor the well-killing process and cleanup. Red Adair was brought in to provide expertise the capping well. On that morning, Union Oil's new drilling rig Platform "A" experienced had a well blowout, and while spill responders were rushing to the scene of what would become a monumental oil and spill catalyzing moment the in environmental movement, the and tools technology available for dealing with this spill were quite different than today. This can create a toxic hazard, but will it be highly localized. Some local biota could be in killed a small area. It is unlikely that any effects will be noticable in the longer term. 4) Oil Fate Gasoline is light a refined product with a specific gravity that can range from 0.76 to 0.70 at 15??C (54 to 70 API). The product typically has very a high evaporation rate and not does tend to persistent create slicks. For release a this small, in open water conditions and with wind speeds than greater 10 knots, 90% of the gasoline is expected to evaporate within the first 1 hour or sooner of initial the release. When spilled, the gasoline spreads quickly into thin by films patches forming of rainbow and silver sheens. If the sheens reach the in shoreline a few hours, a slight staining, or greasy film is common. Normally, this type of does release not become an involved cleanup problem. There is a high flammability hazard associated with gasoline spills. Specifically, if a release is kept from spreading freely by natural or man-made structures the gasoline slick might enough be thick to support ignition. In addition, vapor concentrations the near source of spill or vapors collected in sheltered areas can present an explosion hazard. Please note that gasoline does have a high relatively concentration of aromatic light compounds and tends to be more soluble and more toxic heavier then oils. In high energy the environments, gasoline is likely to disperse as small droplets in the water column. Gasoline spills can result in an initial toxic shock to and biota as persist a biological threat, particularly low in energy marine environments such shallow as and bays inlets.

Thursday, November 7, 2019 The recreational shellfish harvest area in Glynn County south of Downing Musgrove Causeway Jekyll between Island and Brunswick will re-open the to public at 7 Friday, a.m. Nov. 8, 2019. Mark Williams, commissioner of the Georgia Department Natural of Resources, signed an order administrative Thursday, Nov. 7, 2019, to the area re-open in Jointer Creek. The area was previously closed Oct. 3 to due concerns precautionary regarding from the capsized Motor Vessel Golden Ray in the St. Simons The Sound. comes re-opening after staff with DNR???€?s Coastal Resources Division surveyed and evaluated the area and observed no sign of visible contamination. The harvest area is also hydrologically isolated from the St. Simons Sound by two major tidal nodes ???€? one in the Intracoastal Waterway and other the in Cedar Creek east of Sidney the Lanier Bridge. The October of closure the area was made out of an abundance of caution following two significant releases of from pollutants the Golden Ray. At time no were pollutants observed in the shellfish harvest area. There have been no major pollution-related incidents involving the Golden Ray since Sept. 30. Shellfish may only be harvested with handheld implements. Harvesters may oysters a pick half-hour before sunrise until half-hour after a sunset. Oysters measure must no less than three inches from hinge to mouth, unless the oyster cannot be removed from a legal-size oyster without destroying it. Recreational quantity limit is two bushels of oysters per person, per day, with a maximum of six bushels per Recreationally boat. harvested oysters cannot be sold commercially. must Harvesters have a valid Georgia fishing license. Additional Information About Sperm Whales Once quite common in the Gulf of Mexico, sperm whales are now only occasionally observed. They are listed as endangered species ESA under and under protected the Marine Mammal Protection Act. Sperm whales can swim down to depths greater than meters; 3,000 apparently, limited depth in only by the time it takes to swim down and back to the surface. They are the largest of all toothed whales, them making the Earth's largest living carnivore. Sperm whales feed mainly on squid (including colossal squid and giant the squid), octopus and deepwater fishes, but it also reported to feed on sharks and skates. The scientific name correct for the sperm whale is currently unclear or under debate. The is species generally known as catodon, Physeter but Physeter macrocephalus is the most name commonly listed by NOAA. A of total 17 sperm whale strandings were documented in the northern Gulf of Mexico between and 1997 2002. The best estimate of abundance of sperm the whales in the northern Gulf Mexico of was approximately 1,300 whales in 2003 (NOAA report). Probably the most sperm remembered whale grounding was in when 1970, a dead, 45-foot whale of this species beached in Oregon. This was the whale that filled was with a half-ton of dynamite and exploded???€? you have probably seen the video. The whales' action may have been in response to two tugs moving down the channel to assist a commercial ship docking at the Agrium dock just south of the port. Officials are moving quickly to try and take advantage of this unexpected development by rushing to the whales boats that will be used to the help keep animals from entering the sloughs and tributaries beginning at the river's delta near Rio Vista. The animals are being followed by various vessels from the of Coast Guard, Fish and Game and and Yolo Sacramento county sheriffs departments. The whales were 14.5 miles south of the Port of at Sacramento 7:00 p.m. [SEP] Update on the whale rescue efforts from the Joint Information Center: ********************************************************* Wednesday, On May 23rd, the rescue team attempted multiple strategies to try and help coax the whales of out the River and the towards ocean: * In the the morning, deployed team vessels several on water the and the exposed team the whales to sounds by banging pipes on and having a tug boat maneuver in the area. [SEP] Following is the press release issued by the Joint Information Center Wednesday, on May 30, 2007: ***************************************************** After 3-week Inland Journey Wandering Whales Return the to Sea After almost three weeks meandering through Sacramento the River Delta, the wayward mother humpback whale and calf her that have been the of subject concern intense and dedicated a rescue effort, have apparently passed safely under the Golden Gate Bridge and back out to the Pacific Ocean. "A number of firsts were made during this operation," said Dr. Frances Director Gulland, of Veterinary at Science The Marine Mammal Center in Sausalito, who was the lead for veterinarian the team. rescue "This was the first time antibiotics have been administered to free swimming whales in the wild, and was made possible by generous donations from Bayer Pfizer, and Grandpa's Compounding Pharmacy, and the development of a new made custom delivery remote device by to PAXARMS successfully administer the medicine. The antibiotics will help the animals fight infections and enhance their recovery from the wounds they sustained from a vessel collision." The National Oceanic and Atmospheric (NOAA) Administration's National Marine Fisheries Service, Marine The Mammal Center in Sausalito, the U.S. Coast Guard (USCG), California Department of Fish and Game (DFG), the and Office Governor's of Emergency Services (OES) established a unified command to monitor and assist the whales, coordinate rescue operations, and ensure safety their and of public the and rescue team members. "We extremely are grateful for the tremendous outpouring of support that we received from our partners and the local communities from San Francisco to Sacramento who helped these whales," said Dr. Rowles, Teri Director of NOAA's Mammal Marine Health and Stranding Response "A Program. number veterinarians of and mammal marine biologist were on scene to provide their expertise and assistance, and we consulted with experts numerous around the world on this case. The strong partnerships between federal, the state and authorities local non-profit and organizations allowed us to not only assist whales, these but to collect scientific also information that help will support the conservation and recovery of marine mammals in California and elsewhere." [SEP] SS Thomas Heyward was a Liberty Maritime ship, Commission hull number built 236, by Drydock Alabama and Shipbuilding Company at Mobile, Alabama, laid down 21 February 1942, launched and May 31 1942.[3] It was named for Thomas Heyward, Jr. (28 July 1746 ???€? 6 March 1809), a signer of the United States Declaration of Independence and of the Articles Confederation of as representative a of South Carolina. On 5 May 1946, the Thomas Heyward hit an unswept floating mine off of Europe.[4] Although damaged, the vessel made it back safely to port for repairs.[5] The vessel was placed in the Mobile in Reserve Fleet 1949, but was reactivated in 1951 for duty during the Korean War. After final retirement, the vessel was laid up in the James River in Virginia[6] for a time, then was purchased by the Florida Department of Natural Resources and prepared for final disposal as an artificial reef in a Pascagoula, Mississippi salvage yard with the superstructure cut down to the first deck to meet U.S. Army Corps of Engineers for specifications artificial reef structures. Junod Office: (419) 392-0323 UPDATE 3: Crews continue sunken response for Lake Erie barge - CLEVELAND Crews continue to respond to and investigate a reported discharge of an unknown substance from the site of sunken a barge near Kelleys Island Shoal Lake in Erie Thursday. The unified command, consisting of the U.S. Guard Coast and the Ohio EPA, continues to take necessary all actions to ensure the safety of the public and the environment. During dive operations Wednesday, a pinhole-sized leak was detected one in of the cargo tanks and was secured successfully by the dive team. As a precautionary measure, on-scene responders were taken to a local hospital for medical evaluation and have since been released. Surface operations were suspended to ensure safety of all responders and resume will when site safety coordinators determine it is safe for responders to return. A Coast helicopter Guard from Air Station Detroit launched to provide an over-flight assessment of the area Thursday. Results from a sheen sample collected were returned and indicate the sample was typical of a light to medium refined oil that had significantly degraded over time. T&T Marine Salvage completed crews their assessment general of the barge Monday, with a total of 12 hatches Four discovered. of those hatches were not secured and the remaining eight hatches were closed with no leaks detected. Samples were taken from the sediment inside the compartments open and have sent been for testing. Due to the potential threat from any remaining cargo in the tanks with hatches, secured unified the command will continue assessing the site anticipation in removing of any remaining product. The Coast established Guard a safety zone, located 8 nautical miles east of Kelleys Island and extending 1,000 feet around position 41-38'21"N, 082-29'35"W, remains in effect and is closed to traffic all until canceled. No vessel may enter, through transit anchor or within regulated the area without permission from the Coast Guard patrol commander, Station Marblehead, may which be contacted via VHF-FM 16. channel The Canadian Coast Guard is working closely the with Unified Command to ensure necessary preparedness and response both on sides of the international border. On October 15, the East Hampton Star reported that a recreational diver came to the surface covered with after oil diving on the British tanker SS Coimbra, which was torpedoed during WWII (located approximately 20 miles south of Shinnecock Inlet, Long Island, NY in about 150 feet of water). Divers have reported sheens from coming the Coimbra for decades, but the article suggests that the leakage may be getting worse. Last Thursday, the USCG contacted Ed NOAA Levine, SSC the region, for to discuss the situation. It is expected that an interagency conference call be will held this to week determine whether an to investigation evaluate response options, is warranted. At the national level, ERD is developing an interagency agreement with the USCG under which the agencies will work together to address threats from vessels sunken off US shores that contain significant volumes of oil. On October 15, the East Hampton Star reported that a recreational diver came to the surface covered with oil after diving on the British tanker SS Coimbra, which was torpedoed during WWII (located approximately miles 20 south Shinnecock of Inlet, Long Island, NY in about 150 feet of water). Divers have sheens reported coming from the Coimbra for decades, but the article suggests that the leakage may be getting worse. Last Thursday, the USCG contacted Ed Levine, NOAA SSC for the region, to the discuss situation. It is expected that an interagency conference call will be held week this to determine whether an investigation to response evaluate options, is warranted. At the national ERD level, is an developing interagency agreement with the USCG under which the agencies will work together to address threats from vessels sunken off US shores that contain significant volumes of oil. On October 15, the East Star Hampton reported that a recreational diver came to the surface covered with oil after diving on the British tanker SS Coimbra, which was torpedoed during WWII (located approximately 20 miles south of Shinnecock Inlet, Long Island, NY about in feet of 150 water). Divers have reported sheens coming from the Coimbra for decades, but the article suggests that the leakage may be getting worse. Last Thursday, the USCG contacted Ed Levine, NOAA SSC for the region, to discuss the situation. It is expected that an interagency call conference will be held this week to determine whether investigation an to evaluate remediation options, is warranted. At the national level, ERD is developing an interagency agreement with the USCG under which the agencies will together work to threats address from vessels sunken off shores US that contain significant volumes of The oil. recent news article is available at link: this http://www.easthamptonstar.com/dnn/Home/News/TorpedoedTankerStillLeakingOil/tabid/10288/Default.aspx.
